Kyrgyzstan's central bank keeps key interest rate unchanged at 12 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:29 CST
14:30:29 KST

BISHKEK, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Board of the National Bank of Kyrgyzstan has decided to keep its key interest rate unchanged at 12 percent, the bank's press service said on Tuesday.
Since the beginning of 2026, consumer prices have risen by 7.3 percent, while annual inflation has reached 11.7 percent. Rising fuel and lubricant prices, as well as higher food prices amid volatility in global food markets, have been among the main drivers of inflation.
At the same time, economic activity remains strong, with real GDP growing 11.1 percent in January-July 2026. Growth has been supported by high investment activity, particularly in construction, as well as increased domestic consumption.
The National Bank said persistent external inflationary risks require maintaining tight monetary conditions. Keeping the key rate at its current level will help contain secondary inflationary effects and create conditions for a sustainable decline in inflation over the medium term. ■

Russia is escalating hybrid attacks and Europe has no answer
Unknown

Russia is escalating hybrid attacks and Europe has no answer
- Russia is increasing hybrid attacks like cyber strikes, armed drones, and arson against European countries supporting Ukraine, causing rising tensions and security concerns.
- Europe lacks a strong, proactive response and remains mostly defensive, encouraging Russia to test limits and escalate its campaign.
- European nations are preparing new sanctions and military aid for Ukraine, but Russia continues covert efforts to destabilise the West and weaken support for Kyiv.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – Russia is expanding its campaign of hybrid attacks against countries that supply weapons and money to Kyiv and has caught Europe without a plan to respond.
From cyberattacks to armed drones and mysterious cases of arson, tensions are rising across the continent as the war in Ukraine is set to enter its fifth winter.
Poland said in August that it thwarted an attempted assassination of a US citizen originally from Ukraine that was ordered by Russia, while Estonia accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone maker.
Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Aug 25 that those responsible for hybrid attacks “will pay the price” after an explosive-laden drone was discovered at an airport in Leipzig near a Ukrainian cargo plane, raising speculation that Moscow was involved in an attempted strike.
European officials have been anticipating for months that Russia may escalate its aggressive campaign against the continent.
But the bloc has yet to change its fundamentally defensive posture, according to people familiar with how the institutions gauge outside threats, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
That has likely encouraged Moscow to probe how far it can go in trying to intimidate and wear down Western allies as it remains locked in a war of attrition with Ukraine.
“NATO, European and national responses have largely been reactive and defensive,” said Agnia Grigas, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council in Vilnius.
“They have focused on detecting and countering individual provocations, but have not built a record of effective deterrence by consistently dissuading Moscow from continuing or escalating them.”
That lack of preparedness comes as Europe has taken on the primary role in supporting Ukraine, with the US shifting away from the continent.
While NATO’s mutual defence clause commits member states to help one another in case of an attack, Russia’s alleged actions have so far fallen short of what would become a trigger for such a response.
Moscow has increasingly relied on recruitment via social media to carry out arson or other sabotage attacks after large-scale expulsions of its diplomats following the invasion of Ukraine.
Two Ukrainian nationals were handed prison sentences in Britain in June after a jury found them guilty of conspiring to commit arson attacks on a car and property linked to then Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
The prosecution said during the trial that one of the perpetrators was recruited online by a Russian-speaking Telegram user.
Lithuanian prosecutor-general Nida Grunskiene said last week that the drone attack in Germany has “links” to an ongoing investigation into an attempt to detonate a parcel on a DHL cargo plane in 2024.
Lithuania has charged five in the attempted sabotage, allegedly hired by Russia’s military intelligence.
While Germany has not singled out Russia as being behind the armed drone or the recent discovery of a cache of weapons on the outskirts of Berlin, a slew of investigative media reports have pointed the finger at Moscow.
It also added to fresh warnings that Europe’s biggest economy must grapple with the new dimensions of asymmetrical risks.
There are indications that Russian intelligence and security services are looking at hybrid warfare operations against the Baltic states and Poland, an intelligence official told Bloomberg earlier in August.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Moscow is weighing a potential false flag operation using captured Ukrainian drones to strike critical infrastructure in the Baltic region.
“Russia’s ongoing hybrid warfare in Europe is a highly coordinated, sub-threshold campaign aimed at destabilising Western political systems, fracturing NATO and EU unity, and eroding support for Ukraine,” said Alex Kokcharov, geoeconomics analyst at Bloomberg Economics in London.
“To achieve these goals, the Kremlin maintains plausible deniability by exploiting anonymity and utilising proxies to obfuscate direct state attribution.”
Some European Union members have called on the bloc to respond by adopting the sanctions that have been blocked, including seizing assets, a ban on transporting Russian liquefied natural gas and restricting visas, according to people familiar with the matter.
The EU is preparing another package of sanctions on hundreds of individuals and entities, which it aims to adopt in the fall, they said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
But as previous such measures have failed to restrain Moscow, it is unlikely they will do now.
“Russia is willing to use kinetic means because until now, they have been unsuccessful in discouraging support for Ukraine,” said Marek Kohv, head of the security and resilience programme at the Tallinn-based International Centre for Defence and Security.
“It is directly connected to how Russia is doing on the front line.”
NATO members have pledged US$80 billion (S$101.5 billion) in military aid to Ukraine for 2026 and “at least the equivalent levels” in 2027 at the alliance’s July summit in Ankara.
The money is overwhelmingly coming from Europe.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham handed over cruise missile blueprints to Kyiv in a visit on Aug 24.
He also compared Ukraine’s fight with Britain’s resistance to the Nazis in World War II, drawing a response from Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
He accused Britain of “methodically and regularly adding fuel to the fire” and “methodically and regularly plotting to prevent any progress in the peace process” in his remarks to reporters on Aug 24.
Russia has also warned that Britain would face “consequences for which it will have to answer” after reports that Kyiv used drones made by British companies to carry out strikes inside Russian territory.
In August, the Estonian authorities said they were investigating Russian involvement in a fire at Milrem Robotics, a drone manufacturer that supplies Ukraine.
A Latvian charity for Ukraine said its warehouse was the subject of an arson attack in July.
“Russia is clearly seeking to escalate the situation – not through direct military escalation, but perhaps by influencing Western countries, particularly those supporting Ukraine,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in Helsinki on Aug 24. “But it is not working. In fact, it is having the opposite effect.” BLOOMBERG

South Korea said on Wednesday it had scrambled fighter jets in response to Russian military aircraft entering its air defence zone, the second such incursion in weeks.
The relationship between the countries has worsened since South Korea joined Western sanctions following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and since Moscow built stronger ties with North Korea.
Seoul’s defence ministry said multiple Russian aircraft had entered and then left its air defence identification zone over the East Sea, also called the Sea of Japan.

An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area where countries require foreign aircraft to identify themselves for security purposes.

35 on 35 – Independent Ukraine Through the Eyes of a Ukrainian Woman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:27:00 UTC
14:27:00 KST

Yana Oller was born in a small village in Ukraine’s Vinnytsia region on May 4, 1991. Three months and 20 days later, Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada adopted the country’s Act of Declaration of Independence.
“I still have a birth certificate that says in Russian, in a Soviet Union paper, that I was born this and this, in the Russian language,” she tells Kyiv Post.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
As the country slowly built its identity over the past 35 years, Ukrainians such as Oller, like their nation, have also been forging a path of their own.
A small village in Vinnytsia region
Oller was born into a Ukrainian-speaking family from the village of Dzhulynka, in central Ukraine’s Vinnytsia region.
It was the 1990s, and the whole family lived in a house built by her grandfather – not particularly Soviet, she says, but not exactly modern either.
Like most former Soviet Republics in the 1990s, the newfound freedom also came with a crippled economy inherited from the fallen Soviet empire – between 1991-96, the Ukrainian economy contracted between 9.7 and 22.7 percent annually, compounded by hyperinflation, according to a 2012 study by think tank Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
Life, according to Oller, was far from abundant.
“My family was extremely poor, like so poor that we couldn’t afford to buy meat, or to bake something,” she explains. “I remember that we always ate soup. It was just potatoes, carrots, and nothing else.”
From Soviet Republic to EU Applicant: Ukraine’s Identity Shift
The Ukrainian revival of the 1990s
Childhood at Dzhulynka is a vague memory for Oller, but the visible changes, or rather, audible ones, came in the form of music.
“I guess what changed was mostly what we watched… or what we listened to. Like the culture was changing. The music, the movies, the shows,” she continues.
And long before the Ukrainian language law was passed in the Verkhovna Rada in 2019, the 1990s already saw a small revival of the Ukrainian language in media.
“Probably everything was in Russian… and then in 1998, and later, we began watching Ukrainian channels,” she says.
And for young Oller, the surge in Ukrainian language in media wasn’t just a sense of familiarity – it represented something exciting.
“I don’t know why but I always wanted to watch something in Ukrainian… all the Western movies that started coming, they were all translated into Ukrainian. I loved Western stuff, and it was so nice to hear,” she says.
At some point, young Oller would come to the TV just to wait for the end credits to play from one particular show because the song was sung by Okean Elzy, one of the most famous Ukrainian bands.
“I was always waiting for the titles just to hear that song,” Oller recalls.
2000s and the Orange Revolution
After nine years in Dzhulynka, Oller moved to a nearby town because her father, a Protestant church pastor, started a new church.
“I don’t know how, [but] we bought an apartment in town on the third floor. It was my first apartment… I really loved it because I always wanted to live in the big city,” she says.
The highlight for young Oller? The cinema in town.
“We had one movie theater. A movie theater! You don’t have such things in a village,” she says.
But just a few years later, the Orange Revolution would begin – the first test of democracy in independent Ukraine, where electoral fraud claims against presidential candidate Viktor Yanukovych (who later became president in 2010 and was ousted in 2014) led to a popular revolution, which brought reformist leader Viktor Yushchenko to victory.
But for Oller and her family, far from Kyiv, the revolution remained a topic spoken of between adults, now more of a distant memory for Oller.
“It was discussed by parents. It was discussed by adults… You don’t really watch news because you’re a kid,” she says.
“One thing I always remember… during the Orange Revolution, my dad would always complain about it,” she recalls. “He would say everybody’s bad, politicians are bad, everything is horrible, and everybody will go to hell. That’s all I remember.”
She did remember wearing orange – but that doesn’t mean she understood what any of it meant.
“I think we were wearing something orange just because everybody was doing it. Did I understand what it meant? No,” she says.
Moving to the big city
Oller moved to Kyiv in 2008 to study philology at university – and moving to the capital was both an exciting and difficult ordeal.
At the time, the exchange rate to the US dollar had fallen to around 1 to 5, partly in the wake of the US financial crisis, and with little prospect of improvement, according to then-National Bank supervisory board chairman Petro Poroshenko – the same man who would become Ukraine’s president in 2014 in the wake of Euromaidan.
But while the world dealt with the fallout of the crisis, that was the last thing on young Oller’s mind.
“When I came to Kyiv, the news was the last thing I wanted to hear about. I was not aware of anything going on then,” she says.
Ordinary students from outside Kyiv would typically stay in a dormitory, which cost Hr. 600 (around $120) per semester – but since it was overcrowded, Oller had to pay Hr.700 (around $140) for a private room per month, bunking with her flat mate in the same room, on the same bed.
Oller’s memory of university years was mostly of hours of strenuous study, as it also meant a Hr. 500 (about $100 at the time) scholarship to supplement her family’s meager income – but the system did not work in her favor.
“I received a scholarship because I was a good student. But it only lasted, like, the first year or something. Then they failed you,” she says. “In my university, they would fail your last exam on purpose, just to avoid paying you.”
While the issue might not necessarily be attributed to corruption, many Ukrainians have had a similar taste of Soviet-style bureaucracy in different aspects of life – a system that many are still fighting against to this day.
“And even Hr. 500 seemed like, ‘Wow, I can actually buy food.’ Basic food, like pasta and grains,” she adds.
Graduation and the Euromaidan
Oller graduated in 2012 and soon found herself a job teaching English in Kyiv – by then, the exchange rate to the US dollar had fallen to around 1 to 8.
Her first full-time job was teaching at the American English Center in Kyiv, where she first worked as a tutor for around Hr. 20 ($2.5) per hour, or around Hr. 4,000 ($500) per month, before they made her a teacher with higher pay.
“It was enough,” she says, adding that rent per month for a room was about Hr.1,000 ($125) per month at the time.
It was also at work where she met her future husband Jeff, a US citizen who was teaching at the same center, though the two wouldn’t start dating until a few years later.
Then came late 2013, when the Euromaidan – also known as the Revolution of Dignity – would erupt in Kyiv into early 2014, and bring about unprecedented changes for the country.
At the time, protesters rallied against former President Yanukovych’s decision to backtrack on a trade deal with the EU he personally promised in 2010 after meetings with Russia. The protest later grew into a wider mandate against Russian influence and corruption.
Thousands gathered. Then shots were fired. When the smoke was clear, over a hundred were shot dead by Yanukovych’s government near the capital’s central Maidan square, and Yanukovych himself fled to Russia.
But for Oller, while the protests raged on near the central square, the city was relatively calm on the left bank, where she worked – but not for her future husband Jeff, who had to go to work near Maidan.
“I was already friends with Jeff, and he worked there… And he had to go through this, and there were blockposts. Every time, you had to show your documents, especially if you were a foreigner,” she recalls.
“It was hard every day… It was really affecting people here, but I remember that all the time I just didn’t go to Maidan,” she continued. “I love spending my weekend here on Khreshatyk, you know, I love this place. But when it was the revolution, I was scared.”
When Russia later annexed Crimea and started waging a war in eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region, the ripples also came to Oller as she began to notice a change in some people.
A question of national identity
“At the time, one of my best friends was from Sevastopol in Crimea,” Oller says.
“We met at work, and we were had a great time. She was living with a boyfriend who was from Kyiv… and they often went to Crimea before 2014 to visit her mom,” she added.
While Oller says she “was not very aware of what exactly [was] happening,” she began noticing strange comments from her friend as the events unfolded in Crimea.
“I remember loving this friend, but at the same time, she said some weird things,” Oller continues.
“It’s crazy what was happening in Crimea, but you know, they [Russians] were promising them a better life,” Oller recalls.
Eventually, her friend moved to Moscow with her family, and they severed all contact.
“She was not one of those people who would do propaganda or tell you that Russia is better,” she added. “She just moved to Russia because they were worried about her mom or something.”
“I remember this – I was listening to it, but I didn’t understand it, or I didn’t want to understand it,” she says.
Calm before the storm
The exchange rate plummeted to around Hr.2 2-27 per US dollar in the years that followed, as Russia’s 2014 invasion of Ukraine continued in the ensuing years and the country was still reeling from the revolution.
That same year, Poroshenko became Ukraine’s first post-revolution president, and for Oller and many others, things were slowly getting better despite the turmoil.
In 2014, she also moved to a new flat with a private room all to herself, and with a balcony as the cherry on top.
“There were three rooms, three girls, and I chose the best room because it was with the balcony,” she says. “It wasn’t like a super fancy room. But I was so happy and everything seemed great to me.”
She also took vacations from work for the first time to travel abroad.
“This was the year when I first traveled abroad twice a year,” Oller recalls. “On the first trip I went to Egypt because Egypt was the one place that people could afford. It was with my roommate and her friend.”
Then the next trip was to Paris.
“We couldn’t afford flying, I think. Package tours were very popular around Europe as bus tours,” she says. “So we visited three countries, and it was really great.”
She would also start dating her future husband, and life was going well despite small hiccups during COVID-19.
“I didn’t want to teach online, but we had no choice,” she explains.
But later came Feb. 24, 2022 – a day that Ukrainians would never forget.
Russia’s full-scale invasion
In the early hours of Feb. 24, 2022, Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Tanks began marching across the border, and missiles began raining down across Ukraine as gunshots echoed through the streets.
“We woke up at 9 a.m. without an alarm because it was a Thursday,” she says. “I remember this very well because work started at 12 that day.”
Like many Ukrainians, while different countries warned of an impending Russian invasion, life went on as usual until it didn’t.
“Of course, the war was in the air before that, and everybody was expecting something,” she says. “The first thing that we were thinking about is like run to the windows
See what’s happening… And I just remember that the lessons were canceled.”
That night, Oller and her husband – like many Ukrainians – spent the night at the shelter.
Eventually, Oller’s mother said she found them a driver, and after hours of driving through dark streets and avoiding the highway, they found their way to the village of Dzhulynka.
There, they spent a week with her parents before deciding that it was best to leave the country.
Moldova was their next destination, but they were also stuck for a week because the airport was closed. Then they went to Romania, and eventually to the US – home to around half a million displaced Ukrainians by 2026.
But Oller says she never wanted to stay in the US.
“I never wanted to live there. I never thought of doing the protection program there. It’s just temporary,” she says. “I never wanted to live in another country. I always liked living in Kyiv.”
“This is the city where I want to live forever.”
According to Oller, she and her husband wanted to return to Ukraine, but the blackouts in Kyiv at the time stopped them in their tracks as they had to work online.
Eventually, after their brief six-month stay in the US, they found themselves briefly in Sweden, then Slovakia – before they heard that a friend had returned in 2023, and the decision was made.
“Somebody said, ‘Let’s do Shashlik in Rusanivka,’ and we’re like, that’s it,” she says, referring to their old district in Kyiv where they would do barbeques (shashlik) by the Dnipro river.
“I texted the landlord and we decided in five minutes that we were going back to Ukraine,” she says.
“It was the best decision I have made in my life,” she continues. “It doesn’t matter how bad this war is; the moment we arrived, I wanted to kiss the asphalt.”
On Aug. 24, 2026, as Ukraine marks its 35th independence anniversary, Oller says she decided to make borscht – Ukraine’s national dish – for dinner after a long working day while listening to Okean Elzy, the same band little Oller was looking toward at the end of the TV show, back in the village of Dzhulynka.
Asked about what she looks forward to should the war end soon, she has a simple and humble wish – to stay in the big city she always dreamed of living in, without the fear of war.
“I want to continue living in this beautiful city and this beautiful country, without ever fearing any threat.”

Cyclone from Balkans and anticyclone from Scandinavia affect weather - forecast for August 26
Kyiv • UNN
On August 26, rain and thunderstorms are expected in some regions of Ukraine, while the rest of the country will remain dry. Temperatures will reach 30°C during the day.
The weather in Ukraine on August 26 will be influenced by a cyclone from the Balkans and an anticyclone from Scandinavia; it will be rainy in some places and dry in others, while daytime temperatures will reach 30 degrees Celsius, the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center reported, writes UNN.
On August 26, an atmospheric front from the cyclone over the Balkans will bring unsettled weather to the central regions, Zakarpattia, Chernivtsi, and, during the day, most southern regions, while also affecting the southern districts of Kyiv region. Weather without precipitation in the rest of the country will be determined by a high-pressure field from an anticyclone centered over southern Scandinavia. Moderate northeastern winds will prevail, bringing cool air to Ukraine; its influence will be most noticeable in the northern part, especially at night
According to the forecast, today will be partly cloudy.
In the central regions, Zakarpattia, Chernivtsi, during the day also in most southern regions and in Kyiv region, there will be moderate, locally heavy rain and thunderstorms; elsewhere, no precipitation.
The wind will be predominantly northeastern, 5–10 m/s.
Temperatures will be 14–19° at night, 8–13° in the northern part; 21–26° during the day, and 25–30° in the southeast of the country.

Iceland to vote on reopening EU membership talks in close referendum

Iceland to vote on reopening EU membership talks in close referendum
Icelanders will vote in a referendum on Saturday whether to resume entry talks with the European Union amid growing global insecurity. Voters are not being asked to decide just yet if they want to join the 27-member bloc – only whether they want their government to negotiate possible terms.
Icelanders are to vote Saturday on whether to resume entry talks with the European Union amid growing global insecurity, in a referendum seen as going down to the wire.
Icelanders are not being asked to decide just yet if they want to join the 27-member bloc – only whether they want their government to negotiate possible terms, including on the highly sensitive fishing issue.
"This is an opportunity, it's not a final decision," Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir told AFP, arguing that the referendum paved the way for a "risk-reducing 'Yes'".
"This way you get a deal on the table, you're able to see all the questions, the answers to all the questions we get here," she said.
She was speaking to AFP after a "listening meeting" in Selfoss, one of the many small towns the Social Democratic leader has visited to hear Icelanders' questions and concerns on the issue.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
On Saturday, voters will be asked to answer "Yes" or "No" to the question: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"
Implied is the question of whether the country of 400,000 inhabitants ultimately thinks it best to remain the captain of its own ship, or hitch its cart to the EU.
If the "Yes" side wins, an accession agreement negotiated with Brussels would be put to a new referendum and likely require a change to Iceland's constitution, as well as ratification by EU member states.
The north Atlantic island applied to join the bloc in 2009, a year after the 2008 financial crisis led to the collapse of its banks and economy.
Membership negotiations began in 2010 but were suspended in 2013 after a eurosceptic government came to power.
The world has changed radically since then.
Read moreIceland to hold EU referendum 'in the coming months', PM says
"The EU is looking around, it's finishing deals with India, with Mercosur. We're seeing changes in the global climate when it comes to how people are using tariffs as weapons," Frostadottir noted.
Divisive question
While Iceland's economy is flourishing again – albeit with a volatile currency – households are struggling with rising inflation and soaring interest rates, with the central bank raising rates three times so far this year to eight percent. This makes the euro an attractive option to indebted households.
On the global stage, the return of war in Europe with Russia's invasion of Ukraine has shaken established security doctrines.
US President Donald Trump's threats to take over neighbouring Greenland have added to Icelanders' concerns. Their island is strategically located in the sub-Arctic, has no military and depends on NATO and a 1951 bilateral agreement with the United States for its defence.
"The geopolitical upheaval that we have seen recently is not the root cause of this referendum. But obviously, those concerns are impacting the debate," Bifrost University professor Eirikur Bergmann told AFP.
"Mainly the aggression towards Greenland has caused great concern in Iceland and caused many people here to pause and reassess where Iceland belongs."
Opinion polls suggest Icelanders are deeply divided on the EU question.
Office worker Vilborg Inga Magnusdottir said she saw no reason to change the status quo.
"Why would we want to enter the European Union? What would we benefit from it when things are already good?" the 33-year-old told AFP.
Unlike her, Hrafnkell Gudnason plans to vote "Yes".
"It's getting more dangerous for a small country to stand outside the EU," the 59-year-old consultant and horse-breeder said.
"I think it's safer to be a part of a bigger family."
Compromise on fishing?
In a country where seafood products account for around 40 percent of exports of goods, fishing – an integral part of Iceland's national identity – would inevitably be the key issue in EU negotiations.
Half a century after the last "Cod Wars" with Britain, many Icelanders are reluctant to yield even the tiniest bit of control of their hard-won national waters to Brussels.
Even Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir, a staunch europhile, has made it clear that in any future negotiations Reykjavik would insist on retaining "sovereign control over all fisheries".
That would be difficult to reconcile with the EU's current Common Fisheries Policy.
Brussels has stayed out of the fray ahead of the referendum, but has sent positive signals, even on the sensitive fisheries issue.
For the EU, the prospect of welcoming a wealthy, stable country already largely integrated in the single market through its membership in the European Economic Area would provide a strong showcase for its enlargement policy and strengthen its presence in a coveted region.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Several oil companies to avoid using ships on Iran's blacklist over security concerns, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:18:14 UTC
14:18:14 KST

At least three Indian oil refiners and a global energy major plan to stop using vessels on Iran's new blacklist, including for ship-to-ship transfers, due to security concerns, four sources with direct knowledge of the matter said this week.
Tehran announced on Sunday a blacklist of 45 ships it said had broken its rules for crossing the Strait of Hormuz, and would take action against any vessels transferring loads with them, escalating its threats over the key waterway for global energy supplies six months into the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Iran's announcement appears designed to impede the so-called shuttle runs Gulf oil producers such as the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia have undertaken with dedicated tankers to move oil from the Gulf through Hormuz for unloading through STS transfers in the Gulf of Oman onto ships to end-users.
The shuttle runs have kept alive oil flows from the Middle East that have been curtailed by Iran's clampdown on shipping through the strait because of the war.
The named vessels could be fined, detained, and have their cargoes confiscated, according to a post on social media site X/Twitter from the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a new body Iran set up to manage the strait.
"We will avoid our chartered vessels dealing or STS or anything to do with non-compliant ships for Middle Eastern cargoes," said one of the sources, who works at an Indian refinery.
The sources declined to be identified because of the sensitivity of the issue.
Some of the tankers Iran listed are owned or chartered by Saudi Aramco and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co (ADNOC). The ships have been used for shuttling crude, refined products and liquefied natural gas (LNG) out of the Gulf for STS transfer off Fujairah in the UAE or Sohar, Oman, according to shipping data.
Saudi Aramco and ADNOC declined to comment.
Ana Subasic, a trade risk analyst at shipping tracking firm Kpler, said the most compliance-sensitive buyers are expected to avoid these vessels moving forward, but the trade is more likely to reroute through alternative tonnage, counterparties or transfer locations than disappear altogether.
Internal discussions
Several charterers and shipping firms are discussing internally whether to continue their STS operations or not and are evaluating Iran's warning, multiple other trade and shipping sources said, with one of them, a Gulf crude buyer, saying it would be safer to buy oil on a delivered basis shipped to a final destination instead of free-on-board at STS locations in the Gulf of Oman.
Those sources also declined to be identified because of the sensitivity of the matter.
"Our internal departments are still in discussion on how to proceed with crude deliveries from the Strait of Hormuz via ship-to-ship transfers in the long term,” said Formosa Petrochemical Corp President KY Lin.
Iran has previously attacked several of the tankers, including the Wedyan, Mombasa B and Al Bahyah.
Two crude ships no longer giving location
Two of the 12 very large crude carriers on Iran's blacklist were no longer giving their location through their automatic identification systems (AIS) by Tuesday after the list was released, while the rest have had their AIS transponders switched off for weeks.
"The key issue is contagion," Kpler's Subasic said.
"If Iran follows through on threats to penalize vessels that conduct STS transfers with blacklisted tankers, that should narrow the pool of willing shipowners, charterers and buyers, particularly among firms with material Gulf exposure, while increasing due-diligence requirements and potentially freight, insurance and risk premia."

SpaceX to build $100 billion Starship rocket complex in Louisiana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:17:20 UTC
14:17:20 KST

SpaceX unveiled plans on Tuesday to build its largest rocket launch complex yet in southern Louisiana, a $100 billion effort to transform coastal wetlands into a critical base for the company's Starship and AI satellite launch ambitions.
The 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) site on Pecan Island, which SpaceX named Starbase Louisiana, is an expansion of the company's Starship launch operations beyond South Texas and those planned for Florida as its next-generation rocket remains in late-stage development.
The company's second Starbase campus will eventually launch thousands of Starship flights a year, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said, reiterating its goals for an ambitious cadence contingent on solving steep engineering challenges and regulatory hurdles.
Construction will begin next year with the first Starship launch in 2029, SpaceX said. Shotwell detailed the plans near the proposed site in Louisiana's Vermilion Parish at an event with Governor Jeff Landry and other senior state officials.
The "self-sustaining" spaceport envisioned by SpaceX will include its own methane production for propellant, power generation, deep-water shipping capabilities to transport Starships from Texas, vehicle processing facilities, and probably an airport, Shotwell said.
The marshland site is more than eight times the size of Manhattan. Shotwell said "very large portions" of the land will remain natural wetlands with no infrastructure, while an animated SpaceX video showed the area dotted with several launch pads surrounded by greenery.
Site at center of ExxonMobil lawsuit
The site had been at the center of a decade-long lawsuit against ExxonMobil brought by local parishes alleging the oil major's coastal drilling and canal dredging contributed to the state's wetland loss. The state reached an agreement with Exxon to settle the lawsuit in June, prompting its dismissal the following month, a court order shows.
That cleared the way for SpaceX's launch plans for the 18-mile (29-km) coastal strip, which the company had been discussing with the state since February, Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois said.
SpaceX has significantly expanded its southern US footprint in recent years, having built Colossus AI data centers in Tennessee and Mississippi and Starlink facilities in Austin, Texas. It is planning a chip plant in central Texas.
"This project means more than just steel, technology, and capital," Landry said. "It represents jobs for our families. It represents momentum for our communities, and it represents protection for our coast."
SpaceX said the Louisiana site will add more than 3,000 jobs to the region. The governor's office said those jobs are expected to pay an average salary of $92,600, or 192% higher than the average wage in Vermilion Parish.
Second starbase
The launch site, which will be SpaceX's fourth in the US, appears to replicate, at a larger scale, its widening footprint in South Texas, the site of its first Starbase rocket campus. However, the Louisiana site will not have rocket production facilities.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk sees Starship as central to the company's goals of expanding its Starlink constellation and eventually deploying up to 1 million AI data-processing satellites in orbit. The rocket also plays a key role in NASA's Artemis moon program.
Pecan Island is situated in a geographically convenient location for Musk's satellite ambitions. It allows a rocket to launch south over the Gulf waters and into a sun-synchronous orbit that offers plenty of sunlight for solar-powered AI satellites.
Starbase Texas is Starship's only active launch site as the rocket remains in development, while SpaceX builds two Starship pads in Florida next to its flagship Falcon 9 launch pads. The company also has Falcon 9 launch facilities at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
As SpaceX developed Boca Chica, Texas, into the company town of Starbase with support from local government officials, it has faced resistance from residents concerned about water, environmental, and noise pollution and pressure to sell their land.
Shotwell highlighted environmental plans and outlined efforts to restore Pecan Island's receding marshlands and coastline, which act as a natural buffer to protect inland areas from flooding during heavy rainfall.
Pecan Island is a protected hub for dozens of migratory bird species seasonally traveling throughout the Western Hemisphere. At Starbase Texas, Starship launches have blasted shorebirds and their nests with gravel and debris, according to environmental groups.
"The birds might fly away during a launch, but I guarantee they come back," Shotwell said, prompting applause from state officials. "As soon as the rocket's gone, the birds come back. It's not like months later."
She said SpaceX will help fund environmental "protection, restoration, and stewardship" while the launch site is constructed.

Anatolia’s giant pyramids defy the passage of time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:16:31 UTC
14:16:31 KST

Studies indicate that the Bintepeler tumuli were built through extensive planning and sophisticated engineering, rather than simply by piling up soil.
The Bintepeler tumulus field in the western province of Manisa’s Salihli district, known as the “Pyramids of Anatolia,” sheds light on ancient history with its monumental royal tombs and vast necropolis.
Located next to Sardes, the capital of the ancient Lydian Kingdom, the site is considered one of the largest tumulus burial grounds in the world.
Among hundreds of tumuli of various sizes in the area, the most striking is the monumental tomb of King Alyattes, father of the famed Lydian ruler Croesus. Standing about 70 meters high and measuring approximately 300 meters at its base, the tumulus is regarded as the largest known tumulus in the world.
Its enormous scale has drawn comparisons with the pyramids of Egypt. Ancient historian Herodotus also praised the monument in his writings, describing the Alyattes Tumulus as one of the largest monuments built by humans. Its imposing silhouette can still be seen from kilometers away across the Gediz Plain.
Archaeological and geological studies indicate that the Bintepeler tumuli were not created simply by piling up soil. Their construction involved extensive planning and sophisticated engineering.
Different types of soil were deliberately brought from various geographical areas and geological layers to create a stable structure and prevent collapse and erosion. The soils were blended and compacted layer by layer, helping the monumental tombs withstand natural disasters and the passage of thousands of years.
The world’s largest cemetery
Nicholas Cahill, the excavation director of the ancient city of Sardes, said around 125 tombs have survived in the Bintepeler area, while historical evidence indicates that the site once contained about 160. Covering approximately 73 square kilometers, the necropolis is considered the world’s largest cemetery.
“There are three very large tumuli here. The Alyattes Tumulus is the largest tumulus in the world. There is no larger monument anywhere,” Cahill said, noting that the monument is about 70 meters high and 300 meters wide.
He added that Herodotus also mentioned the burial grounds, saying that apart from the monuments of Babylon and Egypt, the largest monument was in Lydia and was the Alyattes Tumulus.
Cahill said studies by Teoman Yalçınkaya, the Turkish representative of the Sardes excavations, suggest that the tumulus was built by a workforce of about 300 people over approximately 15 years.
“Very little machinery was used. About 300 people and a few carts were involved in the construction,” Cahill said, emphasizing that large amounts of water were needed to compact the soil.
He noted that different layers of soil have been identified inside the tumulus, including black soil and sandy soil, indicating that construction teams brought soil from different regions and used the materials in successive layers.
With its vast scale and architectural significance, Bintepeler represents an important part of the cultural heritage not only of Manisa but also of the wider world. Viewed from above, its monumental burial mounds resemble giant pyramids scattered across the plain, preserving evidence of the burial traditions and displays of status associated with Lydian kings and aristocrats.

Seljuk stone bearing name of Prophet Muhammad found at Ani
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:15:36 UTC
14:15:36 KST

The name of Prophet Muhammad is repeated six times in Kufic script around an eight-pointed star motif at the center of the stone. (AA photo)
A decorated stone bearing the name of Prophet Muhammad six times in Kufic script has been discovered at the Seljuk Cemetery at the UNESCO-listed Ani Archaeological Site in eastern Türkiye, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has announced.
Ersoy said the artifact was unearthed during archaeological excavations that have been ongoing at the Seljuk Cemetery since 2021.
“We found a unique artifact in Ani, where Sultan Alparslan’s conquest in 1064 opened the door to Turkish-Islamic history in Anatolia,” Ersoy said.
The 51-by-21-centimeter stone was carved using the relief technique. The name of Prophet Muhammad is repeated six times in Kufic script around an eight-pointed star motif at the center of the stone. Since only half of the artifact has survived, three of the six inscriptions are currently visible.
The stone is believed to be an architectural element from one of the Seljuk tombs in the cemetery.
“The name ‘Hz. Muhammed’ appears three times in the inscription band surrounding an eight-pointed star-shaped motif at its center,” Ersoy said. “This artifact, believed to have belonged to a Seljuk tomb, is a centuries-old stone testament to the deep love our ancestors held for the Prophet Muhammad.”
According to the Culture and Tourism Ministry, the artifact provides tangible evidence of Ani’s Turkic-Islamic identity, the religious beliefs of the period and the region’s burial culture.
Archaeological findings indicate that the Seljuk Cemetery at Ani is the earliest known Turkic-Islamic cemetery and Turkish martyrdom site in Anatolia.
Ani, conquered by Sultan Alparslan in 1064, is considered one of the key starting points of Turkish-Islamic history in Anatolia. The site also holds particular significance for the region’s architectural heritage, with monuments described as the first conquest mosque, first mosque and first masjid in Anatolia.
Similar decorative designs can be seen at the 1191 Mama Hatun Tomb in Tercan, the 1224 Grand Mosque of Malatya, the Eşrefoğlu Mosque in Beyşehir and the Tahir and Zühre Mosque in 
Konya.

Divers exploring the Princes’ Islands off Istanbul encountered rare species including tope sharks and angular roughsharks, revealing a thriving underwater ecosystem in the Marmara Sea despite environmental pressures.
Dives at Viranbağlar, Yelkenkaya, Kurşun Burnu, Sivri Ada, Kalpazankaya, Hastane Altı, Terk-i Dünya and At Mezarlığı captured returning species. While exploring At Mezarlığı, south of Büyükada facing Sedef Island, divers found large horse bones mingling with active marine life, dive instructor Mehmet Karail said.

Human activities like heavy fishing and urban waste threaten this ecosystem.
“We do not want to say to our children and grandchildren, ‘This used to be a sea,’” he said, urging the public to stop polluting the waters.
The Marmara Sea, an inland body of water entirely within Türkiye, connects the Black Sea to the Aegean Sea. It has faced severe ecological challenges recently, including a massive marine mucilage outbreak in 2021 caused by agricultural runoff and untreated wastewater.

Next Atlantic tropical storm will be named Dolly but no connection to Parton's death

Storm systems are named by procedures set by the World Meteorological Organisation and the lists of names are reused every six years.
The next tropical storm that develops in the Atlantic this hurricane season will be named Dolly, but the timing is pure coincidence and has no connection to country music star Dolly Parton’s death on Tuesday.
Storm systems are named by procedures set by the World Meteorological Organisation and the lists of names are reused every six years. For the Atlantic region, the lists are alphabetical and alternate between male and female names.
This season started with Tropical Storm Arthur coming ashore on the US Gulf Coast in June, and Tropical Storm Bertha dumped rain in Louisiana and Texas in July.
Tropical Storm Cristobal formed and quickly dissipated in the Atlantic earlier in August.
The National Hurricane Centre was monitoring a weather system off Africa that may strengthen into a named tropical storm.
Conditions were favourable for the area of thunderstorms south of the Cabo Verde Islands to become a tropical depression sometime in the next week, forecasters at the Miami-based centre said on Tuesday evening.
If it further develops, with maximum sustained winds of at least 63 kph, the system would be named Tropical Storm Dolly.
Forecasters said another weather system in the Atlantic far northeast of Bermuda was disorganized Tuesday and had a poor chance of further development.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has forecast a below-average Atlantic hurricane season due to the El Niño climate phenomenon.
It forecast eight to 14 named storms, with three to six of them reaching hurricane strength and one to three of those intensifying to major hurricanes.
The NHC and other weather agencies name storms to easily communicate warnings about them to people and to avoid confusion. The WMO says names are chosen to be short, easy to pronounce and familiar to the regions of the world where the storm names are used.
It meets regularly to evaluate potential names, and some names are retired for reasons of sensitivity, particularly for deadly or destructive storms.
Country music star Dolly Parton died on Tuesday at the age of 80 after “bravely facing a brief battle with cancer,” her team said.

Türkiye’s ageing population is increasing demand for residential care, with nursing homes struggling to keep pace, particularly in major cities.
The share of people aged 65 and over has risen to 11.1 percent of the country’s total population, according to data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK), highlighting growing pressure on elderly care and accommodation services.
Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Özdemir Göktaş said in a statement that 15,263 people are currently receiving care at 178 nursing homes and elderly care and rehabilitation centers operated by the ministry. There are also 290 privately run nursing homes and 18 facilities operated by other public institutions.
Göktaş said applicants to nursing homes have an average age of 78, while capacity expansion efforts are continuing. Six new care facilities with a combined capacity of 710 people are planned, while construction is underway at 24 nursing homes. Fourteen of those facilities are expected to be completed in 2027.
The ministry is also conducting feasibility and project studies for 26 additional nursing homes. Facilities whose projects are completed are expected to be proposed for inclusion in the 2027 Presidential Investment Program.
Waiting lists are particularly long in major cities and at certain facilities, Göktaş said. Preferences for single rooms, as well as climate, dietary habits and a desire to remain in the city where people were born and raised, are among factors contributing to longer waits.
The ministry also plans to expand day care centers and develop community-based care models, allowing older people to receive support while remaining connected to their homes and social surroundings. The approach offers alternatives to institutional care as the country’s demographic profile continues to change.

Academics map Istanbul gravestones to preserve heritage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:15:04 UTC
14:15:04 KST

A state-backed project launched two years ago has academics mapping and cataloging historic gravestones across Istanbul’s iconic mosque courtyards, safeguarding centuries of architectural and historical data.
The Islamic Inscriptions and Gravestones Inventory Project operates under the auspices of the Presidency with support from the Culture and Tourism Ministry and the General Directorate of Cultural Heritage and Museums.
An eight- to 10-person team conducts active fieldwork in the Üsküdar district, photographing each stone, recording precise measurements and capturing GPS coordinates immediately upon entering a site.
Data from headpiece types, plan and section features, decorations and script forms is entered into the ministry’s Museum National Inventory System after a detailed expert examination process. Istanbul Medeniyet University art history faculty member Professor Kadir Pektaş coordinates the work.
He told state-run Anadolu Agency the gravestones should not be viewed merely as grave markers, but rather as vital historical records and significant artworks. “We clarify their locations by taking coordinates with GPS,” he said. “We are essentially taking the title deed of the artifact.”
He said the stones are as important as the Ayazma Mosque where they stand, providing direct dates, names, naive craftsmanship and aesthetic features revealing the deceased person’s profession and social status through their headpieces.
Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University theology faculty research assistant Betül Eser said gravestones feature symbols representing the afterlife, such as fruit bowls symbolizing heaven’s blessings and cypress trees representing eternity.
She said classical Ottoman gravestones carry phrases of surrender to God, while 19th-century Westernization introduced expressions of worldly attachment and lamentation like scorching death and scorching separation.
“Even if these gravestones occupy a 1- or 2-square-meter area, they are artifacts reflecting the entire belief and social situation of their era,” she said.
Marmara University geography faculty member Assistant Professor Emre Duman said they use geographic information systems to map spatial and attribute data, preventing future losses of relocated or damaged artifacts.
These enclosed burial areas, traditionally reserved for state officials, religious figures and local notables in the Ottoman Empire, are scattered throughout the city’s older districts.
The ministry’s centralized database allows researchers and authorities to track Türkiye’s cultural heritage assets, monitoring their conservation status and preventing the illegal sale of historical artifacts.

Partial lunar eclipse on Friday: Where to see it in Spain, Italy, France, Portugal and Germany

At maximum eclipse on 27–28 August, Earth’s dark umbral shadow will cover 96% of the Moon’s face - an almost total eclipse.
Europeans will be treated to a “very deep” partial lunar eclipse in the early hours of Friday (28 August) morning, just before dawn.
A partial eclipse always happens about two weeks before or after a solar eclipse, so this one follows the total solar eclipse that captivated Europeans earlier this month.
During a partial eclipse, an imperfect alignment of the Sun, Earth and Moon means a Full Moon passes through only part of Earth’s shadow in space. The shadow grows and then recedes without ever entirely covering the Moon, creating a rare celestial phenomenon.
Friday’s is a Full Sturgeon Moon, named after North America’s largest fish. The moon could turn a rusty red as it gets 96.2 per cent covered by Earth’s dark inner shadow. The change of colour is caused by Earth: “the edge of Earth’s shadow in space has a reddish glow that comes from sunlight streaming through the atmosphere that surrounds our planet”, according to timeanddate.
You won’t need the special glasses that were necessary to safely view the total solar eclipse earlier this month. Looking directly at the moon during a partial eclipse is totally safe.
If you happen to have binoculars or a telescope, they will make the shadow clearer to see.
Location and weather will determine where in Europe that will get the best view of the eclipse. The places facing west with the least cloud cover will get the most spectacular experience.
If you won’t be able to see the eclipse in person, it will be streamed during a live show by timeanddate on YouTube.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Spain
Just like with the solar eclipse, Spain will get the best views. The lunar eclipse will be visible from anywhere in the Iberian Peninsula, the Balearic Islands, the Canary Islands, Ceuta and Melilla, provided the skies remain clear with no clouds.
There will be a difference in viewing time, however. In central and eastern Spain, the Balearic Islands, as well as Melilla, the moon will set before the partial eclipse has finished, whereas in the rest of the country, including the Canaries and Ceuta, you will be able to see the whole process of the eclipse.
The moon will rise in Spain at 9.01pm on 27 August and set at 7.47am on 28 August. The partial phase of the eclipse will begin at 4.34am and end at 7.52am – one hour earlier in the Canary Islands.
The peak of the eclipse, which is when Earth’s shadow covers the largest percentage of the moon, will occur at approximately 6.12am, just before sunrise. At that moment, Earth’s shadow will be projected onto 93 percent of the lunar disk.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Italy
Based on current weather forecasts, some of Italy’s biggest cities are set to have the best views: Naples, Rome and Venice are forecast to have the least cloud cover, meaning they should see a 93 per cent eclipse. Bologna is one of the next best, followed by Turin. Genoa and Milan will also have 93 per cent coverage but they are forecast to be very cloudy.
The partial eclipse will start at 03.23am in Italy, it will be at best coverage at 06.12am and it will end at 09.01am.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in France
Current weather forecasts are predicting a lot of cloud and some rain for Friday morning in France so it may not be the best place for a viewing.
The moon will not begin crossing into Earth’s shadow until around 03.20am, with the colouration effects seen around 04.34am. The peak of the event – when the majority of the moon is in the Earth’s shadow and the red colour its deepest – will take place at around 06.13am. At this point however, the moon will be only around 8° above the horizon, and early morning sunshine may interfere.
Marseille and Strasbourg currently have the best chance at a viewing as they’ll have low cloud cover, though there may be heavy rain or lightning.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Portugal
Anyone in Portugal wanting to catch the partial lunar eclipse from the start will be in for an early start - it begins at 02.23am local time and ends at 08.01am.
Lisbon and Amadora currently have the clearest skies forecast, with Braga and Coimbra also in with a good chance.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Germany
As with the rest of the Central European Summer Time time zone, the eclipse will be at its best at 06.13am in Germany. This is after the Moon has set and the Sun has risen in eastern Germany. It begins at 04.33am.
In the far west of the country, however, the rise and set times for the Sun and Moon are delayed by a little more than half an hour, so that more of the eclipse will be visible. The Moon’s exit from the umbra at 7:53am will, in any case, occur long after sunrise and moonset as seen from Germany, according to the Haus der Astronomie.

Armenia plans EU bid, rules out renewed role in Russia-led bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:11:23 UTC
14:11:23 KST

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said his government plans to begin work on a formal application for European Union membership and will not resume active participation in the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) over the next five years.
Addressing parliament on Aug. 24 during debate on his government’s 2026-2031 program, Pashinyan said the CSTO had not addressed the security concerns raised by Yerevan.
“It is clearly stated in our program that we have no plans to return to the CSTO over the next five years. I can say with certainty that we will not step up our activities in the CSTO,” he said.
Pashinyan said discussions were underway within the alliance about potentially expelling Armenia and that he would welcome such an outcome.
“I would be very happy if the organization decided to expel Armenia from the CSTO. It would free us from the dilemma of whether or not to withdraw,” he said.
Armenia froze its participation in the six-member security alliance in early 2024 but remains a formal member.
Turning to the country’s European ambitions, Pashinyan said Yerevan must first submit an official application before determining whether EU membership is achievable.
“Armenia must first submit an official application for EU membership,” he said, adding that preparations would probably begin “in the near future.”
Pashinyan said Yerevan would assess Brussels’ response and prepare an accession road map before putting the issue to a referendum. Armenia’s parliament adopted legislation in 2025 launching the EU accession process, but the country has yet to file a formal application.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Armenia was free to leave the CSTO if it no longer considered membership necessary.
On the proposed EU application, Peskov pointed to Türkiye and other countries whose accession processes have continued for decades.
He also said aligning Armenian legislation with EU trade, customs and food safety rules would create conflicts with the standards of the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union, of which Armenia remains a member.
Pashinyan’s Civil Contract party won 49.7 percent of the vote in Armenia’s June 7 parliamentary election and retained its majority, allowing it to form a government alone.
Russia imposed restrictions on a range of Armenian agricultural products and beverages before the vote, citing sanitary and phytosanitary violations.
The European Union described the measures as “economic coercion,” while Moscow denied that they were politically motivated.
Separately, former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan and his eldest son, Sedrak, were detained on Aug. 25 as part of a corruption investigation, the Prosecutor General’s Office said.
Four other people were also detained.
Prosecutors opened proceedings against Kocharyan on suspicion of abuse of authority, bribery and large-scale money laundering. Investigators are examining allegations that state-owned buildings and land were sold below market value to private companies during his presidency from 1998 to 2008.
Kocharyan, who leads the opposition Armenia Alliance, has denied wrongdoing. His allies described the investigation as politically motivated.

Erdoğan urges restraint as anti-terror process advances

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on Aug. 25 called on people across the political spectrum to support the government’s “terror-free Türkiye” initiative, describing it as a matter of state shared by the country’s 86 million citizens.
Speaking after a cabinet meeting at the Ahlat Presidential Complex in the eastern province of Bitlis, Erdoğan said the process had cleared several critical hurdles over the past two years but still needed to be handled carefully.
“Today, I am once again calling upon everyone, regardless of their political views, to be a part of the solution,” he said.
Erdoğan urged political actors, media outlets and journalists to use measured language and avoid statements or actions that could inflame public sensitivities. He said the government remained determined to resolve the issue permanently and leave future generations “a country and region free of terror.”
The Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration, which sets out the legal framework for the process, was approved by parliament on Aug. 10 with 467 votes and entered into force on Aug. 18.
Its measures are tied to official verification that the PKK and affiliated groups have ended their operational presence and surrendered their weapons.
Turning to regional developments, Erdoğan said Türkiye would not allow what he described as “bloody scenarios” being drawn up for the region to be carried out.
“The Republic of Türkiye will compromise neither its principles nor its national interests,” he said.
Erdoğan said Ankara would continue working for peace and supporting the recovery of neighboring countries. Türkiye’s only objectives in the region were peace, justice, stability and security, he added, rejecting claims that the country had a hidden agenda.
On the economy, Erdoğan said the government would continue prioritizing employment, limiting the impact of volatility in commodity prices and pursuing opportunities in defense and international investment.

SDF formally dissolves after integration into Syrian state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:07:00 UTC
14:07:00 KST

The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) announced its formal dissolution on Aug. 25 after completing the integration of its military, security and administrative structures into Syrian state institutions.
Speaking at a press conference at the People’s Palace in Damascus, SDF commander Mazloum Abdi said the decision followed an agreement with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and the incorporation of the group’s forces into Syrian army brigades.
“We announce today the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and announce with full responsibility its dissolution as an independent military force,” Abdi said.
He said the dissolution also covered the Kurdish-led autonomous administration in northeastern Syria and all military and civilian bodies affiliated with it.
All had been fully integrated into state institutions, he added.
“We want this day to mark a genuine transition from the battlefields to the fields of construction, and from the era of weapons to the era of peace,” Abdi said.
The declaration formalized the outcome of a ceasefire and phased-integration agreement reached by Damascus and the SDF on Jan. 29.
Abdi said on Aug. 20 that the integration of the group’s military, security and administrative institutions had been completed.
Following the announcement, al-Sharaa received Abdi and his delegation at the palace.
The Syrian presidency said the talks covered the next steps in the integration process and efforts to strengthen state authority, security and stability.
U.S. Ambassador to Türkiye and special presidential envoy for Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack called the development “absolutely historic” in a post on X.
"This is what real integration looks like: not winners and losers, but former counterparts with differing points of view crafting a diplomatic solution to strengthen the sovereign nation of Syria. One army, one government, one state," said Barrack.
Türkiye regards the YPG, the main component of the SDF, as the PKK’s Syrian branch.
The PKK is designated as a terrorist organization by Türkiye, the United States and the European Union.

Scientists turn plastic bottles into protein-rich cookies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:03:30 UTC
14:03:30 KST

Scientists turn plastic bottles into protein-rich cookies
Scientists at Southern Illinois University Carbondale (SIU) have developed a way to make 3D-printed cookies using genetically engineered yeast to produce protein and nutrients from plastic and agricultural waste.
The project aims to tackle two of the planet’s crises: plastic waste accumulation and food insecurity.
The team first set out to develop ways to make use of waste plastics, Lahiru Jayakody, an associate professor of microbiology at Southern Illinois University said in an interview with the American Chemical Society (ACS) published on Monday.
“We thought, why not focus on making food? Because plastic is carbon and food is carbon,” he said.
The process starts by breaking down plastic and plant waste with water and oxygen under high temperature and pressure. Genetically engineered yeasts then consume the resulting compounds and produce proteins, fats, and acids. With the addition of fiber, starch, and sweetener, the resulting mix is fed into a 3D printer which molds the paste into any desired shape.
With this technology, the scientists created small protein-rich cookies they dubbed “µBites” or “microbites.” They are waiting for the safety go-ahead from their university to actually taste-test them, however.
The novel technology could be useful in hostile environments, according to Jayakody.
“If you want to produce food in a very extreme environment using the resource you have, carbon resource waste like Arctic, or the desert, and potentially one day in the Mars or the lunar surface, microbeids can do that job,” he told Reuters.
SIU researchers have been developing the technology since 2021, when their µBites concept was selected for NASA’s Deep Space Food Challenge.
The news comes as scientists are paying closer attention to how plastic already unintentionally enters the human food chain.
Researchers have reported microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics in human tissues. A 2025 study published in Nature Medicine detected them in the liver, kidneys, and brain, while a 2026 review published last month said particles had also been found in blood, placenta, and heart tissue.
The particles could pose health risks, with studies linking exposure to inflammation, oxidative stress, cell death, and disruptions to metabolism and immune function. However, researchers say more evidence is needed to determine the effects of long-term exposure in humans.

====================================================================================================

"The response seems very timid": where does ecology fit in the presidential race?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

After a summer of extreme weather, political action on the climate crisis seems timid and below French expectations, say several women experts interviewed by Euronews.
Massive wildfires in Gironde, in the Landes and in the Var. Episodes of repeated heatwaves across the country. Severe drought is seriously affecting agriculture. This summer, France has been severely tested by the elements.
Last winter, the country had already experienced several months marked by a series of weather fronts and storms (Goretti, Ingrid, Nils, Pedro), causing major flooding across France.
With only a few months to go before the next presidential election, environmental issues are expected to take an unprecedented place in the political debate. Historically championed by the left, the topic has become inescapable, forcing the right and the far right to take it up.
Because today, "given the delays and the seriousness of the situation, France no longer has a choice: it must adapt, and fast", warns the Climate Action Network (Réseau Action Climat), which challenges the record of recent successive governments, saying they "have not taken the necessary measures to adapt the country to the effects of climate change".
Yet the warnings have been sounding for several years. As early as 2013, the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) stated that "warming of the climate system is unequivocal and, since the 1950s, many of the observed changes are unprecedented over decades to millennia".
"The years 1983 to 2012 are probably the warmest 30-year period the Northern Hemisphere has experienced in at least 1,400 years", the report also noted.
Politicians out of touch
An issue that is being taken on board by more and more citizens. In a survey published on Monday 24 August (source in French), Ipsos reveals that 64% of French people felt "anxiety or fear" for the health of their loved ones and 48% for their own health during the summer of 2026.
The polling institute also reports that French people "expect above all solutions from the public authorities": 79% of respondents want government measures to help the population cope with heatwaves.
For its part, a study by the French Environment and Energy Management Agency (Ademe) published last year put at 6.3 million the number of moderately eco-anxious French people, showing initial symptoms that should not be allowed to worsen. "2.1 million are thought to be highly eco-anxious, with intense, chronic symptoms" and "420,000 of them have mental health that is genuinely at risk", the study (source in French) noted.
The problem is that they are not necessarily being heard by political leaders. "Most parties and presidential candidates seem out of touch with the realities of everyday life for French people who have been badly affected" by these events, says Anne Bringault, programme director at the Climate Action Network, speaking to Euronews.
"Faced with an unprecedented challenge for humanity and biodiversity, with the many deaths caused by heatwaves, the economic losses, particularly for farmers, homes destroyed by wildfires and nature dried out, the political response seems very timid and not at all commensurate with what French people expect or with their perception of the concrete impacts of climate change", she says.
Appearing on France Inter (source in French) this Tuesday, Jean-Marc Jancovici, founder and president of the climate-transition think tank The Shift Project, was even more scathing, claiming that the political class is "in a form of denial" about climate change.
Causes swept under the carpet
A view shared by Eva Morel, secretary-general of the association QuotaClimat. "We have the feeling that elections are moments when ecology really struggles to find a way through", she laments to Euronews, before trying to explain the reason for this lack of interest. "In fact, they themselves are not encouraged to understand the issue and make ambitious proposals on it, because the media reception of their statements on the subject is generally quite favourable."
She goes even further. "Above all, we cannot hope for a constructive debate on the subject if, when climate disasters occur, we talk only about what is happening and do not try to understand the underlying factors – both the causes and the structural solutions that would allow us to address them", stresses Eva Morel.
She cites the events of the summer of 2026, which sparked discussions focused "mainly on observations and not necessarily on explanations". "So, for example, we talked more about climate, which was almost unavoidable. But we talked less about fossil energy", she regrets. "From there, we cannot really expect the proposals of the various candidates to be convincing when it comes to addressing the root of the problem", the expert continues.
Politicians doing... politics
"Which of the candidates puts at the centre of their programme the fact that the world is going to change? None of them", snaps Jean-Marc Jancovici. In his view, the programmes of potential or declared candidates for the next presidential election are stripped of coherent environmental measures. "You find inconsistencies everywhere", says The Shift Project's president.
For Eva Morel, this situation is explained in particular by how hard it is, in "a political system that rewards demagoguery, to ask candidates to confront a crisis that profoundly destabilises citizens' ways of life and still come up with a desirable project".
On the right, climate issues struggle to break through against traditionally favoured themes such as immigration or law-and-order questions. "Right-wing and centrist parties stay in their lane, like Édouard Philippe, who chose to highlight immigration issues during his trip to Mayotte ", says Anne Bringault. Eva Morel agrees: "Even just on adaptation, the right as a political family still considers that it is not a political question."
In his manifesto, the former prime minister uses the word "ecology" only once. "We believe that this ambition requires the introduction of an effective policy to decarbonise our economy, preserve biodiversity and increase investment in the excellence of French energy and agricultural sectors", he writes, without providing further detail.
For his rival in the centrist bloc, Gabriel Attal, ecology for now seems framed more in terms of competitiveness and innovation than constraint. The Renaissance candidate advocates an energy mix combining nuclear and renewables and wants to turn climate transition into a driver of investment and growth. In early August, Attal also said he refused to leave the water crisis "to the left and the far left around Jean-Luc Mélenchon", promising to create a "ministry for water" if elected.
As for the left, "electoral opportunism, in a context of competition to harvest the green vote, seems to play a significant role", Anne Bringault continues. This competition is all the stronger as ecologists are struggling to appear united and to impose their line in the run-up to 2027, while the La France insoumise candidate seeks to occupy this space by putting forward proposals such as "eco-regions" or enshrining in the Constitution the principle of the "green rule", under which we do not take more from nature than it is able to regenerate.
"What we see is that, today, the environmental programmes of parties on the left are still more substantiated than those on the right, and that has been the case for several years", continues Eva Morel. "What we find interesting is the extent to which political discourse mirrors scientific discourse. And today, that seems to be happening more on the left than elsewhere."
RN, king of disinformation?
On the other side of the political spectrum, the National Rally strongly rejects so-called "punitive" environmental policies and opposes wind power, instead making nuclear energy a pillar of decarbonisation.
The far-right party "is trying in haste to dress itself up in green by advocating simplistic solutions that are barely realistic financially or technically, such as widespread air conditioning", analyses Anne Bringault.
"In fact, they focus on hot-button issues. And since climate is now one of those hot topics, they focus on it. It is purely opportunistic", adds Eva Morel, who acknowledges that the National Rally has rowed back on its statements questioning the IPCC's credibility or the reality of global warming, even if that "is not enough". "The problem is that their political software has not integrated the environmental question at all. They have no proposals that genuinely protect us from the consequences, let alone address the causes."
She also accuses the party led by Jordan Bardella of circulating, in her view, misleading information. "These are narratives that are deliberately orchestrated because they work with public opinion, instrumentalising moments that attract a great deal of attention. [...] It has been shown that this is an obstruction strategy that works. It blocks the implementation of public policies that are supposed to be effective", the expert explains, citing the example of low-emission zones.
"And what we fear is that, alongside this obstruction, there is an effort to disqualify political opponents and environmental defenders by demonising them. And by doing that, they push solutions away from the problem, even though the problem is highly visible", concludes Eva Morel.
