"Which of the candidates puts at the centre of their programme the fact that the world is going to change? None of them", snaps Jean-Marc Jancovici. In his view, the programmes of potential or declared candidates for the next presidential election are stripped of coherent environmental measures. "You find inconsistencies everywhere", says The Shift Project's president.
For Eva Morel, this situation is explained in particular by how hard it is, in "a political system that rewards demagoguery, to ask candidates to confront a crisis that profoundly destabilises citizens' ways of life and still come up with a desirable project".
On the right, climate issues struggle to break through against traditionally favoured themes such as immigration or law-and-order questions. "Right-wing and centrist parties stay in their lane, like Édouard Philippe, who chose to highlight immigration issues during his trip to Mayotte ", says Anne Bringault. Eva Morel agrees: "Even just on adaptation, the right as a political family still considers that it is not a political question."
In his manifesto, the former prime minister uses the word "ecology" only once. "We believe that this ambition requires the introduction of an effective policy to decarbonise our economy, preserve biodiversity and increase investment in the excellence of French energy and agricultural sectors", he writes, without providing further detail.
For his rival in the centrist bloc, Gabriel Attal, ecology for now seems framed more in terms of competitiveness and innovation than constraint. The Renaissance candidate advocates an energy mix combining nuclear and renewables and wants to turn climate transition into a driver of investment and growth. In early August, Attal also said he refused to leave the water crisis "to the left and the far left around Jean-Luc Mélenchon", promising to create a "ministry for water" if elected.
As for the left, "electoral opportunism, in a context of competition to harvest the green vote, seems to play a significant role", Anne Bringault continues. This competition is all the stronger as ecologists are struggling to appear united and to impose their line in the run-up to 2027, while the La France insoumise candidate seeks to occupy this space by putting forward proposals such as "eco-regions" or enshrining in the Constitution the principle of the "green rule", under which we do not take more from nature than it is able to regenerate.
"What we see is that, today, the environmental programmes of parties on the left are still more substantiated than those on the right, and that has been the case for several years", continues Eva Morel. "What we find interesting is the extent to which political discourse mirrors scientific discourse. And today, that seems to be happening more on the left than elsewhere."
RN, king of disinformation?
On the other side of the political spectrum, the National Rally strongly rejects so-called "punitive" environmental policies and opposes wind power, instead making nuclear energy a pillar of decarbonisation.
The far-right party "is trying in haste to dress itself up in green by advocating simplistic solutions that are barely realistic financially or technically, such as widespread air conditioning", analyses Anne Bringault.
"In fact, they focus on hot-button issues. And since climate is now one of those hot topics, they focus on it. It is purely opportunistic", adds Eva Morel, who acknowledges that the National Rally has rowed back on its statements questioning the IPCC's credibility or the reality of global warming, even if that "is not enough". "The problem is that their political software has not integrated the environmental question at all. They have no proposals that genuinely protect us from the consequences, let alone address the causes."
She also accuses the party led by Jordan Bardella of circulating, in her view, misleading information. "These are narratives that are deliberately orchestrated because they work with public opinion, instrumentalising moments that attract a great deal of attention. [...] It has been shown that this is an obstruction strategy that works. It blocks the implementation of public policies that are supposed to be effective", the expert explains, citing the example of low-emission zones.
"And what we fear is that, alongside this obstruction, there is an effort to disqualify political opponents and environmental defenders by demonising them. And by doing that, they push solutions away from the problem, even though the problem is highly visible", concludes Eva Morel.

"The response seems timid": what role for the environment in the presidential campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

After a summer of extreme weather, political action on the climate crisis seems timid and below French expectations, say several women experts interviewed by Euronews.
Massive wildfires in Gironde, in the Landes and in the Var. Episodes of repeated heatwaves across the country. Severe drought is seriously affecting agriculture. This summer, France has been severely tested by the elements.
Last winter, the country had already experienced several months marked by a series of weather fronts and storms (Goretti, Ingrid, Nils, Pedro), causing major flooding across France.
With only a few months to go before the next presidential election, environmental issues are expected to take an unprecedented place in the political debate. Historically championed by the left, the topic has become inescapable, forcing the right and the far right to take it up.
Because today, "given the delays and the seriousness of the situation, France no longer has a choice: it must adapt, and fast", warns the Climate Action Network (Réseau Action Climat), which challenges the record of recent successive governments, saying they "have not taken the necessary measures to adapt the country to the effects of climate change".
Yet the warnings have been sounding for several years. As early as 2013, the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) stated that "warming of the climate system is unequivocal and, since the 1950s, many of the observed changes are unprecedented over decades to millennia".
"The years 1983 to 2012 are probably the warmest 30-year period the Northern Hemisphere has experienced in at least 1,400 years", the report also noted.
Politicians out of touch
An issue that is being taken on board by more and more citizens. In a survey published on Monday 24 August (source in French), Ipsos reveals that 64% of French people felt "anxiety or fear" for the health of their loved ones and 48% for their own health during the summer of 2026.
The polling institute also reports that French people "expect above all solutions from the public authorities": 79% of respondents want government measures to help the population cope with heatwaves.
For its part, a study by the French Environment and Energy Management Agency (Ademe) published last year put at 6.3 million the number of moderately eco-anxious French people, showing initial symptoms that should not be allowed to worsen. "2.1 million are thought to be highly eco-anxious, with intense, chronic symptoms" and "420,000 of them have mental health that is genuinely at risk", the study (source in French) noted.
The problem is that they are not necessarily being heard by political leaders. "Most parties and presidential candidates seem out of touch with the realities of everyday life for French people who have been badly affected" by these events, says Anne Bringault, programme director at the Climate Action Network, speaking to Euronews.
"Faced with an unprecedented challenge for humanity and biodiversity, with the many deaths caused by heatwaves, the economic losses, particularly for farmers, homes destroyed by wildfires and nature dried out, the political response seems very timid and not at all commensurate with what French people expect or with their perception of the concrete impacts of climate change", she says.
Appearing on France Inter (source in French) this Tuesday, Jean-Marc Jancovici, founder and president of the climate-transition think tank The Shift Project, was even more scathing, claiming that the political class is "in a form of denial" about climate change.
Causes swept under the carpet
A view shared by Eva Morel, secretary-general of the association QuotaClimat. "We have the feeling that elections are moments when ecology really struggles to find a way through", she laments to Euronews, before trying to explain the reason for this lack of interest. "In fact, they themselves are not encouraged to understand the issue and make ambitious proposals on it, because the media reception of their statements on the subject is generally quite favourable."
She goes even further. "Above all, we cannot hope for a constructive debate on the subject if, when climate disasters occur, we talk only about what is happening and do not try to understand the underlying factors – both the causes and the structural solutions that would allow us to address them", stresses Eva Morel.
She cites the events of the summer of 2026, which sparked discussions focused "mainly on observations and not necessarily on explanations". "So, for example, we talked more about climate, which was almost unavoidable. But we talked less about fossil energy", she regrets. "From there, we cannot really expect the proposals of the various candidates to be convincing when it comes to addressing the root of the problem", the expert continues.
Politicians doing... politics
"Which of the candidates puts at the centre of their programme the fact that the world is going to change? None of them", snaps Jean-Marc Jancovici. In his view, the programmes of potential or declared candidates for the next presidential election are stripped of coherent environmental measures. "You find inconsistencies everywhere", says The Shift Project's president.
For Eva Morel, this situation is explained in particular by how hard it is, in "a political system that rewards demagoguery, to ask candidates to confront a crisis that profoundly destabilises citizens' ways of life and still come up with a desirable project".
On the right, climate issues struggle to break through against traditionally favoured themes such as immigration or law-and-order questions. "Right-wing and centrist parties stay in their lane, like Édouard Philippe, who chose to highlight immigration issues during his trip to Mayotte ", says Anne Bringault. Eva Morel agrees: "Even just on adaptation, the right as a political family still considers that it is not a political question."
In his manifesto, the former prime minister uses the word "ecology" only once. "We believe that this ambition requires the introduction of an effective policy to decarbonise our economy, preserve biodiversity and increase investment in the excellence of French energy and agricultural sectors", he writes, without providing further detail.
For his rival in the centrist bloc, Gabriel Attal, ecology for now seems framed more in terms of competitiveness and innovation than constraint. The Renaissance candidate advocates an energy mix combining nuclear and renewables and wants to turn climate transition into a driver of investment and growth. In early August, Attal also said he refused to leave the water crisis "to the left and the far left around Jean-Luc Mélenchon", promising to create a "ministry for water" if elected.
As for the left, "electoral opportunism, in a context of competition to harvest the green vote, seems to play a significant role", Anne Bringault continues. This competition is all the stronger as ecologists are struggling to appear united and to impose their line in the run-up to 2027, while the La France insoumise candidate seeks to occupy this space by putting forward proposals such as "eco-regions" or enshrining in the Constitution the principle of the "green rule", under which we do not take more from nature than it is able to regenerate.
"What we see is that, today, the environmental programmes of parties on the left are still more substantiated than those on the right, and that has been the case for several years", continues Eva Morel. "What we find interesting is the extent to which political discourse mirrors scientific discourse. And today, that seems to be happening more on the left than elsewhere."
RN, king of disinformation?
On the other side of the political spectrum, the National Rally strongly rejects so-called "punitive" environmental policies and opposes wind power, instead making nuclear energy a pillar of decarbonisation.
The far-right party "is trying in haste to dress itself up in green by advocating simplistic solutions that are barely realistic financially or technically, such as widespread air conditioning", analyses Anne Bringault.
"In fact, they focus on hot-button issues. And since climate is now one of those hot topics, they focus on it. It is purely opportunistic", adds Eva Morel, who acknowledges that the National Rally has rowed back on its statements questioning the IPCC's credibility or the reality of global warming, even if that "is not enough". "The problem is that their political software has not integrated the environmental question at all. They have no proposals that genuinely protect us from the consequences, let alone address the causes."
She also accuses the party led by Jordan Bardella of circulating, in her view, misleading information. "These are narratives that are deliberately orchestrated because they work with public opinion, instrumentalising moments that attract a great deal of attention. [...] It has been shown that this is an obstruction strategy that works. It blocks the implementation of public policies that are supposed to be effective", the expert explains, citing the example of low-emission zones.
"And what we fear is that, alongside this obstruction, there is an effort to disqualify political opponents and environmental defenders by demonising them. And by doing that, they push solutions away from the problem, even though the problem is highly visible", concludes Eva Morel.

Day trips in Europe: Top 10 sightseeing stops beyond the beaten track for autumn 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:49 UTC
14:00:49 KST

An itinerary doesn’t have to include stops at the big-name cities. This autumn, here are the sightseeing destinations worth adding to your trip that offer scenic spots, historic towns and adventurous foods to try.
The summer months may soon be behind us, but who says travel also has to abruptly draw to a halt?
If you ask me, the crunch of reddish-brown leaves beneath your feet, the milder climate and seasonal delicacies make autumn an ideal time to venture across Europe – not to mention fewer crowds during the shoulder season.
Now, European hotspots may spring to mind as you plan your next escape, and I won’t sway your mind otherwise, but have you considered adding additional stops to your itinerary?
In a survey of booking data primarily from American travellers planning trips across Europe, Daytrip, a platform specialising in city-to-city travel with car transfers, found a recently developing trend.
Instead of just sticking to visiting major cities, more holidaymakers are turning transfers between major spots into opportunities to explore smaller cities overshadowed by popular destinations.
“A transfer that once meant hours on the highway now includes a stop at a historic town, a museum, a viewpoint, or a UNESCO World Heritage Site, effectively adding a destination to the itinerary without adding an extra day to the vacation,” Daytrip said.
So, where could a few hours in between destinations take you?
Popular off the beaten path autumn sightseeing spots
Topping Daytrip’s top 10 ranking is Pompeii in Italy. Less than an hour's drive from Naples, this ancient Roman city is an archaeological treasure trove of public squares, temples and other ruins spanning a vast area of around 440,000 square meters.
If you’re short on time, you don’t have to cover the whole area – you could just see a few sites. For instance, Pompeii's two theatres are within the same area of the city. The Large Theatre was once where Greek-Roman plays were performed, while the smaller Odeon was where poetry and musical performances used to take place. Or, for greener scenery, Julia Felix's Villa, an aristocratic complex from 1st-century BC, features an expansive ornamental garden.
Second on Daytrip’s list is Český Krumlov, nestled in the south of Czechia.
About four hours away from Prague, this historic town is home to centuries-old buildings, including the Český Krumlov Castle. Once the residence of the South Bohemian aristocracy, the building's original layout has been preserved – keeping much of its material structure, interior installations and architectural structure from the 14th to the 19th centuries.
Rounding off Daytrip’s top three sightseeing spots to visit this autumn is Coimbra. This central Portuguese city also welcomes visitors to explore its historic monuments and unique architecture. Beyond its history, the city is also a must-visit destination for foodies.
For those with adventurous palettes, the lamprey fish and eel are local delicacies in Coimbra, thanks to its proximity to the Mondego River – the largest of the exclusively Portuguese rivers. Other delicacies include local cheeses such
Daytrip's top 10 European sightseeing stops for autumn 2026
- 1. Pompeii, Italy
- 2. Český Krumlov, Czechia
- 3. Coimbra, Portugal
- 4. Óbidos, Portugal
- 5. Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia
- 6. Bratislava, Slovakia
- 7. Aveiro, Portugal
- 8. Kutná Hora, Czechia
- 9. Montepulciano, Italy
- 10. Nazaré, Portugal

====================================================================================================

Two years in limbo: the residents still paying mortgages on flats destroyed in east London fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:36 UTC
14:00:36 KST

Sarah Williams vividly remembers the night in 2016 when she camped overnight in a car park to put down a deposit on a flat in the newly completed Spectrum Building in Dagenham, east London.
“People started queuing for those flats 24 hours before they went on sale,” she said. “It was basically the only flat I could afford in London. This was a year before Grenfell, and the flats market in London was completely crazy.”
Four years later, her flat became unsellable when they realised it was covered in dangerous, flammable cladding. Another four years and it, like Grenfell Tower in west London in 2017, had burned down.
It has been two years since the fire at the Spectrum Building on 26 August 2024, which left more than 80 people homeless. They were forced to flee a blaze that broke out in the early hours of the morning, fuelled by the scaffolding that covered the building while the cladding was replaced.
Williams, like many leaseholders, is stuck in a legal limbo, paying the mortgage on a flat that no longer exists, with no idea how much she will get back.
The building’s freeholder, Arinium Ltd, went bankrupt shortly after the fire, and administrators are now responsible for distributing any remaining money, including insurance payouts for loss and damages.
“We still haven’t got our money, and we have no idea whether it will even cover the value of the flats,” said Williams, a charity worker. “We don’t know when we’re going to get it. We’ve still got to pay our mortgages. We’ve still got to pay our rent.
“So many people have told us: ‘It’s terrible what happened to you, and this is a priority for us.’ But our lives are still on hold.”
Insurance payouts are covering emergency accommodation for leaseholders for three years – no one knows what will happen if compensation hasn’t been awarded by then, and people are left to pay both rent and a mortgage.
James Allchurch, who owned two flats which burned down in the fire, said the arduous legal process was compounding the trauma many experienced that night. He and his partner ran from their third-floor flat when he woke up by chance and saw embers and blue flashing lights outside the window.
“We just grabbed whatever clothes we had and ran out the building, leaving everything behind. Because the last thing you think is, we’ll never go back in our flat,” he said.
“It wears you down. I still have nightmares about the fire, I have nightmares about watching our building being demolished, losing everything. There’s an underlying sense of anxiety that has been with me most days since that fire.”
Leaseholders are also concerned that if the freeholder is prosecuted over any fire safety breaches and ultimately fined, that money could come out of the pot of money that would otherwise be distributed to them.
“You want some justice, you want to feel that someone’s taking responsibility and there’s accountability,” Allchurch said. “But the result of that might be that we’re all thousands of pounds worse off.”
As well as frustration at the delays in getting any money back, residents are angry at what they describe as the painfully slow pace of work to replace flammable cladding on buildings across the country.
The day after the fire, the then deputy prime minister, Angela Rayner, told reporters at the site that cladding remediation was going “far too slowly” and vowed to “speed up the process”. But the number of buildings in need of cladding remediation where work has started or been completed has only increased from 50% to 53% in the past two years.
“I don’t want anybody else to go through this,” said Williams. “Do not stand in front of my smouldering building saying this is a priority then fail to follow up on that. I expected fast and urgent action, but I haven’t seen that for the residents of Spectrum and I haven’t seen that for the country.”
Giles Grover, from the End Our Cladding Scandal campaign group, said they were still waiting for Labour to keep its manifesto commitments on building safety.
“Progress has been very slow in the last couple of years,” he said. “There’s been a couple of small steps forward, but it’s piecemeal.
“It feels like Labour prioritised building 1.5m homes, and that’s meant they’ve swept ending the building safety crisis under the carpet. But this fire was a warning, and they need to heed it. There’s hundreds of thousands of people still living in unsafe buildings.”
A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “The residents of the Spectrum Building must be fully and urgently compensated so they can start to rebuild their lives – and we urge the building’s administrators to resolve the insurance settlements as quickly as possible.
“More broadly, we’re speeding up cladding removal to bring the building safety crisis to an end, and introducing a new legal duty to remediate, to force those responsible to fix unsafe buildings or face criminal prosecution.”

====================================================================================================

Iran seeks to criminalise all contact with foreign media in latest ‘chilling’ crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:35 UTC
14:00:35 KST

Iran has taken the first step towards criminalising contact with foreign media, in a move human rights groups have said attempts to “sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world”.
For journalists, researchers and even ordinary citizens, the proposed law being discussed by Iranian lawmakers this month could make speaking to international audiences and groups a potential criminal act and restrict coverage of events such as January’s mass anti-regime protests.
Even social media platforms that the regime considers to be “financed” by another country, such as Instagram and X, would fall under the bill, said Moein Khazaeli, an Iranian human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists.
“It means any kind of interview, contact, or sending photographs to them [foreign media or organisations] could lead to six months to two years’ imprisonment. Not just the US and Israel, but any contact with foreign media in any country could be considered a crime if one doesn’t inform the intelligence ministry beforehand,” said Khazaeli.
Among the recent examples of the risks facing Iranian journalists is the case of Yalda Moaiery, an acclaimed photographerwho was sentenced this month to 15 years in prison in Tehran for documenting the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Although Moaiery was charged under the espionage law introduced after last year’s 12-day war between Iran and Israel, Khazaeli said the new bill signalled a broader effort to regulate and punish contact between Iranians and foreign media and institutions. “It could move [Iran] to a North Korea kind of situation,” he said.
Moaiery, 44, has spent two decades covering the harsh realities faced by people in Iran, including the nationwide Woman, Life, Freedom protests in 2022 and the anti-regime protests that led to thousands being killed in January.
She came to international prominence in 2019 after criticising Trump’s use of one of her photos of a woman at a demonstration near Tehran University, saying Trump’s sanctions were damaging Iranian lives, including those of her friends and family. “This image shows my people and is for my people, and shouldn’t be abused by these men in Washington,” she wrote.
Now, in a cruel irony, Moaiery said she had been sentenced in absentia for her work covering the US-Israeli war in Iran and accused of media activity deemed to strengthen and aid Israel and the US.
“I have been a critic of Israel and its policies all my life. I am not an Israel supporter, never, ever. And I have always been a critic of American politics. It was like something that you are against, and they want to stick it to you. So it’s hard. It’s super hard,” she told the Guardian.
 Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), said the new law on media contact risked turning Iran into an “isolated black hole”.
“It is not simply an attack on journalists and citizen journalists; it is an attempt to sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world by criminalising the free flow of information itself.
“It sends a chilling message and threatens to turn ordinary academic, professional and civic engagement into a potential national security crime,” he said.
Moaiery was arrested and sentenced to eight years in prison in 2022, but later received an amnesty. This time, however, she fears her sentence could be upheld and she might be jailed.
“Of course, I am scared,” she said. “The only thing that I’m worried about is wasting my life if I have to be there for 15 years. When I get out, I’ll be 60 years old.”
  She also criticised foreign journalists who travelled to Tehran to cover the funeral in July of the late supreme leader, Ali Khamenei.
“I have one word for them: shameful. They just want to say, ‘We were in Tehran.’ OK, but what did you do? They didn’t go and ask people about the economic situation or talk to the families of the thousands who died in January. Why were you here? To participate in their propaganda?”

A Tamil summer vegetarian feast: Cynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry and gooseberry pickle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:35 UTC
14:00:35 KST

This lovely summery “curry” is a cold, refreshing dish from Karnataka in India, and is eaten widely in Tamil Nadu, just 20 miles across the Palk Strait from my ancestral Tamil homeland in north and eastern Sri Lanka. Along with chefs Louis and Seb in our development kitchen, we decided that smacking the cucumbers helps give them a silky texture, and means the fragrant yoghurt base can get into all the nooks and crannies. It’s wonderful with plain rice and a side of fenugreek-heavy hot Tamil pickle, made with English gooseberries rather than superfood nelli, both of which are said to make your skin shine and hair bouncy.
Hot gooseberry pickle
Prep 10 min
Cook 10 min
Pickle 10 min
Chill 2 hr+
Serves 4
250g gooseberries
  250ml apple cider vinegar
  1 tbsp caster sugar
  1 tsp salt
  1 tsp fenugreek seeds
  1 tbsp mustard seeds
  4 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed
3 tbsp vegetable oil
4 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  Some salt
Wash the gooseberries well, then spread them out on a cloth and leave to dry.
Put the vinegar, 250ml water, the sugar and salt in a saucepan and cook on a high heat until the sugar and salt have dissolved and the liquid is simmering. Add the gooseberries, turn off the heat and leave to pickle for 10 minutes.
In a small frying pan, dry roast the fenugreek for about 60 seconds, until fragrant, then leave to cool. Tip the cooled fenugreek into a small spice grinder or mortar, add the mustard seeds and crushed garlic, then blitz or grind to a paste. Scrape the mix into a small bowl, add the drained gooseberries, the oil, chilli powder and salt, then cover and put in the fridge for at least two hours.
Cucumber yoghurt curry
Prep 15 min
Cook 10 min
Serves 4
2 cucumbers
80g desiccated coconut (frozen or freshly grated), soaked in water for 15 minutes, then drained
2 green chillies, roughly chopped
  4 garlic cloves, peeled and roughly chopped
30g fresh coriander, stalks and leaves
  ½ tsp black peppercorns
  2 tsp sesame seeds
  100g natural yoghurt
  Salt, to taste
Boiled white rice, to serve
For the temper
4 tsp vegetable oil, or coconut oil
10 fresh curry leaves
1 tsp fenugreek seeds (optional)
2 tsp mustard seeds
  2 tsp cumin seeds
  3 dried red chillies, ideally cascabel
First, make a coconut-cucumber paste. Peel the cucumbers, reserving the skins. Wrap each cucumber in clingfilm, then bash them lightly with a rolling pin. Remove the clingfilm, keeping the seeds, and cut the flesh on a slight diagonal into 1cm slices. Put a few of the chopped cucumbers, the cucumber seeds and skins into a blender, add the drained coconut, green chillies, garlic, coriander, black peppercorns and sesame seeds, then blitz smooth.
Put the yoghurt in a medium bowl, and whisk until smooth, then beat in enough water, if need be, to get it to a pouring consistency. Add salt to taste, stir in the cucumber paste and remaining chopped cucumber, then pour into a serving bowl and put in the fridge to chill.
When you’re ready to eat, make the temper. Put the oil in a small frying pan on a high heat, add the curry leaves and, after about 30 seconds, when they’re sizzling, stir in the fenugreek (if using), mustard seeds, cumin seeds and red chillies – stand well back, because the spices will probably splutter. Pour the hot temper, oil and all, over the cucumber yoghurt curry and serve with plain boiled white rice.
- 
  Cynthia Shanmugalingam is chef/proprietor of Rambutan, London SE1

Autism and ADHD care complaints more than triple in five years in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:34 UTC
14:00:34 KST

Complaints about autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder services in England have more than tripled in five years, official figures show, with the NHS ombudsman warning of years-long waits and patients paying thousands of pounds for private care.
One woman was removed from an ADHD medication waiting list without warning after almost four years, leaving her without the support she needed for about six months. Another patient was given an autism assessment lasting just 50 minutes that failed to follow guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, while a man referred to an ADHD service that was not yet operational ended up paying almost £4,000 for private treatment.
Complaints rose from 410 in 2021-22 to 1,257 in 2025-26, an increase of more than 200%, as referrals and the number of people waiting for assessment, treatment and support also increased.
Demand for ADHD and autism assessment and support services has surged dramatically across England, with open NHS referrals reaching roughly 562,000. More than 60% of adults and children face waiting lists exceeding a year, while prescribing data shows historic multi-year increases.
The parliamentary and health service ombudsman, Paula Sussex, said ADHD and autism services were “under significant pressure, with demand outstripping capacity”, adding: “While commissioning cannot solve these supply constraints, the way services are designed, commissioned and delivered can compound the pressure people experience and make it harder to make the best use of available resources.”
She said: “Right now, the system is too complex and inconsistent, leaving too many patients falling through the gaps.”
A report, called Improving ADHD and Autism Services: Commissioning With Confidence, shares the ombudsman’s findings based on 3,000 complaints. It found recurring issues, including uncertainty around patients’ right to choose a provider. Under right to choose, patients in England can choose from eligible NHS-funded providers for certain services, including some independent providers. However, the ombudsman found uncertainty around how this right applied, with patients sometimes being told wrongly that they could not exercise it.
Other problems included inconsistent recognition of diagnoses across NHS and independent providers, and lengthy waits for assessment and treatment.
In one case, Rich, 48, asked to be referred to Psychiatry UK for his ADHD treatment. NHS South East London integrated care board denied Rich’s request and wrongly insisted he be referred to a local ADHD service, which was still being developed and had no opening date. The ombudsman found his NHS treatment was delayed by five months. Rich felt he had no choice but to pay for private care, amounting to almost £4,000.
In another investigation, South London and Maudsley NHS foundation trust removed a woman from the ADHD medication titration (the process of adjusting medication to find the right balance) waiting list without warning or valid reason, leaving her without specialist monitoring support for about six months. This delay may have affected her symptoms and her ability to carry out everyday activities, causing frustration and distress.
Sussex said: “People should not have to fight their way through a confusing system to get ADHD and autism care.”
The ombudsman’s office itself has a six-month waiting time because of the rise in complaints it is receiving.
A government spokesperson said: “Last December, we asked clinical psychologist Professor Peter Fonagy to lead an independent review, examining the prevalence of - and support for - ADHD, autism, and mental health conditions. Professor Fonagy’s final report will be published later this summer, and will inform our new national approach in this area.”

National lottery faces questions over new boss’s record in gambling industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:34 UTC
14:00:34 KST

The national lottery is facing questions over its new boss’s record in the gambling industry, including a lucrative role in the 24-hour slot machine sector singled out by the prime minister as a blight on British high streets.
Allwyn UK, which holds a licence to run the Lottery until 2034, said last week that it had appointed William Hill’s former UK and Ireland boss Phil Walker as its interim chief executive, replacing Andria Vidler.
While Walker may not get the job on a permanent basis, MPs have written to the Gambling Commission, the industry regulator, about his selection as a steward of the UK’s most high-profile gambling brand, given the lottery’s “unique position” in public life.
In a letter seen by the Guardian, Labour’s Dawn Butler and Conservative MP Iain Duncan Smith told the regulator they were “deeply concerned” by the appointment.
They cited a personal sanction the regulator imposed on Walker in 2024 over “widespread and alarming” failures to enforce money laundering and terrorist financing controls at William Hill, which was fined a record £19.2m the previous year.
They also raised concerns about a boardroom role he holds with Game Nation, the UK’s third-largest chain of adult gaming centres (AGCs).
AGCs are high street gambling venues that are often referred to as “slot farms” due to their high concentration of slot machines, and are open 24 hours a day in most cases.
Last year, upon taking a job with City Gaming Ltd, which owns Game Nation, Walker said he was excited to “develop and grow [the company] over the coming years”.
That view appears to put the industry veteran at odds with the government, just as he prepares to take the reins of the lottery, frequently described as the UK’s largest public sector contract, worth £6.5bn in revenue over 10 years.
While still mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham hit out at AGCs, accusing the sector of “targeting some of the most vulnerable in our communities”.
This month, he announced plans to tighten up the permissive licensing regime that has allowed the sector to achieve the growth Walker has previously advocated for.
Butler, who was instrumental in Burnham’s decision to crack down on AGCs, has written to the Gambling Commission raising concerns about the appointment.
In a letter co-signed by Duncan Smith she said the pair were seeking clarity on whether Walker’s work for City Gaming was “compatible” with the decision to select him to run the lottery.
With regard to his tenure at William Hill, they asked the regulator to “explain what consideration, if any, was given to this history when assessing his suitability for his present position”.
A Gambling Commission spokesperson said: “We would not publicly comment on an operator’s personnel decisions.”
Jackie Olden, a campaigner whose terminally ill mother lost thousands of pounds to Merkur, the AGC sector’s second-largest company, also questioned Walker’s suitability to run the lottery, played by about 20 million people on a regular basis.
“It’s awful that someone heavily involved with 24-hour slot farms that destroy families and communities can run the country’s biggest public sector contract,” she said.
Companies House filings indicate that Walker is likely to have earned more than £50,000 from his non-executive directorship with Game Nation, a role that typically requires attendance at a small number of board meetings each year.
On Tuesday, Game Nation said that Walker would “step back” from his role with the company, with effect from 1 September, for the duration of his interim contract with the national lottery.
A spokesperson for Allwyn said: “As we navigate an increasingly competitive environment, Phil Walker brings valuable operational, digital and marketing experience alongside a significant understanding of our operating landscape.
“His appointment will help deliver the next stage of growth and innovation of the national lottery, and we look forward to welcoming Phil to the role of interim CEO.”
Allwyn, which is ultimately owned by the Czech billionaire Karel Komárek, has previously highlighted that Walker did not lose his personal licence from the Gambling Commission over the sanction imposed while at William Hill, indicating that the regulator believes him fit and proper to run a business in the sector.
The national lottery is regulated separately from the rest of the gambling sector. It is run under a 10-year licence from the Gambling Commission and mandated to donate billions of pounds to good causes.
By contrast, City Gaming is owned by investors in a “tactical value” fund, run by the Wall Street bank Morgan Stanley.
Last year, an employment tribunal judge heard a case of unfair dismissal brought by a former employee of its Game Nation chain.
According to a witness statement submitted during the case, a customer who disliked the staff member once paid a homeless man to defecate on the floor of the shop toilet, so that she was forced to clear it up.
Game Nation was ordered to pay the staff member £6,598.44, albeit for a technicality related to its dismissal procedure rather than the incident. Based on its £32m revenues last year, the company made the money back in less than two hours.
The Guardian has approached the government for comment.

Is the Trump Treasury panicking over the level of US debt?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:34 UTC
14:00:34 KST

Are we seeing the first signs of panic in Donald Trump’s Treasury? The US is by far the world’s biggest debtor, and the steady rise in global long-term interest rates – which I have long argued was inevitable – is starting to cause real pain.
Until now, the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has dismissed concerns about US debt, which recently surpassed $40tn, as a big nothingburger. Growth, in his telling, will be so spectacular the US will easily be able to meet its interest obligations without any significant tax rises or spending cuts, while the rest of the world will happily keep feeding it money. But if Bessent really believes that, why is he trying to strong-arm the bond market by fiddling with the maturity structure of government debt?
The obvious first move, and the one the markets are looking for, is to address the underlying problem by reining in America’s massive federal deficit, which is now running at roughly 6% of GDP. Bessent has repeatedly assured markets that the Trump administration’s voracious borrowing is temporary, and that AI-led growth will generate an abundance of tax revenues that will soon bring the deficit down to a somewhat more manageable 3% of GDP.
That could happen, but there are many reasons to think that pain-free budget consolidation is wishful thinking, not least because AI profits are likely to prove much harder to tax than labour income. In the near term, the costs of supporting an ageing population, paying for what appears to be an inevitable surge in military spending and caving to intense populist pressure for more public spending will probably rise at least as fast as revenues.
Making matters worse, the premium on long-term US treasuries – a major part of the dollar’s “exorbitant privilege” as the global reserve currency – has largely evaporated. US debt no longer trades as a special safe asset relative to that of other advanced economies. The value of dollar dominance is thus fading even under the best of circumstances. And if budget pressures eventually trigger a crisis, the result could be a rapid loss of the dollar’s global market share that might otherwise take decades.
What, then, should the US Treasury do? The textbook answer, as Bessent well knows, is to take steps toward major budget consolidation, and not the blundering, heavy-handed random cuts that Elon Musk and his Doge acolytes pursued in 2025. Bessent’s problem is that his boss, Trump, understands that American taxpayers are not prepared for any kind of genuine austerity.
That is why Bessent’s turn toward bond buyback gimmicks is worrying. In effect, Bessent is promising to take long-term debt out of the system and replace it with short-term debt, much as the Federal Reserve does when it engages in quantitative easing. Such an approach can make sense in a panic, when there is a good chance long-term rates will come back down, but there is little evidence that the market is the one panicking right now.
In fact, global long-term real interest rates are rising everywhere, suggesting that US exceptionalism no longer applies, at least not to the same degree. Bessent has argued for some time that long-term rates are too high, favouring short-term borrowing as a way to wait out the spike that he believes will soon subside.
He may be right. Plenty of prominent economists, particularly those who have long insisted that interest rates would remain ultra-low for ever, still cling to the view that today’s elevated rates are an aberration. Unfortunately, studies based on historical data suggest that the recent increase is better thought of as a normalisation and that over the long term rates are more likely to rise than to fall.
With the national debt now exceeding $40tn, this is not the time to tell investors that there is “nothing magic” about that number. Taken with the growing fiscal deficit, higher long-term interest rates and mounting spending pressures, America’s debt burden is a very real concern.
More troubling still, Bessent’s ham-fisted attempt to control the bond market undermines his hard-earned credibility as the safest pair of hands on the Trump 2.0 economic team. Until now, Bessent has managed to steer Trump away from some – albeit not all – of his most damaging impulses, whether on tariffs or the appointment of the Fed chair. Of course, he has to toe the line on hot-button issues near and dear to Trump’s heart, insisting that the US has in effect defeated Iran and that nothing will benefit working Americans more than upending the international trade order. Otherwise, he would be fired immediately. But bond markets are not so easily pushed around.
Bessent, the former bond trader and hedge fund manager, scored a major win when he supported the Argentinian peso last autumn, and he probably did not do too much damage by unexpectedly backing the Japanese yen over the summer, even if the effects faded fairly quickly. By contrast, his attempt at a Treasury-led quantitative easing has done little to stem the rise in long-term yields. Given that there is not going to be any meaningful debt reduction before November’s midterm elections, bond markets have good reason to remain deeply sceptical of America’s fiscal trajectory.
Kenneth Rogoff is a professor of economics and public policy at Harvard University. He was the IMF’s chief economist from 2001 to 2003.

Europe’s gas prices are surging. Who will be the first to pay more?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

Europe could face its toughest winter gas season since 2022 as wholesale prices trade near their highest level in more than three years. Household bills could rise quickly in the Netherlands while taking nearly a year to fully adjust in Germany and Austria.
Gas and electricity bills could increase in Europe this winter if wholesale prices remain elevated long enough to feed through to consumers.
The benchmark European wholesale natural gas price, the Dutch front-month TTF, was trading at over €66 per megawatt-hour (MWh) later on Tuesday, down from above €68 earlier in the session. This compares with around €29/MWh at the beginning of the year.
The rally has been fuelled by growing investor concerns that the Strait of Hormuz could remain closed into the winter.
This comes at a time when the EU’s gas-storage levels remain historically low ahead of the heating season.
EU gas storage was 62.99% full at the end of the gas day on 24 August, according to data from Gas Infrastructure Europe.
“Europe's gas stores are unusually low for the time of year,“ Natasha Fielding, editorial manager for gas, LNG, coal and biomass at Argus Media, told Euronews Business. She added that this level was far below the five-year average of 79%.
“The only other time in the last 15 years that stocks were close to as low was in 2021, ahead of the last major gas crisis,” Fielding said.
Among the larger European markets with the lowest storage levels, Germany’s stores were only 51% full, while those in the Netherlands stood at 44.3%.
Oxford Economics pointed out in a report published on 13 August — before the latest icrease in gas prices — that EU gas consumption is around 15%-20% lower than in 2021.
It said the EU can operate with lower storage levels, although that would mean relying on more winter LNG imports. And that could leave the EU more exposed to competition with Asian buyers for available cargoes.
The competition is already intensified due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting a route that normally carries almost one-fifth of global LNG trade.
In a potential EU-Asia bidding war, wholesale prices could climb further.
At current levels, prices "will not be enough for Europe to manage storage through winter," Goldman Sachs analysts Samantha Dart and Laura Cyr wrote in a note cited by Bloomberg.
"In a scenario where Middle East energy exports normalise only gradually through 2027, we estimate that December 2026 TTF would likely need to move above €100/MWh," they said. That is 110% above Goldman’s €50/MWh base case, they added.
Oxford Economics said the EU might be forced to suspend parts of its ban on Russian gas imports if supplies tightened further. According to the latest European Commission calculation, Russia’s share of combined pipeline and LNG imports was around 12.5% in 2025.
In January 2026, the Council of the EU adopted a regulation to prohibit both LNG and pipeline gas imports from Russia beginning 18 March 2026, with transition periods for existing contracts. By the end of 2027, all Russian gas imports are due to be prohibited.
How quickly could household bills follow?
A brief price spike may have a limited effect, but a prolonged rally would gradually feed into new and renewed household contracts.
A jump in wholesale prices does not immediately push retail prices up. The headline TTF price can rise much faster than the EU’s effective import price, which reflects what importers actually pay after existing contracts and hedging arrangements are taken into account.
However, as suppliers’ contracts expire and they buy or hedge more gas at the new, higher market price, the effective import price gradually moves closer to the wholesale price.
Those higher costs may then be passed on to households when tariffs are revised or contracts renewed.
According to Fielding, the extent to which energy bills rise will depend on how long the price rally lasts and whether prices climb further in the coming months. Across the EU, "households on variable gas tariffs would be among the first to feel the effects of higher wholesale prices," she said, adding that the pass-through from gas to electricity bills is typically weaker.
"Countries with more liberalised retail markets tend to experience a more rapid pass-through," Fielding said.
According to Oxford Economics, it takes an average of about six months for changes in wholesale prices to be fully reflected in consumer prices. However, the timing varies widely between countries.
“The prevailing market structure — with 12- or even 24-month fixed-price contracts dominating — means that it takes nearly a year for peak pass-through in markets such as Germany and Austria,” the report said.
Consumer gas prices may respond within a few months in countries like France, Italy and Spain. In some markets, like the Netherlands, pass-through is almost immediate.
Oxford Economics named Italy as the most exposed country to a gas price shock among the large European economies, due to the “interplay of a relatively fast pass-through and a considerably above-average reliance on gas.”
However, the country currently has one of the highest gas-storage levels, according to data from Gas Infrastructure Europe.
Much depends on how cold the winter is.
Oxford Economics said, “The backbone of the EU’s space heating remains gas; hence, the EU’s gas prices remain hostage to outside temperatures in the coming winter.” The consultancy added that a sustained cold spell this winter would push up demand for heating and gas.
In their report predating the latest natural gas price spike, Oxford Economics said eurozone consumer energy prices — including gas, electricity and other household energy costs — could be as much as 15% higher year on year in the fourth quarter.

US consumer confidence hits seven-month low on worse outlook
US consumer confidence fell in August to the lowest level since the start of 2026 on a deteriorating outlook for business conditions and the labour market.
The Conference Board’s gauge of confidence decreased 0.8 points to 89.4 after a downwards revision to the prior month, data released on Aug 25 showed. A measure of expectations for the next six months fell to the lowest level since January, even as an indicator of present conditions rose to a four-month high.
The report suggests high petrol prices and broader cost-of-living pressures alongside a slowdown in hiring continued to weigh on American households in August. Recent data showed US retail sales fell in July by the most in more than a year as consumers pulled back after strong growth in the first half of 2026.
The survey period for the report was Aug 3 to Aug 16, a span that saw average pump prices hover above US$4 a gallon as renewed hostilities in the US-Iran conflict sent oil prices higher. The US on Aug 24 announced plans to increase economic pressure on Tehran, a move that could keep fuel costs elevated if supply concerns persist.
The Conference Board survey showed that perceptions of the current state of the job market improved in August. The share of consumers who said jobs were plentiful rose, while the share saying jobs were hard to get fell. The difference between the two – a metric closely followed by economists – matched the widest reading in 2026.
Looking ahead, however, consumers were more negative about future job and income prospects. They also were less optimistic about future business conditions, though the share of respondents saying they intend to take a vacation within the next six months rose to the highest level since January.
“Anticipated spending on services pared back in August after a pop in most discretionary activities last month, as lower gas prices and the summer’s World Cup likely boosted consumer’s desire to spend in July,” the report said. “Despite this, consumers still planned to spend more overall on services over the next six months.”
A separate measure of consumer sentiment by the University of Michigan fell in August for the first time in three months as households worried about worsening business conditions and rising inflation.
The Commerce Department will release July consumer spending, income and inflation data on Aug 26. Economists expect the report to show inflation-adjusted spending stalled in July. BLOOMBERG

Deputy FM sheds light on Iran-Oman deal on Strait of Hormuz

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:48:09 UTC
13:48:09 KST

Kazem Gharibabadi, deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, told state television that Iran remains in a state of war. He said the strait had become a matter of Iran's national security and that basic changes in entry and exit routes were required.
He said that for the past 58 years ships had passed through Omani waters, causing severe damage to Iran. Under the new temporary arrangement, the entry lane into the Persian Gulf will run through Iranian waters, while the exit lane will pass through Omani territorial waters. In both directions, ships will transit through Iranian waters. The corridor will function like a two-way highway with a total width of about seven miles, he said.
Gharibabadi said the route was temporary, and that Iran and Oman must negotiate a permanent new route within 30 to 60 days to replace the previous maritime traffic scheme.
"From a military standpoint, the Strait of Hormuz is closed," he said. Under the understanding, no military vessels will be allowed to pass, and only commercial ships will be permitted to transit.
He dismissed claims by Donald Trump about demining the strait, saying no one but Iran knows the location of mines in the waterway. "If that claim were true, why is no vessel passing through the strait?" he asked.
Gharibabadi said the negotiations with Oman took place through a joint working group that included the foreign ministry, the ports and maritime organisation, the IRGC and its navy force, and the General Staff of the Armed Forces. He said the armed forces had presented the maps and all sides had consensus on them.
On possible talks with the United States, he said conditions had changed, and that any future negotiations would not be like the past. He also said Iran could carry out preemptive actions to defend its national security. "Why must we always wait for America to attack us so that we defend ourselves? If we do not see conditions as appropriate, why should we not take actions against American interests? These are now within the framework of the Islamic Republic's policy," he said.
Regarding Pakistan's army chief, who visited Tehran this week, Gharibabadi said, "We told him we do not trust America. It was not the Islamic Republic of Iran that violated the Islamabad MoU. America has not been honest in talks and has proven it does not abide by its commitments. If the Americans want nothing to happen in the Strait of Hormuz and want action toward its reopening, they must implement Iran's conditions in the agreement."

Finns turning to ad-supported streaming to curb costs
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
07:45:15 EEST
13:45:15 KST

After a booming period of ever-increasing media streaming subscribers during the Covid pandemic, the companies behind those services have been forced to rethink their strategies.
Now, lower-priced ad-supported subscriptions have emerged as the industry's answer to lagging growth.
The shift towards so-called hybrid subscriptions — cheaper packages that include advertising breaks — marks a big departure from the ad-free model that drove the sector's initial expansion.
"For a long time the market was driven by pure subscription revenue where consumers paid to avoid adverts. Now advertisements are being integrated again," said Fredrik Liljeqvist, a media analyst at Mediavision in Stockholm told Yle.
He said that subscribers who opt for the ad breaks can substantially reduce their subscription costs.
Costs and strategies
"If you watch movies and TV series, and choose a subscription without a sports package, it gets between 30 and 50 percent cheaper if you allow the adverts," he explained.
Households in Finland have embraced the cheaper options more readily than their Nordic counterparts, replacing older, more expensive ad-free subscriptions with the new partially ad-funded alternatives.
The market share of so-called hybrid subscriptions in Finland rose from 15 percent last year to 21 percent this year. Streaming giant Netflix is set to launch advertising subsidised versions in Denmark, Norway and Sweden during 2027, and according to Mediavision, it is only a matter of time before that happens in Finland as well.
Alongside the introduction of hybrid subscriptions, streaming services have intensified efforts to prevent users from sharing accounts, using stricter controls on IP addresses and geolocation.
"It is easier to convert a user who is not paying, but who gets a subscription shared with them, than to find a completely new customer," Liljeqvist said.
€62 per month
Finnish households spend an average of 62 euros per month on digital media — including video, text, audio and video games. That's significantly less than elsewhere in the Nordic region. In Sweden, the sum has grown rapidly in recent years and now the average stands at 87 euros.
Price comparisons reveal stark differences for identical products across borders. Viaplay's ad-free monthly sports package costs approximately 65 euros in Sweden but just 46 euros in Finland, despite broadly similar content.
Those price differences are deliberate, and reflect the streamers' assessments of what consumers across various markets will pay, according to Liljeqvist.
"It is about willingness to pay. That differs greatly between Finland and the rest of the Nordic region," he said.
On average, consumers in Finland spend around half of their media euros on video services, around 20 percent on text-based content, 20 percent on audio and about 10 percent on video gaming.
Finland's free-to-air tradition
In Finland, only about 50 percent of consumers' media spending goes towards TV and video content, compared with nearly 60 percent in Denmark, Norway and Sweden.
"Finland has historically had a very broad free offering in traditional TV. Not only public service, but also large commercial TV channels. Therefore Finns do not want to pay for large TV packages in the same way," Liljeqvist explained.
He noted that in other Nordic countries, viewers need a paid subscription to access the number of free channels that Finns take for granted.
According to Mediavision, content from public broadcaster Yle accounts for 26 percent of total viewing time in Finland. At the same time, Sweden's public broadcaster SVT has 16 percent of the Swedish market.
However, Liljeqvist noted that the smaller paid market in Finland was primarily due to traditional television's broad free content offerings, rather than solely Yle's market dominance.
This article is based on this article by Svenska Yle, the public broadcaster's Swedish-language news unit.

Central American countries declare a state of emergency over severe drought
Kyiv • UNN
Panama has become the third Central American country to introduce emergency measures due to the drought caused by El Niño. Water shortages have already reduced the number of vessels passing through the Panama Canal.
On Tuesday, Panama declared a state of emergency due to severe drought caused by the El Niño phenomenon. It has become the third Central American country, after Honduras and El Salvador, to introduce emergency measures because of a lack of rainfall. LRT reports, according to UNN.
Details
Panama’s Minister of the Interior, Dinoska Montalvo, said the decision would allow the authorities to better prepare for the consequences of the drought, which is already destroying crops and posing risks to food security.
Due to falling water levels, the Panama Canal has been forced to reduce the number of vessels that can pass through it. This creates additional problems for one of the world’s key trade routes.
The situation in other countries
In El Salvador, the authorities declared the highest, red alert level because of meteorological and agricultural drought. The country is intensifying monitoring of the situation and preparing food aid for rural families that lack irrigation systems.
Honduras has also reported a serious threat to a significant part of its territory. The Central American Dry Corridor, which encompasses parts of Honduras, El Salvador, and Nicaragua, has been particularly affected.

The situation is being worsened by abnormal heat. Record temperatures were recorded in all three countries in June and July, while in August alone, 14 temperature records were broken in El Salvador.
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon during which the surface water in the central and eastern parts of the equatorial Pacific Ocean warms. It changes precipitation and wind patterns and can cause extreme weather in various regions of the world.

A $1.4 billion question: The case for a new tax on Australians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:42:12 UTC
13:42:12 KST

In brief
- Sugar-sweetened drink consumption could fall 24 per cent if a sugar tax is introduced, new research has found.
- The tax could raise revenue for health services and dental care initiatives.
A 20 per cent tax on sugary drinks could prevent millions of tooth cavities and add hundreds of thousands of years to Australians' lives collectively, according to new research,
A Griffith University study published in BMJ Public Health on Wednesday found a levy applied to non-alcoholic drinks with added sugar, such as soft drinks and most juices, could prevent 3.7 million cases of tooth decay, 191,000 cases of gum disease, and 115,000 cases of complete tooth loss across Australia over the next 25 years.
The study suggested that tax revenue could be used to strengthen health services and to implement a universal health care approach to dental care, but co-author Lennert Veerman said the benefits would extend beyond oral health.
"The study also estimates a 20 per cent sugar tax would generate approximately half a million health-adjusted life years for the 2019 Australian population over their lifetime, both from dental health improvements and reductions in weight-related illness," the Griffith University public health professor said.
As of 2017–2018, approximately 9.1 per cent of Australians adults reported drinking sugar-sweetened beverages every day, while nearly one-third of Australians aged 15 and older had untreated tooth decay or cavities, according to the study.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Using a computer-based simulation, researchers found that for every 1 per cent increase in the price of sugar-sweetened drinks, consumption was expected to drop by 1.2 per cent.
Assuming a 20 per cent tax is passed on in full to consumers, the study predicted the price increase would result in a 24 per cent reduction in consumption.
Marco Peres from SingHealth Duke-NUS in Singapore said the findings highlighted the oral health benefits of sugar taxes.
"Importantly, a sugar tax is a population-level measure," he said.
"It does not rely solely on individuals changing their behaviour but helps create an environment in which healthier choices become easier.
"This is particularly important if we want prevention strategies to reach the whole population and reduce health inequalities."
United Kingdom tax reduced sugar content
Oral diseases are a growing public health concern, affecting approximately 3.5 billion people globally.
The study found that oral diseases contributed to 2.4 per cent of Australia’s total health burden — the impact of a health problem on a population — and ranked among the top 10 diseases.
According to the World Health Organization, 116 countries have an excise tax on at least one type of sugar-sweetened beverage. The study notes there is a high level of support among the Australian public for policies that reduce sugar intake.
In 2018, the United Kingdom introduced a tax of 19.4 or 25.9 pence per litre, depending on the sugar content of beverages.
It led to a 46 per cent reduction in the sugar contained in soft drinks, the UK government said, with nearly 90 per cent of the market now containing sugar below the level at which the tax applies.
A 2024 parliamentary inquiry into Australia's diabetes epidemic recommended Australia introduce a 20 per cent tax on sugar-sweetened drinks.
The Parliamentary Budget Office estimated that, after allowing for collection costs and a drop in GST revenue, such a tax would raise nearly $1.4 billion in the following two financial years.
At the time, the Australian Medical Association said it was "100 per cent behind" the tax.
"Our modelling shows we can prevent thousands of cases of diabetes if we act," the association's president Steve Robson said.
In 2024, the Australian Beverages Council — the peak body for the non-alcoholic drinks industry in the country — rejected calls for a sugar tax, claiming it was a "misguided measure that misses the mark and will only hit hardest those households that can least afford it".
While critics argue a sugar tax would disproportionately affect lower-income households, a 2017 Deakin University study found those households stood to gain the greatest health benefits.

Asia-Pacific Community: Chinese-built wastewater plant revives Mongolian capital's green lifeline
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
12:40:52 CST
13:40:52 KST

ULAN BATOR, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Ulan Bator's Tuul River, long choked by untreated sewage and plagued by acrid odors, has seen a remarkable environmental turnaround thanks to a landmark Chinese-Mongolian wastewater treatment facility, with local staff like Urnaa devoting years to preparing for its full handover to local operators.
Urnaa works as the chief translator at the Ulan Bator central sewage treatment plant, the nation's largest and most advanced sewage plant that began construction in early 2019 and was inaugurated on June 15 this year.
Every working day, she shuttles across the sprawling facility's workshops, providing real-time interpretation for Mongolian technical teams and compiling operation and maintenance manuals to smooth the handover process to the local team. Over the past year, she has watched how the plant, built entirely to Chinese standards and using Chinese technology by China Railway No. 4 Engineering Group Co., Ltd., has evolved from early construction to full operation.
Standing on the rooftop on the fourth floor of the plant's comprehensive service building, eight massive secondary sedimentation tanks stretch outward like polished mirrors, their clear treated water reflecting Mongolia's boundless blue skies and white clouds.
Covering a total area of 178,000 square meters with 55 standalone buildings, the plant boasts a daily treatment capacity of 250,000 cubic meters. It can process nearly all residential and industrial wastewater produced in Ulan Bator, serving roughly half of Mongolia's entire population.
Two side-by-side display boards in the facility's lobby lay bare the capital's decades-long sewage crisis, drawing a stark contrast between this modern, recycling-focused new plant and its outdated predecessor.
Constructed back in the 1960s and expanded three times over the years, the aging plant only handled 160,000 to 170,000 cubic meters of wastewater each day. As the capital's population exploded, sewage output surged, triggering equipment malfunctions.
For years, vast volumes of inadequately treated wastewater were discharged directly into the Tuul, Ulan Bator's mother river -- a foul reality Urnaa remembers all too clearly from her early career. Ten years ago, while working on a Mongolian disabled children's rehabilitation project run by the same Chinese contractor, the stench from the polluted river lingered constantly around the work compound. Today, stable operation of the new treatment plant has delivered visible improvements to surrounding air quality and the river's water clarity.
Lyu Haiyun, project manager from China Railway No. 4 Engineering Group Co., Ltd, noted that the plant's value stretches far beyond simply producing clean discharged water, as it delivers a complete low-carbon circular development concept tailored for Mongolia. Its integrated design unifies wastewater treatment, clean energy production and resource recycling.
Design teams took full account of Mongolia's sludge, which contains high organic matter, installing four large medium-temperature anaerobic reactors on-site to ferment sludge into biogas for power and heating. Once fully operational, the biogas system will meet 25 to 30 percent of the plant's electricity and heating demands, slashing long-term operating expenses.
Beyond filling Mongolia's critical domestic sewage treatment technology gap, the project prioritizes cultivating independent local operational capacity through systematic training. Starting in 2023, around 70 Mongolian operation and maintenance technicians have traveled to China for specialized training courses. In July, Urnaa accompanied local regulatory officials to Beijing to attend training sessions on biogas power generation.
"Many Mongolian engineers have learned so much through this project," Urnaa said. "For me personally, all the training and on-site practice have given me full confidence to work for similar infrastructure projects in the future." ■

Median hourly earnings from wages and salaries rose 2.7 percent to 35.96 NZ dollars (about 21.43 U.S. dollars) in the year to June 2026, the department said, adding that for men, median hourly earnings increased 3.6 percent to 36.92 NZ dollars, while those for women rose 3.4 percent to 34.95 NZ dollars.

UK concerned about possible changes to backpacker visa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:39:32 UTC
13:39:32 KST

PM rules out British backpackers being forced to work in regions
In short:
The government was considering imposing regional work requirements on British backpackers to make the scheme less attractive in a bid to bring down migration numbers.
The prime minister has publicly poured cold water on that idea, heading off a diplomatic stoush.
What's next?
No date has been set for the government to unveil its changes in migration policy after Tony Burke postponed a National Press Club address earlier this month.
The prime minister has vowed not to make British backpackers work in regional areas as part of a looming migration overhaul, defusing a potential diplomatic stoush with the United Kingdom.
British citizens on Working Holiday Maker, or backpacker, visas are allowed to live in Australia for up to three years without any specific work requirements under a free trade deal which came into force in 2023.
Working holiday makers from all other countries must work in regional or remote areas to have their visas extended beyond a year.
The favourable treatment has led to a steep increase in the number of UK backpackers coming to Australia, up from 47,238 in 2023/24 to 79,412 in 2024/25 according to Home Affairs data.
Under pressure to clamp down on temporary visas and reduce overseas arrivals, the government was considering a plan to impose regional work requirements on British backpackers to make the scheme less attractive.
But some in the government were concerned that would clearly breach the free trade agreement between Australia and the United Kingdom at a time when the government had positioned itself as an international champion for trade rules.
Anthony Albanese quashed the proposal on Wednesday afternoon, ruling out any changes to the deal.
"The UK situation is a separate agreement as a result of the UK free trade agreement which we are certainly honouring," Mr Albanese said.
He intervened not long after UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke on the sidelines of a Five Eyes meeting in Sydney.
After that meeting, Mr Burke did not deny the issue had been canvassed.
"We talk regularly about all migration issues, about the issues we are managing in each of our countries," Mr Burke told reporters in Sydney.
"In terms of anything coming forward, as to any changes we'd made to the migration program, those are decisions that would be made by the Australian cabinet."
The possible change to UK arrangements was one of several under consideration as part of a wider crackdown on immigration which Mr Burke was due to announce three weeks ago before being forced to postpone.
No new date has been set for the policy announcement, which is designed to ensure Labor meets its own target of cutting net overseas migration (NOM) from the current 300,000 to 225,000 by 2028.
Backpackers are a significant contributor to the NOM with a record 321,116 visas being issued last year, up from 234,556 the year before.
Mr Burke last month paused the processing of applications from 24 countries including Argentina, Chile, Spain, Poland, Thailand and Malaysia, and pushed workers applying for overseas skilled visas to the back of the queue.
"The processing of backpacker visas across the entire program is happening more slowly than it was," Mr Burke said.
"And similarly there are changes we've made to the permanent program in preferencing, at the moment, onshore positions rather than offshore."
The far-reaching directive is designed to stop, or dramatically slow, the number of overseas arrivals but has created an enormous amount of confusion and concern within the business, hospitality and tourism sectors which rely on migrant workers.
As one business figure told the ABC, "everything has ground to a halt".
One Nation and the Coalition are promising dramatic cuts to migration, but both have ruled out any cuts to backpacker visas given their popularity in regional areas.

Lok Sabha Speaker seeks response from 20 rebel TMC MPs on disqualification petitions
Edited by: Karan Manral / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 26, 2026, 12:52 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Rebel TMC MPs with Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla in June
NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla has issued notices to 20 rebel Trinamool Congress (TMC) MPs who are now affiliated with the little-known Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI), seeking their responses within seven days to disqualification petitions filed by the TMC.The disqualification petitions are currently pending before Birla.This comes after Solicitor General of India Tushar Mehta on Tuesday informed the Supreme Court that the Speaker had already issued notices to the 20 MPs on the disqualification petitions filed by the TMC under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution.
Mehta made the submission before a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant while appearing for the Lok Sabha Speaker and the Secretary General of the House. The bench was hearing a plea filed by senior TMC leader Abhishek Banerjee, challenging the delay in deciding the petitions seeking the disqualification of the rebels.Responding to the submission, the bench said, "It is not a question of issuing notices, it is a question of concluding the proceedings within a time frame."During the hearing, the bench indicated that it was inclined to issue notices to the respondents on Abhishek Banerjee’s writ petition.
Mehta, however, submitted that there was no need to issue notices to the Speaker or his office, stating that he would appear on behalf of Birla.The TMC has accused the 20 MPs of “abandoning” the party and subsequently joining the NCPI. Abhishek Banerjee has contended that their conduct attracts disqualification under the anti-defection provisions of the Constitution.
The petition names the Lok Sabha Speaker and the Secretary General of the House as the principal respondents and also impleads the MPs whose disqualification is being sought.
Karan Manral is a journalist at the Times of India. He covers politics, social issues, and international affairs, exploring stories that affect people’s everyday lives. He also writes explainers to make these stories easier for readers to follow.

Unknown Publisher

WASHINGTON, August 26. /TASS/. So far this year, the US Department of State has channeled almost $40 million to purchase unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to combat crime in Ukraine, according to documents released on the US public procurement portal, seen by TASS.
In February, the Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement (INL) at the US Department of State allocated some $32 million to Ukraine’s Stream Techno for drone and UAV ground control station purchases under two contracts, the data showed. In August, the sum was raised to $39.9 million.
According to data released on the State Department’s data, the authority works with foreign governments, law enforcement agencies and the private sector to combat "narco-terrorism, drug trafficking, transnational organized crime, and other criminal threats at the source."
