One boat, more than 400 people and 25 years of consequences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
19:34:32 UTC
04:34:32 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
"We were terrified."
For Farid — a pseudonym used to protect his identity — those three words still carry him back 25 years, to a ship in the Indian Ocean, a teenage boy surrounded by hundreds of strangers, and the sudden arrival of Australian authorities after the vessel that had rescued him was prevented from reaching Christmas Island — an Australian territory.
He was 17. He had fled Afghanistan, leaving behind his single mother and siblings, and spent eight months moving from one boat to another in search of safety.
By the time the Norwegian freighter MV Tampa rescued him and 432 other asylum seekers — most of them Hazara Afghans — from a stricken fishing boat named the Palapa in August 2001, he had already endured storms, days at sea and the uncertainty of not knowing where the journey would end. At the time, Hazaras were fleeing Afghanistan, fearing persecution from the resurgent Taliban.
Then came another uncertainty.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We weren't clearly told where they were going to take us. When we first saw the authorities' ship, I thought they were going to take us to Australia," Farid tells SBS News.
Instead, he was taken to Naoero (formerly known as Nauru), where he would spend years caught up in Australia's newly established offshore processing system before eventually returning to Afghanistan.
"It was like a camp. We get our turns, about once a month, to go out for a few hours," he says.
"For the first year we didn't get to go out at all. We were not very hopeful. It was just tents at first, but then they set up portable rooms," Farid says.
Today, he is 42 and lives in Melbourne's south-east, where he works as a painter after completing trade courses and an apprenticeship. He was granted asylum in Australia in 2012.
The ordinary life Farid has built in Australia is a long way from the journey that brought him here, one that began when he was a teenager fleeing Afghanistan and led him into the centre of the 'Tampa crisis' and Australia's emerging offshore processing system.
Twenty-five years on, his experience offers a human window into the events surrounding the Tampa and the policy that followed, known as the Pacific Solution, as Australia continues to debate how it responds to people seeking protection.
When the Tampa answered the call
On 24 August 2001, the Palapa ran into trouble in rough seas about 140km north of Christmas Island, leaving those on board facing the prospect of sinking.
Two days later, on 26 August, Australia's Rescue Coordination Centre alerted ships in the area that the vessel was in distress, with the words "HELP" and "SOS" painted across its roof.
The closest vessel was MV Tampa, whose captain, Arne Rinnan, agreed to come to their aid. Guided by an Australian Coastwatch aircraft, the Tampa reached the stricken fishing boat and began taking those on board to safety.
For Farid, the rescue should have marked the end of a terrifying journey. Instead, it was followed by a confrontation that would reshape Australia's approach to asylum seekers arriving by boat.
Rinnan initially headed towards the ferry port of Merak, Indonesia, but several asylum seekers reportedly pressured him to take them to Australia instead. According to a subsequent Senate inquiry, some threatened to jump overboard or hurt themselves if they were taken to Indonesia.
Fearing for their safety, Rinnan changed course for Christmas Island.
Australian authorities refused permission for the vessel to enter Australian territorial waters and directed Rinnan to take those aboard to Indonesia.
As the standoff continued, Rinnan raised concerns about the deteriorating health of some passengers.
Australian authorities arranged for food, water, and medical assistance, but the deadlock continued.
On 29 August, Rinnan declared a state of emergency and sailed into Australian waters without permission, prompting the government to send 45 Special Air Service (SAS) troops to board the vessel.
Farid remembers the arrival of the authorities as another moment of fear.
"I was nervous and frightened because they [authorities] wore face coverings and had their fingers on the trigger."
It was like seeing something in the movies. We were confused because the captain explained to us that he was not permitted to enter into Australian waters.
Christmas Island caught in the middle
Gordon Thomson was a Christmas Island Shire councillor at the time and had direct contact with Rinnan during the standoff, including through fax.
On 28 August 2001, Thomson and other elected representatives issued a statement calling on the then-prime minister John Howard to allow the Tampa into the island's port.
"We applaud the captain and crew of the Tampa for their correct application of humanitarian principles and the law in taking onto their ship asylum seekers by offering safe refuge on Christmas Island," the statement read.
But a day later, as the government moved to prevent the Tampa from reaching the island, Thomson says the atmosphere on Christmas Island changed.
"The government brought in the SAS, armed boats and attack craft, effectively taking control of and, in many people's eyes, pirating the Tampa and forcing it back out to sea," he tells SBS News.
"They also closed the port, which meant local people couldn't go out on the water. No-one was allowed to get into a boat, despite fishing being a daily necessity for many people on Christmas Island."
"The government was determined that journalists couldn't get onto boats and reach the Tampa to tell their stories. There was a real clampdown on movement across the island," Thomson says.
With the standoff unresolved, the government turned to an alternative: those aboard would be taken elsewhere, where their claims for protection would be processed.
Life in Naoero
Hassan Ghulam was a community elder in Australia when nearly 300 asylum seekers were transferred to Naoero in September 2001.
Naoero is a tiny Pacific island nation about 3,000km north-east of Australia, and had a population of roughly 12,000 people at the time.
In the weeks after the Tampa crisis, Australia reached an agreement with the Naoero government to establish an offshore processing centre at Topside, in the island's remote interior. In return for hosting the asylum seekers, Naoero received financial and development assistance from Australia.
The centre was still being built when the first arrivals were sent there, with many initially housed in large tents while Australian personnel worked to establish the facility.
As more asylum seekers arrived, Topside quickly became crowded, with conditions marked by extreme heat, water shortages and limited electricity.
From Australia, people like Ghulam became crucial links to those inside, advising the Hazara refugees and gathering information about life inside the camp from journalists and detainees via satellite phone.
When they were taken on the boat [to Naoero], the conditions were terrible and many suffered from severe physical distress.
"What they endured throughout felt like it was a punishment to scare them into coming into Australia … it was [also] a message intended to the [people] smugglers," Ghulam says.
The now 75-year-old says smugglers charged large sums to put people on boats that were often poorly equipped and unseaworthy, with water sometimes flooding into the vessels as they crossed open seas.
"We Hazaras are mountain people, not sea people," he says.
"If you leave us on a mountainside, we can climb like goats. But in the sea, we are not fish — we would drown."
The first Naoero facility was established rapidly in the aftermath of the crisis, and accounts from the period describe difficult conditions, including shortages of water and other basic services. The island's remoteness also meant limited access to medical care and other support.
Ghulam says he made several attempts to reach Naoero, including one with an Australian documentary news crew hoping to record the conditions inside the detention centre, but they were stopped before they could even board the plane.
Letters from limbo
Instead, detainees began sending Ghulam letters from Naoero — some describing the harsh living conditions, others sharing their hopes for the future, and many reflecting on the pain of being separated from the people they loved.
The letters that made their way from Naoero painted a picture of lives suspended in uncertainty.
In one dated 27 October 2002, a detainee wrote of the ongoing water shortages: "Sometimes God helps us, rain is a great source of water, people come out of containers and take bath in the rain."
They also described the emotional toll of being separated from family: "Normally I do not like to think of my sisters because such feelings make me upset and weak and the circle of life becomes slower here."
SBS News has seen some of the letters, but has not independently verified them in their entirety.
Elaine Smith, an advocacy worker who worked closely on the Tampa affair in Australia at the time, also reviewed copies.
The letters also show some detainees trying to maintain hope despite their circumstances.
One wrote that he did not want to burden the person receiving his letters with his troubles, saying he wanted to "share" his joys.
He described starting a small mathematics class for fellow detainees, while teaching himself English grammar and fiction from the Naoero library.
He said those were among the few subjects available, unlike the mathematics and physics he wanted to study, and asked whether he could pursue further education by distance.
The politics of the Tampa
On 1 September 2001, Howard announced that Naoero and New Zealand had agreed to receive the Tampa passengers for refugee-status processing outside Australia. The arrangement became the foundation of what was later known as the Pacific Solution.
The Tampa's arrival came just weeks before Australia's federal election, which was shaping up around issues including border protection and asylum seekers.
Government figures showed boat arrivals had risen sharply in the years before the Tampa affair — from 921 in 1998-99 to 4,137 in 2000-01. The Howard government argued that Australia was being "targeted by organised people smugglers" because its "refugee determination outcomes were overly generous".
At the launch of his 2001 election campaign in Sydney, Howard famously delivered a line that would come to define his political legacy on border protection: "We will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come."
In a sit-down interview with SBS News 25 years later, he continues to defend his approach and says he reflects positively on his immigration policies.
We were ahead of our time … you couldn't maintain domestic support for strong immigration policies if you allow people to come willy-nilly to live in our country.
"What we adopted was a common sense approach. You cannot maintain local support for high immigration if people feel that the government no longer controls either the number of people or who they are."
Children overboard controversy
The Howard government's hardline approach to boat arrivals reshaped Australia's border policy, but also gave rise to some of the most controversial episodes of the 2001 campaign, including the "children overboard" affair.
The controversy centred on events surrounding SIEV 4, a vessel intercepted by the Australian Navy's HMAS Adelaide on 6 October 2001, about 100 nautical miles north of Christmas Island.
The following day, 7 October, a report emerged that asylum seekers had thrown children overboard as the Navy attempted to intercept the vessel. A subsequent Senate inquiry found no children had been thrown overboard from SIEV 4.
On 8 October, SIEV 4 started to sink while under tow, and photographs taken during the rescue were later presented as evidence associated with the alleged incident.
The inquiry found the photographs had been wrongly associated with the "children overboard" claim.
Howard has previously defended his handling of the affair, saying he relied on the advice he received at the time. In 2002, he told ABC Lateline he had never been told the original advice was wrong. Twenty years later, in an interview with the Guardian, he again defended the claims, saying: "It was the advice we had at the time."
But in his interview with SBS News 25 years on, Howard offers a somewhat different characterisation of the episode.
That was a mistake, that was a miscommunication.
"I don't think anybody is to be blamed for that," he says.
He says the reaction was understandable given the "enormous turmoil" and emotion of the time, before shifting focus to what he sees as the policy's longer-term outcome.
"All I can say is it's good we are not having accidents at sea now, like we used to have then."
The legacy of 'stopping the boats'
Howard's reference to "accidents at sea" points to the deadly period of boat arrivals that followed the Tampa affair.
In December 2010, 50 people died when SIEV 221, carrying asylum seekers, crashed into the rocky shoreline of Christmas Island in treacherous seas — a tragedy the WA coroner later described as the largest loss of life in an Australian maritime incident in peacetime in 115 years.
It was one of a series of boat journeys in the years that followed, with hundreds of asylum seekers dying at sea as boats attempted to reach Australia.
Since December 2013, the Australian government has reported no known deaths at sea from maritime people-smuggling ventures targeting Australia.
Howard views that outcome as evidence that Australia's approach was ultimately vindicated — and argues that other countries are now confronting similar challenges.
We were right and the rest of the world is adopting our approach.
Howard says the position he took during the 2001 election was criticised at the time, particularly by some Europeans who regarded it as insensitive. But, he argues, many of those same countries are now grappling with the challenges of irregular migration and border control.
"You can't have an open, tolerant, non-discriminatory immigration policy if it's open slather," he says.
"You can't. And we decided a long time ago. And the rest of the world is now adopting the approach we adopted then."
The challenges Howard describes remain evident across Europe. On 21 August, French police were filmed intercepting an inflatable boat as migrants attempted to cross the English Channel to Britain, part of an intensified effort to prevent small-boat departures.
At the end of July, thousands of people tried to cross from Morocco into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta, in a mass influx that resulted in dozens of deaths.
Asked how he would judge his own legacy on immigration and border protection, Howard declines to do so himself.
"That's for other people. I cannot be my own judge. Others will be my judge.
"I think we ran an immigration policy that most Australians support, one that still allows us to adopt a humanitarian approach."
The debate over 'stopping the boats'
Graham Thom, advocacy coordinator at the Refugee Council of Australia, acknowledges immigration is a complex issue, but disagrees offshore processing was responsible for 'stopping the boats'.
"One of the key myths that is very difficult to dispel is that somehow offshore processing stops the boats from arriving," he tells SBS News.
"There's this whole narrative around 'stopping the boats', when what we saw after Tampa was the Howard government starting to intercept boats and push them back," Thom says.
Tampa didn't stop the boats. People kept coming.
"Until we acknowledge that the Pacific Solution had nothing to do with stopping the boats, we're sort of trapped in a system that has bipartisan support for cruelty."
Thom says Australia should instead work with countries across the region, including Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, to ensure people have basic rights, access to work and study, and protection from detention or removal while longer-term solutions are found.
"[We] don't need to resettle everyone," he says.
"As long as there is hope that those most at risk can get to some sort of safety, then you remove the incentive for people to get on dangerous boat journeys."
When asked about critics who argue that the arrival of asylum seekers by boat is not Australia's responsibility, Thom says the issue needs to be considered as part of a broader global system.
"I say to any critic, we are part of a global system and we have to look at our responsibility globally.
"If we don't solve the problem at its source, people are going to keep moving, and they will keep moving until they find safety and security.
Demonising, criminalising and isolating people is not the solution.
Thom says the debate over border protection has continued to shape how migration is discussed in Australia.
"I think the whole migration debate is blowing up on all proportions and it is always easy when times are tough to blame someone … and migrants are often first to face those attacks," Thom says.
"Ultimately, how we treat them is a reflection of us, not a reflection of people trying to seek a better life."
Howard rejects that characterisation of his approach. He says he hadn't been concerned with how the decision might be viewed 25 years later; he was thinking of "what's right at the time" and that "we had to say no".
"We have a proud record of taking people in from all around the world and a generous humanitarian program.
"We wanted to maintain that."
Life after Tampa
But Naoero was not the end of Farid's story. His asylum application was rejected and he was eventually returned to Afghanistan, where he lived for eight years before being granted asylum and returning to Australia in 2012.
Today Farid is a painter, but his hopes of pursuing a career as an educator have not disappeared.
Since leaving Afghanistan, he has helped establish a primary school of 320 students in his old village, a dream he has relished, having grown up determined that no other child in his community would have to travel hours to reach the nearest school.
Farid's life now straddles two places: the community he left behind in Afghanistan and the life he has built in Australia. His experience offers a personal lens into a question at the heart of Australia's migration debate: what does it mean to become Australian?
Howard views it differently, rejecting the idea that Australia's identity needs to be defined as either "mono" or multicultural.
"It's all pointless. I don't think we should fret about definition, what it is.
The thing is, migration to Australia since World War Two has been a huge success.
"[But] what we should not do is ignore people who want greater control over immigration. They want a ceiling on the number of people who come here, and they don't want people who aren't willing to adopt our ways coming here. How you enforce those two things is a matter of debate."

"Adolf Hitler, huge autist, massive autist, like all these incredible men, some of the best men that ever lived," Thomas Sewell tells viewers online.
Sewell, a neo-Nazi who led the National Socialist Network (NSN), now White Australia, is 10 minutes into a 22-minute monologue giving his "take" on autism.
His argument begins with what he sees as the problem.

"What's wrong with them is they've been coddled," the white supremacist says.
"We used to bully nerds and now we coddle them. Now we're like, 'Oh, you have a disability. You're autistic.' And we treat them like that they're f---ing retarded."
Then, a compliment: "They're not. They're actually usually a lot smarter."
Adolf Hitler, huge autist, massive autist, like all these incredible men, some of the best men that ever lived.
Sewell repeatedly returns to the idea that autistic men do not need to be treated differently, but instead need challenge, male role models and to ‘channel their fixations’. He suggests joining the military — Sewell is ex-Army himself — learning a trade or pursuing higher education.
"It won't fix you, but it'll fully build your character," he says.
"They're not being challenged."
Sewell dismisses expert understanding of autism repeatedly in his videos — "none of these experts understand autism" — and argues instead that those who struggle have not had "the right mentoring from the right male role models".
Running through his commentary is Sewell’s own movement. Sewell claims that at one point about one-fifth of NSN members were autistic and tells viewers about one former NSN member he says he took under his wing.
"I became like his big brother, and I taught him how to lift [weights], and I taught him how to fight and I taught him how to talk to girls and after two years of just intense bullying … he became like a normal person."
A year later, in 2025, Sewell shared another video speaking about autism. This time as he criticised a Countering Violent Extremism program.
"I've recruited hundreds of autistic teenagers and zero of them have stabbed anyone," Sewell jokes.
We contacted Sewell and he denied that he ever actively recruited autistic people.
But his comments come as the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and researchers stress that extremist groups target young people, who they see as vulnerable, including those who are neurodivergent.
'It is a recruitment video'
Peta Lowe, who spent years leading the NSW government’s Countering Violent Extremism program for young people, has no doubts about the video.
"It is a recruitment video. Whether he frames it that way for himself or not," she tells The Feed.
"For a lot of neurodivergent people, one of the things they really struggle with is social interactions and understanding what people mean and the various layers of communication," she says.
What Lowe sees in Sewell’s language is an attempt to reframe difference as an asset. Something that may leave a person feeling out of place elsewhere is presented as something valued inside his group.
"One thing that extremist groups do is they accept you. 'If you want to come, we're going to accept you. And not only are we going to accept you, you become part of a brotherhood,'" she says.
"It's the idea that the thing that is your vulnerability can be a positive here."
"He used a lot of that language. Be more productive, be more successful, be more valuable."
Sewell led the NSN, which disbanded in January after the government introduced new hate laws in the wake of the Bondi terror attack.
But in May, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the group had effectively "phoenixed", re-emerging in its latest form as White Australia, which was subsequently banned under the laws.
The ban makes it a crime to join, support, recruit and raise funds for the group. The decision followed advice from ASIO, which Burke said considered whether an organisation could heighten the risk of violence.
Sewell has been convicted of violent offences, including an attack on a Channel Nine security guard that resulted in a community service order, and an attack on a group of hikers, for which he served five weeks in jail.
He is currently on trial for violent disorder, affray and other offences after allegedly inciting about 40 men to storm an Indigenous sacred site in Melbourne.
For years, he has tried to push a neo-Nazi movement in Australia, organising rallies and public stunts across the country to garner attention and recruit more neo-Nazis.
Sewell is still streaming some of those views online.
Recruiters looking for neurodivergent people
A 2022 analysis published in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders looked at how autism is discussed in alt-right spaces online.
Analysing more than 700 posts on the alt-right platform Gab, specifically the term "weaponised autism", it found that it was largely used by non-autistic users who portrayed autistic people both negatively and as possessing traits that could be useful to the mobilisation of the movement.
For Lowe, recruitment of neurodivergent people is not confined to the far right.
An Islamic State recruiter she spoke to described becoming adept at identifying people online who appeared vulnerable or were searching for a sense of belonging.
"You can't possibly target everyone all the time so you get very good at knowing who to specifically target based on things they say, comments they make on different posts."
That can mean going to online spaces where those vulnerabilities are already being discussed.
"There's actual forums where they talk about things like neurodiversity," she said.
"Recruiters will actively go into those forums and try and encourage people through identifying their vulnerabilities and offering them something."
A growing focus on neurodivergence
In recent years, the AFP has identified a range of factors that can make some young people more vulnerable to radicalisation.
"These include social dislocation, peer influence, mental health challenges, neurodiversity factors, active online engagement with extremists, and triggering or traumatic events," the AFP said in a submission during a statutory review of the Online Safety Act in 2024.
The AFP also shared warnings that extremist groups are deliberately targeting young people in their recruitment strategies based on these vulnerabilities.
But researchers and psychologists caution against drawing a simple line between autism and extremism.
Dr Katie Seidler has worked in forensic psychology for almost 30 years and has assessed violent extremism cases for Australian courts.
"It's unhelpful and it's untrue to suggest that autism spectrum disorder or autistic features make somebody more likely to be violent in an extremist way," she tells The Feed.
"The vast majority of those people who present with ASD [autism spectrum disorder] do not go on to hold violent or extremist ideological positions, nor do they go on to commit acts of violent extremism."
Where autism can be relevant, Seidler says, is when particular traits intersect with other circumstances in a person's life.
"It’s kind of a bit of a perfect storm of events," she says.
"It's not just the autism spectrum disorder, but it's the autism spectrum disorder in constellation with exposure to material online that appeals to that person's thoughts ... with maybe an absence of effective social connections outside of that."
This intersection is also showing up in intervention programs. Academics from Victoria University told a Senate inquiry in 2024 there had been an increase in neurodivergent people referred to extremist violence prevention programs in Australia, particularly young people and those involved in online offending.
Similar trends have emerged overseas. In the UK, one in five referrals to the Prevent counterterrorism program had autism, according to figures released this month.
This is higher than the prevalence of autism in the general population. In Australia, about 1 per cent of the population has autism, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, and less than 1 per cent worldwide, according to the World Health Organization.
'Unbelievably manipulative'
Nicole Rogerson, CEO of Autism Australia, has spent two decades at the forefront of autism advocacy in Australia.
She says there are characteristics associated with autism that, for some people, can create vulnerabilities online.
And it would be tragic that they would consider individuals with autism low-hanging fruit to try and join that movement.
"Some of the vulnerabilities can be things such as an immense interest or focus on something. It can be a misinterpretation. It can be a literal interpretation. There are a whole range of things."
Communication can be another. Some autistic people may misread cues that others pick up on.
When shown Sewell’s videos about autistic young men, Rogerson said it made her sick.
"It's fair to say this is a group of very unwell young men looking to build and grow their network based on hate. And it would be tragic that they would consider individuals with autism low-hanging fruit to try and join that movement."
"Even just thinking like that is unbelievably manipulative to take a group of young men who may have trouble with social interactions," she said.
"And they might be quite lonely."
But for counterterrorism expert, Peta Lowe, she says in the absence of supports, young people will keep being drawn in.
"What worries me is that we haven't yet found a way to counter those effective recruitment strategies."

Trains between Britain and Europe on track to run every 15 minutes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
19:30:00 UTC
04:30:00 KST

A Eurostar passenger train enters the Channel Tunnel, operated by the company Eurotunnel, in Coquelles, northern France. | Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP via Getty Images
LONDON — High-speed trains linking the U.K. to the continent through the Channel Tunnel may soon depart every 15 minutes — thanks to competition from new operators on the route.
The number of daily services between London St Pancras and destinations like Paris, Brussels and Amsterdam is on track to rise from the 25 round trips currently operated by Eurostar each day to 55 by the end of the decade — around four departures per hour — according to POLITICO calculations.
The Channel Tunnel has been running under capacity since it opened in 1994 and infrastructure owners have long encouraged a “second operator” to challenge incumbent Eurostar on the rail line to the continent.
Advertisement
That idea seems to have finally left the station. Virgin Trains was last week given the green signal by the U.K. regulator to run up to 20 daily return trips between London, Paris, Brussels and Amsterdam, the first of several authorizations required for international trains. Virgin wants to begin the services in 2030.
Martin Jones, deputy director, access and international at the U.K.’s Office of Rail and Road (ORR), said the approval of Virgin’s track access rights was “an important next step in bringing competition and growth to the market for international rail services.”
But it looks increasingly likely that it won’t just be Virgin competing with Eurostar on the route to London.
Italian competition
Trenitalia, Italy’s state railway, is adamant it will be running services on the Channel route by 2029. It has promised 10 round trips a day, with operations starting from 2029.
The operator has put its money where its mouth is, this month placing a €2 billion order with manufacturer Hitachi for 19 new high-speed trains, some of which it says will be for use in the Channel Tunnel.
The state-owned company says it can stable the trains in France, at a new €80 million facility at Maisons-Alfort Pompadour, south of Paris. The depot is already under construction and will also be used to maintain rolling stock for its increasingly popular trains between Italy and France.
Advertisement
Using this new facility will allow Trenitalia to bypass capacity limits at the Temple Mills International depot in east London, where Eurostar keeps its fleet and where Virgin is also expected to do so. The U.K. regulator allocated the last space in the facility to Virgin last year.
Mark Smith, a former rail manager who runs the popular Man In Seat 61 travel website, told POLITICO: “Both contenders appear to have the ability and financial backing to make this happen, but there are many steps in a long process before any train runs. Trenitalia are in pole position with a 2029 start date, helped by having ordered trains of a type already approved for France and a continuation of an existing production line.”
Travellers check their phones while standing next to a Eurostar train at St. Pancras station in London on December 30, 2025. | Carlos Jasso/AFP via Getty Images
“I see no reason why experience in Italy or Spain should not be repeated, where competition has raised standards, increased capacity and lowered average fares. The whole market has gown, in Italy Trenitalia is carrying more passengers than it did before competition from Italo arrived. Passengers have won, the biggest loser has been short haul flights.”
Reasons to be cautious
There’s still plenty of time for it all to go wrong — as it has before.
German state railway Deutsche Bahn once planned services through the tunnel, going so far as to send a promotional train to St Pancras for a photo op in October 2010. The operator was ultimately stymied by Brexit and backed away from the idea, although it has since shown some renewed interest.
There is also room for the new entrants to revise their plans. Operators don’t necessarily have to run every service they get authorization to operate from the ORR. Each operator also needs separate authorizations in each country and for the Channel Tunnel itself, meaning there are still regulatory hurdles to clear.
Advertisement
It also wouldn’t be the first (or even second) time a company brought trains to use in the Channel Tunnel and never ran them there. DB ended up using its ICE3 sets built for the tunnel to shore up reliability on other routes, including on the notoriously delay-prone route between Brussels and Germany.
Meanwhile, sleeper cars built to run never-realized Nightstar overnight services back in the 1990s are now running long-distance routes in Canada.
For now, all three new operators plan to compete on the existing routes and are yet to formally propose any new destinations — meaning Italy’s state railway would be running trains that go nowhere near Italy.
But this is increasingly common in Europe’s new age of liberalized railway competition, where national operators go wherever they see a gap in the market.
France’s state operator, for example, creams off lucrative domestic high-speed services in Spain, while Austria’s federal railways runs a sleeper between Germany and Switzerland.
Even before Brexit, adding new railway destinations from London was expensive and operationally difficult, thanks to the U.K.’s decision to remain outside the Schengen passport-free travel area.
Advertisement
This means that any station to be properly served from London needs expensive manned passport control, security checks, and a spare platform fenced off from others by a de facto international border. International and domestic passengers must be kept separate, too. These hurdles also make it commercially unviable to directly serve other destinations in the U.K. beyond London.
Piling in
Despite these challenges, the London route is deemed so lucrative that companies seem to be piling in.
Another would-be competitor, Gemini Trains, says it still wants to run 11 trains a day through the Tunnel by 2030 despite failing in its application for space at the Temple Mills depot. As of August 2026 Gemini is now looking at opening its own depot in Kent, on the site of a mothballed facility at Chart Leacon.
It has a partnership with global mobility giant Uber, but no trains, track access, nor yet a depot. If it is able to run its planned services, too, it would take the total number of cross Channel return services to 66 a day.
Eurostar has also announced plans to increase its own offering, and says a €2 billion (£1.7 billion) fleet of up to 50 new train sets will be delivered in the early 2030s, allowing a 30 percent increase in its own services and expansion to new destinations including Frankfurt and Geneva.
While the high-speed line on the U.K. side of the channel has plenty of spare capacity for all these plans — it was built with space for eight international trains an hour — whether they can come to fruition will also depend on capacity elsewhere. Train paths in France, Belgium and beyond will need to be secured.
Another major constraint will be passenger capacity at stations. In the international terminal at London St Pancras station terminal, there is already often nowhere to sit once through passport control. The station’s owner has commissioned architects Hawkins\Brown to fix this — with a brief to double passenger capacity there by 2028 and more expansions planned in the 2030s. St Pancras sits on a constrained site, sandwiched between neighboring King’s Cross station, the British Library, and a canal — limiting room for expansion.
Speaking last month, Gwendoline Cazenave, CEO of Eurostar, said the U.K. needed “a bold vision to match the private investment on the table.” She called for “more depot capacity, a bold expansion of St Pancras and a seamless border.”

Two People Have Died of Measles in Pennsylvania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
19:27:49 UTC
04:27:49 KST

Two people in Pennsylvania have died from measles, marking the first reported deaths from the disease in the U.S. this year.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health said on Tuesday, Aug. 25, that the two people who died were unvaccinated and lived in Lancaster County, the epicenter of a statewide measles outbreak that has sickened hundreds.
No additional information has been released about the two people who died. State health officials said the deaths are the first measles-associated fatalities in Pennsylvania in 35 years.
“Because measles was largely eliminated in the [state] for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness,” said Dr. Debra Bogen, Pennsylvania’s health secretary, in a statement.
More than 2,700 measles cases have been reported in the U.S. this year—the highest number of cases since the disease was considered eliminated in the country in 2000. In just the past two years, the U.S. has recorded more measles cases than it did from 2000 through 2024 combined.
Measles is a highly contagious viral disease that can cause high fever, a tell-tale rash, cough, and other symptoms. The disease can be mild for some, but about one in four people sickened with measles is hospitalized. Young children, pregnant women, and the elderly are among those who are at risk of more severe disease.
No specific treatment for measles exists. The measles vaccine—delivered as a combination measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) shot series—is 97% effective at preventing the disease and lowers the risk of complications if someone is infected.
“As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand that the MMR vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles,” said Bogen.
Within communities, a vaccination rate of above 95% is considered ideal for robust herd immunity against measles. The national MMR vaccination rate among kindergarteners surpassed 95% in the 2019-2020 school year, but it has been declining ever since, according to U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. In 2025-2026, MMR vaccination coverage was just 92.4% nationally, and about 93% in Pennsylvania. In Lancaster County, home of the largest Amish settlement in the country, the vaccination rate was under 88%. An estimated 25% of the Amish population in Lancaster County is vaccinated against measles, according to the Association of Immunization Managers, an organization of state and local immunization officials.
Vaccination rates began notably declining in the U.S. during the COVID pandemic and have continued dropping amid increasing anti-vaccine rhetoric and policy under the Trump Administration. On Aug. 10, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that called for U.S. children to receive fewer vaccines and ordered the MMR vaccine to be split into three separate shots, despite a lack of scientific evidence to back the changes.
“Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal,” Trump said of the combined shot, which has been in use for more than 50 years and has a strong safety and efficacy record.
Doctors and vaccine scientists said Trump’s executive order and comments were unscientific and misleading. "As measles cases reach a 35-year high in the U.S. and with cold and flu season quickly approaching, [the] executive order on vaccines is not only disheartening but dangerous,” Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), said in a statement at the time.
The CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend that all children get two doses of the MMR vaccine, starting with the first dose at 12 through 15 months of age.
An additional early dose of the vaccine can also be given to children aged 6 to 11 months under some circumstances, says Dr. Elizabeth Murray, a pediatric emergency medicine physician in Rochester, N.Y. “With the ongoing measles outbreak, make sure your children are immunized. If your child is under age 1, talk to your doctor. Depending on how much measles is circulating where you live, your doctor may recommend an earlier dose,” she says.
The CDC also advises adults who haven’t been immunized against measles or who are unsure about their vaccination status to get the vaccine. The agency recommends that people who were vaccinated before 1968 with an older version of the shot get at least one dose of the vaccine in use now, which is more effective.
For people fully vaccinated after 1968, however, there is no need to get a booster, the CDC says, as two doses of the vaccine should offer adequate, lifelong protection.

Anthropic's 'massive' AI data centre plans revealed in emails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
19:26:52 UTC
04:26:52 KST

AI giant Anthropic wanted 'massive' data centre capacity in NSW, emails reveal
In short:
The US tech giant behind popular AI chatbot Claude wanted to meet with the NSW government earlier this year about locating up to 5 gigawatts of data centres in the state, the ABC can reveal.
That would be more than three times the current capacity of all Australia's data centres.
What's next?
National cabinet is meeting today to consider new water and energy rules for AI data centres amid mounting community concern about their rollout in Australia.
Internal NSW government emails reveal AI giant Anthropic was interested in building up to 5 gigawatts of AI data centre capacity in NSW alone, a capacity that would be three times the size of Australia's entire data centre infrastructure.
This grand ambition from the US company behind Claude would require tens of billions of dollars in investment and a significant expansion in the number of data centres across the country, to meet just one company's demand in a single state.
"That is a massive amount," Olivia Shen, director of the Strategic Technologies Program at the United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney, said.
It comes as the Albanese government negotiates new rules for large-scale data centres with the states, which are vying with each other to attract investment from Silicon Valley.
The speed and scale of the AI data centre boom has prompted a growing backlash from local communities concerned about the impacts of building this physical infrastructure in their local communities.
Training and running generative AI needs an enormous amount of computing capacity, which requires expensive computing hardware and tremendous amounts of power. They can also be hot and noisy.
With Silicon Valley rushing out new AI models at a breakneck pace, there has been a race to build the physical infrastructure required to serve the billions of people using popular AI services launched since late 2022.
Emails reveal plans to meet Anthropic CEO
Documents released by NSW parliament earlier this year reveal how a senior public servant shared information about Anthropic's interest in building out its AI computing capacity in NSW.
Dena Jacobs, executive director of independent state government agency Infrastructure NSW, wrote to two senior public servants at the Department of Premier's Investment NSW in March about a conversation with Anthropic adviser John Garnaut.
Ms Jacobs told the staff she wanted to organise a meeting between Investment NSW staff and Mr Garnaut ahead of a "a more senior level meeting".
"The context is that the CEO of Anthropic is visiting Sydney and would like to speak to NSW government about the opportunities to locate up to 5GW of AI training capacity in NSW. i.e. there's an opportunity to locate this outside Sydney," she wrote on March 18.
Ms Jacobs's email did not specify Anthropic's intended timeframe for this computing goal.
The ABC understands the 5GW goal only reflected initial interest from Anthropic, which was one of a handful of major tech companies that Infrastructure NSW had spoken with about their future computing demands.
Both Anthropic and NSW Investment declined to comment.
Mr Garnaut told the ABC that he "work[s] with AI firms" but said he "did not put in this particular request".
Two weeks later, Anthropic's senior executives, including CEO Dario Amodei, visited Australia.
Mr Amodei met the prime minister and treasurer when they signed a memorandum of understanding between the company and the government, which included, among other things, a promise to "expand [Anthropic]'s presence in Australia".
The AI company has not publicly stated how much computing capacity it would like to obtain in Australia.
The ABC reported in June that Anthropic wanted 5GW of new Australian computing capacity by 2030, with a longer-term goal of 20GW.
The Australian Financial Review reported in July about a confidential tender sent by the AI company to Australian data centre builders asking for 1.4GW of capacity, valued at more than $20 billion.
Australia an attractive destination for centres
Anthropic's interest in up to 5GW for a single state would dwarf the projections for the total amount of computing capacity expected to be built by the end of the decade.
New data released in a report from lobby group Data Centre Australia today calculated that Australia currently has 1.6GW of computing capacity in total.
The report projects that Australia's data centre capacity will grow to 3.9GW by 2030.
These figures are a marked increase from data released by the same group earlier this year.
In April, Data Centres Australia said there were 1.5GW of current capacity and 3.2GW projected by 2030, suggesting demand for computing capacity, and the ability to satisfy that demand, was growing even faster than anticipated.
Analysts estimated global data centre capacity was somewhere around 55 and 82 gigawatts in 2025.
Ms Shen said Australia had emerged as an attractive destination for US AI companies for several reasons.
"One is just that we have lots of land. Another is that we have huge amounts of renewable capacity, particularly solar energy, and the third is that we are a stable democracy," she said.
While Australians are among the most distrustful populations in the world of AI, they are also some of the fastest adopters of the technology.
Anthropic released data in June claiming that Australia ranked first in the world for use of its Claude project, when adjusted for the working-age population.
Ms Shen said Anthropic, out of all of the global tech companies, was particularly incentivised to move some of its operations abroad.
Anthropic remains locked in a high-stakes legal battle with the US government over export controls placed on its cutting-edge models.
The company is also reportedly looking at going public at a $US2 trillion ($2.8 trillion) valuation as soon as late this year.
"In the face of this uncertainty about the regulatory landscape in the US, including a lot of local opposition to data centres, it makes sense for Anthropic to want to diversify its compute and its business outside of the United States," Ms Shen said.
Governments looking to attract business
Australian governments, too, have indicated their interest in attracting US tech companies to establish themselves here.
Other internal NSW government emails released by parliamentary order show that the office of NSW Innovation, Science and Technology Minister Anoulack Chanthivong set up a meeting with one US Anthropic executive during their trip.
The ABC understands that meeting did not go ahead.
Mr Chanthivong told the ABC his government did not comment on private discussions but would regularly discuss investment opportunities with the companies.
"The Minns Labor government continues to welcome investment from leading technology companies," he said.
Last week, NSW announced a set of new energy, water, environmental and community requirements for data centres.
In return, developers would receive a commitment to have their development applications assessed within 75 days.
The state said qualifying projects must fund additional water and energy supply and impose no net cost on consumers and communities.
These rules come on top of Anthony Albanese's recent announcement that the federal government would create a set of "Australian standards" that he hoped would attract investment from top tech companies while avoiding a US-style community backlash.
This comes as polling from multiple outlets shows that a plurality of Australians would oppose data centres being built in their local community.
The Albanese government is pursuing new requirements around the use of energy and water, copyright protections, workers' rights and computing capacity for Australian businesses and researchers.
Mr Albanese is set for a showdown over these standards at national cabinet later today, as both Queensland and the Northern Territory have signalled that they will not accept a requirement to guarantee that all data centres bring enough new renewable energy to account for their added demand.
The rest of the new data centre rules will be developed as the Albanese government seeks to legislate the standards in early 2027.

Earlier, Financial Times journalist Christopher Miller reported that representatives of the Donald Trump administration last week asked Kyiv not to launch strikes against Moscow, St. Petersburg, and other regions of Russia on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday — precisely during the period when the U.S. side was scheduled to send a high-ranking official to Moscow. According to him, Ukraine agreed to this.
This is Ratcliffe’s first visit to Russia since his appointment as CIA director and one of the highest-level contacts between the Trump administration and Moscow in recent times.
The CIA, the Department of Defense, and the U.S. Air Force declined to comment on the visit.
The C-17 Globemaster III is a large military transport aircraft which, according to the U.S. Air Force website, can be used for strategic and tactical airlift and airdrop missions, as well as for aeromedical evacuation.

Ukraine’s metals industry on verge of systemic shutdown — agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
19:24:54 UTC
04:24:54 KST

MOSCOW, August 25. /TASS/. Ukraine’s metals industry has plunged into a deep crisis, the RBC-Ukraine news agency reported.
In August, two key enterprises, Zaporozhstal and ArcelorMittal Krivoy Rog, which together accounted for around 72% of Ukraine’s steel production in 2025, were put out of action as a result of explosions, according to the report.
For Ukraine, a systemic crisis entails a loss of export revenues, rising construction costs, and issues with the hryvnia exchange rate, the agency noted. If the two steel plants remain idle for an extended period, Ukraine risks losing roughly 72% of its steel production. According to the publication, this could result in a production cut of around 2 mln tons by the end of 2026, which in turn could lead to a loss of exports and foreign currency earnings.
President of the Ukrmetallurgprom industry association Alexander Kalenkov said earlier that the halt in maritime exports for mining and metallurgical enterprises threatens Ukraine’s macroeconomic stability as they could cease operations in the coming weeks. The situation is further complicated by the crisis within the Ukrainian steel industry itself. Import quotas imposed by the European Union on Ukrainian steel automatically reduce domestic demand for iron ore used to produce it. According to Kalenkov, unless the situation changes, the first to shut down will be the mining and processing plants that rely heavily on exports. Enterprises focused on the domestic market will be able to hold out longer, but they will also ultimately face a drop in demand.

Trump floats 'Lake America' name for Lake Ontario amid Canada row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
19:23:00 UTC
04:23:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump suggested renaming Lake Ontario "Lake America" as his trade dispute with Canada escalated, drawing swift pushback from the United States' northern neighbor.
"He can blow out his hole as much as he wants to, but it’s never going to happen, because Canadians are strong,” said Patricia Wiseman, an Ontario resident, as she walked along the waterfront of Lake Erie.
It may be more complicated than that. Trump has wide latitude over how the U.S. government recognizes geographic places and landmarks. But he cannot force Canada or individual citizens on either side of the border to follow his preferred naming conventions. And his latest branding idea - reminiscent of his move to rechristen the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America” - highlights how much his rhetoric and trade policy have sundered the previously warm relationship between Washington and Ottawa.
"I believe the American people love us, and we love them,” Wiseman said. "They’re going through as much turmoil as we are. Hopefully, one day we can reunite.”
Trump introduced the idea of renaming the easternmost area of the Great Lakes hours before Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's scheduled announcement of reciprocal tariffs on U.S. imports into his country.
"The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer,” Trump posted Monday on Truth Social.
The White House followed later in the day by posting on social media a toy Lego map of the U.S. labeling the Gulf of Mexico with Trump's preferred name, Gulf of America,
The U.S. and Canada, which share borders along multiple Great Lakes, including Lake Ontario, are locked in an extended trade dispute, with the Trump administration imposing 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down. That ratcheted up lower tariffs that Trump imposed in 2025, shortly after his second presidency began.
Trump has also threatened new 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel, while Carney said U.S. trade demands showed that Washington wanted to "destroy our major industries,” including autos, steel and aluminum.
The official U.S.-Canada border stretches across the water between Lake Ontario's northern and southern shores. The body of water forms much of New York State’s coastline and separates Buffalo from Toronto, the capital of the province of Ontario. Toronto is Canada's most populous city and Ontario its most populous province.
Ontario is also the single largest export destination for more than a dozen U.S. states.
"It’s disappointing,” Ontario resident Paul Butler said of Trump's policy and rhetoric. "The more you hear it, it just gets downright infuriating.”
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who traded personal insults with Trump on Monday, dismissed the Lake Ontario threat as "a lot of rhetoric” and urged the two countries to resume negotiations. Ford acknowledged in a CNN interview that the dispute "got a little personal” and agreed it was time to lower the temperature, saying the trade fight was hurting both countries and that Canada and the United States should "get back to the table” to negotiate.
The lake's name comes from the Huron Indigenous people's word "oniatarí:io,” which means "lake of shining waters,” and it predates European settlement in the region. The province, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
The International Hydrographic Organization - of which both the United States and Canada are members - works to ensure that the world’s seas, oceans and navigable waters are surveyed and charted uniformly, and also names some of them. But there is no single international body that determines names of international bodies of water.
"It’s been like that for so long, so, why do we need to change it?” said Nancy Minard, an Ontario resident. "It seems to work for Canada and I think probably works for the U.S., too.”
Trump has at least some support for his idea on Ontario's south shoreline.
"I like it. Absolutely. Because I like America, and right now Canada’s not treating us very nicely,” said Jim Fetterhoff, a resident and fisherman in Port Ontario in upstate New York.
He cited Canadian tariffs on dairy and other products. Nothing against Canadians themselves, Fetterhoff added, "just the Canadian government. I love Canadians.”
Canada and Mexico are the largest U.S. trading partners but have drawn Trump's ire throughout his second presidency on trade, immigration and crime. He has called for Canada to become the 51st state, alternating between joking tones and seemingly serious assertions that Carney and other Canadians have rejected and mocked.
On the day of his second inauguration, Trump fulfilled one of his 2024 campaign promises with an executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. The body of water forms a shared border between Mexico and the U.S.
Mexico does not recognize the change, nor do many other countries and international bodies.
In 2015, President Barack Obama changed the name of Alaska's Mount McKinley, named for the 25th U.S. president, to Denali, its historical name given by Alaska Natives as well as the preference of many Alaska residents. Trump, the same day he ordered the Gulf of Mexico to be renamed, returned McKinley's name to the Alaska mountain to honor "a great president.”
That back-and-forth in Alaska could be a preview for a certain ancient lake. Said Wiseman of Trump, "He’s not going to be in the presidency forever.”

====================================================================================================

Why automation and repression go hand in hand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
19:18:48 UTC
04:18:48 KST

analysis
When are the pitchforks coming?
Wealth inequality is becoming extreme. Political corruption is rampant in the United States.
Billionaires are building fortified bunkers to protect themselves from the inevitable social upheaval that lies in our future (they fear).
"What do I see in our future now? I see pitchforks," US tech entrepreneur Nick Hanauer famously warned in 2014.
"There is no example in human history where wealth accumulated like this and the pitchforks didn't eventually come out.
"You show me a highly unequal society, and I will show you a police state. Or an uprising. There are no counter-examples."
Some tech leaders say it is inevitable that people will revolt against automation.
"This is the real underlying threat posed by automation: tremendous social upheaval, public unrest, and political collapse stemming from widespread unemployment and grotesque inequality," warned Kai-Fu Lee, a former president of Google China, in 2022.
It's why 100 millionaires signed an open letter for the Davos Summit in 2025 with a simple message for their wealthy colleagues: "It's taxes or pitchforks!"
So where is society headed?
Daron Acemoglu, a winner of the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences (2024), published a working paper recently, with Mehdi Shadmehr and Arda Gitmez that grappled with these issues.
It was titled Automation and Repression, and its conclusion was disquieting.
Redistribution or repression?
The economists argued in their paper that, when faced with the threat of a popular revolt against greater automation, political leaders would have two choices, and they would choose the option most people wouldn't like.
"We show that the capitalist state can use redistribution or repression to reduce the threat of a revolt," they say.
"[And] greater automation makes repression more attractive to the capitalist state," they argue.
Why is that the result?
Because according to their model, more automation will require more redistribution to cushion the disruptive effects of automation, so as a country automates more, the tax burden will keep increasing on "capitalists".
So, the "capitalist state" will opt for repression, since repression only has a fixed cost (as a proportion of output), whereas the cost of redistribution keeps increasing with the extent of automation.
It's a strange use of language.
They're talking about the "cost" of repression like it's a basic financial cost of running a state, and they write in negative terms about the "cost" of redistribution when that redistribution is being used to keep people alive and democratic society functioning.
But that's the language these economic models use.
A lot of surveillance, forced compliance
And it's the language some wealthy individuals and business leaders employ.
The paper references an interview with Mo Gawdat, former chief business officer at Google X, who spoke of the attitudes of many tech leaders as rushing toward full-scale automation and then using other tools to control the population who lose their jobs, in these terms:
"And so you're going to see a world where unfortunately there's going to be a lot of control, a lot of surveillance, a lot of forced compliance."
According to Acemoglu, Shadmehr and Gitmez, these types of debates have become prominent in popular media and the business world.
So they have tried to incorporate revolts, triggered by inequality between capital and labour, into a task-based model of automation.
In essence, they have modelled how workers would try to coordinate in an uprising, and how a capitalist state would try to prevent an uprising occurring, in an environment in which automation and inequality are increasing.
Their paper contributes to growing literature on the historical evidence on political and social reactions to automation.
They say the novel finding of their paper is that automation and repression complement and reinforce each other.
Its full dynamic model shows that if society develops to the point where there is a credible threat of revolt against automation, "the economy will ultimately converge to repression and the 'pitchforks' will be met with 'guns' from the capitalist state".
"In a further extension, we show that if society first starts in a democracy, democratic decision-making will become less and less acceptable to capitalists as the level of the capital stock grows, and society will experience an anti-democratic coup, once again transitioning to repression," the paper notes.
Data centre and AI boom at risk from backlash
The three economists acknowledge that their paper is only a "first step" in the investigation of the dynamics between political regimes and technology choices, especially automation.
They say it would be great to incorporate richer political interactions into their model, including the reality of lobbying and political donations and other forms of democratic capture.
And they say it would be interesting to explore how advances in AI can change politics in other ways that interact with automation and repression.
But their paper comes at an interesting time.
In recent months, The Economist magazine has been warning that the data centre and AI boom is at risk from a growing public backlash in countries like the United States, Britain and Australia.
In Australia, there has also been public unease about the increasing use of new surveillance tools used by the state.
The NSW Police Force is currently running an Australian-first trial in Moree (an area with a high Indigenous population) using rooftop drones to "fight crime" in the area, controlled by people hundreds of kilometres away at Bankstown Airport.
The same police force has been using software developed by Israeli digital forensics company Cellebrite to download the contents of a suspected criminal's phone, including deleted messages and images, and new legislation before NSW parliament seeks to extend those powers for police, which is raising concerns that that capability will eventually shift into routine policing.
Back in 2017, the Fairfax Media reported that Centrelink, the Australian Taxation Office, the Australian Securities and Investment Commission, and the Australian Federal Police were already using Cellebrite technology.
In another Australian-first trial, the Western Australian Police have been using live facial recognition software to scan people walking on the streets of Perth and Fremantle, comparing their faces against a police watchlist in real time.
And AFL clubs are now exploring using facial recognition technology instead of digital or paper tickets.
It's clear we're heading in a certain direction with this technology. Is the state already rehearsing for a more repressive role?

First deaths in US measles crisis reported

First deaths in US measles crisis reported
Two people have died of measles in Pennsylvania, decades after the disease was considered eradicated. Measles is currently making a resurgence in the US, with cases at a 35-year high.
The two victims were residents of Lancaster County, a largely rural county west of Philadelphia, state health officials announced on Tuesday. No additional details were provided, except that neither victim was vaccinated.
Fatal cases of measles are exceedingly rare in the US, but infections are rising. 2,289 cases of the disease were recorded in 2025, the highest number since 1991, when 9,643 cases were recorded. Last year’s number was surpassed by this July, and as of August 20, 2,777 cases have been recorded this year, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Outbreaks have occurred in 47 US states and territories, with 94% of cases occurring among the unvaccinated.
Measles is a highly contagious viral respiratory disease that was officially eliminated in the US in 2000 following a successful mass vaccination campaign. Before mass vaccination began in the 1960s, measles killed between 400 and 500 Americans every year, according to CDC data.
Dr. Adam Ratner, an adviser to the CDC, told the JAMA medical journal last year that skepticism about Covid-19 vaccines has “bled over” into other vaccines, due to the Covid shots becoming “this insanely polarized political thing” from 2020 onwards.
“Once there was that kind of hesitancy out there and that kind of divisiveness, it’s not surprising that it has bled over into people thinking about vaccine mandates and childhood vaccines in general,” Rather said.
US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine skeptic, has vouched for the safety of the combined measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, but noted “the decision to vaccinate is a personal one.”
A vaccination rate of around 95% is required to prevent measles outbreaks. In November, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a division of the World Health Organization (WHO), will meet to determine whether the US and Mexico can still claim to be “measles free” after recent outbreaks.

Big disagreement looms over crowded national cabinet agenda
In short:
Premiers are heading into national cabinet divided over how Australia should meet the rapidly growing energy demands of AI data centres.
The leaders meeting will also consider domestic violence, bird flu, fuel security and gun laws, but GST is not on the agenda.
What's next?
Premiers and chief ministers will meet Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Sydney today to discuss the plan to impose data centre standards and other national priorities.
A stoush over energy rules for data centres will dominate national cabinet as leaders confront a crowded agenda where progress on guns, GST and other contentious issues is unlikely.
Premiers and chief ministers will meet with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Sydney today to discuss AI data centres, bird flu, domestic violence, fuel security and the national gun buyback.
The federal government's plan to impose national standards for data centres, which would require developers to bring their own renewable energy and set other parameters around water usage and community contributions, is expected to be the biggest source of disagreement.
The Queensland and Northern Territory governments are opposed to the renewables-focused standards and have been scathing of threats the Commonwealth would force their will on states if necessary.
Loading...
Despite a long-running public stoush about GST, the tax issue is not on the agenda, with multiple state sources telling the ABC their respective views on the current deal were already no secret.
Agreement around progressing the next five-year national plan to end violence against women and children is likely, but Mr Albanese is facing calls from the federal crossbench to use the meeting to progress more reforms to help tackle the scourge.
The leaders are not due to discuss federal Labor's plan to standardise the private health rebate for all ages, effectively reducing the benefit for older Australians, which the South Australian government this week became the latest jurisdiction to oppose.
Premiers and chief ministers will get a briefing from Australia's chief veterinary officer on the outbreak of H5N1 bird flu, which has now been detected in all six states.
Energy and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen will provide an update on the latest moves to ensure Australia's fuel security amid ongoing disruptions caused by the US war with Iran.
Bowen dismisses nuclear reactors powering data centres
The Australian Energy Market Operator has estimated data centres would grow from currently consuming 3 per cent of the nation's electricity supply to 13 per cent in a decade.
Mr Bowen said yesterday if the government got the policy settings "right", he was confident Australia could handle the electricity demands of data centres.
"That's why we're requiring new data centres to bring their own renewable energy, backed by gas firming," he said.
Mr Bowen has maintained the Commonwealth is prepared to legislate over the top of states, if necessary, though he has not outlined specifics.
"The constitution is pretty clear about, if there's a dispute between Commonwealth legislation and state legislation, which legislation prevails," he said.
He also rubbished the suggestion of data centres running on nuclear small modular reactors, which he described as the "most expensive form of energy and the longest to deploy".
Bowen's data centre energy threat dismissed as foolish
Queensland Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie told the ABC his government would not be "forced" into a particular energy pathway by the Commonwealth.
"We're our own state and we're pushing back," he said.
"We believe that there are potential investment opportunities in Queensland for data centres, but it's going to be all forms of electricity and we're not going to force renewable energy on regional communities."
Mr Bleijie said Mr Bowen was a "fool" for threatening to override states and suggested the federal minister "doesn't understand the constitution".
"Chris Bowen should be trying to work with state and territories government, not be a big brother bully as he's trying to do in this case," he said.
Asked if Queensland would mount a challenge to any Commonwealth attempt to override the state, Mr Bleijie said he did not believe it would be necessary.
"No-one's going to have to challenge anything because the type of investment won't come because businesses will not invest it if there's only one form of electricity on the table," he said.
Northern Territory Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said she was opposed to national AI data centre standards, arguing states and territories should be free to make laws that "suit" the views of their community.
"We don't need the federal government coming in heavy-handed and trying to dictate to states and territories, how they should be developing data centres or not, and what energy mix they should be using," she told ABC Radio National.
Ms Finocchiaro said the NT had an "incredibly unique situation" where the Beetaloo Basin had enough gas to power out the nation for 200 years and more.
"We want recognised by the federal government," she said.
"Because if data centres are to want to develop in the territory, they should be utilising that enormous energy resource we have."
Ms Finocchiaro said the national cabinet meeting was the first "real chance" leaders have had to discuss the issue directly.
"There's nothing territorians hate more than a heavy-handed federal government, and I'll be here to stand our ground and make sure that territorians are put first at national cabinet," she said.
Crossbench calls for audit of dollars spent tackling DV
Also at national cabinet, Mr Albanese will raise domestic and sexual violence against women, with states and territories expected to agree to accelerate efforts to respond to the epidemic.
They will also discuss priority areas for the next five-year national action plan to end violence against women and children, which is due to be released early next year.
Yesterday, more than a dozen crossbenchers signed a letter to Mr Albanese asking him to use the national cabinet meeting to prioritise their calls to beef up the powers of the Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commission.
The MPs and senators, including Allegra Spender, Andrew Wilkie, Helen Haines, Dai Le, Lidia Thorpe, Jacqui Lambie and Fatima Payman, have asked that the commission be made a statutory authority and given the ability to compel data, audit spending and track whether measures governments have funded are "actually working".
"A decade of reviews and inquiries into domestic, family and sexual violence has produced more than 1,000 recommendations, yet women and children continue to die, and too many systemic failures remain," the letter said.
"Billions of dollars flow to states and territories every year for these programs, but there is no equivalent oversight of where that money goes or whether it is reducing harm."
Gun buyback far from national
Mr Albanese's attempt to establish a national gun buyback in the wake of the Bondi terror attack will be discussed at the meeting though developments are unlikely.
Only NSW and the ACT have signed up to the proposal so far, while Western Australia recently completed its own voluntary program.
But no further jurisdictions are likely to join the scheme.
Cooperation is far more likely in the ongoing response to the deadly outbreak of H5N1 bird flu, which has reached all states although not the ACT and NT, and recently been detected in a mammal.

Kurdish-led forces in Syria dissolve after merging with army
