Airman Among 8 Killed in Crash at Remote Alaska Radar Site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:48:38 UTC
03:48:38 KST

A 23-year-old Air Force civil engineer was among the eight people who were killed in a plane crash near a remote Alaskan radar site last week, officials announced Aug. 24.
2nd Lt. Leah A. Borsich was a member of the 611th Civil Engineer Squadron at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, flying on a Cessna 441, which was contracted by the U.S. military, to the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site on Aug. 20 when the plane crashed, killing all aboard.
The 611th is part of the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center under the 11th Air Force and helps to maintain more than 40 remote or austere radar sites across the region.
Col. Timothey Meerstein, commander of the center, described Borsich as “a positive leader who brought tremendous energy and enthusiasm to our command. She led with professionalism, compassion and purpose, and her presence strengthened the bonds between the people around her.”
According to social media posts and profiles, Borsich was an Ohio native who participated in the Air Force ROTC program while attending the University of Dayton.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers also identified two employees as victims of the crash on Aug. 24: Sabrina Hansen and Hayden Scalise, both of Anchorage, Alaska. Officials have yet to release the names of non-Pentagon personnel in the crash.
The Army Corps of Engineers also said in its statement that it had contracted with the air charter company Security Aviation for a flight to Cape Newenham to “inspect and perform maintenance on a new fire suppression system” at the site.
Cape Newenham is part of the Alaska Radar System, a network of 15 remote long-range radar sites and three remote radio sites that monitor Alaskan airspace, particularly for Russian activity. Built in the 1950s to host dozens of Air Force personnel, the site is now run by just a handful of contractors supported by the Air Force.
In an Aug. 21 media briefing hosted by the National Transportation Safety Board, Alaska Region Chief Clint Johnson said preliminary data indicates the crash “happened after one missed approach” as the two pilots had no visibility and were navigating solely using their instruments.
“What we understand is after the second missed approach, Anchorage … lost contact with the airplane, and then a search began shortly after that,” Johnson said.
An HH-60W helicopter, an HC-130 personnel recovery plane, and Guardian Angel Airmen from the Alaska Air National Guard all responded to the crash, according to the 11th Air Force.

UGVs and UAVs Instead of Sappers: U.S. Conducts Sandhills Tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:48:11 UTC
03:48:11 KST

The U.S. conducted tests of unmanned systems for mine clearance and drone interception as part of the Sandhills Project.
Participants in the tests reported on the progress of the trials in an interview with Defense Daily.
The 20th Engineer Brigade of the U.S. 18th Airborne Corps, which uses various UAVs and UGVs for engineering tasks, was involved in the exercises. On August 21, engineers tested the Safe Pro AI-based mine detection technology on an UGV in conjunction with a Black Widow UAV to assess routes and determine the boundaries of minefields.
“In particular, when it comes to operations that are not fully autonomous, we want to ensure that a human remains in the control loop. Before using any lethal means, such as detonating a linear charge, we want to ensure that a human confirms such an action,” said Colonel Jeff Burgess, commander of the 20th Engineer Brigade.
Spotlight AI technology, which uses geospatial fusion of drone imagery, detects and identifies the type of munition that might be hidden from human sight.
According to the developer, the system analyzes a database of approximately 3 million images and identifies specific types from among 150 varieties of munitions.
After identifying threats, the AI plans optimal routes for the user.
The system is capable of operating not only on servers but also on standalone devices, such as laptops.
According to Safe Pro Group, AI is actively used for humanitarian and agricultural missions in Ukraine.
In addition, the 18th Airborne Corps tested the Bumblebee V2 interceptor drone, equipped with AI for autonomous identification and targeting of aerial targets.
These interceptors are stored in a special “Bee Hive” container equipped for remote drone launch. In particular, an Ford F-250-based UGV, equipped with an Edda turret featuring an automatic shotgun for countering UAVs, was spotted during the tests.
The turret-equipped platform successfully neutralized several drones with a diameter of approximately 7 inches at distances ranging from 10 to 100 meters.
The U.S. Army notes that such systems will be used to support engineering teams clearing minefields, barbed wire, and other obstacles.
The U.S. Army conducted the Sandhills project to integrate operational units, government agencies, and industrial companies, and to gather feedback from service members to establish a framework for engineering solutions to be carried out by unmanned system operators.
As part of the first Sandhills exercise in 2024, an experiment was conducted to use robotic, autonomous systems to breach obstacles during large-scale combat operations.

Here's why America's debt binge should worry Australians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:46:36 UTC
03:46:36 KST

US government debt surges to $US40 trillion and could lead to higher rates in Australia
Interest rates are rising a world away, but the ripple effects may soon spread to Australian shores.
World debt markets are groaning under the weight of elevated inflation, ballooning US government debt, and tech companies spending big on AI data centres.
There's basically too much demand for money, and the cost of that funding is leading to higher interest rates.
Australian borrowers are in the firing line because the cost of fixed-rate mortgages is connected to US longer-term interest rates.
So why are we talking about bonds and debt now?
Earlier this month, two forces collided.
The first is America's national debt hitting a record high of $US40 trillion.
US debt has more than doubled in the past decade, reflecting years of heavy spending under both the Trump and Biden administrations.
The other factor is the US Treasury announcing it will buy back even more bonds than it usually does.
The bond buying, without getting into the nitty-gritty, is an effort to keep longer-term interest rates down.
Here's what's playing out and how it could affect you.
Why did the US debt hit $US40 trillion?
If we want to spend money we need to get a job and earn the cash first.
The US government, though, can issue bonds or IOUs if its spending exceeds its income through tax revenue.
If you have lots of deficits, or you keep spending more than you earn, you need to borrow more.
To fund its spending the US government, via its Treasury, has needed to borrow more than $US40 trillion from Wall Street, pension or superannuation funds, and other central banks.
So why does it matter that the debt keeps growing? Growing debt is a problem because money isn't free.
Indeed, money has become more expensive since the pandemic.
Several governments, including the US and Australia, flooded their countries with cash to keep businesses afloat, shoppers spending and workers from being sacked.
When borders were shut during the COVID-19 pandemic there was a surge in spending, which led to higher inflation.
Loading...
That inflation hasn't yet come back to levels policymakers are comfortable with.
So central banks, including Australia's Reserve Bank, raised interest rates to reduce overall levels of demand in the economy.
As inflation and interest rates remain elevated, it means anyone borrowing money is going to be on the hook.
Now the US government's annual interest bill is more than $US1 trillion, and it's only growing.
How bad is the global debt binge?
It's not just the US government mired in debt.
China's national debt recently surpassed 100 trillion yuan, or roughly $20.8 trillion.
Britain's debt is just shy of 3 trillion pounds, or just over $5.7 trillion.
Loading...
Australia's gross national debt has reached $1 trillion, which is small in comparison.
The easiest way to track how global financial markets feel about growing debt is looking at how they price it.
Basically, the more expensive it gets the riskier it's perceived to be.
The global so-called risk-free interest rate is the US 10-year Treasury bond.
It's supposedly risk-free because if you're going to lend anyone money for 10 years it's considered as safe as it gets with the US government.
It's currently tracking at about 4.7 per cent. For context, the 10-year rate hovered around the 2.5 per cent mark from 2010 to 2020.
Loading
The interest rate on the US 30-year Treasury bond is 5.2 per cent. That's when you lend your money to the American government for an even longer period of three decades.
"Whether the market looks to test [US Treasury Secretary Scott] Bessent and co and tries to push the 30-year Treasury yield through 5.3 per cent in the coming days or weeks remains to be seen," Pepperstone's Chris Weston wrote in a note to clients.
"But I think we can [rely on Mr Bessent's] determination to respond, and potentially upscale that response, and that's ultimately what the market will be looking for."
What could happen next?
The big picture here is that the global bond market is concerned that central banks like the US Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan and Bank of England do not have a handle on inflation.
I have no doubt you feel the associated pain when you do your shopping.
The debt market will continue to sell bonds in the meantime, which drives up the interest rates on those bonds and the yield on the investment.
The US administration stands poised, it seems, to counter any bond market sell-off with bond-buying of its own.
It's a clash of the Titans.
If the bond market wins, global interest rates — including those in Australia — will rise.
This will likely affect Australian fixed-rate mortgages, as opposed to variable-rate mortgage products, which are influenced by the Reserve Bank's cash rate.
Materially higher interest rates could also see big share market falls and much weaker global economic growth.
Loading...
If the financial firepower of the US government prevails, the status quo remains and debt keeps rising.
Either way, there is a lot at stake.
The next major test for global financial markets could be mid-September when the world's largest central bank, the Federal Reserve, meets to decide on interest rates.
"Long end Treasury yields have pushed to their highest levels in almost two decades this month as heavy fiscal supply, sticky inflation and a fresh spike in oil prices collide just weeks before the Federal Reserve's September 15–16 meeting," said Amundi's head of global fixed income for Asia, Rajesh Puri.
"Global equities have wobbled on the move, crude has rallied on renewed tension around the Strait of Hormuz, and gold has climbed as investors look for protection against fiscal and inflation risk."
There's clearly something in the air.

Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold Review: Better, Not Best
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:45:00 UTC
03:45:00 KST

Good camera. Slightly improved design. IP68 water and dust resistance. Qi2 25W wireless charging. Slick AI features and software.
TIRED
Significantly weaker specs than other Pro models. Comparatively chunky. $100 more than last year’s 10 Pro Fold.
The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a predictably iterative improvement over last year’s foldable, with slight upgrades to performance and the camera, but it comes with an unwelcome $100 price bump. The IP68 rating for water and dust resistance and the Qi2 25W support for faster magnetic charging are standouts in a category where Google is lagging, but it has never been known for its hardware. Software is where the company excels, and some folks will appreciate the unrivaled AI-infused software features.
Google is good at elevating its devices beyond the spec sheet, but the 11 Pro Fold is perilously close to the Pixel 11 on paper, a phone that’s less than half its price. Beyond the big unfolding screen and customizable rear LEDs, little else justifies the “Pro” tag. With Samsung’s fresh Fold8 form factor and a folding iPhone on the horizon, I’m not convinced Google has done enough to make this the foldable you drop $1,900 on.
Devil in the Details
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold doesn’t look different from the 10 Pro Fold, but Google has shaved off a fraction of a millimeter and 19 grams. Sadly, the 11 Pro Fold is still heavier and thicker (239 grams and 10.1 mm) than Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold8 (201 grams and 9.7 mm), the Fold8 Ultra (215 grams and 8.9 mm), and the Honor Magic V6 (219 grams and 8.75 mm, not sold in the US). That makes it a little trickier to handle, though the horizontal camera bar means less rocking than Samsung’s phones when they lie flat.
The double-camera module has had a makeover, so it looks less chunky, and the back is matte-textured glass that feels lovely. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold scores an impressive IP68 rating for water and dust resistance. That compares favorably to Samsung’s IP48 ratings, which means both can survive shallow submersion, but Google’s phone is dust-tight, whereas Samsung’s phones are at risk from fine dust and sand.
Photograph: Simon Hill
It’s a shame the Fold is only available in two colors: Obsidian, the color of my review unit, looks more like a dark matte gray than black, while Olive Green has a shinier gold frame.
I’m not a fan of Google’s asymmetrical design. With the Pixel 11 Pro Fold closed, there’s a curved corner cutout, and when you open the phone, the two halves have slightly different thicknesses. All folding phones still have a detectable fold line in the middle of the screen when you open them, but Google’s is among the most noticeable. Some folks won’t notice or care, but I’m the kind of guy who goes upstairs to turn the light on so the downstairs switches aren’t misaligned.
The fingerprint sensor in the power button always bugs me when I switch to a folding phone, because I have to pick it up to touch it and unlock the screen, rather than pressing on the screen like most phones. You do have face unlock with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and it works well provided there’s ample light, but it still doesn’t work in a dark room, which is still annoying.
You get two lovely, sharp OLED displays in the Pixel 11 Pro Fold: an 8-inch main screen and a 6.5-inch cover screen. Both push peak brightness to 3,600 nits, remaining legible in direct sunlight, and boast a variable refresh rate up to 120 Hz. They’re smooth, with rich colors, and I have nothing to complain about beyond that crease.
Pro Pretender
I’m not convinced the 11 Pro Fold earns the “Pro” in its title. It does have the new HiLight feature, a group of color LEDs in the camera module’s flash that light up different colors based on who is calling, or swirl through the rainbow while you chat to Gemini. It’s neat, if a little underbaked. It’s handy if you put your phone face down when you’re working or trying to relax, but it’s a very minor feature.
All the Pixels get the new Tensor G6 processor, and the Fold has 16 GB of RAM paired with 256 GB, 512 GB, or 1 TB of storage. Switching from the Pixel 10 Pro XL, it was mostly smooth sailing. But it froze a couple of times in split-screen view in Gmail and after launching an app on the outer display, then unfolding the inner display.
The 11 Pro Fold actually has more in common with the regular Pixel 11, because it misses out on the high-end camera in its Pro siblings. Folding phones struggle to match flagships on camera specs because of form-factor limitations, and they must include two front-facing cameras (one for open and one for closed).
Photograph: Simon Hill
You get the same 48-megapixel main camera and 10.8-megapixel telephoto for 5X optical zoom as on the Pixel 11, but the Fold drops to a 10.5-megapixel ultrawide. The main camera is excellent in a wide range of scenarios, and I used the telephoto lens a lot. The 5X zoom produces sharp, detailed shots, though things get a little fuzzy if you push up to the maximum digital zoom capability at 30X. The ultrawide is a very obvious weak spot, producing relatively grainy images, though it doubles as a macro lens for decent, if slightly distorted, close-ups. The 10-megapixel front-facing cameras are passable for selfies.
The 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL cameras are superior across the board (50-MP main, 48-MP ultrawide, 48-MP telephoto, and 42-MP front-facing). They also boast instant Night Sight, 120X digital zoom, and better video capture. That said, I took some great shots with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold; its camera results compare favorably to other foldables, and a good telephoto is more useful than an ultrawide.
I like the new camera tricks: Camera Looks lets you define your preferred style, dictating contrast and colors; Magic Capture makes it easy to get video and photos from an event without focusing on the viewfinder; and Creator Suite will delight content creators with some useful tools, like a built-in teleprompter. You can even use Circle to Search in the camera app to get info on anything you circle without snapping a shot first.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, main camera
Unfortunately, there’s one significant area where the Fold looks amateur, and that’s battery life. The 4,806-mAh battery is smaller than the one in last year’s 10 Pro Fold (5,015 mAh). While that downgrade is mitigated by greater power efficiency in the new Tensor chip, Google suggests 24 hours for the 11 Pro Fold, compared to 30-plus for the other Pixel 11 models.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Compared to a folding phone with a silicon-carbon battery, like the Honor Magic V6, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold lacks stamina, but it shouldn’t be an issue for most folks. The battery lost 6 percent in an hour of video streaming, and an hour of casual gaming claimed 9 percent. It will get you through an average day easily, but when I pushed the Fold with a lot of photography and graphically demanding gaming, I had to engage the battery saver before bedtime.
There’s 30-watt wired charging, but you should definitely embrace Qi2 wireless charging with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold as it tops out at 25 watts and is so much more convenient. The magnets stick firmly and ensure perfect alignment. It’s nice to see Qi2 25W in a folding phone, since many competitors haven’t even adopted it in their regular flagships yet.
Software Save
I’m a big fan of Google’s Pixel-exclusive software features. Call Screen saves me from telemarketers daily; I use Now Playing often to add songs to my playlist, and several new features may just persuade you to board the Pixel train. My colleague Julian Chokkattu talked about Rambler in his Pixel 11 Pro review as a more conversational voice-to-text message-drafting tool. I also like that AI overviews pop up contextually to save you a step, offering a Calendar link when someone texts to suggest a meet-up, for example, though it does mean granting Gemini access.
But one of the most useful new features for the Fold is Bubbles. With this, you can keep a floating circular profile picture from an open chat and open or minimize it with a tap. It’s not a new idea (Facebook Chat Heads did it more than a decade ago), but it lets you get on with other things without leaving the chat, potentially floating above two apps in split-screen mode. It also minimizes to a bar at the bottom right when you’re using the main screen.
With folding phones, people always talk about the ability to watch movies and play games on a big screen, but their real strength is multitasking. Message apps can show the list and a preview simultaneously. You can read a café review and check the location on a map, or watch a movie while you skim your emails.
Photograph: Simon Hill
That said, many apps still aren’t optimized for folding phones, so they can look clownishly big or occasionally obscure buttons. As mentioned, I ran into freezing issues and had to restart apps more than once. Sometimes, when you switch from the cover display to the big screen, it fails to scale up, and you might get a prompt to restart the game for full-screen view, as I did with Bloons TD 6.
Foldable newcomers should also beware of the big black bars. You must rotate the opened Fold for maximum screen viewing, but virtually nothing is made for this weird, almost square aspect ratio. You get more room when browsing something like Netflix, but start a video and you’re not much better off than with a large flagship phone like the Pixel 11 Pro XL.
Games fare a little better, and the 11 Pro Fold is great for titles like Clash of Clans, point-and-click adventures like Machinarium, and tower defense games like Bloons TD 6. It’s also a good option for older games via emulators, but for anything too demanding, like Wuthering Waves or Genshin Impact, you can expect dropped frames galore.
The other reason I find myself unfurling the big screen is to read. For browsing the web, doomscrolling Reddit, or, best of all, reading an ebook, a folding phone is a big step up from a regular phone screen. Whether it’s worth the premium you pay is debatable. It’s a little too easy to forget to use the big screen in daily life.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Photograph: Simon Hill
Folding phones have been around for years, but they still feel a bit gimmicky. For folks who think they’re a tough sell when they can get both a higher-spec flagship phone and a tablet for the price, it’s worth laying hands on one to get a feel for the experience. Foldables may not be an inevitable next step for phones, but there’s a reason they’ve carved out a niche.
The 11 Pro Fold starts at $1,899; that’s $100 more than last year’s 10 Pro Fold, but it doesn’t have a storage bump to soften the blow, as the Google Pixel 11 ($899) does. It also lacks the Pro features you’ll find in the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL ($1,099 and $1,299). If you’re set on a foldable, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 and Fold8 Ultra ($1,900 and $2,100) demand consideration, and if you don’t live in the US, check out the Honor Magic V6 ($2,100). There are other options and form factors in our best folding phones, but rumors of a folding iPhone persist, so you might want to wait and see what that looks like.
Simon Hill is a senior writer for WIRED and has been testing and writing about technology for around 20 years. You can find his previous work at Business Insider, Reviewed, TechRadar, Android Authority, USA Today, Digital Trends, and many other places. Syria’s economy poised for improvement after US sanctions removal
Removal of US sanctions offers Syria a chance to fully rejoin the global financial system after years of isolation.
Syria’s removal by the United States from its “state sponsors of terrorism” list clears one of the last major hurdles to the country’s integration into the global financial system, analysts tell Al Jazeera.
On July 8, US President Donald Trump announced he was formally notifying Congress of his intention to rescind Syria’s designation, which had been in place since 1979. A 45-day congressional review period passed on Saturday, and the US completed the formal delisting on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump’s latest wave of Iran sanctions: Which 60 entities are targeted?
- list 2 of 3France, Saudi Arabia agree on $7bn theme park project near Paris
- list 3 of 3US removes Syria from ‘state sponsor of terrorism’ list
While Washington had already lifted many of the restrictions preventing transactions with Syrian banks, the “terrorism” designation continued to carry additional financial and trade restrictions, and Syria’s removal will give the country – still struggling to pick itself up after a nearly 14-year war – a badly needed economic boost.
“The momentum is great for this announcement, and it was the last main barrier to banks reconnecting [with the global community],” Vittorio Maresca di Serracapriola, sanctions lead analyst for Karam Shaar Advisory, a consulting company with a focus on the political economy of the Middle East, told Al Jazeera.
Longstanding sanctions
Syria was first designated by the US as a “state sponsor of terrorism” in 1979 under the presidency of Hafez al-Assad.
The country was originally placed on the list for its support of Palestinian armed groups. Syrian-US relations were later strained when the US invaded Iraq in 2003, just a few years after Hafez died and his son Bashar succeeded him. Washington pulled out of its embassy in Syria in 2012, a year after Syrians rose up against the al-Assad regime, which responded with brutal suppression and violence, leading to war.
During the conflict, Syria became increasingly isolated from the global community as more international sanctions were placed on the regime.
When the al-Assad regime finally collapsed in December 2024, a new government, including members of former rebel groups, took its place. One of its first priorities was trying to reintegrate Syria into the regional and international community by removing the sanctions, which has largely been accomplished.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, the former rebel group he led, were also previously under US sanctions, which have been removed.
While Syria has moved on from its isolation since the fall of al-Assad, its economy remains weak with almost 90 percent of the population living below the poverty line.
“For nearly five decades, Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism resulted in severe restrictions on financing and exports and contributed to significant hesitation and overcompliance among banks and investors who were reluctant to engage with Syria, fearing secondary sanctions,” Obai Kurd Ali, a Syrian expert with the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, told Al Jazeera.
“People in Syria are suffering from severe poverty and a deteriorating economic situation with decent living standards becoming unaffordable day after day,” he added. “For Syrians, any step that may lead to better living conditions is worth celebrating, and removing [the] designation is not only one such step but also one of the final major actions toward dismantling the complex web of US sanctions that isolated Syria for so long.”
‘Great momentum’ for Syria’s economy
Maresca di Serracapriola said the decision to lift Syria’s designation reduces legal risks for banks working on Syria-related financing or transactions and allows US foreign assistance to Syria.
“The removal of restrictions on US foreign assistance and government contracting has the potential to open additional channels for development and reconstruction support,” he said, adding that “the biggest impact will likely be on financial flows and investment.”
International banks would often cite the designation as a reason against working with banks in Syria.
“The timing of the announcement is important because the Central Bank of Syria reactivated its account at the Federal Reserve Bank in New York in March, and recently, the World Bank has approved a $100m grant for financial sector modernisation in Syria,” Maresca di Serracapriola said.
Ibrahim Kochaji, a Syrian banking and economic expert, called the lifting of the sanctions “a pivotal moment in the trajectory of the national economy” but said it was “not an immediate remedy” for the country’s deep economic struggles.
Kochaji said any resolution to Syria’s issues requires “a long path of reforms and measures” that would be bolstered by stability and sound governance.
Kurd Ali agreed. “The transitional government must seize this opportunity to put its own house in order,” he said. “Good governance, transparency, robust anticorruption measures and meaningful judicial reform are essential to regain investors’ confidence and ensure that investment contributes to a sustainable and inclusive recovery that puts people’s priorities at its heart.”
Impacts on daily life
The fall of the al-Assad regime was met with jubilation across Syria. And many Syrians still speak about the improvements to their day-to-day lives since the regime’s demise.
But increasingly, Syrians are expressing frustration at the soaring cost of energy and the stuttering local economy.
Kochaji said the removal of sanctions would impact Syrians daily lives but the impact may not be as immediate as some may hope.
“The realistic answer is that the impact will be gradual, but it can become tangible if the government manages the transition wisely,” he said, adding that if managed correctly, production and transportation costs could decrease and new job opportunities could develop, among other potential benefits.
While many of the main economic barriers have been removed, analysts said they believe Syria’s banking sector is not guaranteed to automatically rebound.
“International banks and investors will still look at Syria’s antimoney-laundering and counter-financing of terrorism framework and overall risk environment, also general governance and political stability,” Maresca di Serracapriola said. “So that will not necessarily shift the picture entirely with respect to banking.”

SRINAGAR: Jammu & Kashmir is grappling with power shortages and unscheduled outages after key hydroelectric projects, including the 450MW Baglihar stage I and the Salal project, were shut for silt-flushing operations. Baglihar stage-I in Ramban district has remained non-operational for a week, with accumulated silt at its gates delaying restoration work.Officials said desilting work at Baglihar stages I and II and the Salal project began on Aug 18. While Baglihar stage II resumed generation on Aug 22, stage I is yet to restart. Salal is expected to resume operations on Tuesday.
The prolonged shutdown has widened the region’s power deficit. Jammu & Kashmir’s peak electricity demand stands at about 2,500MW in summer and 3,000MW in winter. With both Baglihar units largely unavailable for most of the past week, Jammu & Kashmir faced a shortfall of nearly 900MW.Built on the Chenab river, Baglihar stages I and II are among Jammu & Kashmir’s key power sources. Following the disruption, the power department is exploring alternative arrangements to bridge the supply gap.The crisis comes amid criticism of the Omar Abdullah-led govt over rising electricity tariffs. From Sept 1, power consumers in Jammu & Kashmir will face a 6.83% tariff hike.

Country Music Icon Dolly Parton Dies at 80
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:34:54 UTC
03:34:54 KST

Dolly Parton, the country music legend behind hits like “Jolene” and “9 to 5” as well as actress, businesswoman, fashion icon, and philanthropist, died on Tuesday. She was 80.
Her death was announced in a video featuring her nephew, Bryan Seaver, that was shared on Parton’s social media accounts. Seaver didn’t disclose a cause of death in the video. He said that his aunt “has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by” her loved ones, including her husband Carl Dean, who died last year, as well as her parents and “countless others who have watched her and longed for her to meet them in the heavens.”
“She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history,” Seaver said. “My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you. She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD, and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family whether you liked it or not.”
Read More: Dolly Parton Loved Us All, Darlin'
A statement shared on Parton’s social media page said Parton “died peacefully today in Nashville.” The statement referenced her decades-long legacy in both music and philanthropy. It also said that a small, private funeral service will be held for Parton’s immediate family, per her wishes, while it encouraged fans to share tributes to Parton online.
Parton’s family also asked that, instead of flowers, people who wish to express their condolences donate to Parton’s Imagination Library, a program that mails books to children for free. Parton founded the initiative in 1995 in her home state of Tennessee, and it has since expanded to other states and even internationally, donating hundreds of millions of books worldwide.
“I am as proud of the Imagination Library,” Parton told PBS News in 2020, “as I ever will be, anything I ever do for the rest of my life.”
Health issues persist
Last year, fans expressed concerns about the state of Parton’s health after she announced that she would need to postpone upcoming shows in Las Vegas, which she later canceled, because of “some health challenges” that she was dealing with. Parton said that her doctors told her she needed to have “a few procedures,” which she didn’t elaborate on, but she sought to allay any concerns.
“Don’t worry about me quittin’ the business because God hasn’t said anything about stopping yet,” Parton said in a post in September. “But, I believe He is telling me to slow down right now so I can be ready for more big adventures with all of you.”
Amid growing online speculation over her health, Parton posted a video in October, captioned “I ain’t dead yet!” in which she said, “I know lately, everybody thinks that I am sicker than I am. Do I look sick to you? I’m working hard here! Anyway, I wanted to put everybody’s mind at ease.”
She said in the video that when her husband was sick, and after he died, “I didn't take care of myself, so I let a lot of things go that I should’ve been taking care of. So anyway when I got around to it, the doctors said, ‘We need to take care of this, we need to take care of that.’ Nothing major.” She added that she had to cancel some appearances so that she could be near her home and Vanderbilt University Medical Center, which was where she was having “a few treatments here and there.”
In May, Parton shared another video update on her health, in which she said that it would take her more time to be ready to perform on stage again “because some of the meds and treatments make me a little bit swimmy-headed.”
“The good news,” she said at the time, “I’m responding really well to meds and treatments, and I’m improving every day.” She went on to say that she has “always had problems” with kidney stones but that, in recent years, her immune and digestive systems “got all out of whack” and her doctors were “working real hard on rebuilding and strengthening those.” She added that her doctors assured her that her health issues were treatable.
Just four days before her death, Parton told PEOPLE in a statement: “As I’ve shared in video messages throughout the past year, I am dealing with some health issues that I just didn’t pay attention to when I was watching over Carl.”
She reiterated that she hates to cancel things, such as her Las Vegas residency, but admitted, “I just couldn’t do the shows at the level I would want them to be, and in the way that I know my fans would expect them to be. I definitely plan to do special performances in the future, but I won’t tour anymore like I used to.” Parton added that she was in the early stages of developing “avatar performances” that would allow her to put on a show without having to “show up in person.”
“Seriously, though,” Parton told PEOPLE, “even though I’m still healin’, I’m still workin’! You know me — as I’ve often said — I’ve dreamed myself into a corner and I still have so many things I want to achieve, so I’m gonna keep on working as long as I can to see everything come to life.”
Tributes pour in
Tributes for the country music icon began pouring in on Tuesday afternoon, including from U.S. President Donald Trump, who called Parton “one of the greatest Country singers.” The President said that, in Parton’s honor, he was ordering American flags across the country to be lowered for a week, starting at 6 p.m. that evening.
“This is a true loss for millions of people,” Trump said on Truth Social. “There has never been anyone like her, and never will.”
Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee said in a social media post that she and her husband were “absolutely heartbroken and saddened to hear of the passing of our friend.”
“Dolly’s life and career are forever woven into Tennessee’s music, culture, and history,” Blackburn said. “Her extraordinary talent, generosity, and love for the Volunteer State touched hearts around the world and will continue to inspire generations to come. Tennessee will forever be grateful for Dolly.”
Other politicians mourned the loss of Parton as well, remembering not only her contribution to the music industry but also her philanthropic legacy and advocacy.
Former President Bill Clinton said in a post on X that he and his wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, “were big fans” of Parton and “will always be grateful for the music and the memories,” including seeing her perform in 1974. “Dolly Parton was one of a kind—a great songwriter and performer who told the stories of everyday Americans with honesty, humility, and heart,” Clinton said. “She rose high from her East Tennessee roots and never forgot where she came from. And she always believed in giving back, especially in her efforts to promote literacy.”
Former Vice President Kamala Harris called Parton “a true American icon” and listed her many accolades in a social media post. “All at once she was kind, modest, and funny,” Harris said. “With her music, her philanthropy, and her style, Dolly was one of one.”
“Dolly Parton was one of the great entertainers of our era,” Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont said on X. “She was not only a talented musician & songwriter, but a lifelong philanthropist and advocate for literacy, education, LGBTQ+ rights, healthcare and disaster relief. Her music and humanity touched millions. She will be sorely missed.”
Education Secretary Linda McMahon said, “America lost an icon today. Dolly Parton embodied so much of what is possible in America - a remarkable singer, songwriter, entertainer, businesswoman, and philanthropist.” McMahon added that Parton’s “greatest legacy extends far beyond her music,” praising and linking to Parton’s Imagination Library.
Harry Potter author J.K. Rowling called Parton’s Imagination Library “the best contribution to child literacy ever made by a celebrity.” Rowling added in a post on X, “Our paths crossed once, in the 90s, backstage at a talk show, and I was completely tongue-tied and starstruck. RIP Dolly. You were a complete, irreplaceable one-off.”
Conservative media personality Megyn Kelly was among many who remarked on Parton’s broad appeal. “Dolly Parton seemed as close to total goodness as any mere mortal could come,” Kelly said in a post on X. “She united us all in our love and admiration for her and, now, in mourning her.”
Many musicians also shared tributes for Parton.
Fellow octogenarian entertainer and friend Dionne Warwick posted on X a photo with Parton and said, “I will certainly miss her laugher, jokes and her being. Rest well and in total peace my friend. My heart is heavy.”
Country singer and actress Reba McEntire honored her friend in a statement, thanking her “for all the wonderful things [she] did for us here on earth.”
“We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang,” McEntire said. “Thank you, Lord, for Dolly. She’s gonna have a blast in heaven singing all her favorite songs with all her family and friends who have gone on before her.”
“Dolly Parton had a way of making everyone feel special, and seen, and welcomed, and as if you were old friends,” Kelly Clarkson said in a social media post. “I will miss her heart and her voice as I am sure millions will. What an incredible gift and talent she was and still is with an amazing catalogue of art she has left behind for all of us.”
Kacey Musgraves shared multiple posts on X about the news, saying in one that she was glad Parton was reunited with her late husband and summing up her sadness in another: “The world feels a lot less sparkly all of a sudden.”
‘Head honcho’ of heaven
Parton’s co-stars from her first feature film, 9 to 5 (1980), for which she also provided the Academy Award-nominated and chart-topping theme song, also paid their respects to Parton after her death.
Lily Tomlin called Parton “The Great Harmonizer of Humanity” in a post on X, while Jane Fonda shared a lengthy tribute on Instagram.
“I know that millions are mourning and I want to say this – more than anyone I have ever known, Dolly will always be with us because she was so present, so powerful, so generous and playful that she is woven into all our lives and hearts forever,” Fonda said.
“I never knew anyone like her,” Fonda added. “She was simultaneously a naughty, playful southern gal from the hollows of Tennessee and a deep, soulful thinker who could see through people right down to their true selves. She was many things…lyricist, songstress, player of many instruments, writer, prankster, visionary, loyal friend […] She was the voluptuous embodiment of empathy. That’s something of hers she’d want us all to take with us.”
“To her gay and trans fans,” Fonda continued, “I want you to know that she loved you. You know that without me telling you. She loved all her fans and they are legion. And you know she doesn’t want y’all to mourn now. Dress up and celebrate her spirit. But first, watch the final episode of Grace and Frankie,” Fonda said, referring to her Netflix show with Tomlin that concluded in 2022 with a guest appearance by Parton, “where she’s an Angel, the head honcho working class angel in Heaven.”

Legendary US country music singer Dolly Parton dies at 80
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:34:33 UTC
03:34:33 KST

Efe Özkan
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Legendary American Country musician Dolly Parton, whose decades-long career produced hits including “Jolene” and “I Will Always Love You,” has died at the age of 80, her family announced Tuesday.
The announcement was made through Parton’s social media accounts in a video posted by her nephew, Bryan Seaver, on behalf of the Parton family. No cause of death was disclosed.
US President Donald Trump released a statement on Truth Social that said, “In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM. Rest in Peace, Dolly! The World loves you.”
Parton had faced health problems in recent months and was forced to cancel appearances and postpone her planned Las Vegas residency. Days before her death, she told fans she was recovering from health issues and responding well to medication and treatment.
Parton’s career, rise to icon-status
Born in 1946 in Sevierville, Tennessee, Parton grew up in a poor family and began performing at a young age. She was singing on local radio by 10 and recorded her first single, “Puppy Love,” at 13, the same year she made her debut at Nashville’s Grand Ole Opry.
She moved to Nashville in 1964 and quickly made a name as a songwriter, with other artists recording her compositions. Her profile grew further after she joined Porter Wagoner’s television variety show, where she performed from 1967 to 1974.
Parton went on to establish herself as a solo artist, releasing some of her most enduring songs in the 1970s, including “Jolene” and “I Will Always Love You,” which was later transformed into a global hit by Whitney Houston.
Her career extended well beyond music. She starred in films including 9 to 5 and Steel Magnolias and became equally known for her philanthropic work, particularly through the Imagination Library, which provides free books to children.
Across a career spanning more than six decades, Parton sold more than 100 million records and received 11 Grammy Awards, alongside numerous other accolades. She was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

- Watson was detained at a protest holding a sign demanding impeachment, conviction, and removal of Trump and Vance.
- He is charged under Article 88 for contempt towards officials, with the Air Force confirming pre-trial confinement and due process rights.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - A US military service member who called for President Donald Trump and Vice-President J.D. Vance to be impeached is facing charges under the military justice system, his lawyer and the Air Force said on Aug 25.
The active-duty officer, Major Jason Watson, denounced Trump and Vance in July for actions including going to war with Iran without congressional authorisation, according to a video of the protest event posted online.
In the video, the US Capitol Police can be seen detaining Watson, who held a protest sign calling for their impeachment, conviction and removal.
Watson's lawyer said in a statement that the airman would face charges under three articles, including Article 88 - a rarely used provision which accuses him of contempt towards officials.
“Major Watson acted knowing the risks to his career and his liberty,” said Christopher Mutimer, counsel for Watson.
“It is my hope that other Americans who feel powerless in this moment will take some measure of courage from his willingness to speak and to stand by his convictions,” Mutimer said.
The Air Force confirmed Watson had been charged and said he would continue to be held in pre-trial confinement and be afforded the right to due process.
Laws governing US military service members place restrictions on their political activities, particularly while in uniform.
Article 88 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice prohibits officers from using “contemptuous words against the President, the Vice-President, Congress” and other US representatives. REUTERS

India and China to continue to seek political settlement of border issue
India and China agreed to continue to seek a political settlement of their border dispute in talks between top officials held in Beijing on Tuesday.
Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, the designated special representatives for the border talks mechanism, “had a candid and in-depth exchange of views on the India-China boundary question, and agreed to continue their work in seeking a political settlement of the boundary question in the context of their overall and long-term interests,” the Indian Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
It said the two sides expressed satisfaction at the steady resumption of people-to-people and cross-border exchanges, including the ongoing Kailash Manasarovar pilgrimage and resumption of border trade through the Himalayan passes.
The special representatives noted the progress made in implementing the consensus reached between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Kazan, Russia on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in October 2024, and again in Tianjin, China in August 2025 on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit.
ICYMI: Doval, Wang Yi Hold 25th Round Of India-China Boundary Talks 
New Delhi and Beijing agreed to continue working towards a “fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable” settlement of their boundary question, while stressing the importance of maintaining peace along the border.… pic.twitter.com/L0jbSFQcjd
Kazan was the first formal bilateral meeting between Modi and Xi in four years, since a skirmish in the Ladakh region of the Himalayas in 2020 left 20 Indian soldiers and at least four Chinese soldiers dead.
At Kazan, Modi and Xi agreed to use the special representatives mechanism and foreign minister dialogues to seek solutions to the border question and maintain peace in border areas.
The Beijing talks were held under the strategic guidance of Modi and Xi and in a constructive and forward-looking spirit, the statement said, adding that India highlighted the importance of maintaining peace and tranquility in the border areas for the continued development and progress of bilateral relations.
Doval and Wang also discussed bilateral, regional, and international issues of mutual interest, as the two neighbors prepare for this year’s SCO summit next week in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan and the BRICS summit next month in New Delhi.
Xi is expected to attend the BRICS meeting with a large delegation, according to reports.
Doval also called on Chinese Vice President Han Zheng before the special representative talks.

Economic war against Iran could end in defeat for US allies — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:32:01 UTC
03:32:01 KST

LONDON, August 25. /TASS/. Iran possesses greater capacity to inflict damage on energy sectors of the United States and its allies in the Persian Gulf than vice versa, Jorge Leon, Rystad Energy’s senior vice president and head of geopolitical analysis, said in a comment to TASS.
"The biggest oil-market risk may not be the [US] sanctions themselves, but Iran’s response to them. Tehran has threatened to treat countries supporting the US campaign as participants in the war and has again raised the prospect of preventing oil from leaving the Persian Gulf. This creates an important asymmetry for the oil market: there may be relatively little additional Iranian oil left for [US] sanctions to remove, but Iran still has considerable capacity to disrupt everybody else’s exports," he explained.
Meanwhile, Washington’s statements appear tougher than its actual actions now, Leon noted. "The actual announcement came across as much less dramatic than anticipated, with a wide gap between the rhetoric and the substance, at least going by the initial comments. What we have seen so far looks much more like an expansion of the existing sanctions regime than a fundamentally new economic weapon," he said.
According to the expert, "what matters now is not the announcement itself, but whether China complies and whether Iran retaliates." "The real question now is how aggressively Washington is prepared to enforce secondary sanctions against Iran’s remaining trading partners. China is the key. Iranian crude exports have already fallen sharply because of the blockade, and Beijing is essentially the only significant buyer left. Unless China materially reduces purchases further, the additional impact on Iranian oil revenues could be relatively limited," he said.
"Washington is trying to turn the military blockade into a much broader economic blockade. But after decades of sanctions, Iran has developed a highly resilient survival economy," Leon added. "More economic pain does not necessarily translate into political capitulation," he concluded.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced earlier that Washington planned to sharply tighten its unilateral sanctions regime against Iran, aiming to completely block Tehran’s revenue sources. The US would be prepared to impose secondary sanctions on any countries refusing to comply with new restrictive measures against Iran, Bessent said. He also threatened such nations with a loss of access to the dollar.
On August 24, the US administration added 48 legal entities, 24 individuals, and six oil tankers to its sanctions list against Iran. Citizens and companies from Azerbaijan, Greece, India, Iran, China, Malaysia, the Marshall Islands, the UAE, Singapore, Turkey, Ukraine, France, and Switzerland were blacklisted.

Trump goes all in on Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, as primary losses pile up

South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham staved off a challenge from Rep. Ralph Norman in the state's Senate primary runoff election, and with the help of President Donald Trump's endorsement will advance to November's general election.
Graham — the sister of Sen. Lindsey Graham, whose seat she was appointed to fill after he died unexpectedly in July — was leading Norman by 4 percentage points when the Associated Press called the race.
She'll face Democrat Annie Andrews in November's general election. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter labels the race "Solid R." Lindsey Graham was favored to win reelection before his death.
The race was a test of Trump's power of the party, as he threw his full support behind Graham. Trump, the de facto head of the party, has traditionally played kingmaker, but has suffered a series of recent losses.
Graham and Norman are both Trump allies. But Norman, a hard-line member of the House Freedom Caucus, found himself crosswise with Trump on occasion, in part owing to his initial support for former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley in the 2024 GOP presidential primaries. Norman also has a tendency to raise fiscal concerns about some of the president's priorities, at times straining his relationship with the president.
Trump throughout this election cycle has targeted fellow Republican lawmakers who have opposed him or his policies.
Graham, who has a brief political track record, has enjoyed Trump's enthusiastic support since the days after her brother's unexpected death.. Trump, who had a close relationship with Lindsey Graham, traveled to South Carolina to campaign with Graham last week and held a tele-rally for her on Monday.
″[T]here is nobody better to honor the legacy of her beloved brother, Lindsey. Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life, and has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina," Trump posted to TruthSocial on Monday.
Graham, who has never been elected to office but was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster in July to serve out the remainder of her brother's term, came into Tuesday on somewhat shaky ground. She suffered an embarrassing moment in a debate with Norman last week.
Asked to comment on the importance of Taiwan to U.S. interests, Graham copped that she was "not that informed on national security," raising questions about her fitness for the job. Graham has since defended her performance, arguing during an appearance on Fox News that she doesn't "speak politician."
Norman, who launched an unsuccessful bid for South Carolina governor earlier this year, seized on the moment, casting himself as the proven conservative in the race.
"My opponent is unknown. She's being backed by the Washington establishment," Norman said in a recent appearance on Fox News. "She's a propped-up candidate. You could tell that during the debates. This is an important job. There is no training on the job that you can effectively do."
The stakes were high for Trump, some of whose picks in South Carolina, as well as other parts of the country, have fallen short of late.
Trump in May endorsed South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette in the GOP primary for governor, though he eventually co-endorsed state Attorney General Alan Wilson, who bested Evette in a runoff in June. GOP lawmakers in the South Carolina legislature also dealt a blow to Trump in May when they scuttled his push for partisan mid-decade redistricting.
Elsewhere, too, Trump's once-powerful endorsement has come up short. Rep. Randy Feenstra, R-Iowa, in June lost to Zach Lahn in the state's GOP gubernatorial primary, despite notching support from Trump.
A Trump-endorsed candidate lost this month in Wyoming's Republican gubernatorial primary. And two candidates Trump had backed for the House in Florida — Rep. Cory Mills and Catalina Lauf — lost their respective primaries earlier this month.
In total, 10 Trump-endorsed candidates have lost their races this election cycle, equal to the total number of Trump-backed candidates who lost in 2018, 2020 and 2024 primaries combined, according to a CNN analysis.

Is this movie high art or dangerous filth? It took Australia decades to decide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Is Salò high art or dangerous filth? It took Australia decades to decide
There's a new Halloween game coming out next month, but Australians and New Zealanders hoping to cosplay as Michael Myers may be disappointed.
It's because Halloween: The Game has been "refused classification" by the Australian Classification Board, not because of the presence of a violent killer, but because in the game the consumption of cannabis can alert players to Myers's location.
In a statement, the Australian Classification Board gave its reasons: "Games containing illicit drug use related to incentives or rewards cannot be accommodated within the R18+ classification category and must be Refused Classification under the Guidelines."
This means the game cannot legally be sold in Australia, and it's not the first piece of media to be caught in Australia's classification net.
Existing in some form for more than 100 years, the Australian Classification Board (ACB) consists of a director, deputy and a revolving set of board members who assess every film, video game and publication submitted for public distribution against legally enshrined classification guidelines.
The ACB does not directly censor media, but its decisions can lead studios and production companies to alter their product.
When a piece of media receives a restrictive classification or is refused classification in Australia, studios and distributors have two basic options: Accept it's been restricted, or alter the content and reapply to the ACB in the hopes of receiving a new rating.
That's what happened with Greta Gerwig's Oscar-winning drama Ladybird back in 2018 when the ACB gave it a MA15+ rating for "brief strong nudity", restricting it to those over 15 — not exactly ideal for a coming-of-age movie.
So, distributor Universal cut the offending scene — a fleeting shot of a penis on the back of the magazine — and the ACB agreed to a lowered M rating.
"Neurotic" is how professor and author of The Money Shot: Cinema, Sin and Censorship Jane Mills describes Australia's relationship with media classification.
"There's all these euphemisms and mealy-mouthed sort of words used to describe what is very paternalistic at its least bad," she tells ABC Arts.
"But at its worst, I think it's denying people the right to know and make informed judgement, which is the basis of democracy."
Innocence and ignorance
Halloween: The Game is far from the first piece of media cast out into Australia's refused-classification wasteland.
In 2003, a dozen police officers raided Sydney's Balmain Town Hall and arrested five people, including movie critic Margaret Pomeranz, over an illegal screening of Larry Clark's Ken Park.
The psychological thriller had been refused classification over "actual sex, sexualised violence and what appeared to be child sex abuse". It remains illegal to stream, rent, buy or screen Ken Park in Australia.
"I think there's often a confusion between innocence and ignorance. We keep people ignorant in the interest of keeping them innocent," Mills says.
"People should be allowed to see, hear, read what they want when we consider that they're of an age to make that decision. One might not necessarily like what one hears or reads, but the right of someone to write it or speak it, I think, is a crucial thing to protect.
"It makes us different from fascist countries."
Pier Paolo Pasolini's Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom, has one of the most storied censorship journeys in Australian film history. Banned shortly after its Australian release in 1976, the controversial political art horror was submitted for appeal in 1993 and rated R for theatrical release, turning the film into a political football as it bounced around Australian cinemas.
A campaign to have the film re-banned, led by Christian figureheads like then-National Party senator Julian McGauran, succeeded in 1998, and the movie was once again refused classification. After another failed distributor application in 2008, a 2010 DVD release was submitted again, this time with 176 minutes of 'contextual material'. The application was successful, drawing the ire of McGauran and the Australian Christian Lobby.
Forty years after it was banished from Australia, Salò is set to be screened as a centrepiece of Sydney's Festival of Dangerous Ideas' inaugural Dangerous Films slate.
"Being the first year, we had to do Salò because it's the one that, if people go, dangerous ideas, banned films, films that are really hard to watch — that's the one," festival director Danielle Harvey tells the ABC.
"It's been quite the journey for me even to be able to watch it, to know exactly what I'm going to be subjecting people to.
"Subjecting, I think, is the right word because it is unwatchable and everyone should watch it."
Shock and awe
Salò's infamous scenes of rape, abuse, coprophilia, violence and murder, along with the furious debate around its legality, have seen it detached from the deep political analysis lurking beneath its cruelty.
Set in 1944 in fascist-controlled Italy, the film centres on four wealthy, powerful men — the Duke, the Bishop, the Magistrate and the President — as they collect lower-class victims upon which to unleash their reckless depravity.
"It's not just shocking for its own sake. That's the first thing. It's a very serious argument about power, about fascism, about consumerism, and it puts the audience in a really uncomfortable position to get them to think about these things," Harvey says.
"There is no titillation to this. It is absolute horror, but horror because it is talking about what humans let happen to other humans, and that is fascism, that is consumerism."
Mills, who edited a 2023 retrospective of Pasolini's work, has seen Salò three times — first closer to release in a "dirty" London cinema ("it must have been illegal"), once for the retrospective and a third time to prepare to introduce it for The Festival of Dangerous Ideas.
Every viewing brought a new appreciation for Pasolini's intent.
"I was actually surprised by how well made it is. Pasolini only took 37 days to film it. It's supremely intellectual and cleverly thought out. I was very, more impressed by it than shocked," she says.
"The set designers and the set decorators need Oscars. It's got this incredibly beautiful, elegant 1930s art deco decor, that elegance in the context of the barbarity of some of the sex and violence and you can't really distinguish where it begins and ends."
Who can hack it?
Harvey says it wasn't easy to track down a copy of Salò — the film isn't streaming, and physical copies are hard to come by — but the effort was worth it.
"It's been this hilarious journey of finding the last Blu-ray player in Sydney for me to watch it ahead of time and to make sure that I'm not doing something stupid in showing this film," she says.
"It stands up as incredibly audacious filmmaking. Inviting people to come and experience this in a communal setting and watch these really young people be absolutely brutalised incessantly — it is a big statement, but at the same time, where else are you going to see this?
"It's the idea of how do we talk about power and what power is, and as humans, how do we allow bad things to happen to other humans? Of course that's in my mind right now. It's in everybody's mind."
Mills says that beyond Salò, the banning of film, books, video games, and even social media often boils down to moral panic.
"The masses can't get hold of something very dangerous because we don't want the masses to have access to ideas about individual freedom and choice," she says.
"I think the only way one can counteract this is by saying, well, people must be allowed to see, read, hear what they like to judge for themselves."
Ultimately, Harvey is excited about the opportunity to screen Salò, not just to share an important piece of art with a wide audience, but for what it represents for other pieces of media that have been refused classification and can't make it into an arts festival.
"Banning a film just makes it less available. It doesn't mean that it ceases to exist. What you're doing is you're encouraging a form of elitism in who can and can't access art, and that is really problematic," she says.
Harvey says there is a difference between banning a film because the content breaks laws, like in the extremely rare case of snuff films, and prohibiting a film because of what it represents.
"A film that is using artistic trickery and storytelling gets banned because it's trying to say something, then by banning it, you're also making a statement about who can cope with these kinds of ideas," she continues.
"That to me is much more interesting. Why do we think that audiences are so feeble that they can't cope with the hard facts about things or be pushed into uncomfortable territory? What are you saying about people?"
Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom, will screen as part of the Festival of Dangerous Ideas on August 29.

Can you eat too much tinned tuna?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Can you eat too much tinned tuna?
Tinned tuna is a lunch box staple for many people. It's affordable, high in protein and doesn't need cooking, making it a nutritious and convenient option for busy days.
But if you're eating tuna most days, you may have wondered whether it's possible to have too much. Or perhaps you've watched your child happily eat a tuna sandwich every day for a week and wondered if that's too much of a good thing.
The concern usually comes down to mercury. Mercury can be harmful in high amounts, particularly during pregnancy and early childhood. But the amount of mercury in seafood varies considerably between species — and that's where much of the confusion begins.
For most Australians, the evidence on tinned tuna is reassuring. Let's unpack this.
Why does tuna contain mercury?
Mercury is a naturally occurring element in the environment. It enters rivers and oceans through natural processes, such as volcanic activity and weathering of rocks, as well as from some industrial activities.
In water, bacteria convert mercury into a form called methylmercury. Fish absorb it from the water and food they eat.
When larger fish eat smaller fish, the mercury builds up inside them over time. Because bigger fish usually live longer, they often contain more mercury than smaller fish.
This isn't unique to tuna. Large fish such as shark (flake), swordfish and some marlin can also contain higher mercury levels because they are larger predatory fish.
Is all tuna the same?
No. Most tinned tuna sold in Australia comes from smaller tuna species, such as skipjack and yellowfin. Because these are generally younger and smaller than the species commonly sold as fresh tuna steaks, they typically contain much lower levels of mercury.
This is why health advice distinguishes between tinned tuna and larger predatory fish.
How much mercury is safe to eat?
Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ) uses international safety guidelines to estimate how much mercury people can consume over time without increasing health risks. This limit is called the provisional tolerable weekly intake (PTWI).
For most people, the PTWI is 3.3 micrograms (µg) per kilogram of body weight per week. For pregnant women, the limit is about half that, at 1.6µg per kilogram of body weight per week.
To put this into perspective, a person weighing 70kg would have a PTWI of about 231µg of mercury per week. But if pregnant, that drops to 112µg of mercury a week.
Limited research has specifically examined mercury concentrations in canned tuna products sold in Australia. So evidence from international studies is often used to indicate expected mercury concentrations. But levels may vary between countries, species and products.
A 2025 Spanish study analysed 60 cans of tuna and found an average mercury concentration of 0.138mg/kg.
Based on these findings, a small 95g can of tuna could contain about 13µg of mercury.
For a person of 70kg, this means:
- one can of tuna per week may provide roughly 13µg of mercury, or less than 6 per cent of the recommended weekly limit
- one can of tuna every day for a week may provide about 92µg of mercury per week, or approximately one-third (40 per cent) of the recommended weekly limit.
For a typical four-year-old who weighs 20kg, they can eat up to 66µg of mercury per week. One can of tuna may use up about 20 per cent of a four-year-old's weekly mercury allowance.
This means two to three cans of tuna a week, which is what you'd use to make a week's worth of tuna sandwiches, is unlikely to be a concern.
But overall, children have a much lower mercury limit than adults because they are smaller and weigh less.
What is mercury poisoning?
Mercury poisoning occurs after prolonged exposure to high levels of mercury.
Depending on the amount and duration of exposure, symptoms can include numbness or tingling in the hands and feet, muscle weakness, problems with coordination, changes in vision or hearing, and difficulties with memory or concentration.
These symptoms are extremely unlikely to occur from eating the amounts of tinned tuna typically in an Australian diet.
What about other fish?
Some Australian fish contain much higher levels of mercury than canned tuna, and their intake should be limited. It's recommended you consume no more than one serving of shark (flake), swordfish, broadbill or marlin per week and avoid other fish during the same week.
Should I eat the same protein every day?
Even though tinned tuna is a healthy choice, eating the same food every day isn't ideal. Not because of mercury, but because no single food provides every nutrient we need.
Fish provides omega-3 fats and iodine.
But there are health benefits from other sources of protein:
- eggs are rich in choline (a nutrient important for metabolism)
- legumes provide fibre and plant protein
- lean meats contribute iron and vitamin B12
- tofu provides plant protein and can also be a source of calcium
- nuts and seeds provide healthy fats, fibre and a range of vitamins and minerals.
Including a variety of these foods across the week makes it easier to meet your nutritional needs than relying on any single food.
The bottom line
Tinned tuna is a nutritious, affordable and convenient source of protein.
For most Australians, eating tinned tuna regularly, even every day, is unlikely to result in unsafe mercury exposure.
Rather than avoiding it because of concerns about mercury, it's best enjoyed as one of a variety of protein-rich foods that together make up a healthy, balanced diet.
Lauren Ball is Professor of Community Health and Wellbeing at the University of Queensland and Emily Burch is an accredited practising dietitian and lecturer at Southern Cross University. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.
