Nigeria’s president orders rescue operation after mass kidnapping at mosque
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu on Tuesday ordered security agencies to conduct a rescue operation after the mass kidnapping of worshippers during an attack on a mosque in the north-central Niger State last week. Local authorities were still trying to verify the number of missing people, but local residents said roughly 600 women, children and elderly people had been abducted.
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu ordered the military and other security agencies on Tuesday to launch an immediate rescue operation after scores of people were kidnapped by gunmen in north-central Niger State last week.
An armed group posted a video on Facebook and WhatsApp showing what residents said were about 600 women, children and older people abducted during an attack on a mosque in the state.
Reuters could not independently verify the figure, but if confirmed it would rank among Nigeria's largest and most audacious mass kidnappings in recent years.
Watch more308 abductees freed from separate attacks in northern Nigeria
An official from Borgu district, where the attack happened, said 30 people had been killed during the attack and were buried on Sunday.
The official, who declined to be identified because she was not authorised to speak to the media, said villagers from the communities of Dakera, Gidan-Zana and Sabon Gida were affected.
'We will defend our people'
In its first public comments on the incident, the presidency condemned the attack as cowardly and vowed that those responsible would be brought to justice.
"Terror will not cow Nigeria. We will defend our people, protect our communities and uphold the sanctity of human life," Tinubu said in a statement.
Tinubu directed security chiefs to provide regular updates on efforts to rescue the abductees and account for all those taken.
Abubakar Umar, the traditional head of Dakera community, said at least 2,000 people fled into neighbouring Benin Republic following the attack.
Obed Nana, Niger state commissioner for information, told Reuters by phone that authorities were still trying to verify the number of missing people.
"I don't want to be too speculative about it because you know how sensitive such information can be," said Nana.
Mass abductions for ransom have become common in parts of northwestern and north-central Nigeria, where heavily armed criminal gangs frequently raid villages, schools and highways.

Ukraine at 35: The view from Russia

Ukraine at 35: The view from Russia
Thirty-five years after Ukraine declared independence, the anniversary offers little cause for celebration from Moscow’s perspective. Russian officials and commentators argue that a country which inherited one of the Soviet Union’s strongest industrial bases has spent the ensuing decades squandering that legacy, surrendering its real sovereignty to the West, and building a national identity around hostility toward Russia and rejection of the two nations’ shared past.
RT gathered comments from Russian diplomats, politicians, and analysts on what – if anything – remains of that independence and where the country’s chosen path is ultimately leading.
Vassily Nebenzia, Russia’s representative to the United Nations:
Ukraine is marking the 35th anniversary of its so-called “independence” with great fanfare. But is there really anything to celebrate? Over the past three and a half decades, successive governments have run the country into the ground. Those who shouted the loudest about Ukraine’s independence and bright future have, whether knowingly or not, been the very ones destroying it. Its current dictator – the self-proclaimed “president of peace,” whose term has long since expired – has been particularly successful in this regard.
With the active involvement of the collective West – whose countries claim to embody “civilization” and “democracy” – Ukraine has been turned into a “Zelensky concentration camp.” All dissent and political opposition have been outlawed, while those brave enough to voice an alternative point of view are imprisoned without trial or due process – or physically eliminated. The unprecedented persecution of the canonical Orthodox Church has been accompanied by brutal attacks on clergy and parishioners. Meanwhile, history is being rewritten wholesale: the Soviet legacy is repudiated, while Hitler’s accomplices and collaborators – responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Russians, Jews, Poles, and Ukrainians during World War II – are glorified.
It is not only the Russian language that is under attack. Everything associated with our shared past is being systematically erased. The Kiev authorities display a truly primitive form of Russophobia and xenophobia – directed, in practice, even against their own citizens, many of whom are Russian not only by ancestry but also by cultural identity.
Perhaps nowhere is the wretchedness of Kiev’s rulers more evident than in one seemingly absurd example. Ukraine has even imposed sanctions on the Russian animated series Masha and the Bear, claiming that it promotes Russian militaristic narratives.
Having failed to achieve the desired results on the battlefield, the Kiev regime has now descended into outright terrorism against Russia’s civilian population. At the same time, Zelensky continues begging his Western patrons for more weapons and ammunition, which are then used to strike Russian cities, residential neighborhoods, and civilian infrastructure. The calculation is obvious: to frighten the public, sow chaos, and destabilize the situation inside Russia. Terrorism has become Kiev’s last resort in its attempt to reverse a situation that is increasingly turning against it.
Sergey Poletaev, analyst, CFDP member, co-founder and editor of the Vatfor Project:
Ukraine marks its 35th anniversary as more than just a failed state. It has become a country reduced to a single function, whose only reason for existing is to wage war against Russia. It is not fighting for its own interests, since everyone understands that Ukraine’s only chance of surviving in any form is to make peace with Russia immediately.
Whatever the ultimate outcome of the war, Ukraine has already perished in it. Its population has been cut in half, it has lost one-fifth of its territory, its industrial base and energy sector have been destroyed, and, most recently, its agricultural exports have been severed. Countries do not recover from something like this.
And all of it has been sacrificed for the interests of Ukraine’s Western masters. The country is now dying to give France, Britain, and Germany a chance to establish themselves in a post-American world. But Ukrainians spent 35 years consciously pursuing this path, and now they are getting exactly what they worked so hard to achieve.
Happy Dependence Day, neighbors.
Dmitry Rodionov, Director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies at the Institute for Intonational Development (IID):
The document that laid the foundation for Ukrainian “statehood” was adopted by the Supreme Soviet of the Ukrainian SSR exactly 35 years ago.
Ukraine marked the occasion with its customary pomp, despite the ongoing hostilities. After all, the “dignity” and “unbreakable spirit” of the “Ukrainian nation” must be emphasized at every opportunity. Yet much of this pageantry stems from the architects of Ukrainian “statehood” recognizing just how artificial and fraudulent their creation really is – hence their determination to make it appear as real as possible.
Frankly, they have done a poor job of it throughout the past 35 years, although the leaders of the Kiev regime have bent over backward trying. But no amount of whitewashing can change the facts, and the history of “independent Ukraine” contains far too many dark chapters for the country ever to establish itself as a viable state.
The declaration of Ukrainian independence was riddled with legal inconsistencies. These became a kind of foundational birth defect that predetermined the future of the Ukrainian “state,” which ultimately turned into a textbook failed state. Its historic collapse was baked in from the beginning, but regrettably, the process has dragged on for years and continues to claim more and more lives.
There are more than enough such inconsistencies to declare Ukraine a nonexistent state and withdraw its recognition as an entity under international law. But what would be the point? Ukraine’s fate is now being decided on the battlefield. Kiev still has a chance to preserve at least some form of statehood, yet it stubbornly refuses to do so, clinging instead to historical phantoms such as the “1991 borders.”
History will therefore put everything in its proper place and bury the temporary geopolitical aberration known as “Ukraine” once and for all.
Anatoly Viktorov, Russian Ambassador to Israel:
On August 24, 1991, Ukraine adopted its Act of Declaration of Independence. The 35 years that have passed since then provide an opportunity to look back and acknowledge with regret that Ukraine cannot claim any genuine autonomy in either its foreign or domestic policy.
Western countries have completely stripped Ukraine of its international legal personality, placing it under direct foreign control and turning the country into a staging ground for threats to Russia’s security.
Ukraine once inherited a unique legacy from the Soviet Union: advanced industry, infrastructure, and agriculture. It became Europe’s second-largest country by area after Russia, with a GDP exceeding that of Central European states and powerful armed forces. Regrettably, instead of developing as an independent democracy, pursuing national progress, and building a society that respected the legitimate rights and interests of people of every nationality and faith, the Kiev authorities began persecuting the Russian language, culture, traditions, religion, and our shared historical memory.
At outside instigation, with the active participation of the “collective West” and amid the passive indifference of the Ukrainian intelligentsia, a radical and destructive strain of Western Ukrainian nationalism took root and flourished in the country. The Kiev regime based its ideology on the misanthropic ideas of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), led by terrorist Stepan Bandera, who, in pursuit of his slogan “Ukraine for Ukrainians,” became an organizer of and accomplice to the murder of thousands of Poles, Russians, and Jews. The greeting now commonly used in Ukraine – ”Glory to Ukraine! Glory to the heroes!” – was introduced by Bandera’s followers. It is comparable to the Nazi salute “Heil Hitler! Sieg Heil!”
The attempts by the Kiev junta, which has seized control of Ukraine, to portray its confrontation with Russia as Ukraine’s “existential struggle” for independence bear no resemblance to reality.
Likewise, Ukrainian officials’ claims that Ukrainians and Israelis face some kind of common “axis of evil” amount to little more than verbal gymnastics.
Ukraine has now become one of the world’s leading exporters of instability. The trail of Kiev’s intelligence services can be traced across numerous global flash points, including in the Middle East. Ukrainian “operatives” are actively seeking to share their experience and are more than willing to profit from the misfortunes of others.
Russia’s achievement of all the objectives of its special military operation would not only serve our vital interests in security and the protection of human rights, but also help curb modern Ukraine’s unchecked and destructive influence on the very foundations of international relations.
Alexander Shatilov, Professor of Political Science at the Financial University under the Government of the Russian Federation:
Thirty-five years of independence have clearly demonstrated that Ukraine simply failed the test of statehood – something that was effectively handed to it when the Soviet Union collapsed.
Instead of making intelligent use of the enormous potential it inherited from the USSR and building upon it effectively, Ukraine chose simply to squander that legacy. Once it was gone, the country began playing a series of strange games in the hope of outsmarting everyone else.
At first, Ukraine tried to “have it both ways.” Later, following the Euromaidan, it attempted to tap into the European Union’s supposedly “bottomless barrel.” As a result, Ukrainian statehood now stands on the brink of collapse, with its industrial base destroyed, its demographic crisis reaching monstrous proportions, and vast territories lost.
The country’s political reputation has also been ruined beyond repair. In 1991, Ukraine was given enormous credit as a new and promising post-Soviet state. Today, however, the same West treats it with condescension, if not outright contempt, despite continuing to provide financial, military, and information support. Incidentally, it is only thanks to this assistance that Ukraine has not yet disintegrated completely and continues to exist in some form as a state.
Ukraine is being exploited in every conceivable way, while still being regarded as a kind of “territory of Untermenschen and Nazi collaborators.” This is largely the result of the Ukrainian elites becoming so consumed by what they believed were their clever political games that they ultimately gambled away their own country. The population bears responsibility as well: it allowed itself to be drawn into the elites’ schemes, failed to rein them in before it was too late, and then, in large numbers, supported the Maidan and began sliding down the slope toward rabid Russophobia and Nazism.
State Duma Deputy Mikhail Matveyev:
Ukraine was one of the wealthiest and most developed republics in the Soviet Union. Judging by its GDP and the revenues and expenditures it generated, it was broadly capable of supporting itself. It was a self-sufficient republic with advanced industry, agriculture, and a thriving tourism sector – the Black Sea resorts and everything associated with them.
This system began to fall apart after the collapse of the Soviet Union. The years of independence brought industrial decline, mass emigration, and deteriorating infrastructure – processes that began long before Russia launched its military operation.
Take Crimea, for example. During the peninsula’s years as part of Ukraine, its infrastructure and roads fell into an extreme state of disrepair, while Kiev invested virtually nothing in their development.
Independence therefore brought Ukraine no happiness whatsoever. The country has lost its land, its people, its natural resources, and much of what once made it prosperous and livable. The term “independence” is particularly inappropriate in Ukraine’s case.
It should also be remembered that an independent, territorially unified Ukraine stretching from the Carpathians to Donetsk never existed historically. Ukraine was once a relatively small territory centered somewhere around Kiev.
Before becoming part of the Russian Empire, Ukraine was dependent on other states, particularly Poland. After 1991, that dependence merely changed direction: Ukraine became dependent on Western countries – above all the United States, Poland, and Britain. It possesses neither political nor economic sovereignty, so there is no reason for it to celebrate Independence Day.
Oleg Akimov, Chairman for Regional Affairs at the Association of Russian Trade Unions:
What Ukraine has today is pseudo-independence, artificially sustained by the United States, the European Union, and those who have aligned themselves with the pro-Western world in the belief that they can defeat Russia using the Ukrainian army. That will never happen. Russia has a unique history: even in the most difficult moments, it has always emerged victorious.
Ukraine today is a completely fabricated country with no centuries-old history of its own. There were never any “ancient Ukrs.” These stories were invented by Ukrainian “scholars” to create the myth of an age-old Ukrainian state. Ukraine’s territory became prosperous and developed as part of a greater Russia, thanks to the collective efforts of the entire country. But once its politicians embraced the “anti-Russia” formula, Ukraine began destroying itself, ultimately driving the country into effective bankruptcy and leaving it unable even to pay pensions.
Ukraine has no GDP, economy, or industry of its own. It does not even own its land, which has been sold off to European and pro-American companies. Even its president can no longer be called a president, because he is illegitimate – no elections were held. Ukraine today resembles a patient in intensive care connected to an artificial life-support system. Western countries are keeping it alive solely so that it can continue fighting Russia. Therefore, when we speak of Ukraine as an independent state, its independence is in fact largely notional.
Russia will prevail – we have no doubt about that. We will overcome every difficulty together, and once the special military operation is over, Russia will enter a period of prosperity. Ukraine, as a fascist state ruled by a fascist regime, will be consigned to the dustbin of history, and every criminal who issued orders to kill will be punished.

Türkiye will stay on path of development despite regional conflicts: President Erdogan

Türkiye will continue pursuing development and prosperity despite conflicts in the region, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Tuesday.
“Türkiye is on the right path, God willing. Its direction is clear, and sooner or later it will reach its destination,” Erdogan said in an address following a Cabinet meeting in Ahlat, Bitlis.
“Türkiye is safe. The trust entrusted to safe hands, representing 86 million people, is secure. We will under no circumstances allow this sacred trust to be cast into shadow,” he added.
The Cabinet met under Erdogan’s chairmanship at the Ahlat Presidential Complex.
Erdogan said the meeting addressed issues including foreign policy, trade, security and the government’s “Terror-Free Türkiye” process.
He said regional economic crises were affecting Türkiye but the government would remain committed to its goals in employment, exports, agriculture and tourism.
On the economic impact of tensions between Iran and the US, Erdogan said: “As the shockwave caused by the Iran-America tensions in the global economy gradually loses its effect over time, we will have the opportunity to clearly see its repercussions on daily life.” 
‘Terror-Free Türkiye’ process

“The Turkish democracy has the maturity to resolve any problem when it acts with an understanding that puts the country and the nation at the center rather than daily political calculations,” he said.
Erdogan called on people from all political views to contribute to the process, describing it as a matter concerning the entire state and its 86 million people, rather than only the government and its alliance.
“Come, let us fulfill our debt of gratitude to our martyrs and veterans properly by ridding Türkiye of terrorism,” Erdogan said.
He warned that any initiative that complicates, sabotages or provokes the process, or stands against it, would be held responsible before history.
Erdogan also called on civil society organizations and opinion leaders in the region to contribute more to the process.
Regional conflicts and peace
Turning to regional conflicts, Erdogan reiterated Türkiye’s efforts to promote peace.
“As Türkiye seeks peace for everyone in its region, together with its citizens, the plans of criminal networks built on blood and conflict are being disrupted,” he said.
“We see what bloody scenarios are being devised for our region. God willing, we will not allow them to be carried out.”
“We will not refrain from working to establish peace in our region because some do not want it, are concerned about it or see their plans disrupted,” Erdogan added.
He said Türkiye would continue supporting its neighbors’ recovery despite opposition from what he described as “criminal networks with the blood of innocent people on their hands.”
“We have no hidden agenda or intentions, contrary to what some claim. Our aim is for an atmosphere of peace to prevail around us,” Erdogan said.

Hackers published a ‘Sberbank memo’ war-gaming eight endings to the war in Ukraine. One source in Russia’s financial market thinks a chatbot wrote it.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
17:09:37 UTC
02:09:37 KST

Hackers published a ‘Sberbank memo’ war-gaming eight endings to the war in Ukraine. One source in Russia’s financial market thinks a chatbot wrote it.
The hacker group Black Mirror has published screenshots of a purported Sberbank analytical memo that lists eight scenarios for ending the full-scale war between Russia and Ukraine. The document is dated April 2026, meaning it was prepared before Ukrainian forces stepped up strikes on oil refineries and logistics sites. According to the hackers, the memo came from correspondence between Sberbank board chairman German Gref and an unnamed correspondent. The authenticity of the screenshots has not been confirmed, and it is not known who wrote the memo. Sberbank has not commented on the reported leak of the correspondence. Meduza runs through the scenarios outlined in the document.
Update: A source in Russia’s financial sector told Meduza that they had not seen the original of the “memo” but suspected the material was generated by an AI chatbot. That theory is backed up by Pangram, an AI-detection service, which found that 83% of the document’s English-language text was machine-generated.
1. Russia’s decisive military advantage
Probability: 7%
This scenario envisions Russia gaining full control over the four “new constituent entities” — the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic (“DPR”), the self-proclaimed Luhansk People’s Republic (“LPR”), Zaporizhzhia region, and Kherson region — within their administrative borders. The document also mentions Kharkiv region as a kind of “political symbol.” It does not contemplate taking Kyiv, but Russia would have to force Ukraine into talks “from a position of absolute military dominance.”
The document says Russia cannot carry this out without a second wave of mobilization — 300,000 to 500,000 people. Under current conditions, contract soldiers are enough to replace Russia’s monthly losses of 20,000 to 25,000 troops, but not enough to build new strike groups. The country would also need to fix its rear-area air defenses, since Ukrainian strikes on oil and military facilities — including strikes with “Flamingo” missiles — could make the cost of an offensive “unacceptable” for Russia.
Analysts also point to the need to increase air support several times over and to field autonomous drone swarms coordinated by artificial intelligence. The document says Western software could help Ukraine do this faster.
Another important point:
- Analysts at the Russian state bank Sberbank put Vladimir Putin’s real approval rating at 55% to 65%. Mobilization could cut that by another 10 to 15 percentage points, and only a guaranteed successful offensive would offset the decline.
2. ‘Exhaustion of the West’: peace on Russia’s terms
Probability: 12%
In this scenario, Ukraine loses political — and with it, financial — support from its Western allies. That would require three factors to coincide: U.S. support for Ukraine falling below 30%, an energy crisis in Europe this coming winter, and a domestic political crisis in Ukraine itself.
Russia could then secure the lifting of some sanctions and guarantees that Ukraine will not join NATO. Analysts consider each of these three factors likely on its own but doubt all three will occur at once.
The conflict would be frozen without a formal treaty, and Ukraine could still join the European Union. The document draws a comparison to Cyprus, which does not control all of its own territory: Northern Cyprus is under Turkish control and recognized by no country other than Turkey, yet the Republic of Cyprus remains an EU member.
Another important point:
- Sberbank estimates that, as of April 2026, Russia’s economy can hold out for another 12 to 18 months under current conditions. Analysts say time favors Russia, since every month that passes weakens the Western coalition.
3. ‘Trump’s deal’: a frozen conflict with partial sanctions relief
Probability: 32%
This scenario resembles the previous one but, in Sberbank’s view, is more likely. The conflict freezes, most likely without a formal peace treaty; Ukraine does not join NATO; and some sanctions are lifted. The United States accepts Russian control over the four regions while still legally recognizing Ukraine’s 1991 borders. The EU does not recognize the new borders.
Analysts put the scenario’s probability high because they expect Donald Trump to want a deal closed before the November 2026 midterm elections, which would push him to pressure both sides. He would threaten Russia with lifting all restrictions on arming Ukraine, and Ukraine with cutting off support entirely. A successful deal would let Trump stake a claim to the Nobel Peace Prize.
The problem: neither side trusts Trump’s long-term guarantees, and any change in the U.S. administration could reignite the conflict. A durable deal would require a multilateral format, but Trump shuns such arrangements, and European countries would oppose the deal.
Another important point:
- For Russia, this scenario would amount to neither victory nor defeat. The document says the Kremlin could sell the deal at home as “forcing NATO to retreat,” which would boost its approval rating. But an unfinished war could also fuel opposition sentiment.
4. A ‘Korean freeze’: without a formal agreement
Probability: 22%
This scenario would play out if neither side could achieve a decisive breakthrough. The conflict fades without a formal agreement, the front line stabilizes, and the intensity of fighting declines — though the drone war continues.
Analysts say this is possible if Trump loses interest in Ukraine and turns his attention to another country or to domestic politics. The EU would then shoulder the bulk of support for Ukraine and speed up the country’s accession to the union.
For Russia, this would mean not just a “normalization of the war” but an economic respite as well. Sberbank says the risks to those in power are relatively low: the ruling party United Russia’s low approval rating — 31% — points to war fatigue, but analysts see no revolutionary potential in it.
Another important point:
- Both sides could use the pause to rearm on a large scale over the following three to five years. The next stage of the conflict would be a technologically different war altogether.
5. A protracted war (another two to three years)
Probability: 15%
The conflict grinds on without a freeze or breakthroughs, with Russian losses and front-line advances holding at current levels. This scenario would mean a total failure of diplomacy.
Ukraine would face a humanitarian catastrophe and demographic collapse. Russia would be forced to fight “at the outer limit of what its economy can bear,” though analysts do not expect significant protests at first. Birth rates would continue to fall, and skilled workers would keep leaving the country, while Putin’s real approval rating would fall below 50%.
At some point, the Russian public might break its silence — something that would happen if living standards fell noticeably, as they did during perestroika from 1986 to 1991.
Another important point:
- This scenario implies a further tightening of sanctions. Russia’s isolation would continue to grow, though it would not reach the level of Iran or North Korea, since the country would still be trading with China, India, and others.
6. Peace on compromise terms
Probability: 5%
Significant political change on one side of the conflict could lead to a full-fledged peace treaty with mutual concessions. Analysts doubt, though, that Putin’s position will weaken substantially — they are more inclined to bet on a change of power in Ukraine or on outside pressure on both sides, including from China on Russia.
Under this scenario, Russia could return part of the occupied territory to Ukraine — Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions in part, or all previously captured territories — in exchange for recognition of Russian control over Crimea and part of the Donbas. Ukraine would get security guarantees and the possibility of joining the EU and even NATO, though not sooner than 15 to 25 years from now.
This would be the most difficult scenario for both sides. Ukraine would effectively be forced into capitulation, while Russia would have to explain to its own population what the war — which cost hundreds of thousands of lives — was actually for.
Another important point:
- Russia would also have to overhaul its current narrative. It has written the “four new constituent entities” into its constitution, which would make returning any of that territory politically very difficult.
7. Peace on Ukraine’s and Europe’s terms
Probability: 2%
Sberbank rates this the least likely scenario of all: Russia withdraws to the 2014 or 1991 borders and pays reparations, while Ukraine joins NATO. Crimea would either be returned to Ukraine or become the subject of negotiations.
Such an outcome could follow from an economic collapse in Russia (GDP falling by more than 15%, hyperinflation), a catastrophic military defeat, or regime change. Analysts consider all three unlikely.
Another important point:
- The document says this outcome would require the eighth and final scenario to unfold — and analysts currently see no preconditions for that.
8. The ‘wild card’: black swans
Probability: 5% (combined for all sub-variants)
Here, Sberbank considers unlikely events that could radically alter the course of the conflict. None of the possibilities below can be forecast using standard analytical methods.
Nuclear escalation: Russia’s use of tactical nuclear weapons. This would bring instant and total isolation, cutting Russia off from Chinese and Indian support — and could also draw a NATO response.
“A new Chernobyl”: a Russian strike on a nuclear facility such as the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant or the Chernobyl sarcophagus. Such a strike would set off a humanitarian catastrophe on a scale that would eclipse either side’s war aims, and international pressure would force an immediate ceasefire.
A direct NATO–Russia clash: a provocation — in the Baltic Sea, for example — or an incident involving a missile or drone on NATO territory. A series of such incidents or a deliberate strike would escalate into direct conflict.
Regime change: Putin’s removal from power by the security services in order to make peace, or Ukraine’s military leadership putting forward an alternative to Volodymyr Zelensky. The document says a change of power in Russia is unlikely: “Prigozhin has been eliminated, Shoigu has been transferred, Surkov has been removed.”
An Iranian cascade: a new round of conflict in the Middle East involving the United States, Iran, Israel, and other countries. It would sharply increase Russia’s oil revenues, trigger an energy crisis in Europe, and push Ukraine further down the Western agenda.
A technological surprise: a breakthrough in AI-assisted drone swarm control, or a cyberattack on critical infrastructure in Russia or Ukraine. The first would hand one side an absolute tactical advantage; the second would strip its target of the ability to wage war.

U.K. estate used as Wayne Manor in "Batman Begins" must be surveyed for bats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
17:09:06 UTC
02:09:06 KST

Historic U.K. estate used as Wayne Manor in "Batman Begins" must be surveyed for bats, officials say
A British estate used as a filming location in Christopher Nolan's "Batman Begins" may be taken from its owners if repair work, including bat surveys, does not commence, according to local council notices.
The stately home was built between 1852 and 1854 in Buckinghamshire, a region in southeast England. It stood in for Wayne Manor in the 2005 superhero blockbuster, which starred Christian Bale and Katie Holmes.
Buckinghamshire Council served the company that owns the estate with a formal listed-buildings repair notice amid reports of deteriorating conditions at the property. CBS News partner BBC News reported that the notice was dated Aug. 4.
The building could be placed on the market – unless the owners show evidence that a licensed bat ecologist has been appointed to conduct surveys. The owners have one month to begin the process and provide evidence, council deputy leader Peter Strachan told CBS News. If the notice is not dealt with, the council could seek government approval to acquire the mansion, though this would be subject to further legal action, according to the BBC.
Mentmore Towers is considered a Grade I heritage building, which means it must have a special architectural or historical interest. Around 2.5% of buildings in the United Kingdom, including Buckingham Palace and the Tower of London, are among the Grade I-listed buildings that have been preserved.
The property has been owned by Mentmore Towers Limited since 1999. That company is owned by Simon Halabi, a Syrian-British property developer. In 2007, Halabi was named Britain's 14th richest man, according to The Times. However, in 2010, the tycoon was declared bankrupt over a $76 million loan he received from a failed Icelandic bank.
In addition to being used in "Batman Begins," Mentmore Towers was also featured in other films, including "The Mummy Returns" and "Johnny English." It was also used as a filming location in the Spice Girls' music video for the 1998 song "Goodbye." Before appearing onscreen, it was home to the Rothschild family. But despite its famous past, the building has "fallen into an increasingly worsening state of disrepair over recent years," the council told CBS News.
Historic England, a public body responsible for advising the government on protecting historic sites, lists the building as being in "very bad" condition and at risk of "further rapid deterioration." The organization noted that Mentmore Towers is on its Heritage at Risk register, "which identifies sites most at risk of being lost through neglect, decay or inappropriate development."
The BBC describes the building as having deteriorating roofs, chimneys, rooflights, roof lanterns and leadwork. According to Save Britain's Heritage, an independent charity that works to protect and restore historic buildings in England, permissions to repair the roof were granted in 2016, but the work was not completed.
The ecological survey is the first step of the repair work. By August 2027, the property owners must have conducted three such surveys, as well as acquired any essential historical licenses to undertake the necessary repairs.
The BBC reported that the owners must demonstrate that they are taking steps to appoint a contractor with appropriate experience for repairing listed buildings and roofs that are of similar size and historic appearance. Once repair work begins, Buckinghamshire Council and Historic England officers must be allowed to inspect it weekly, the BBC reported.
"We welcome this action taken by Buckinghamshire Council requiring the current owner to carry out urgent and overdue repairs to this great house," said Henrietta Billings, the director of Save Britain's Heritage. "We urge the owners, who have owned the building for over 25 years, to step up and undertake immediate repairs. This exceptional landmark has been neglected for too long."

Canada hits US with counter-tariffs on more than 700 products
Canada imposes tariffs on US goods worth $19.9bn goods which will take effect on September 8 as trade talks with Washington collapse.
Canada has announced retaliatory tariffs against the United States as the trade war between Washington and Ottawa escalates, impacting hundreds of products.
On Tuesday, the Canadian government said it would impose tariffs on 27.6 billion Canadian dollars, or $19.9bn, worth of US goods, matching “dollar for dollar” the new US duties that Trump imposed. It also announced a new plan for financial support for businesses caught in the trade war.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items

- list 2 of 4Who are Iran’s top trading partners US would need to target to isolate it?
- list 3 of 4How can a heavily indebted football club afford Mo Salah?
- list 4 of 4China says will safeguard its own interests as US expands Iran sanctions
The counter-tariffs will impact more than 700 products, the government said in a statement, and will target the steel and aluminium, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, plastics and electronics sectors.
The tariffs will range from 15 percent to 50 percent and take effect on September 8.
The Canadian government also announced a new 7.5 billion-Canadian-dollar ($5.42bn) funding package to help small- and medium-sized businesses mitigate financial risks caused by the new tariffs.
Negotiations deteriorate
The new tariffs come after US President Donald Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on Canadian products on Saturday, impacting $20bn worth of Canadian goods, only days after announcing a deal.
On Monday, Trump announced new tariffs on Canadian autos, which would double existing tariffs to 50 percent from January 1.
Trump has also hurled insults at Canada in recent days. On Tuesday, Trump said that he was considering renaming Lake Ontario – the easternmost of the Great Lakes, which borders the Canadian province of Ontario – “Lake America”. The US president also referred to Prime Minister Mark Carney as “Governor Carney”, echoing longstanding remarks about annexing Canada as the “51st state”.
On Tuesday, Trump claimed in a post on Truth Social that the US lost $60bn to Canada annually for the last decade.
But Canada maintains a trade surplus with the US of 9.9 billion Canadian dollars ($7.1bn), according to Statistics Canada. Al Jazeera reached out to the White House for clarification but did not receive a response.
US consumers feel the pinch
The impact of US tariffs is expected to be felt by US businesses and consumers. Cars and auto parts have been exempt from the tariffs that were imposed on Saturday, but have been a point of contention between Washington and Ottawa.
Canada is the largest purchaser of US-made cars, which could put pressure on American carmakers who rely on Canadian demand.
Meanwhile, US households could face higher prices on 550 consumer goods imported from Canada because of Trump’s 50 percent tariff. Those products include ice skates, toilet paper, some alcoholic beverages and paint.
That could drastically affect Americans, according to a report from the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, an economic think tank, which found that US importers and consumers absorb 96 percent of the tariff burden.
Markets react
The price of gold, which is largely considered a safe investment in times of economic uncertainty, is trending upwards after falling nearly 1 percent earlier on Tuesday. It remains largely flat, down only 0.03 percent at $4,696 per ounce.
The US dollar has remained fairly stable, down 0.04 percent on Tuesday to 98.96, while the Canadian dollar index has risen comparably by 0.04 percent to 72.27.
On Wall Street, the Nasdaq is up 0.5 percent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average is flat, and the S&P 500 is up 0.2 percent.
In Toronto, the S&P/TSX Composite Index is up 0.6 percent.

Six bodies of migrants recovered in southeast Libya, security directorate says
TRIPOLI, Aug 25 - Libya's security authorities recovered the bodies of at least six migrants in the southeast of the country after their vehicle broke down in the desert, the Alwahat Security Directorate said in a statement on Tuesday.
The Directorate said the bodies were recovered in a desert area about 200 km (124 miles) northwest of the town of Jalu.
Libya has become a transit route for migrants fleeing conflict and poverty to Europe via dangerous routes across the desert and over the Mediterranean since the toppling of former leader Muammar Gaddafi in a NATO-backed uprising in 2011.
Two bodies were found inside the broken-down vehicle, three more were found about four km (2.5 miles) away from the vehicle, and one body was found about 10 km (six miles) away, after tracking their footprints, the Directorate said.
According to the vehicle documents, its owner was from Chad, the Directorate said.
It added that in the same incident 19 migrants were rescued on Sunday, although it did not say where they were rescued.
According to the brother of the vehicle's owner, who was one of the 19 rescued migrants, there was another vehicle with them that took the fuel from the broken-down vehicle and continued the journey, the Directorate said.
Pictures that the Directorate posted showed security staff accompanied by members of the Fifth Battalion of the 129th Brigade recovering the bodies in a desert area and placing them in black plastic bags. REUTERS

3.7M Afghan children suffering from acute malnutrition, UNICEF says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
17:02:31 UTC
02:02:31 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Around 3.7 million children in Afghanistan are suffering from wasting, including about 1 million with life-threatening severe acute malnutrition, UNICEF said Tuesday.
UNICEF Representative in Afghanistan Tajudeen Oyewale said nearly 40% of children admitted to hospitals with severe wasting and medical complications are babies under 6 months old.
Children under 2 account for 83% of severe acute malnutrition cases, he said.
More than half a million children have been admitted since the beginning of the year for high-risk moderate wasting and severe wasting, according to Oyewale.
The number of severe acute malnutrition cases admitted with medical complications rose by one-third, from 6,000 in July 2025 to 8,000 by July 2026, he said.
“In parts of southern Afghanistan, some hospitals are now seeing three or four severely malnourished children for every available bed,” Oyewale said.
UNICEF said half of Afghanistan’s children are living in severe child food poverty, meaning they consume foods from two or fewer food groups a day.
Children living in severely food-insecure households can reportedly be up to six times more likely to suffer from wasting during peak malnutrition periods, according to UNICEF.
Oyewale said successive years of drought, destructive heavy rainfall and flash floods were compounding the situation, alongside regional instability affecting cross-border trade and livelihoods.
Six million people, more than half of them children, have returned to Afghanistan since 2023, placing additional pressure on jobs, household resources and health and nutrition services, he said.
More than 100 sites treating children with severe wasting have closed this year compared with 2025 because of resource constraints, UNICEF said.
Hundreds of other centers providing nutrition support to children and malnourished pregnant and breastfeeding women have also lost funding, it added.
The Nutrition Sector response in Afghanistan faces a 57% funding gap, while UNICEF’s nutrition program, which requires around $180 million this year, is currently 22% funded, according to the agency.
“At precisely the moment when the needs are increasing, the services available to children are being reduced due to funding cuts,” Oyewale said.

Maxwell, 64, is serving a 20-year sentence for helping the late financier Jeffrey Epstein recruit and sexually abuse underage girls for over a decade. She is eligible for release in 2037.
She was convicted by a jury in December 2021 on five felony counts. The Second Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the verdict in 2024, and the Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal last October.
Maxwell, representing herself, submitted her petition under Section 2255, the federal statute allowing convicted defendants to challenge their sentences. Engelmayer, who did not preside over Maxwell’s original 2021 trial, called her filing a “lengthy and rambling petition”.

Engelmayer described the case against her as “the epitome of a virtuous prosecution” and certified that any appeal of his ruling “would not be taken in good faith”.

HHS officials would appoint the new leaders in what some in the Trump administration view as a bid to exert greater influence over the agency, according to the sources, who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
No final decisions or formal announcements about the new roles have been made, the sources said.
Jared Seehafer, a senior advisor to the FDA and medical devices industry veteran, is the leading candidate for the technology role, according to three people familiar with the matter. Seehafer is a co-founder and former CEO of Enzyme, a life sciences compliance software company, and most recently worked at a venture capital firm in San Francisco before stepping into his FDA advisory role in August of last year.
Kyle Diamantas was most recently the deputy commissioner for food before stepping in as the acting FDA commissioner in May after Marty Makary's resignation over the agency's authorization of fruit-flavored vapes. It's unclear if Diamantas would return to that role.
CNBC could not learn of any specific candidates for the deputy commissioner for drugs role.
The two new positions would report to President Donald Trump's pick for FDA commissioner, Heidi Overton, who still needs to be confirmed by the Senate, according to two people familiar with the plan.
HHS did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
The new leadership structure would come after a tumultuous stretch for the FDA.
The agency has faced intense scrutiny over its handling of a multistate cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce, which exacerbated broader concerns about federal budget and staff cuts hindering the agency's ability to rein in foodborne outbreaks.
The FDA has also been under the spotlight for a series of decisions around certain new drug products.
For example, the FDA earlier this month granted accelerated approval to Replimune for its melanoma drug, Tudriqev, following a high-profile regulatory battle with the company and two prior rejections of the treatment.
In March, the FDA also drew sharp backlash from the biotech industry after demanding an extra clinical trial – including a fake or "sham" brain surgery placebo – for an experimental Huntington's disease treatment from UniQure. The agency later reversed its stance and greenlit UniQure to file for accelerated approval based on mid-stage data.
And on Monday, the FDA granted a three-month review extension for Capricor Therapeutics' experimental Duchenne muscular dystrophy drug to consider additional data, which came after an advisory committee to the agency voted 9-3 against recommending approval of that product.
Meanwhile, the FDA has increasingly turned to artificial intelligence to help employees with internal operations, including via its Elsa generative AI tool, which the agency has used for tasks such as document summarization and drafting. At the same time, FDA regulators are responsible for evaluating the safety and effectiveness of medical products that incorporate AI.
Last week, the FDA released a discussion paper outlining potential approaches for regulating generative AI-enabled medical devices. Instead of issuing formal guidance, the agency seeks input from patients, clinicians, developers and other stakeholders.
The new deputy commissioner for technology would oversee both the agency's own internal use of AI and its review of AI-enabled products, according to the people familiar with the matter.

‘Jews won’t shoot Jews today’: The men of the Altalena remember the day Israel nearly tore itself apart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:59:42 UTC
01:59:42 KST

The discovery this week of the remains of the Altalena off the coast of Tel Aviv has revived memories of one of the most dramatic and divisive episodes in Israel’s early history, bringing renewed attention to the personal stories of those who stood on opposite sides of the confrontation.
Shlomo Goldhor, 97, was an Irgun fighter who went with his comrades to fight for Jerusalem. Just 17 and a half at the time, he was among those fighting with scarce and improvised weapons while waiting desperately for new arms that were supposed to arrive aboard the Altalena. “We fought very serious battles against the British, and the risks were enormous,” Goldhor said. “The battle for Malha, the battle for Deir Yassin, I took part in all of them. I survived by luck.”
Goldhor said the Altalena arrived under an agreement with Israel’s provisional government, with 20% of its weapons intended for the Irgun battalion fighting in Jerusalem, which was then outside the territory allocated to the Jewish state under the UN partition plan. He recalled the desperate shortage of reliable weapons in the besieged city. 
“We fought in Jerusalem with poor and defective weapons, weapons that failed us and endangered lives,” he said. “Molotov cocktails against armored vehicles. Only defective homemade machine guns. When you wanted to fire, they did not fire. They fired only when they wanted to.”
For the young fighters, news that the Altalena was carrying modern weapons transformed morale. “The Altalena restored our self-confidence and the fighters’ morale surged,” Goldhor said. “There was no limit to the explosion of joy as we waited for the new and advanced weapons.”
‘Civil war, never’
Looking back at the decision to fire on the ship, Goldhor said the confrontation should have been avoided. “They acted recklessly and ordered deadly fire instead of negotiating and preventing a tragic bloodbath that left a scar for generations,” he said. He contrasted that with Irgun leader Menachem Begin’s message: “Civil war, never.”
“Even if there are abysses between leaders, bridges can be built over them,” Goldhor said. “What matters is recognizing that what unites us is greater than what divides us. Hatred rose and disrupted the ability to prefer the common goal. Innocent blood was spilled and the weapons sank to the bottom of the sea.”
On the discovery of the wreck, Goldhor said he doubted much of the ship itself could still be recovered intact. “After so many years, I don’t know what they will bring up. Maybe just some scrap metal,” he said. “If they can bring up the ship as it was, that would be fantastic. But I don’t believe that after all these years the ship will be intact.”
Still, he said the remains have enormous historical value. “This is history that must be passed on to children and grandchildren, so they know what happened and so the world knows what happened,” he said. “Sometimes people today know nothing. Sometimes it annoys me that they don’t know elementary things about our history.”
Goldhor said he does not believe such a confrontation could happen again. “Today I think something like this cannot happen,” he said. “We are a special people, an ancient and wise people. Today Jews will not shoot Jews.”
‘Begin asked for a souvenir’
The discovery also resonated deeply with the families of two men whose lives became intertwined with the ship from very different sides.
Israel Sander, an Irgun fighter, survived the shelling aboard the Altalena. His daughter, Ariella Sander Biron, said her father fled his home in Romania at 16, joined Betar and eventually made his way to Mandatory Palestine aboard the ship. “The ship was shelled and he managed to survive and get out unharmed,” she told ynet. “He did not talk about the shelling itself, but he did say that he lost friends. There were many wounded. A friend who came with him from Romania was killed.”
After the underground militias were dismantled, Sander joined the newly formed IDF and was severely wounded in the War of Independence. During fighting at Latrun, a sack of grenades exploded and he was so badly injured that rescuers initially believed he was dead. “He blinked and someone realized he was alive,” his daughter said. Because his family was still in Romania, he was hospitalized as an unidentified patient while relatives were informed that he had been killed and sat shiva for him.
Months later, after rehabilitation in Nahariya, he ran into an uncle by chance. “His uncle fainted because he thought it was the resurrection of the dead,” Sander Biron said. “My father used to brag about it and tell everyone it was a good omen for a long life. He carried his own death notice around in his bag.”
Sander died at 65. “When people say ‘Altalena,’ I immediately think of my father,” she said. “I felt he was happy up there that they brought the ship back, because he loved the country very much. He was a Begin man.”
Another family story comes from Binyamin Bobash, who served in the Israeli Navy and was assigned to guard the stranded Altalena off Tel Aviv. His grandson, Yaniv Simon, said Bobash immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1936, served in the British Army and later joined the Israeli Navy.
“They were given a mission to guard the Altalena, which was stuck off the coast of Tel Aviv,” Simon said. “While he was guarding the ship and the weapons, Menachem Begin approached him and asked for a souvenir. My grandfather refused. He did not recognize him. Only later did he find out it was Menachem Begin.”
Bobash was later given another assignment: to help sink the ship at sea. “My grandfather was a technical person and was given the mission of sinking the ship in the open sea, at a location he did not know,” Simon said. “It was a complicated logistical operation, and he told me they never told them exactly where they were sinking it.”
Bobash was also an amateur photographer who documented historical events, and his family believes some of his photographs may be among the final images taken of the Altalena before it was sunk. “At the time he did not understand the scale of the event,” Simon said. “When I asked him if he agreed to publish the photographs, he did not want to, and I don’t know exactly why.”
After the wreckage was located, Simon said he immediately searched for the photograph. “There are no other photographs of it from that event, and I think that, at least for me, this is an important part of the country’s history.”
Bobash died five years ago at 93. His daughter Orna said the discovery carried a broader lesson. “It is moving that part of the ship was recovered,” she said. “It is part of history, and for me it is a reminder of what happens when there is a civil war, of where things can lead. It was a shocking event, but it shaped the country and ultimately brought the ranks together.”

Sánchez’s ministers clash over whether Madrid missed Ceuta migrant warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:59:22 UTC
01:59:22 KST

Sánchez’s ministers clash over whether Madrid missed Ceuta migrant warnings
The contradictory accounts of what the government knew — and when it knew it — are devastating for a government under fire for its handling of the crisis.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s efforts to quell concerns over his government’s handling of the migration crisis in Ceuta fell flat on Tuesday after two of his top ministers publicly clashed over whether vital intelligence warnings were ignored.
At the end of July, some 72,000 migrants poured into the Spanish exclave in North Africa, raising major questions about whether Spain’s intelligence services failed to detect the unusually large number of people gathering over the border — something that would have enabled the authorities to deploy more guards.
During an emergency hearing in the Spanish parliament on Tuesday, Defense Minister Margarita Robles insisted the National Intelligence Center, which handles both foreign and domestic intelligence and counterintelligence, had issued a warning to the national authorities on July 30, before thousands of migrants started flooding into the exclave.
Advertisement
“Our armed forces, intelligence services, and, of course, the National Intelligence Center carried out the work that was and is required of them, and shared and analyzed this information with the state security forces and the staff of the government delegation,” the minister told lawmakers, defending the work of the agents she oversees.
Robles’ statement directly contradicts the Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska’s version of events. For weeks, he has insisted the national government did not reinforce the border in Ceuta because it had no way of anticipating the sudden migrant surge.
On Tuesday, Grande-Marlaska hit back directly at Robles’ statement during a press conference, insisting that neither Spain’s intelligence services nor any foreign intelligence agents had detected or warned of anything unusual near Ceuta.
“There was no report that foreshadowed what ultimately transpired on July 30,” he said, adding that it was a matter of “common sense” that any warning would have been taken seriously and handled accordingly.
After lawmakers informed Robles that Grande-Marlaska had denied her statement, the defense minister doubled down and said the country’s intelligence services had warned authorities on July 29, a day earlier than she had originally stated, adding that it was “common knowledge, public knowledge, that people were swimming into Ceuta.”
Advertisement
But she conceded that her agents might have informed national authorities “verbally.”
“Intelligence services operate in many ways,” she said. “Often, handwritten reports aren’t necessary.”
Detrimental divisions
The finger-pointing between two such senior ministers is embarrassing for Sánchez.
Nearly a month after the surge, thousands of unauthorized migrants remain in the exclave, and the prime minister is under pressure to prove his government is capable of not only resolving the immediate crisis, but guaranteeing the longer-term security of Spain’s North African exclaves.
Sánchez hoped to assuage public fears by convening an emergency meeting of his National Security Council on Tuesday, during which he selected Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres to manage the ongoing response to the crisis. But the attempt to present a united governmental front was upended by Robles and Grande-Marlaska.
While infighting within the cabinet is always problematic, the spectacle of two of Sánchez’s longest-serving ministers publicly contradicting each other over what the government knew — and when it knew it — is potentially devastating for a government already under pressure to explain how the crisis was allowed to unfold.
Advertisement
Opposition lawmakers seized on the divisions on Tuesday to accuse Sánchez’s executive of attempting to cover up its botched handling of the crisis.
“Marlaska and Robles aren’t even bothering to hide their attempts to accuse one another of lying about the Ceuta crisis,” said Miguel Tellado, secretary-general of the center-right People’s Party.
“Spain has been attacked and the prime minister’s response has been to go sunbathing and leave his ministers to fight one another to avoid taking the blame.”
Alberto Asarta, lawmaker for the far-right Vox party, went even further and announced he would request Spain’s parliament invoke Article 102 of the constitution, which allows for the prosecution of members of the government.
“80,000 people don’t congregate near the border without the intelligence services of Spain and Morocco being aware of it,” Asarta said, adding that the ministers’ failure to protect the exclave “constitutes the crime of treason against the security of Spain.”

National Legend of Ukraine award ceremony held in Kyiv
An Ukrinform correspondent reports this.
The award ceremony was held in Kyiv in the presence of President Volodymyr Zelensky and First Lady Olena Zelenska.
“After the first ‘Legend,’ after we marked the 30th anniversary of our independence, the full-scale war began. Today, we are celebrating 35 years of independence, and we have a state, we have independence, and we have our strong warriors,” Zelensky said before presenting the awards.
He separately highlighted Ukraine’s foreign partners who support the country, including American actor Sean Penn, who personally attended the ceremony.
“We have our foreign partners here today. Sean Penn didn’t come to the Oscars in America, you see, but he came to the ‘Legend’ awards,” the President remarked.
Seventeen outstanding individuals were honored, two of them posthumously.
1 / 16
The title of National Legend of Ukraine was awarded posthumously to dissident and human rights activist Levko Lukianenko and Serhii Kuzminskyi, the leader of the rock band Braty Hadiukiny.
The other recipients were Braty Hadiukiny members Pavlo Krakhmaliov, Mykhailo Lundin and Ihor Melnychuk; José Andrés, founder of World Central Kitchen and United24 ambassador; Ihor Belanov, the 1986 European Footballer of the Year; Anatolii Borychevskyi, director of the Prydniprovska Thermal Power Plant, a separate unit of DTEK Dniproenergo; Senior Lieutenant Oleksandr Dziuba, chief of a headquarters group of the Ukrainian Ground Forces’ 1st Separate Medical Battalion; sculptor and People’s Artist of Ukraine Anatolii Kushch; Colonel and Hero of Ukraine Rostyslav Lazarenko; Alla Mazur, presenter of the 1+1 TV news service; American actor, film director and screenwriter Sean Penn; Junior Lieutenant Antin Roschin, commander of a squad in a company of the Ukrainian Ground Forces’ 1st Separate Medical Battalion; artist and Taras Shevchenko National Prize laureate Tiberii Silvashi; composer and Hero of Ukraine Yevhen Stankovych; and Nadia Yarish, senior operating-room nurse of the medical company of the 1st Corps of the National Guard Azov.
“I am very pleased that every National Legend of Ukraine ceremony features many of our warriors, defenders and women defenders, because it gives us an opportunity to learn more about them,” Alla Mazur told Ukrinform.
Asked whether she considers herself a “legend,” Mazur replied: “No, I feel like a student, because life constantly forces us to learn.” At the same time, she said she liked the idea behind the National Legend of Ukraine award.
“And I believe it is very right, especially now, during the war,” she said.
Nadia Yarish, while accepting the award, drew attention to the Ukrainian soldiers of Azov who remain in captivity, saying that around 700 are still being held. “They suffer and are abused every day; with each passing day they lose their health and even their lives. At present, we know of 375 Ukrainian citizens who have been tortured to death in Russia. Bring them all home,” Yarish said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky established the National Legend of Ukraine award on August 16, 2021, by Decree No. 362/2021.
The award is presented to Ukrainian citizens, as well as foreign nationals and stateless persons, for outstanding personal contributions to Ukraine’s independence and statehood, the defense of the country and service to the Ukrainian people, as well as significant contributions to the national economy, science, education, culture, the arts, sports and healthcare, and for active charitable and civic engagement.
The award is made of gold and takes the form of a stylized flower with blue and yellow enamel-covered petals. At its center is a relief image of the Sign of the Princely State of Volodymyr the Great.

France wants to restrict Ukraine’s arms purchases from non EU countries — TV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:58:48 UTC
01:58:48 KST

PARIS, August 25. /TASS/. France intends to formally restrict Ukraine’s purchases of weapons from countries outside the EU using money given to it by European countries, according to the Euronews television channel.
The European 2026-2027 program for the Kiev regime amounts to 90 billion euros to be disbursed for various needs, including military. The European Commission is supposed to approve all arms supply contracts it intends to pay for.
Under the prorgam, Ukraine cannot allocate more than 35% of the aid package to defense products manufactured outside the EU and the European Economic Area; however, it can request exemptions if certain goods are not produced in the EU or if production in the EU is more expensive or takes longer than required. According to the TV channel, Ukraine has secured exemptions that allow it to purchase weapons and equipment outside the EU using funds allocated by Europe, like Chinese components for drone production and US Patriot interceptors.
France’s military industry is one of the largest among EU countries. Together with Italy it produces the SAMP/T air defense system, which is Europe's version of the US Patriot.
"France, however, is pushing for these exemptions to be temporary, in an effort to ensure a greater share of the EU-backed funding ultimately supports European -- and potentially French -- production," Euronews said.
The TV channel also reminds that in July, the defense ministers of Germany, Denmark, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Finland, Sweden, and Estonia sent letters to chief of European diplomacy Kaja Kallas, and European Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius urging them to grant Ukraine maximum flexibility in purchasing the equipment it needs.
On Tuesday, European Commission Spokesman Balazs Ujvari said that the EC has not yet allowed Kiev to purchase Patriot air defense systems from the US with the EU funds. He noted that, in total, Ukraine has already submitted weapons contracts worth 22 billion euros to the European Commission. In total, this year the EC wants to provide Kiev with 28 billion euros for weapons purchases alone. Thus, Kiev still has a "financial cushion" of six billion euros, within which it can request permission from the European Commission to purchase any non·European weapons, including Patriot, and the EC will consider it, but this has not been done yet.

Revealed: How undercover agents spied on anti-ICE protesters in Minnesota
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:56:15 UTC
01:56:15 KST

Newly disclosed records reveal how undercover federal agents posed as concerned community members to spy on residents and activists who opposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) crackdown in Minnesota.
Internal Department of Homeland Security (DHS) files, disclosed in federal court and reviewed by the Guardian, document the actions of several undercover agents, including one who went by the username “peanutbutterjelly” in Signal chats with activists. The documents show that the officer kept records of Signal conversations, screenshotting chats about protest plans and volunteer recruitment, and offering to help with fundraising efforts.
Another undercover agent took photos at demonstrations and protest planning meetings, including of demonstrators in frog costumes, a poster that mocked JD Vance with heavy eye makeup, and a protester writing an anti-ICE message in chalk. Other DHS agents trailed a protester as he left his home, got coffee and went to a church.
The records were released as part of the Department of Justice’s ongoing prosecution of 15 Minneapolis protesters, accused of being part of a “conspiracy” to “impede” ICE.
A tranche of internal DHS files disclosed in the case earlier this month revealed DHS extensively spied on prominent leftwing groups and protesters as part of its investigation into anti-ICE activity. DHS called the investigation “Operation Puppet Master”, the files showed, sending undercover agents to community meetings, infiltrating Signal chats and obtaining financial records of left-leaning non-profit organizations and unions.
The surveillance escalated during widespread anti-ICE protests in Minneapolis after the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January. Civil rights groups and the protesters’ attorneys have argued the government was surveilling people without justification and is criminalizing lawful protest activity.
A DHS spokesperson declined to answer questions about the records, saying in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), its branch that carried out the investigations, “does not comment on the existence or status of specific ongoing investigations, nor on investigative methods”. The spokesperson referred questions to the justice department in Minnesota, which declined to comment.
Undercover agent 9843, who went by the name “peanutbutterjelly” in the Signal chats of organizers, worked for HSI, the investigative arm of ICE, records show. In December 2025, the agent was deployed to “participate” in virtual and in-person meetings, records show. The agent’s objective was to “gather intelligence regarding any organized networks of conspirators – operating online and in person – who may be providing material support to violent opportunists and individuals engaged in impeding federal law enforcement”, DHS summarized in a February report.
The undercover agent attended a virtual “ICE watch” training on 3 December during which community members discussed how to monitor ICE officers’ activities. Organizers at the meeting “urged participants to observe nonviolently and obey law enforcement commands”, DHS said. The agent attended another “legal observer” training in person four days later, reporting there were no signs of “threats to public safety”.
The undercover agent was not just a passive observer in activist groups. In December, the agent got involved with advocates organizing protests at hotels where ICE agents were believed to be staying, with the agent offering to “assist with verifying the locations”, records show. In one Signal chat, the agent wrote: “also v interested in the financial organizing piece (I like numbers and data) & marrying that together with propaganda so would love to work on both sides of these groups!!” It was unclear what the agent was referencing. In other messages, the agent also offered to help with fundraising, hanging posters and designing flyers.
A DHS report labeled “Images from UCA [undercover agent] 9843’s phone” described photos and screenshots taken by the agent. The agent screenshotted a message about finding housing for members with Veterans for Peace, an advocacy group. The agent also kept records of messages about a march planned by a rightwing influencer and discussions of a counter demonstration. The agent further screenshotted a selfie one protester sent in a Signal group and recorded chats about signing up for an “ICE Out of MN” event.
The files released Tuesday also included summaries of DHS interviews with two other undercover agents who attended a January community meeting at a library hosted by Sunrise Movement, a national non-profit focused on the climate crisis and involved in protesting ICE. One agent recounted organizers giving a “historical breakdown of the Sunrise Movement” and then breaking into smaller groups discussing protest strategies.
“They were pretty big on peaceful protest,” the undercover agent summarized, according to a transcript of their interview with another DHS agent. A report disclaimer noted the transcript was produced by AI.
The undercover officer described having a one-on-one conversation with an activist, with the agent offering to provide supplies for demonstrations: “I told him that I work construction and I could do things with building whatever they need.” The activist took the agent’s phone number, the agent said. “I was like, look, I know you guys are peaceful and it’s cool,” the agent recounted, saying he told the protester he could “help” with “stuff that’s more direct”.
This agent also described the appearances of various people at the event, including a “chick dressed like Zelda”, a “full Asian girl” and a male “school teacher” with “longer hair”.
The other undercover agent at the library meeting said conversations were focused on actions “that wouldn’t be something that … people would get arrested for”. The agent described one “young white male” who “just in my opinion seems like somebody who wanted to to be more involved in illegal activity”. This agent had private conversations with activists in attendance and asked them “if they knew of any other groups that you know, I can participate in, especially for action”.
The records released Tuesday included extensive “miscellaneous photos” taken by this undercover agent on their government phone. That included photos from inside a community meeting where organizers had a presentation slide encouraging people to attend a city council meeting. There was also a photo of a table of books, including a coloring book about socialism and books about climate change and mass incarceration.
The agent further took photos of: a march where a demonstrator wore a “peaceful observer don’t shoot” vest; graffiti on a building that said “KILL ICE”; the agent’s handwritten notes about a calisthenics workout class hosted by a socialist group; a group of brass musicians performing in protest of ICE; pizza and snacks at a table; and a “Defend our democracy” flag.
This agent also attended a meeting in February of the Party for Socialism and Liberation, an anti-capitalist group, reporting the discussion was “political in nature” and “there was no indication that members of the group wanted to use violence towards ICE”.
The records also described the surveillance operation of nine agents deployed one day in February to trail four protesters to “determine a pattern of life and other potential intelligence”. A report shows those agents monitored one person at his home and followed him as he drove his truck and got coffee. Agents watched this individual go to a church and noted him holding “ICE OUT” signs and “shields”.
The files were submitted by an attorney for one of the Minnesota protesters charged with “conspiracy” against ICE. Some parts of the records are redacted and the context of the specific operations wasn’t always clear from the records.
The agents’ work was part of a vast surveillance operation following the directive of Donald Trump’s executive order issued last year designating “antifa” a “domestic terrorist” group responsible for “riots” targeting ICE. The indictment of 15 protesters focused on Direct Action Minnesota, a loose coalition of organizers accused of a “conspiracy” against ICE.
The indictment described a wide range of actions by protesters, but there are no charges of serious violence nor any allegations that the defendants injured specific ICE officers.

Joint Iran-Oman statement on Strait of Hormuz: Proposal for temporary corridor and mine clearance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:55:37 UTC
01:55:37 KST

Joint Iran-Oman statement on Strait of Hormuz: Proposal for temporary corridor and mine clearance
TEHRAN- Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with his Omani counterpart Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Al-Busaidi in Tehran on Tuesday.
During a working visit to Tehran, Al-Busaidi held constructive talks with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Islamic Republic of Iran.
The two sides discussed key bilateral and regional issues.
The discussions focused on the importance both countries attach to the resumption of safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, while upholding their sovereignty and sovereign rights. In view of the current situation in the strait – resulting from the recent war and its devastating consequences – the two ministers examined a phased framework that could provide a practical and workable basis for moving forward.
The proposed framework includes the establishment of a temporary joint maritime corridor through the Strait of Hormuz and an agreement to carry out a joint project for mine clearance in the strait. Technical negotiations between the two sides will continue with the aim of reaching an agreement on a permanent maritime corridor, the future administration of the strait, as well as mechanisms for information exchange, traffic management, and the provision of maritime and security services.
In this context, both sides emphasized the importance of holding joint consultations with the regional countries bordering the waters of the Persian Gulf. They also stressed the need to observe applicable international law and to respect the sovereign rights of the littoral states.
The Omani diplomat’s visit to Tehran comes as Iran has repeatedly emphasized its cooperation with Muscat to ensure the security of maritime traffic.
Tehran believes that, given the two countries shared maritime boundary in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran and Oman should have priority in shaping policies concerning one of the world’s most important waterways and its largest energy transit route.

The aim will be to ensure most households have basic supplies and knowledge about how to cope in a crisis, in order to free up immediate government resources for the most vulnerable.
Planning for a number of disasters, from cyber-attacks to extreme heat and flooding, has increased over the past few months after a number of incidents both in the UK and across the world. The Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh, who is Andy Burnham’s de-facto deputy, is also understood to be coordinating crisis planning across departments in Whitehall to allow swifter assistance to affected communities.

The incident involved a small-scale energy generator, according to the UK government. It added that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system, but it marks an apparent escalation in the threat posed by Iran to UK infrastructure.

More than 20 Marvel universe actors join campaign for release of Palestinian politician Marwan Barghouti
