Yemen's increased violence leaves thousands hungry, displaced
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:50:44 UTC
22:50:44 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen's increased violence leaves tens of thousands displaced and hungry
The increase of military conflict in Yemen is not limited to traditional front lines, with the fighting impacting different aspects of life.
The UN-sponsored de-escalation agreement reached between the conflicting parties in Yemen in April 2022 failed to protect what remained of the necessities of life amid a new threat of all-out war, bringing the spectre of the ongoing humanitarian disaster to the fore since the Ansar Allah group, also know as the Houthis, took control of the capital Sanaa in September 2014.
During the current military round, infrastructure and service facilities are direct targets in attacks, almost completely paralysing local trade, disrupting supply chains and leaving millions of Yemenis, particularly displaced people, facing a daily struggle for survival in a country where even the most basic rights are an unattainable luxury.
The present fighting also affected Mocha Port, one of the most important arteries for the flow of food supplies along Yemen's western coast, which has come under repeated shelling.
According to port director Abdulmalik Al-Sharaabi, the attacks caused extensive damage to vital facilities, with direct losses estimated at $16 million, as well as deaths and injuries among workers and civilians.
This disruption immediately impacted living conditions for thousands of people, particularly due to the halt of basic goods flows, foremost among them food and fuel products.
Wide areas under the control of the internationally recognised government along the western coast and parts of the neighbouring highlands have been hit by severe shortages.
In addition to the alarming figures related to living conditions, this paralysis has another particularly harsh dimension.
Hundreds of workers at Mokha port suddenly found themselves deprived of their only sources of income, accompanied by severe food shortages and sharp price increases that have placed a heavy burden on all citizens exhausted by years of prolonged war.
Meanwhile, residents of Marib province are facing immense suffering being the largest refuge for internally displaced people.
The province, which carries significant demographic and humanitarian weight, is facing repeated and intense waves of ballistic missile and drone attacks, threatening the lives of hundreds of thousands of civilians, particularly those living in dilapidated tents in informal displacement camps.
Displaced from Al Mahwit province, Umm Ziad told The New Arab, "We are living in a catastrophic situation, as we have no food to live on away from our homes since we were displaced while fleeing the Houthis' brutality. We depend on aid, and we have begun to fear that we will be forced to flee to another province because of the continued shelling of Marib."
The danger of further war extends to harming the main lifeline of livelihoods by targeting energy facilities and domestic gas supplies that serve most Yemeni provinces.
This direct threat risks causing a complete paralysis of supply chains, early signs of which have already emerged in the shortage of domestic gas cylinders in several cities.
From Taiz, Abdu Saif Al-Bakari told TNA, "I have been trying for four days to obtain a gas cylinder. I searched all the petrol stations in Taiz and all the cylinder shops, but I could not find one. They told me that gas was unavailable because of the shelling of Marib, and I was forced to buy it on the black market for 20,000 rials, although its official price is 9,500 rials (One dollar is equivalent to 1,550 rials in areas controlled by the internationally recognised government.)."
The repercussions has also suffocated the capital, Sanaa, under the Houthis' control.
As commercial activity at Mokha port has halted and major supply lines have been cut, Sanaa's markets have suffered severe food shortages, immediately reflected in unprecedented waves of price rises that have consumed what little money remains in residents' pockets.
In a city already suffering a chronic humanitarian crisis because salaries have remained unpaid since 2016, with no prospect of an end to the crisis, the latest escalation has closed the last avenues of survival for millions of families unable to afford food or medicine.
"We have reached a situation in which we can no longer bear living," From Sanaa, Ibrahim told TNA. "For more than 10 years, we have lived without salaries and suffered fear, repression and security crackdowns to the extent that if a person says he is hungry, he is threatened or kidnapped. Despite this, the Houthis impose financial levies on citizens under the pretext of celebrating the Prophet's birthday."
As the health, education and other basic services sectors collapse under the strain of shortages of supplies and fuel, Sanaa is now living through an extremely harsh reality.
Citizens find themselves trapped between the burden of excessive price rises and the complete helplessness imposed by a parallel economy that is draining the resources needed for their daily lives.
Residents are also facing heavy financial levies imposed under the name of commemorating religious occasions, alongside a growing wave of online protests launched by citizens on social media platforms under hashtags denouncing escalating policies of starvation.
Experts warn the current conditions is pushing the country towards extremely dangerous territory.
Wafik Saleh, executive director of the Taiz Centre for Studies, told TNA that Mokha Port going out of service would inevitably trigger a rapid wave of inflation, leading to unprecedented increases in the prices of food and basic goods at a time when markets are unable to absorb the shock or provide sustainable alternatives.
"The spectre of collapse does not stop at food. It extends to the most basic necessities of survival," Saleh explained. "Targeting the vicinity of energy facilities in Marib is emptying markets of their supplies of domestic cooking gas and other petroleum products, automatically fuelling black and parallel markets whose prices double the burden on Yemeni families."
"As people's purchasing power collapses, thousands find themselves forced to exhaust what remains of their income to cope with harsh living conditions, driving a catastrophic deterioration in humanitarian crises on the ground," he added. "These accumulating crises are outlining the features of a comprehensive disaster that is undermining the efficiency of the health and food sectors as a result of interruptions to cold chains and rising hospital operating costs, threatening to increase the number of people in need of urgent assistance to unprecedented levels," Saleh concluded.

Russia Steps Up Recruitment of Women for Ukraine War – Vot Tak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:49:51 UTC
22:49:51 KST

Russia is increasingly recruiting women for the war against Ukraine amid signs that its pool of potential male recruits is shrinking, according to an investigation by the Poland-based news outlet Vot Tak.
At least 50 Russian women serving in the war have been killed, with the annual death toll rising the longer the war has gone on, the outlet found.
Vot Tak identified each of the 50 women and examined how Russia recruits women, what motivates them to enlist and how their roles have expanded from medical and support work to operating drones, firing sniper rifles and taking part in assaults.
Women have traditionally served mainly in civilian and support positions in the Russian military. In early 2022, 310,000 women worked in the armed forces, but only about 40,000 were service members. By March 2023, 1,100 women were deployed in Ukraine, according to then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu, the only official figure released during the war.
Vot Tak found that women are now being recruited for a wider range of combat duties, including as drone operators, snipers, machine gunners and assault troops.
One of the women interviewed by Vot Tak was Yelizaveta Tsybina, a 24-year-old drone operator with the call sign “Bayana” who signed her fourth volunteer contract this summer. She is now based at a barracks in the southwestern Kursk region.
“They present it all beautifully and patriotically,” Tsybina told Vot Tak. “But when you arrive, the situation, the way you are treated and the work itself are completely different.”
She said that although she did not initially want to enlist after Russia invaded Ukraine, many of her friends did, and her boyfriend signed a contract in June 2024. A military enlistment office rejected Tsybina because she lacked medical training. Her boyfriend was killed that August.
She then trained as a drone operator and joined the St. George volunteer assault brigade, formed largely from former Wagner mercenaries and Russians who had fought in eastern Ukraine since 2014. A week after signing a six-month contract, she was sent on her first combat mission.
“I didn’t think I would survive my first contract,” she said.
In late 2024, Tsybina was deployed near Soledar in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, where she used drones for reconnaissance and later helped direct artillery fire. Her unit was subsequently sent to Chasiv Yar, where she said she dropped munitions on a dugout after seeing Ukrainian soldiers enter it.
Tsybina returned to her home region of Krasnoyarsk in May 2025 with a minor wound and concussion. Four months later, she was back in the military.
“It draws you in. Unfortunately, I can’t get out of it anymore,” she told Vot Tak. “When I return to civilian life, everything feels wrong — the environment, the routine, the people, the relationships. It feels as if I’m not where I belong.”
Tsybina has since signed three more fixed-term contracts with volunteer formations. She said she avoided signing with the Defense Ministry because its contracts are effectively impossible to terminate while the war continues.
“If I had the choice, I would choose not to start down this path,” she said. “I am afraid to say this openly, but disappointment with the Russian Armed Forces is the view of most Russian soldiers.”
Short-lived recruitment drives
Women can sign military contracts in any Russian region and are offered the same bonuses, salaries and benefits as men, according to Vot Tak. Advertisements generally seek Russian citizens aged 18 to 45 with at least a secondary education and no criminal record, though the criteria vary.
Like men’s contracts, women’s agreements with the Defense Ministry are automatically extended until the war ends.
Since late 2025, students have been targeted at universities in at least five cities, as well as the Ulyanovsk region, Vot Tak found. A college in Krasnoyarsk held a closed recruitment meeting attended only by women.
The recruitment drives are often short-lived. One in the Tomsk region lasted 10 days. A Telegram channel reopened recruitment in March 2026 and expanded it in June to drone, communications, logistics and supply roles. Two weeks after Vot Tak contacted the channel, a recruiter said applications had closed because of an “extremely large influx” of candidates.
Recruiters also made misleading promises, the outlet reported, including telling prospective recruits that contracts could be terminated after one year and that women would not be transferred to assault units or sent to the front. In practice, Defense Ministry contracts are extended indefinitely and women have served in frontline and assault roles.
Russia had initially tried to recruit women as medics and cooks early in the war. By 2023, volunteer formations were advertising for female snipers, drone operators, electronic warfare specialists and assault troops.
The Defense Ministry has also reportedly recruited female prisoners in exchange for expunging their convictions. More than 80 may have left Siberian prisons to work as medics in late 2024, Vot Tak reported, though the practice appears to have since been phased out.
Rising death toll
Vot Tak said it identified 50 female service members killed since February 2022. The annual toll rose from five in 2022 to 15 in 2025. Twelve were killed in the first half of 2026 alone.
Most were between the ages of 31 and 49. The oldest, Irina Anisimova from the Saratov region, was 57 when her death was reported in October 2024. The youngest was 23-year-old Yana Koshkina, who volunteered in 2023 and was killed in a drone strike near Bakhmut while commanding a casualty evacuation team.
One of the first was Valentina Galatova, 27, who was killed during a combat mission in Mariupol on April 14, 2022.
Galatova first traveled to Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine with humanitarian aid in 2014 and later settled in Donetsk with a commander from a Russia-backed formation. After he was killed in 2020, she joined his regiment.
Officially listed as a paramedic, Galatova worked as a political officer and therapist, her mother told Vot Tak. During the full-scale invasion, she joined assaults and died in mortar fire in Mariupol.
Women have also been implicated in abuses. Vot Tak previously reported that an assault platoon commander with the call sign “Witch” allegedly ordered subordinates to shoot five Ukrainian prisoners of war in May 2024. A female sniper called “Ripley” told a pro-Kremlin correspondent that she would be willing to shoot foreign fighters who try to surrender.
Some women now enlist as soon as they turn 18, while others try to flee after encountering withheld pay, violence by commanders or indefinite contracts, Vot Tak said.
Sofya, who asked that her name be changed, signed a Defense Ministry contract at 19 after graduating from medical college in 2023. Now 22, she trains soldiers in first aid and wants to leave.
She told Vot Tak that recruiters had promised her about 80,000 rubles ($967) a month but did not pay the agreed salary. She dismissed recruitment into drone units as another lure to send young people into Ukraine.
“I am disappointed in today’s army and want to leave as soon as possible,” she said. “Everyone is waiting for the war to end so they can get out — young people and older people alike.”
“At 22, I have no desire to die because of politicians’ wars.”

Sexual Assault Rates Decline in Latest Pentagon Survey Following Reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:49:19 UTC
22:49:19 KST

Sexual assault reports across the military decreased last year, according to the Pentagon’s latest official figures released Aug. 21.
The Department of Defense received 7,998 official reports of sexual assault involving service members in fiscal 2025, a decrease from 8,195 in 2024 and 8,515 in 2023, according to the U.S. military’s annual congressionally mandated report on the issue. The Pentagon said it found sufficient evidence for disciplinary action in 2,220 of those cases.
The Pentagon also estimated that sexual assaults involving service members decreased to 4.3 percent from 6.8 percent for Active-Duty women. It dropped to 1 percent from 1.3 percent for Active-Duty men since the latest available data from 2023.
The Air Force and the Space Force had the lowest rates of sexual assault among the services—2.8 percent for female Airmen and 3.5 percent for female Guardians, and less than 1 percent of male service members for both services.
Those figures come from the Pentagon’s biennial Workplace Experiences Survey, which asks service members whether they have been sexually assaulted, sexually harassed, or experienced sex discrimination in the past year. The total number of reported sexual assaults across the military is released annually. The anonymous survey, which asks about incidents that occurred in the past 12 months, captures a broader set of data and is the primary marker for the Pentagon on how prevalent sexual assault is within the ranks. Responses were collected in the fall of 2025.
“Dignity, respect, and discipline are foundational to the warrior ethos and the overall preparedness of the force,” Undersecretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata said in an Aug. 21 statement. “Sexual assault and sexual harassment undermine these values, eroding trust and threatening the mission.”
The U.S. military estimated that one-third of sexual assaults were reported in 2025, compared to one-fourth in 2023, according to Pentagon data.
Military personnel experts said the trends are an indication that the process for reporting and addressing sexual assaults has improved during the Biden and Trump administrations.
“We’re seeing increased trust in reporting and in the systems that are available,” said Katherine Kuzminski, the director of studies at the Center for a New American Security, which she attributed to “deliberate policy decisions and investments.”
“Not only was that something that was started in the last administration, but this administration also gets to claim credit for continuing on,” she added of the recent reforms.
At the end of 2023, each of the military services established an Office of Special Trial Counsel to prosecute serious crimes, including murder, sexual assault, and domestic violence. The aim was to remove the chain of command from the process to lessen fears of retaliation.
That followed the establishment of an Integrated Primary Prevention Workforce, which has focused on preventing sexual assault, suicide, and other harmful behaviors in 2021. President Joe Biden also ordered that sexual harassment be added as an offense under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
Alex Wagner, who served as the assistant secretary of the Air Force for manpower and reserve affairs under Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin in the Biden administration, said the latest figures showed recent reforms, particularly the hiring of the prevention workforce and the implementation of the Office of Special Trial Counsel, have started “to sink in and demonstrate success.”
Wagner said the survey results represented “clear, strong evidence that the focus on reducing unwanted sexual contact in the military by Secretary Austin and the service secretaries has resulted in a real and positive reduction in harmful behaviors that impact the lived experiences of members of the military.”
This year’s report, under the Trump administration, appears to support continuing many of those efforts.
“[E]ngaged leadership, a fully resourced Integrated Primary Prevention Workforce, and the active mitigation of stressors are critical readiness multipliers that preserve and support our Total Force’s warfighting capability,” the Pentagon wrote in the report released Aug. 21.
According to the Pentagon, trust in the military to handle sexual assault has increased. Still, less than half of Active-Duty women trust the military to “protect their privacy, ensure their safety, and treat them with dignity and respect” compared to around two-thirds of Active-Duty men.
Asked about the new military justice process, 44 percent of Active-Duty women and 64 percent of Active-Duty men said they would trust the Office of Special Trial Counsel to be fair in a hypothetical sexual assault scenario.
Preventing sexual assault, the Pentagon says, is not just a personnel matter but is vital for the military’s combat effectiveness.
“The Department’s commitment to a disciplined, professional fighting force is fundamental to maintaining a lethal, ready, and mission-focused military,” the latest report concludes.
“This commitment is grounded in standards, accountability, and mutual respect across the Total Force. Conduct that undermines that trust—including sexual assault—directly degrades unit cohesion, readiness, and overall warfighting effectiveness. Preventing and responding to sexual assault is therefore a readiness imperative.”

How to Break Up With Your Therapist Without Ghosting Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:48:11 UTC
22:48:11 KST

Your therapist has probably encouraged you to have difficult conversations, advocate for your needs, and resist the urge to avoid things that make you anxious. That’s all well and good—until, one day, the difficult conversation is with them.
If therapy doesn’t feel useful anymore, or if you’ve realized that you and your therapist simply aren’t the right match, it can be tempting to outsource the breakup to the cancel-appointment button. Yet unless there’s an ethical, boundary, or safety concern, experts say it’s usually worth having a conversation with your therapist before ending the relationship. It might improve the therapy. It might also help you find someone better suited to you, or simply allow you to leave without feeling guilty about ghosting the person who knows exactly why you tend to ghost people.
Speaking up could also save you from having to begin the search from scratch. “Your therapist could be the gateway to your next great therapist,” says Ryan Culkin, a licensed professional counselor and chief counselor officer at Thriveworks, which provides therapy and psychiatry services. They might be able to adjust their approach—or recommend someone who would suit you better.
Even if you already know you’re finished, breaking the news doesn’t require a dramatic confrontation or an elaborate defense. Here’s how to decide whether it’s time to call it quits—and how to do it painlessly.
Figure out what kind of discomfort you’re feeling
Good therapy isn’t necessarily easy. “Sometimes therapy can be really uncomfortable, but it can be incredibly productive,” says Eli Kraiem, a clinical psychologist in New York. A therapist might challenge an assumption you’re attached to, point out a pattern you’d rather not see, or encourage you to do something that scares you. Feeling unsettled after a session doesn’t mean it went badly.
Michael G. Wetter, a clinical psychologist in Los Angeles, prefers this question: “What is the discomfort accomplishing?” Productive discomfort generally leads to insight, reflection, behavioral change, or progress toward goals you and your therapist have agreed on, he says. If it’s a poor fit, you might notice you leave therapy feeling misunderstood or have the same conversation week after week without much meaningful movement.
Juliann Siwicki, a licensed clinical professional counselor in Vero Beach, Fla., thinks about it this way: “Are you uncomfortable because you’re talking about something hard? Or because you feel like you’re having coffee with someone and not getting help? Those are two different things.”
You should be able to name what you're working toward—a pattern you're trying to break, a decision you're stuck on, a reaction you'd like to change—and to notice how much airtime your therapist is taking up. "A therapist can share something about themselves if it helps the client," Siwicki says. "It becomes too much when the client is spending the session listening to the therapist's stories, or feels like they need to take care of the therapist."
Kamran Eshtehardi, a clinical psychologist in Pasadena, Calif., has heard the far end of that spectrum. One client described a previous therapist who "thought it would be helpful to tell me about when they cheated on their wife"—including that his wife left him, and that he later saw an escort. "And I'm like, ‘What? Like, a therapist told you?’" Eshtehardi says. "Those are major red flags."
What was once a good fit can also change over time. A therapist who helped you through a crisis might not be right for your next stage. "A great therapist might not be great for you," Culkin says. "It's kind of like dating—you're not going to get it right the first time every time."
Even finding that “the therapist gets on your nerves” doesn’t necessarily mean you should quit, says Eshtehardi. A rupture doesn’t mean the therapy has “rotted on the vine,” he says, and progress sometimes develops “underneath the surface” before reaching a tipping point. But if you’ve explained what you need and nothing changes—or there’s no sense of progress—your frustration deserves attention.
Serious boundary violations, unethical behavior, or anything that makes you feel unsafe are different. You don’t need to attempt a repair before leaving, nor do you owe the therapist another session.
Say what isn’t working
If you’re open to continuing with your therapist, with the appropriate changes, describe what you’ve noticed and need—without turning the conversation into a performance review.
Try: “Our sessions have started to feel conversational, and I need more structure, feedback, and therapeutic insight. Can we talk about that?” Or: “I’m not sure what I’m working toward. Could we revisit my goals?” Culkin suggests language as straightforward as: “That didn’t land with me,” “I want to try something different,” or “I really liked when you did this.”
Eshtehardi recalls a client telling him that the usual sympathetic responses—“I’m so sorry to hear that” or “That must have been so hard”—didn’t work for them. “I just want to get stuff on the table and say, ‘OK, what’s going on here? How do we work with this?’” the client told him. That feedback helped Eshtehardi calibrate his approach. “I’m not saying it’s necessarily the client’s job to help train the therapist,” he says, but clients can explain what they’re looking for and how they prefer to work.
If you know you’re ready to leave
Sometimes you’re not interested in recalibrating the relationship—you’ve already decided to end it. In that case, the goal isn’t to persuade your therapist that you have a good enough reason to go. It’s simply to communicate your decision in whatever way feels most manageable.
You don’t have to deliver the news face-to-face. A call, email, or text is fine: “I don’t want therapy and the therapeutic relationship to be another source of anxiety for my clients,” Eshtehardi says. For someone accustomed to conflict or pushback, sending “I’m sorry, this isn’t working for me” and receiving a calm response can itself be therapeutic. You might realize, he says, that “maybe there’s a way to connect with people that doesn’t feel like I’m always doing the wrong thing.”
Eshtehardi also encourages clients who feel guilty to view the conversation as an opportunity to “practice trusting that someone else is going to be OK,” and trusting themselves to make the right decision. Your therapist’s response will provide useful information. A therapist who responds with openness and a willingness to adjust is giving you one kind of information; defensiveness or guilt-tripping gives you another. If the therapist acts wounded, Eshtehardi thinks of it as a “double whammy.” It might hurt, but it also “confirms that you’ve made the correct decision to stop therapy.”
You don’t need to build a case for your decision. “When it comes to trying to find the right fit, I don’t think clients should have to worry about having to justify their perspective,” Eshtehardi says. He suggests keeping the message simple: “I don’t think it’s the right fit. I’d like to stop sessions, and I really appreciate your time. Thank you.”
And try not to assume you’ve devastated them. Therapists are trained to handle patients leaving, Kraiem says. If yours can’t tolerate it, “then there’s a problem with the therapist, not with the patients.”
Make the transition easier on yourself
If you need consistent support, try to line up a new therapist before leaving your current one. Ask your therapist if they can recommend someone with a different style or specialty.
Before booking, confirm the new therapist accepts your insurance. “There’s nothing worse than getting through that first session” only to discover they don’t, Culkin says. You can also ask how they structure sessions, establish goals, and respond when a client disagrees. Be candid about what helped the first time around, what didn’t, and what’s important to you this time. Culkin encourages therapists to ask what clients appreciated about past providers and what they wish had been different. “Those are gold answers,” he says.
It’s not mandatory, but Kraiem recommends a wrap-up session, if you’re comfortable: “Let’s have one session to reflect on the experiences, process how you’ve improved, how you’ve grown through therapy, and maybe areas that still need improvement,” he says.
Ask the practices about transferring relevant records. You’ll typically sign an authorization specifying what can be shared. Whether you want a direct handoff depends on why you’re leaving, Eshtehardi says. If you felt misunderstood, the former therapist’s perspective could “muddy the waters,” and you might prefer a clean start. If your therapist is referring you to someone with more specialized expertise, a conversation could help them get up to speed more quickly. In that case, Eshtehardi tells clients, “I’ll tell you everything I tell them so you know what they know.”
Finally, cancel future appointments and settle outstanding balances or other loose ends. Eshtehardi suggests asking: “Are there any last things we need to do?” If medication is part of your care, coordinate with your prescribing clinician about refills.
Changing therapists isn’t proof that treatment failed. Sometimes successful therapy means repairing a strained relationship. Other times, it means recognizing that the relationship has run its course—and using the difficult-conversation skills you’ve practiced to say so.

What is phubbing? The tech habit quietly damaging relationships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:45:26 UTC
22:45:26 KST

As our digital footprints grow, questions about digital privacy and tech habits are becoming more common between couples.
"phubbing"Most of us use a variety of apps, social media platforms and scheduling tools as our lives become increasingly digital.
However, for couples, this can lead to interesting dynamics and questions. One of you may love being online and posting frequently on social media, whereas the other could prefer a quieter, more private lifestyle.
As such, how you approach technology and digital privacy as a couple could be completely different to how you handle it individually.
'Phubbing' on the rise
Unsurprisingly, technology can have both a positive and a negative impact on your relationship.
Phone snubbing, commonly known as "phubbing" and a related pattern called "technoference" are both increasingly common.
While "phubbing" refers to ignoring or snubbing a partner in favour of a phone, "technoference" refers to any interruption to couple activities caused by technology, such as constant calls, messages or notifications.
According to a 2025 study published in the journal Human Behavior and Emerging Technologies, survey respondents used their smartphones during 27% of the time they spent around their partner, on average.
Around 86% of respondents also used their phone every day while around their partner.
This was based on objective phone-tracking data rather than self-reports, which may not be as accurate.
The study found that phone use around one's partner could predict lower relationship satisfaction and co-parenting quality, as well as greater depression and lower life satisfaction. The effects were more pronounced for women.
On the other hand, technology can also benefit your relationship by making it easier to stay in touch, schedule important dates and activities, or bond over a favourite show.
When it comes to digital privacy, however, things can get more complicated. Couples today have to navigate a number of situations that did not exist for previous generations.
According to the relationship resource Love Respect, couples may need to discuss digital boundaries around privacy and exclusivity.
This can include whether it is okay to tag each other in pictures and posts or check in somewhere together. Whether to make a relationship status public is another point worth discussing, along with whether partners can follow each other's mutual friends.
However, one of the most important digital privacy questions couples may need to align on is whether they are comfortable using each other's devices.
Another major question is location sharing. According to a Civic Science report published last year, around 52% of Americans share their location with a spouse or partner.
In other cases, couples may disagree over home security and tech due to privacy concerns, as well as over what personal information to share online, for example when shopping, due to fears of scams.
Bridging the privacy gap
One of the first, if most obvious, things you can do when you realise you and your partner have different views on digital privacy is talk to them.
According to Love Respect, you should find out what they are comfortable sharing online while also communicating your own thoughts on what you want and do not want to share. Try to stay as calm and clear as possible.
It may help to discuss social media rules, such as tagging or posting photos of each other, or sharing relationship statuses. For location sharing, temporary sharing or turning off real-time tracking can ease friction.
You can choose to keep your phone and email passwords separate, as part of your personal autonomy.
It can also help to find small compromises, such as regular updates while travelling instead of an all-day live tracking app.
If the conversation is not progressing or is getting heated, it can help to take a break, give each other space and revisit the topic later, once both of you have had time to process things.
Approaching a couples counsellor can also help if you find it difficult to reach a satisfactory agreement.
Love Respect also emphasises that you should never feel pressured, manipulated or guilted into sharing your passwords or logins, or into changing digital habits you are comfortable with.

eHarmony misled Australians over 'free' subscriptions, court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:45:13 UTC
22:45:13 KST

The Federal Court of Australia has ruled eHarmony misled Australian consumers with fake free dating services.
Users who paid for the website and app's one-month premium membership were charged for a six-month subscription and were unable to cancel payments that automatically renewed, even after profiles were deleted.
What's next?
The court will decide on penalties and consumer redress at a later date.
Users of eHarmony's website and app, the fourth largest of its kind in Australia, were misled with fake free dating services and then forced to pay, the Federal Court of Australia has found.
Users of its free basic membership were unable to talk to other single people online without paying, the court found.
Those who paid for a one-month premium membership were then charged for a six-month subscription, had to pay hidden and additional mandatory fees and were unable to cancel payments that automatically renewed, even after profiles were deleted.
"Try before you buy — and no pressure to sign up," a message on the free dating page read.
"We love our site and want you to enjoy it too, which is why we encourage you to sign up for free, review your matches and get to know us a little better."
It was a confusing statement, Justice Christopher Horan said on Tuesday when he found the company deceived its Australian customer base.
"I consider that such an assumption or conclusion was erroneous. Accordingly, the conduct was misleading or deceptive," he said.
"The one-month representation amounted to conduct that was liable to mislead the public.
"I accept the ACCC's submission that it was not possible to use the eHarmony Platform as a Basic member, free of charge, to 'date' other members by engaging in ongoing communications for the purposes of developing a romantic relationship."
The court found about 1.3 million users from Australia registered for a basic membership between 2019 and 2024.
One user who gave evidence to the court — and cannot be named for legal reasons — signed up for a six-month membership at a one-time discounted payment of $155.64, but deleted her profile two months later after failing to meet anyone.
When the six-month period expired, eHarmony renewed her subscription and billed her credit card $478.80.
She told eHarmony she didn't wish to continue her subscription and cancelled her credit card when the platform refused her request.
The company, which refers to itself as "the No.1 trusted dating app" referred the woman to a debt collection agency.
The proceedings were brought before the federal court after the consumer watchdog became aware of the repeated pattern.
The ACCC received hundreds of complaints from consumers, commissioner Luke Woodward said.
"Dating platforms are an important part of Australians' social lives,'' he said on Tuesday.
"Many people use them to meet others and form valuable connections.
"Consumers were not adequately informed about their memberships' duration or that the membership would automatically renew, including, for many, at a much higher price."
The court will decide on penalties and consumer redress at a later date.

One million Afghan children suffer ‘life-threatening’ malnutrition: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25

22:44:00 KST

One million Afghan children suffer ‘life-threatening’ malnutrition: UN
- One million Afghan children face life-threatening severe acute malnutrition amid a worsening crisis, with 3.7 million suffering from wasting, UNICEF warns.
- Hospital admissions for malnourished children have risen sharply, with southern hospitals overcrowded and many cases involving children under two years old.
- Aid cuts have closed over 100 treatment sites, leaving UNICEF's US$180 million nutrition programme only 22% funded, risking more child deaths without urgent action.
AI generated
Geneva – One million children in Afghanistan are suffering from life-threatening malnutrition in a worsening crisis sweeping the country, the United Nations warned on Aug 25.
Across Afghanistan, 3.7 million children suffer from wasting, meaning they are acutely malnourished, the UN children’s agency UNICEF said.
Among them are “one million children who are suffering from life-threatening severe acute malnutrition” – the worst form, said UNICEF’s Afghanistan country representative Tajudeen Oyewale.
“If there is no treatment, and we are not able to act fast, that one million number are at risk of dying,” he told reporters in Geneva, speaking from Kabul.
Afghanistan has endured repeated hunger emergencies in recent decades as it has struggled through civil war and other crises. An economic collapse followed the Taliban government’s return to power after US-led forces withdrew in 2021.
“Malnutrition plays a central role” in the growing numbers of deaths of very young children, Oyewale said.
Nearly 40 per cent of children admitted to hospitals with severe wasting and medical complications were babies under six months old, he said.
Meanwhile, children under two years old make up more than 80 per cent of severe acute malnutrition cases in Afghanistan.
He described a “worsening nutrition crisis” across the country, with more than half a million children admitted to hospital so far in 2026 for high-risk moderate and severe wasting.
In July 2025, around 6,000 severe acute malnutrition cases were admitted; in July 2026, the numbers went above 8,000 – a third higher.
“In parts of southern Afghanistan, some hospitals are now seeing three or four severely malnourished children for every available bed,” he warned.
‘Vicious cycle’
Oyewale said an “increasingly alarming picture” was developing, with families cutting back on nutritious food and meals becoming smaller.
Children’s first food beyond breast milk may be little more than bread with tea, or watered-down yoghurt, “and for a growing child, this is simply not enough”.
He said children could get trapped in a “vicious cycle”: being poorly nourished, developing severe diarrhoea or respiratory infections, and then in turn becoming more malnourished.
These problems are compounded by Afghanistan’s other troubles, such as successive years of drought, flash floods, regional instability and cross-border trade disruptions.
The return of six million Afghans from abroad since 2023 – more than half of whom are children – is also exacerbating the pressures on stretched resources.
While treatment for malnutrition can save lives, if survivors return home to the same conditions, “we frequently see those kind of children relapse and come back”.
Oyewale said that while the needs were increasing, services for children were being slashed due to international aid cuts.
He said more than 100 sites treating children for severe wasting had closed since 2025.
UNICEF’s nutrition programme in Afghanistan is estimated at US$180 million (S$228.5 million) in 2026 but is only 22 per cent funded.
“We should not wait until a child is dangerously thin and lying in a hospital bed before we act,” Oyewale said. AFP

Ukraine Tests World's First Purpose-Built Robot Aircraft Carrier for Drones

A Ukrainian naval drone company unveiled the world’s first dedicated drone aircraft carrier on Monday, confirming months of reports that Kyiv’s military had developed a means of launching airborne strike drones from remote-controlled large motorboats.The 7-meter-long Magura MV11 marine drone was displayed and identified to the public during the Ukrainian Independence Day parade in a sail-by on the Dnipro River, the military information platform Oboronki reported.
The Ukrainian marine drone manufacturer UFORCE has produced Magura model boats since 2023. The motor-boat-resembling sea drones have for the most part been used by Ukrainian naval commandos for kamikaze strikes against Russian ships and shore infrastructure, and more rarely as platforms for special missions.
The MV11, per the Oboronki report, is Ukraine’s first publicly identified sea drone, designed from keel up, to carry and launch other unmanned systems from its onboard, “allowing the drone to act as a mobile naval base” – as a remote-controlled aircraft carrier/drone hanger.
Usable payload of the vessel as a mothership/transport platform is 2,200 kilograms (4,850 pounds). According to developers, the MV11 is capable of operating autonomously up to seven days. The article said the drone was developed jointly by UFORCE designers and R&D bureau in Portugal, with financing from unnamed Ukrainian allied states.
Russian Strikes Injure 35 Across 3 Cities, Including 2-Month-Old Infant
Photos and videos showed the vessel’s deck as a flat top broken into transport sections along the length of the hull, with doors protecting the transport section from sea and spray. The images run on major Ukrainian news platforms showed the compartments in a closed position.
Video published by UFORCE in March 2026 demonstrated a Magura launching an interceptor Unmanned Air Vehicle (UAV) emerging from a container mounted on the deck of a Magura-type robot boat. Ukrainian military information platforms have suggested drones carried in a launch compartment would need to be mechanically restrained in a cradle or rack to protect them from the sometimes-sharp sea maneuvers carried out by Magura pilots.
Given a typically sized Ukrainian first-person-view (FPV) drone armed with a conventional munition sufficient to destroy an armored vehicle, available deck space aboard an MV11 might be sufficient for quick launch of 20-40 aircraft in a single wave, and up to three waves of aircraft if the FPV drones were stored hopper-style in layers, Kyiv Post researchers found. The actual aircraft carrying capacity of the MV11 has not been made public.
According to UFORCE, the MV11, aside from an aircraft carrier configuration, can also be used to perform reconnaissance and surveillance, as a support platform for amphibious operations, and as a supply vessel for fuel and equipment used by their naval drones. According to the developers, the drone can perform these tasks 24/7 and in all weather conditions.
Russia’s military has sometimes struggled to contain Ukraine’s growing sea drone threat, deploying everything from advanced fighter jets to attack helicopters to block ships and shore-based machine guns to interdict Ukrainian robot boat attacks. In May 2025, Ukraine’s special operations command first fielded Maguras armed with anti-aircraft missiles. Russian official sources said the tactic was ineffective. Ukrainian sources said at least three helicopters were shot down before Russian air assets learned to keep a safe distance from the Ukrainian sea drones.
First shown to the public in July 2023, Ukraine’s Magura-series maritime drones operating in kamikaze mode have scored repeated naval successes and become a critical weapon in Kyiv’s increasingly effective campaign to disable or destroy warships of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. The possibly most spectacular attack taking place on Feb. 1, 2024, saw six Maguras overwhelm shipboard defenses to sink the Tarantul-II covette Ivanovets within sight of shore of the Russia-controlled Crimea peninsula. Reportedly, 40 hands lost their lives. A Feb. 14, 2024, nocturnal strike scored multiple hits on and sank the 4,000-ton heavy assault ship Tsezar Kulikov offshore from the Crimea seaside resort Alupa.
Recent high-profile operations using Magura boats as FPV launch platforms include an early August 2026 strike by FPV drones flown from Maguras operating off the Crimea coast to hit a pair of Russian S-400 Triumf interceptor missile launchers and an air defense radar protecting the south shore of the peninsula. A Ukrainian defense intelligence (HUR) statement estimated the value of Russian equipment losses in excess of $50 million dollars. Other Ukrainian drone units, possibly assisted by the take-down of the S-400, touted by the Kremlin to be the world’s most advanced air defense system, struck at least 60 targets across Crimea in the weeks following the HUR air raid, Kyiv Post records showed.
The US-based military maritime equipment company RECONCRAFT and UFORCE, in July 2026, signed a memorandum of understanding for licensed production of Ukrainian Magura boats in Oregon and South Carolina, with the American boatbuilder providing manufacturing capability and UFORCE providing software, guidance systems and command-and-control technology. News reports have mentioned potential production volumes of hundreds of boats annually.
Current Ukrainian production of Magura boats is a military secret. According to open sources, Ukraine’s special forces and navy have almost certainly fielded at least 100 boats since first fielding them in 2023, and possibly as many as 300.
The US, Great Britain, Turkey and China have experimented with drones flown from conventional, human-operated aircraft carriers, but none of those countries has yet fielded an aircraft carrier-launched drone operationally. Iran converted the container ship Shahid Bahman Bagheri into a drone carrier equipped with a ski-jump launch ramp in the early 2020s. US and Israeli air strikes in February-March 2026 sank the vessel in shallow water near the Bandar Abbas/Khuran Strait.

Vatican offers ‘good offices’ to help achieve settlement in Russia-Ukraine war

Burç Eruygur
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
The Vatican offered its “good offices” Tuesday to help achieve a settlement in the Russia-Ukraine war, saying it would continue supporting efforts to create space for dialogue.
Speaking at a joint news conference in Moscow with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher said the Vatican would continue supporting efforts to achieve a settlement.
 
Gallagher, the Vatican's secretary for relations with states, said it would contribute to and offer space for dialogue while continuing its charitable and humanitarian efforts.
“Indeed, we offer our good offices in any way that can help, in the hope that the much desired peace can be achieved as soon as possible,” Gallagher said.
“This is my sincere wish for the people of the Russian Federation, for the Ukrainian people, and all those who continue to suffer on account of this tragic war,” he added.
Gallagher expressed gratitude for what he described as a “frank and constructive” conversation with Lavrov.
He said the Ukraine war was among several topics they discussed and that, despite “substantial” differences and “numerous important points” of convergence, both sides reaffirmed the need to keep communication channels open.
Gallagher said the Vatican continued to follow the war with “deep concern.”
During his meeting with Lavrov, Gallagher said he reiterated Pope Leo XIV’s appeal to end hostilities and begin “authentic negotiations with the support of the international community.”
“The position of the Holy See remains clear. The conflict cannot be resolved by military means. It is essential to create the conditions for a serious political and diplomatic process,” he said.
Gallagher urged Moscow and Kyiv to “demonstrate openness and goodwill so that such dialogue can become a reality.” He also reiterated the need to respect international humanitarian law.
“Peace must be founded on the full respect of international law and of the principles of the Charter of the United Nations,” he added.
For his part, Lavrov said he conveyed Moscow’s gratitude to the Vatican for what he described as its balanced position on the situation in and around Ukraine.
 
“We outlined Russia's principled approaches to resolving the Ukrainian crisis by addressing its root causes and reaffirmed our appreciation for the Vatican's active engagement in resolving a number of pressing humanitarian issues within the conflict in Ukraine,” Lavrov said.
Lavrov said Russia and the Vatican maintained a trusting relationship and that Moscow supported efforts to inject new momentum into inter-church dialogue.
He also expressed hope that Vatican officials would pay attention to issues raised by Russia in their contacts with the Ukrainian side.
Lavrov said he informed Gallagher of Russia's readiness to resume political consultations at the deputy foreign minister level.
He added that Moscow was also ready to resume “targeted” consultations between the two sides' ministries on specific issues at the expert level.

Two UN peacekeepers killed in South Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:42:33 UTC
22:42:33 KST

Two UN peacekeepers killed in South Sudan
Two UN peacekeepers have been killed and seven people injured after unidentified gunmen ambushed a patrol in South Sudan’s eastern Jonglei State, the UN mission in the country (UNMISS) said on Monday.
The patrol was attacked while traveling to Pajut, a remote area in Jonglei, according to the mission. UNMISS deployed a quick reaction force to secure the area and assist with the emergency response. Three other peacekeepers were among those injured, along with two members of the South Sudan National Police Service and two civilian staff. No group has claimed responsibility for the attack so far.
UNMISS chief Anita Kiki Gbeho condemned the attack, describing violence targeting personnel working to support peace in the country as “unacceptable.”
Gbeho called on the authorities to launch a “thorough and prompt investigation” and ensure those responsible are brought to justice. UNMISS also warned that attacks targeting UN peacekeepers may constitute war crimes under international law.
South Sudan broke away from Sudan in 2011 but has remained volatile after a five-year civil war erupted in 2013 over a feud between leaders Salva Kiir and Riek Machar. The two signed a power-sharing deal in 2018, but tensions have escalated since Machar was detained on treason charges last year.
South Sudan has been plagued by political instability and armed conflict since gaining independence in 2011. A five-year civil war erupted in 2013 over a feud between President Salva Kiir Mayardit and former First Vice President Riek Machar, rooted in power struggles within the ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM – the party was founded in Sudan in 1983 and still keeps the same name). The 2018 peace agreement formally ended the civil war, but clashes continue across the country, driven by local militias and resource disputes.
The situation has been further complicated by political upheaval, including the arrest of Machar in March 2025. Machar’s party, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement‑in‑Opposition (SPLM‑IO), has warned that his detention effectively nullifies the 2018 peace agreement. Machar has been accused of supporting the White Army, a militia composed largely of Nuer fighters, which reportedly participated in clashes in Upper Nile state.
Ongoing insecurity has displaced hundreds of thousands, worsening the humanitarian crisis. According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), by the end of 2025, South Sudan had over 2.7 million internally displaced persons, and more than 9 million people in total are in need of humanitarian assistance.
Jonglei has been at the center of renewed fighting in recent months. Opposition forces seized government outposts in the state in December, prompting a government counteroffensive involving ground assaults and aerial bombardments. Violence displaced more than 420,000 people across South Sudan between January and June, primarily in Jonglei, according to UNMISS.
The incident comes amid mounting security risks for humanitarian personnel in South Sudan. At least 36 aid workers have been killed in the country since the beginning of the year, according to the UN, already exceeding the 31 deaths recorded throughout 2025.
More than 450 incidents of violence against humanitarian workers and assets were reported between January and July, more than double the number recorded during the same period in 2025, UN Humanitarian Coordinator for South Sudan Ramanathan Balakrishnan said last week.

Ukrainian company Wild Hornets develops module that can increase drone operating range by up to 50% – photos
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Ukrainian company Wild Hornets develops module that can increase drone operating range by up to 50% – photos
Ukrainian company Wild Hornets has developed the HV VTX Pro video transmitter, which is responsible for transmitting video signals from a drone to a ground station.
Source: Wild Hornets in a conversation with Ukrainska Pravda
Quote: "This upgrade expands the capabilities of both interceptor drones and FPV strike drones. Under comparable conditions, their maximum effective operating range will increase by up to 50%."
Details: The new HV VTX Pro will become part of the Hornet Vision digital video transmission system. Engineers have more than doubled the transmitter's maximum output power, to 4W.
The company explained that the more powerful module is expected to increase the range of digital video transmission and improve the stability and quality of communications when electronic warfare systems are operating.
According to the company, the operating radius of interceptor drones could increase from approximately 20 to 30 km under favourable radio conditions and when using an omnidirectional antenna with 360-degree coverage, which is installed on Hornet Vision ground stations.
Quote: "The more powerful VTX module also expands the capabilities of interceptor drones to engage targets flying at extremely low altitudes. According to pilots' estimates, depending on the conditions, this could increase the effectiveness of intercepting such targets by at least 20%."
More details: Wild Hornets said that when a directional antenna is used, the effective communication range with the new HV VTX Pro could increase even further.
"This will significantly increase the effectiveness of FPV strike drones: their maximum operating range will largely depend on battery capacity," the company explained.
The HV VTX Pro has already entered mass production and is being installed on all new Wild Hornets drones equipped with thermal imaging cameras. In the near future, the company plans to equip drones with daylight cameras with the new modules as well. The company stressed that this will not increase the cost of the drones for the Ukrainian military.
Previously, Wild Hornets also upgraded the Hornet Vision system, increasing the number of independent communication channels from nine to 25. The company said this will allow up to 25 crews to operate with Hornet Vision simultaneously without creating critical radio interference with one another.

NEW DELHI: Opposition MPs on Tuesday clashed with ruling party members during a meeting of the parliamentary standing committee on home affairs over a demand to discuss alleged police excesses against students during the July 20 protest march, news agency ANI reported, citing sources.During the meeting on "crime against children", Congress MP Ajay Maken submitted a letter seeking a discussion on the alleged use of pellet guns and lathicharge against students during the Jantar Mantar protest, sources told ANI.Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra is also learnt to have raised the issue, sources added.Opposition MPs argued that several students injured in the lathicharge were minors and that the matter therefore fell within the broader scope of 'Crime Against Children'.However, committee chairman Radha Mohan Das Agarwal rejected the demand, citing the Supreme Court's decision to set up a high-level committee to examine allegations of police excesses as well as violence by protesters during the demonstrations.Sources told ANI that a heated exchange took place between a BJP and a Congress member during the meeting, leading the chairman to ask members to restrict the discussion to the listed agenda.
This comes days after the Supreme Court constituted a five-member high-powered expert committee to conduct a fact-finding exercise into allegations of police excesses during the march.The committee comprises former Punjab and Haryana high court chief justice Ravi Shankar Jha, former Delhi high court Justice Shalinder Kaur, former CBI director Rishi Kumar Shukla and former Meghalaya DGP LR Bishnoi.
A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the panel would examine grievances raised by both protesters and police authorities in connection with the demonstrations.The bench directed the HPEC to prioritise allegations of excessive use of force by police, violence by protesters, and alleged harassment and molestation of women protesters. It also allowed the panel to examine whether interim compensation should be provided to people injured during the protests, including police personnel and protesters.The Supreme Court further directed that CCTV recordings of the protests and body-camera footage from police and security personnel, which had earlier been ordered to be preserved, be handed over to the committee for examination.The court clarified that the formation of the HPEC would not prevent police or other security authorities from initiating departmental or disciplinary proceedings against officers found to have violated applicable rules.

How TIME and Statista Determined the Best Employers of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:38:18 UTC
22:38:18 KST

TIME, in partnership with Statista, the leading global provider of market and consumer data and rankings, has published the second annual "Best Employers” ranking. Employers can help shape the workforce in a country. However, employee workplace satisfaction not only impacts company culture, but can influence productivity, innovation, profitability, and industry reputation. Here's how the winners were selected.
Methodology
The research project “Best Employers of 2026” was based on surveys conducted using several online access panels to guarantee a representative sample of employees across each country, starting with Brazil, India, and Australia. In Australia, 200,000 employer evaluations were conducted for companies from all sectors employing at least 200 people in the country. In India, 760,000 employer evaluations were conducted from companies employing at least 500 people in the country. In Brazil, more than 900,000 employer evaluations were conducted from companies employing at least 500 people in the country. Participants were asked, through an open-ended question with an auto-complete function, to name their current employer. This method ensures neutrality and prevents companies from influencing the selection of respondents.
Data collection
The survey was conducted using several online access panels to guarantee a representative sample of employees across the country. Participants were asked, through an open-ended question with an auto-complete function, to name their current employer. This method ensures neutrality and prevents companies from influencing the selection of respondents.
Scoring model
The final score combines two types of evaluations: employees’ willingness to recommend their own employer (direct score) and their willingness to recommend other employers in the same industry (indirect perception score), using data from 2025 and 2026.
Direct score: Respondents were asked to rate their willingness to recommend their employer to friends and family. The responses were graded on a scale from 0 to 10, where 0 means “I wouldn’t recommend my employer under any circumstances” and 10 means “I would definitely recommend my employer”.
Indirect score: Employees were also asked about their willingness to recommend other employers within their industry. Respondents were shown an industry list of employers and asked to give an opinion on those that stood out, either positively or negatively (Response options: “would recommend”, “would not recommend”, “no opinion”). Additionally, an open-ended question allowed respondents to name other employers. Greater weight is given to direct recommendations, as they provide the strongest reflection of employee satisfaction.
Ranking and recognition
This ranking reflects not only how employees view their own workplace but also how companies are perceived across their sector, creating a balanced and independent view of the top employers.

State-backed hackers targeted EU officials on WhatsApp, document shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:36:13 UTC
22:36:13 KST

BRUSSELS — Foreign governments have been trying to hack the messaging accounts of high-ranking European Union officials, the bloc’s cyber defense unit said in an internal presentation obtained by POLITICO.
The presentation, given to officials from EU national governments in July, lists “account takeover targeting high-ranking officials” as one of the top threats facing the bloc this year.
The presentation is the first official acknowledgment that EU officials were targeted by cyberattacks through messaging apps, after several national cyber agencies flagged an ongoing campaign linked to Russian threat groups earlier this year. The presentation is also the first reported instance in which an EU authority formally links such attacks to a foreign government.
Advertisement
The officials were the targets of so-called “state-sponsored spearphishing,” the presentation said, a term for state-backed, targeted and bespoke campaigns to get specific people to click on dodgy links or open malicious attachments. Hackers used "social engineering techniques" to trick EU officials, crafting personalized messages that were more likely to get targets to take the bait.
Earlier this year, POLITICO first reported that the European Commission told some of its most senior officials to shut down a Signal group over hacking fears. It came at the same time as a series of warnings by national cyber authorities telling governments to move away from commercial messaging apps like WhatsApp and Signal for official business.
In March, at least five national cyber and intelligence agencies publicly warned about ongoing hacking campaigns on Signal and WhatsApp. Dutch intelligence services specifically pinned this on Russia, and Germany warned that hackers were targeting “high-ranking individuals in politics, the military, and diplomacy, as well as investigative journalists.”
The agencies warned then that hackers were posing as a fake Signal support chatbot to persuade users to share their codes, allowing them to take over an account to read incoming communications and group chats.
EU cybersecurity officials said in the presentation that the bloc's institutions had faced eight "significant incidents" so far this year. One key challenge, they flagged, is that the different EU institutions still use different technical cybersecurity solutions and lack a common solution to exchange sensitive and classified documents.
The European Commission declined to give details on internal security practices in response to POLITICO's questions on the presentation.
WhatsApp and Signal did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Three years after his death, the Met goes after Mohamed Al Fayed. As for his enablers – well, you can’t rush things, can you? | Marina Hyde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:35:23 UTC
22:35:23 KST

How reassuring to learn that police investigating claims of sexual assault against Mohamed Al Fayed have handed a file to the Crown Prosecution Service, a mere three years after the former Harrods owner’s death at the age of 94, and just decades after the first survivors made reports of abuse. The CPS has said it won’t provide a timescale for any decision, to which we might remark: no shit. With this case, the one thing you could never accuse any of the authorities of is being bound by anything approaching a timescale.
The story does, however, certainly have scale. So far, more than 400 allegations including rape, sexual assault, sexual exploitation and human trafficking have been made against Al Fayed by at least 156 women – abuse he got away with, having died without any charges ever being brought against him. The claims span the years 1977 to 2014. At least 21 women came forward while he was alive, and there have been extraordinary rundowns in news articles and documentaries about all the alleged enablers of his wicked behaviour, from lawyers to mouthpieces to security henchmen to the doctors who carried out “purity examinations” on his young female PAs.
So, not to be a Debbie Downer – because any movement on this case is better than none – but perhaps that sense of scale is not immediately discernible from the file that has been sent to the CPS, which relates to a male suspect in his 80s and two indecent assaults on two women in London. The investigation remains ongoing, the Met confirms.
Of course, other under-prosecuted criminal networks are available. During the full-spectrum coverage of the Jeffrey Epstein case, many asked how on earth so many blind eyes could be turned by so many people to so much flagrant abuse by someone who was known to have served prison time for soliciting prostitution from a minor. People marvelled at the vast collective silence – yet anyone who couldn’t quite believe how it could happen should have been reassured that other vast collective silences were very much ongoing. Peter Mandelson’s now notorious message of commiseration to his friend Jeffrey shortly before his 2008 incarceration – “it just could not happen in Britain” – always seems to me ironically resonant. Perhaps his lordship was right, though not in the way he meant.
As the Epstein furore raged on earlier this year, several Al Fayed survivors wrote to me asking why this one case was dominating everything while another, still unresolved one – and so much closer to home – seemed to lack the turbocharge of outrage that pushes something from the places our society would rather forget into the ones where we have our (always belated) reckonings. The answer to that question is normally that significant numbers of people and institutions have a deeply vested interest in not getting to the bottom of it.
It would feel unwise to conclude anything other than that in this case. There has been no equivalent political pressure to let daylight in on Al Fayed’s activities. No one has got wall-to-wall news coverage for asking how he was able to operate an alleged criminal fiefdom in the centre of Knightsbridge, when allegations were repeatedly made and the rumours in rarefied circles were more than deafening. It was, it seems, just the way things were.
And as indicated, for things to be that way for so long, there needed to be whole armies of enablers and hangers-on who facilitated abuse, or looked away, or closed down or ridiculed or trashed those who stepped out of line and said anything about it, including the alleged victims. Only one of Epstein’s helpers, Ghislaine Maxwell, has ever been brought to justice. Typically, no one bar the kingpin in what I think of as the sex-case industrial complex even faces so much as a charge – they simply melt back into society, into other jobs, into the ongoing conspiracy of silence.
Today, the Al Fayed survivors’ group Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors issued a statement pointing out that: “Survivors have spent decades either not being believed or being told that Fayed and those around him were too powerful and that nothing could be done – but today is an important reminder that the passage of time does not, by itself, put accountability beyond reach.” Yet with the best will in the world, the passage of time doesn’t exactly help, does it? Al Fayed himself died unscathed, and we all know that once things tip conveniently into the “historical” file, they are so much harder to prove.
But there are things the public can get behind right now. What Al Fayed’s survivors want is the trafficking investigation they have been requesting for almost two years. As they point out, this was not one bad man, nor some form of corporate abuse. It was, they allege, a trafficking network involving multiple perpetrators and enablers and backed by the global movement of illicit funds. At least five survivors have already been confirmed by the Home Office as victims of modern slavery. Yet the Met has been accused of having failed in its legal duty to offer the victims a referral to the national referral mechanism (it’s understood the police didn’t believe they were obligated to), which identifies modern slavery victims. Yet again, all the running is being made by a survivors’ group. No One Above wants confirmation that human trafficking and modern slavery are the primary framework of the Al Fayed investigation, and to know that financial investigators are being utilised to determine how the network was funded and concealed.
It remains to be seen if any belated percentage of justice will be served in this case. Even if it is, we can expect all manner of blind-eye institutions to immediately resort to their happy place and trot out some trite platitude like “never again”. In fact, it would be more accurate to conclude the opposite. Always again. Always again, until society has the courage to realise that it so often takes a village to do bad things, as well as good ones.

  Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist

Russia extends improvised ship defenses to Baltic Fleet

- Multiple Russian Baltic Fleet vessels were observed during exercises fitted with improvised netting and irregular camouflage patterns.
- Russian naval forces have lost multiple warships to Ukrainian drone and unmanned surface vessel attacks in the Black Sea since 2022.
Russia’s Baltic Fleet has fitted several of its warships with improvised netting and irregular camouflage patterns as makeshift protection against drone strikes, according to footage circulating from a recent fleet exercise.
The images show at least three vessels equipped with different combinations of netting, deformation-pattern paint and other visual countermeasures on their bridges, radar housings and weapons systems.
The netting and camouflage now visible on multiple Baltic Fleet vessels are not part of a standardized Russian navy protection program. Similar improvised measures, including cage-like screens, netting and disruptive paint intended to interfere with visual and optical drone targeting, have appeared on Black Sea Fleet and Caspian Flotilla vessels over the past two years, often applied unevenly across different ships within the same fleet.
The measures follow the first confirmed Ukrainian drone strike on a Baltic Fleet installation. Ukrainian drones struck the corvette Boikiy, a Project 20380 vessel, while it sat in a dry dock at the Kronstadt naval base near St. Petersburg on the morning of June 3.
Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, announced the strike and published video of the attack, saying two Baltic Fleet ships were hit; he did not name the second vessel. Pro-Russian military blogger Boris Rozhin confirmed a drone struck the Boikiy’s superstructure, and video circulating on social media showed a fire at Kronstadt following the attack.
Russia’s Defense Ministry did not comment on the reported strikes, and the extent of the damage to the Boikiy has not been confirmed. The Boikiy had spent 2025 escorting tankers from Russia’s so-called shadow fleet through European waters, according to Brovdi.
Russia’s naval forces have lost multiple warships to Ukrainian drone and unmanned surface vessel attacks since 2022, primarily in the Black Sea. The Black Sea Fleet withdrew much of its surface combat force from Crimea’s western ports following repeated strikes by Ukrainian Neptune missiles, Magura-class unmanned surface vessels and aerial drones. The June 3 strike on the Boikiy was the first confirmed Ukrainian drone attack specifically on a Baltic Fleet installation, according to NV.ua, though
The Insider reported the Boikiy was the third Baltic Fleet vessel damaged by any means since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.

The US president said Tehran could no longer pay large segments of its military and was facing a "humanitarian crisis of epic proportions," days after 32 countries issued a joint statement condemning Iran's use of executions to silence dissent.
US President Donald Trump has renewed his criticism of Iran's execution of protesters, claiming Tehran can no longer afford to fund its armed forces and is facing a humanitarian crisis "of epic proportions".
"The failing Islamic Republic of Iran is not paying large segments of their military, while at the same time killing protesters, even when they are not protesting, at levels not seen before," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday.
"It is a humanitarian crisis of epic proportions, and must be stopped, now," he added.
In January, warning of imminent executions, Trump said the United States would take "very severe action" if they went ahead.
Days later he said reliable sources had informed him that the executions of "more than 800 detained protesters" had been halted, a claim Iranian officials did not confirm.

The January 2026 protests erupted following the collapse of the Iranian rial the month before and spread rapidly to more than 180 cities.
Security forces killed thousands of people during a crackdown on 8 and 9 January in the resulting crackdown.
Iran's Supreme Council of National Security acknowledged a death toll of more than 3,000. The UN Special Rapporteur on Iran put the figure at at least 5,000, while human rights groups and insiders in Iran believe the actual number of those killed may have surpassed 32,000.
At least 1,639 people were executed in Iran in 2025, the highest annual figure since 1989, according to Iran Human Rights and the organisation Together Against the Death Penalty.

Spain to reform asylum laws to align with EU rules as Ceuta crisis remains unresolved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:31:24 UTC
22:31:24 KST

Spain is set to reform its asylum laws as the Ceuta crisis remains unresolved. The European legislation aims to make it easier to reject asylum requests and accelerate returns, in line with demands from the bloc's hardline countries
The Spanish government is expected to present a draft bill to reform immigration and asylum laws as it struggles to contain the political fallout of the Ceuta crisis, which saw 80,000 people cross illegally from Morocco into the Spanish city in one day in July.
Madrid said the aim is to “bring Spanish legislation into line with the European Pact on Migration and Asylum”, which came into force this summer and makes it easier to reject asylum requests and accelerate expulsions, in line with demands from hardline countries.
Spain had initially opposed large parts of the legislation, arguing that a more comprehensive and humane approach to migration would be more beneficial. In practice, aligning with the EU will bring harsher measures into force, even as Spanish sources insist that fundamental rights will be guaranteed under the new system.
The timing comes as the migrant crisis in Ceuta remains unresolved, putting the spotlight on Madrid's handling of irregular migration, as well as its push to regularise up to 500,000 migrants living and working in Spain without legal documents.
While the vast majority of the 80,000 people who crossed the border illegally have returned to Morocco, around 5,000 remain in the Spanish enclave, including an estimated 2,000 minors.
The issue of unaccompanied minors is particularly sensitive, as Madrid seeks to balance strict legal requirements with its commitments to Brussels and Ceuta’s regional authorities to return everyone who entered illegally.
An attempt to transfer the minors to mainland Spain through an emergency decree has stalled, as the Spanish government, the conservative opposition and Ceuta’s regional authorities remain divided over the procedure.
Meanwhile, the European Commission has said Spain must carry out returns where there are no legal grounds for a person to remain in EU territory, while also ensuring that the rights of minors are protected under international conventions.
Madrid has yet to find a solution.
The draft immigration and asylum bill approved on Tuesday goes beyond Ceuta. It will implement the broader European Pact on Migration and Asylum, which came into force on 12 June, and introduce the EU's so-called “screening” procedure. The legislation will also affect the Canary Islands, which have seen an increase in irregular arrivals by boat.
A single command to deal with an unresolved crisis
The Spanish government also declared the Ceuta crisis a matter “of interest to national security” and called for a single command to manage the response.
The decision came almost a month after the crisis began, prompting sharp criticism from the conservative opposition People's Party (PP). Juan Vivas, president of Ceuta, had spent weeks calling on the Spanish government to take control of a situation that had overwhelmed the autonomous city.
Spain has yet to provide a comprehensive explanation of what triggered the mass influx into Ceuta, beyond pointing to human traffickers and a social media campaign that allegedly led young Moroccans and sub-Saharan migrants to believe they could enter the city and automatically claim asylum
While several ministers have been dispatched to the city, Pedro Sánchez is yet to address the migrant crisis in public since visiting Ceuta on July 31, when he declared that Spain’s territorial integrity “had been breached”, without blaming Morocco for the influx.
Rabat has said Madrid’s mass regularisation of migrants earlier this year sent contradictory signals.
