Russian ‘Starlink’ constellation satellites falling from orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:27:58 UTC
18:27:58 KST

- Two satellites from Russia's second Rassvet batch are decaying toward reentry after never performing orbit-raising maneuvers.
- None of the 16 satellites launched July 19 climbed above 360 km, roughly 200 km lower than the first group reached at a similar stage.
Two satellites from Russia’s second Rassvet launch batch are heading toward reentry after never performing orbit-raising maneuvers, according to tracking data reported by Anatoly Zak of RussianSpaceWeb.com. The pair had fallen below 300 km in altitude as of late August and appeared to be on a decay path, the report said.
It is the second time satellites from the Rassvet constellation have failed to reach a stable orbit. The Defence Blog reported in June that the first Rassvet satellite lost, designated Object 4, reentered the atmosphere on June 6 after never performing a single maneuver following its March 23 launch, the first confirmed casualty of the program.
The two newly affected satellites are part of a 16-spacecraft cluster launched July 19 from Plesetsk aboard a Soyuz-2-1b rocket, the same launch site that sent up another classified military satellite on August 24. The July batch was the second group of Rassvet-3 satellites built by Bureau 1440, a Russian company developing a low Earth orbit broadband constellation the Kremlin has promoted as a domestic counterpart to Starlink. Neither Roscosmos nor Russia’s Ministry of Defense has publicly acknowledged the July 19 launch.
The U.S. Space Force catalogued 17 objects, the 16 satellites plus the rocket’s upper stage, on July 24 in an orbit averaging 289 by 327 km with an inclination of 82.3 degrees, RussianSpaceWeb reported, citing Space Force tracking data. Nine of the 16 satellites began orbit-raising maneuvers between late July and early August, but their resulting altitudes ranged from 313 to 332 km, roughly 200 km lower than where the first Rassvet batch stood at a comparable point after its own March 23 launch.
By August 5, 11 satellites in the second group were climbing, according to the tracking data cited in the report. By the end of August, three of those had stopped climbing and begun a slow decay at altitudes between 310 and 330 km. None of the 16 satellites in the batch managed to climb above 360 km, the report said.
Bureau 1440 confirmed the July 19 launch’s success in a statement posted to Telegram the following day, saying the satellites had separated from the rocket and established contact with mission control.
“After completion of checks and the operational activation of sub-systems, the satellites will begin transfer to a target orbit for providing communications services,” the company said in the statement.
The company did not disclose a launch time or the satellites’ official designations in that statement.
Rassvet’s stated goal is to provide Russia with an independent satellite broadband network after Starlink terminals were effectively cut off from unauthorized use inside the country. Bureau 1440 has said it aims to expand the constellation to roughly 250 satellites by 2027, when it plans to begin commercial service, and to as many as 900 satellites by 2035, according to company figures. Militarnyi has reported that Russia plans to place 292 Rassvet satellites into orbit by the end of 2027.
Ukrainian officials and analysts have said the first Rassvet batch, launched in March, has already begun providing measurable coverage over Ukraine despite Object 4’s loss. Ukrainian satellite communications expert Volodymyr Stepanets told Militarnyi in early August that the first group provides at least two daily communications windows over Ukraine, each lasting more than an hour, based on his analysis of the satellites’ orbital tracks. Serhii Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential adviser known by the call sign Flash, has said Russia would need at least 200 to 250 satellites in orbit to provide stable, continuous coverage.
Plesetsk, the launch site for both Rassvet batches, has drawn repeated Ukrainian drone activity in 2026. Roscosmos director general Dmitry Bakanov said Ukrainian forces attempted a drone attack on the site during preparations for the March 25 launch, and Ukrainian drones reached the surrounding Arkhangelsk region again on August 23, a day before Russia’s next classified satellite launch from the same complex.
The second batch’s orbital plane sits more than 100 degrees away from that of the March launch group, according to RussianSpaceWeb, based on differences in each group’s right ascension of the ascending node. No official update on the fate of the underperforming satellites has been issued by Roscosmos, the Russian military or Bureau 1440.

The oil refinery in the Russian city of Perm suspended operations following a Ukrainian drone strike.
Reuters reported the incident, citing industry sources.
The attack on the facility took place on August 21. The refinery in question is one of Russia’s largest – LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez.
The drone strike caused a fire and damaged process units at the AVT-4 crude oil distillation unit, which accounts for nearly 40% of the refinery’s capacity.
Before the damage, the unit could process 14,000 metric tons of crude oil per day.
Preliminary estimates suggest repair work could take one to two weeks.
In addition, sources say another primary oil distillation unit, AVT-5, which accounts for 34% of the refinery’s capacity, has been out of operation since the drone attack on July 29.
The LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery is a key industrial facility in Russia’s Perm Krai.
The refinery has a designed processing capacity of about 13 million tonnes of crude oil per year, making it Russia’s seventh-largest oil refinery by processing volume. The refinery produces gasoline, diesel fuel, jet fuel, and lubricants, and also processes associated petroleum gas.
The facility’s products meet domestic demand in the aggressor country and, prior to Ukrainian strikes, were also used for export shipments.
LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez has been repeatedly targeted by drones operated by Ukraine’s Defense Forces. The refinery was attacked on May 8 and May 7. Another drone attack took place on April 30. The facility is more than 1,500 kilometers from the frontline.
Strikes on Russian oil refineries aim to reduce fuel production needed to supply Russian troops and support the country’s economy. Damage to equipment at these facilities reduces oil processing and creates fuel shortages in the domestic market.

You invested money in a brand, but you could lose it: a lawyer warned about the main pitfall for businesses
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:24:24 EEST
18:24:24 KST

You invested money in a brand, but you could lose it: a lawyer warned about the main pitfall for businesses
Kyiv • UNN
The name of a legal entity does not grant exclusive rights to a brand. The lawyer advises registering a trademark separately to avoid disputes and expenses.
Registration of a legal entity in itself does not guarantee a business the exclusive right to use the company name as a brand. Proper legal protection of a trademark requires separate trademark registration. Alina Parkhuta, an intellectual property lawyer at LLC "Law Company "LOGIC"", told UNN about this.
According to her, entrepreneurs often make the mistake of believing that after a company is state-registered, its name automatically receives the same protection as a registered trademark.
Entrepreneurs often begin actively developing a brand before taking care of its legal protection. They invest in marketing, advertising, website development and increasing the company's recognition, but postpone trademark registration. If a dispute arises, this may lead not only to financial losses but also to the need to completely change a brand that has already become known to consumers
She clarified that when a legal entity is state-registered, its name is entered in the Unified State Register. It is used to identify the company in legal relations, conclude contracts and conduct business activities.
In turn, according to Parkhuta, a trademark has a different purpose - it helps distinguish the goods or services of one business from the goods or services of other companies on the market.
A trademark may be a word, logo, graphic image, slogan, combination of letters or numbers, or another designation used to individualize goods and services, the lawyer clarified.
After a trademark is registered, its owner obtains the exclusive right to use the relevant designation and may also permit or prohibit its use by other persons, the lawyer emphasized.
According to Parkhuta, postponing trademark registration may create legal and financial risks for a business.
If another person registers an identical or similar designation as a trademark for the relevant goods or services, that person will obtain legal mechanisms to protect their rights.
In such a case, a company that has already operated under the relevant name for a long time may face claims concerning the use of the brand. This may relate to the website name, advertising materials, signs, product packaging, social media pages and other elements of the corporate identity, Parkhuta said.
If a dispute arises, the company may be forced to spend money on legal protection and, in some cases, change the name and brand elements into which significant resources have already been invested.
In today's competitive environment, a brand is not merely a means of identifying a company. It builds business recognition, consumer trust and its reputation on the market.
Companies invest in advertising, marketing, social media, website creation and the development of their own style. Over time, these investments increase the economic value of the brand and its recognition among customers.
Today, a brand is one of the most valuable intangible assets of a business. Its creation requires time, financial investment and systematic work, so the issue of legal protection should not be postponed. Trademark registration helps not only secure rights to the brand but also creates a reliable foundation for the company's further development, entry into new markets, conclusion of partnership agreements and business scaling
Thus, state registration of a legal entity and trademark registration serve different functions. Company registration allows a business to officially conduct economic activities, whereas trademark registration provides legal protection for a specific brand.
For a business planning long-term development and investing in its reputation, timely trademark registration can help reduce legal risks and avoid additional costs in the future, the lawyer emphasized.

Who are Iran’s top trading partners US would need to target to isolate it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:23:05 UTC
18:23:05 KST

Who are Iran’s top trading partners US would need to target to isolate it?
The US wants to isolate Iran from the global economy. Here is who Tehran trades with, and how much is at stake.
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has unveiled a new wave of sanctions on Iran, branded “Operation Economic Outcast”, designating close to 60 entities, individuals and vessels and widening secondary sanctions to cover shipping, gold, aviation, technology and digital assets.
He said the aim was to sever every economic lifeline sustaining the government in Tehran until it stands alone, and that President Donald Trump was telephoning world leaders with specific requests to halt their dealings with Iran, though he named no countries and set no deadline.
Below, we break down Iran’s top trading partners using official customs figures compiled by Trade Data Monitor, which exclude the unrecorded flows sustaining much of Iran’s oil exports.
Iran’s top export partners
Iran has spent much of the past two decades under Western sanctions, a pressure that has pushed its economy away from Europe and towards a narrowing group of Asian and regional partners.
In 2024, Iran exported some $56bn worth of goods to at least 112 countries and territories, according to official customs figures. Its top export partners were:
- China ($14.58bn) – The largest buyer of Iranian oil, taking more than 80 percent of Iran’s seaborne crude exports, according to tanker-tracking analysts. Much of it is discounted and moved by shadow-fleet vessels, barely registering in either country’s customs records.
- Iraq ($11.7bn) – Iran has been a major supplier of gas to Iraq for electricity generation, and sells electricity directly to Iraqi provinces in the south. It is also a leading source of food products, building materials and manufactured goods.
- UAE ($7.16bn) – Has long been a financial and re-export lifeline for Iran, accounting for 13 percent of its exports. Abu Dhabi imposed an indefinite trade embargo last week after accusing Iran of firing missiles at its territory. Tehran denied the allegations.
- Turkiye ($6.1bn) – Iran has long supplied Turkiye with pipeline gas via the Tabriz-Ankara Pipeline, along with petrochemicals, food products, and construction materials.
- Afghanistan ($2.3bn) Iran supplies its landlocked neighbour with fuel, food and construction materials, and Afghanistan depends heavily on Iranian ports and overland routes to access wider markets.
Iran’s top import partners
In 2024, Iran imported some $68.5bn worth of goods from at least 87 countries and territories, according to official customs figures. Its top import partners were:
- UAE ($21bn) – Supplied just above 30 percent of Iran’s imports, most of them re-exported goods rather than Emirati production, giving Tehran indirect access to Western machinery, electronics and consumer goods. Abu Dhabi’s indefinite trade embargo has severed that route.
- China ($17.8bn) – The main supplier of machinery, electronics, vehicles and industrial components, and the partner Iran has leaned on most heavily as Western trade has closed off.
- Turkiye ($11.1bn) – A shared land border and longstanding commercial ties make Turkiye a key overland supply route, sending machinery, chemicals, vehicles and manufactured goods. Trade in both directions has fallen since the war began.
- European Union ($6.1bn) – European sales are now a fraction of pre-2018 levels, concentrated in pharmaceuticals, medical equipment and machinery.
- India ($1.6bn) – Trade has fallen sharply in recent years. New Delhi has kept commercial links narrow and weighted towards agricultural goods including rice, tea and pharmaceuticals.

Russian military confirms classified satellite launch from Plesetsk

09:22:50 UTC
18:22:50 KST

- Russia launched a classified military satellite from Plesetsk on August 24, a day after Ukrainian drones reached the surrounding region.
- Russian officials confirmed the satellite reached orbit but did not disclose its identity or mission.
Russia launched a classified military satellite from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on August 24, the country’s Ministry of Defense said, a day after Ukrainian drones reached the surrounding Arkhangelsk region in an apparent attempt to disrupt the launch. A Soyuz-2-1b rocket lifted off from Site 43, Pad 3, at 05:40 Moscow time.
Russian officials said the payload, listed only under the generic designation “Kosmos,” reached orbit as planned and that ground stations established telemetry contact with the satellite. The Ministry of Defense did not identify the spacecraft’s mission or specifications.
Ukrainian and Russian monitoring channels reported drones over Arkhangelsk region on August 23, with local officials describing the targets as “strategic facilities.” The Russian monitoring channel Locator Russia said at least two drones reached the vicinity of Plesetsk, and residents in the area filmed footage of drones overhead, according to the Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi. Governor Alexander Tsybulsky of Arkhangelsk region ordered residents to take shelter and said mobile internet service would be suspended, without disclosing the outcome of the attack. Russian authorities said 40 drones were shot down over the region in total.
It was the first reported case of Ukrainian drones reaching Arkhangelsk region, according to Militarnyi. Roscosmos director general Dmitry Bakanov said in April that Ukrainian forces had previously attempted a drone attack on Plesetsk during preparations for a March 25 satellite launch, an attack he said Russian space and air defense units repelled.
Plesetsk is Russia’s primary launch site for military satellites and has also been used to test the Sarmat intercontinental ballistic missile, according to Militarnyi. The site has hosted multiple Soyuz-2 and Angara rocket launches in 2026 carrying military satellites and batches of Rassvet-series communications satellites, built by the Russian company Bureau 1440.
Similar warnings reappeared in mid-August for a period between August 19 and August 30, overlapping with separate restriction notices tied to a presumed Angara-1.2 launch. On August 15, authorities in the Komi Republic announced closures of the Vashka and Zheleznodorozhny rocket-debris impact zones, sites previously used for GLONASS satellite launches on Soyuz rockets, without specifying an exact launch window beyond “the second half of August.” A similar warning followed on August 21 from officials in the Tyumen region regarding a debris impact zone in the Uvatsky district.

China's Xi Jinping to visit India with 400-member delegation for Brics: Report

China's Xi Jinping to visit India with 400-member delegation for Brics: Report
Edited by: Trisha Mahajan / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 25, 2026, 15:38 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Xi’s expected visit comes as India and China step up high-level talks to maintain peace along the border and rebuild ties. (File photo)
Chinese President Xi Jinping is likely to attend next month’s BRICS summit in New Delhi with a large delegation, more than double the Chinese contingent that accompanied him on his last India visit in 2019.Xi’s expected visit on September 12-13 with 400 officials, marking his first trip to India in seven years and comes as the two countries work to stabilise ties after years of tensions over their disputed border, reported Reuters, citing sources.Two Indian sources said Xi was likely to be accompanied by around 400 officials, compared with fewer than 200 during his 2019 visit. “Chinese officials are busy finalising hotels and security protocols,” one Indian source with direct knowledge told Reuters.
Xi’s final travel plans and the agenda for any possible bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi are yet to be finalised, the sources said.The Chinese foreign ministry said, “China attaches great importance to and actively participates in BRICS cooperation, and supports India, the current chair, in successfully hosting this year's BRICS summit.”“We currently have no information available to provide” about Xi’s visit, it added.
The expected visit comes as India and China continue high-level efforts to improve ties. National Security Advisor Ajit Doval on Tuesday met Chinese Vice President Han Zheng in Beijing, with the two sides discussing ways to maintain peace and tranquillity along the border and strengthen relations across economic, political and multilateral platforms.“On 25 August, NSA and Special Representative on the India-China Boundary Question, Ajit Doval called on Han Zheng, Vice President of the People's Republic of China,” the Embassy of India in China said.Read more: Ajit Doval’s China visit: NSA, Chinese VP Han Zheng discuss border peace, bilateral tiesThe two sides discussed strengthening peace and tranquillity in the border areas and improving bilateral ties “across economic, political and multilateral fora”, the embassy said.Doval is in Beijing for the 25th round of Special Representatives talks on the India-China boundary question with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. The talks are expected to cover the border dispute as well as bilateral, regional and international issues.
India-China ties were badly strained after the 2020 Galwan Valley clash, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed. The confrontation led to a prolonged military stand-off along the Line of Actual Control before the two sides reached a disengagement agreement in October 2024.
Relations have improved gradually since then, with a series of high-level engagements between Modi and Xi. Their possible meeting in New Delhi during the BRICS summit could give fresh momentum to those efforts.

Occupation officials involved in deportation of 53 Ukrainian children to Russia served with notices of suspicion in absentia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25

Occupation officials involved in deportation of 53 Ukrainian children to Russia served with notices of suspicion in absentia
Four occupation "officials" involved in the deportation of 53 children from three children's homes in temporarily occupied Donetsk and Makiivka to Russia have been served with notices of suspicion in absentia.
Source: Ukraine's Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko
Details: The children were illegally taken to Russia in October 2022.
"This was not an evacuation. This was a planned deportation of Ukrainian children, organised at the highest level of Russia's military-political leadership," Kravchenko said.
According to the investigation, four officials carried out the crime in the occupied territory:
- "Donetsk People's Republic" health minister Dmytro Hartsev provided administrative processing
- Svitlana Maiboroda, head of the occupation "State Service for Family and Children's Affairs", coordinated transport, the transfer of personal files and subsequent placement of the children
- heads of children's homes Viacheslav Vysiahin and Viktor Honcharov organised the gathering of the children and personally accompanied them during their removal
Law enforcement established that the Ukrainian children were transported by bus to Rostov-on-Don, Russia. From there, they were flown by a special Rossiya flight detachment aircraft to Moscow Oblast and distributed among social centres.
Immediately after arrival, Russian agencies began processing documents under Russian law: granting the Ukrainian children Russian citizenship, entering them into the state database and placing them with Russian families.
The children's profiles subsequently appeared on an adoption portal. The investigation established that 28 Ukrainian children were placed under the guardianship of Russian families.
"To this day, not a single child from this group has been returned to Ukraine. They have effectively spent their entire conscious lives in the aggressor state. They are growing up in a Russian educational, informational and cultural environment. A foreign identity is being imposed on them and attempts are being made to permanently sever their connection with Ukraine.
This is not a side effect of deportation. This is its continuation: a deliberate state policy of Russification of Ukrainian children," the prosecutor general said.
Dmytro Hartsev, Svitlana Maiboroda, Viacheslav Vysiahin and Viktor Honcharov have been served with in absentia suspicion notices for violations of the laws and customs of war committed by prior conspiracy of a group of individuals.
"Their decisions, orders, meetings held, transfer of documents and the entire deportation route have been documented in detail. Notices of suspicion served in absentia are only the first step towards the personal accountability of each of them. War crimes have no statute of limitations," Kravchenko stressed.
Background: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine previously named 10 more individuals involved in the militarisation of Ukrainian children under occupation.

Sitting volleyball captain Alipourian dropped from Asian Para Games squad
TEHRAN - Iran’s sitting volleyball captain Davoud Alipourian has been left out of the national team squad for the upcoming Asian Para Games in Nagoya, Japan.
The national team are set to begin a new training camp in preparation for the Asian Para Games, but Alipourian will not be among the players called up for the upcoming camp.
The World Sitting Volleyball Championships and Paralympic qualifying tournament in Hangzhou was the last competition in which Alipourian represented Iran. Iran won the title at the tournament and secured their place at the Paralympic Games. Following the event, however, Alipourian declined to join his teammates in subsequent training camps amid a dispute with the team management.
He had initially been included among the 15 players invited to Iran’s first training camp following the World Championships, but chose not to attend as part of his protest.
For the next camp, which will be the national team’s second training camp since the World Championships, Alipourian has been removed from the squad. As a result, the camp will feature the 14 players who participated in the previous camp.
Ali Kashfian, head of Iran’s Sitting Volleyball Association, confirmed the decision, adding that the dates for the new training camp would be finalized soon.
With Alipourian no longer part of the national team setup, Iran will also have to appoint a new captain ahead of the Asian Para Games.
The fifth Asian Para Games will be held in Nagoya, Japan, from Oct. 18 to 24, with Iran’s sitting volleyball team entering the competition as the defending champions.

First K2 Black Panther Tanks Under Second Contract Arrive in Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:19:31 UTC
18:19:31 KST

The first shipment of South Korean K2 Black Panther main battle tanks, ordered under a contract effective August 1, 2025, has arrived in Poland.
Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, the country’s Minister of National Defense, announced this.
The military received 28 K2 tanks, which will soon join the arsenal of the Polish Armed Forces’ 16th Pomeranian Mechanized Division.
This delivery marks the start of implementing the agreement, which includes supplying both base vehicles and a specially developed K2PL version.
In subsequent batches, Poland will receive the K2PL version, manufactured using components produced in Poland.
Poland’s large-scale rearmament of its armored forces with South Korean equipment began in the summer of 2022, when the two sides signed a framework agreement to purchase 980 K2 tanks.
The first firm contract was signed in August 2022 and called for the direct delivery of 180 K2 tanks in their basic configuration from South Korea.
Hyundai Rotem has fully completed the first contract by delivering all 180 vehicles to the Polish military.
The second agreement, signed on August 1, 2025, provides for the manufacture and delivery of the next batch of 180 K2 and K2PL tanks.
Under this second contract, some of the tanks will be manufactured directly in South Korea, while the K2PL versions will be produced at facilities within the Polish defense industry.
The K2 Black Panther tanks will replace the outdated Soviet T-72s and their Polish PT-91 Twardy upgrades in the 16th Mechanized Division, many of which were transferred to Ukraine.
The final F-35A Husarz fighter jet for the Polish Air Force has previously been completed in the U.S. Subsequent aircraft will be manufactured in Italy.

On highway in Zakarpattia region, car at high speed struck and killed child: holding of race is being investigated
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:16:45 EEST
18:16:45 KST

On highway in Zakarpattia region, car at high speed struck and killed child: holding of race is being investigated
Kyiv • UNN
In Zakarpattia region, a 19-year-old driver was served with a notice of suspicion following the fatal collision with a child. Possible illegal racing is also being investigated.
In Zakarpattia region, an 11-year-old boy was killed in a road accident on the Kyiv–Chop highway; the driver was notified of suspicion, and the prosecutor's office is checking information that illegal speed races were held here shortly before the tragedy, the Zakarpattia Regional Prosecutor's Office reported, UNN writes.
Details
"A 19-year-old man who hit an 11-year-old boy with a car has been notified of suspicion. The child died at the scene from the injuries sustained," the statement said.
The tragedy occurred at around 5:20 p.m. on August 23 on the international Kyiv–Chop highway near the village of Solomonovo in Uzhhorod district.
"According to the investigation, the suspect was driving a Volkswagen Vento at a speed of approximately 100 km/h, exceeding the established limit. According to preliminary information, at that moment the child ran onto the road and suddenly turned back," the prosecutor's office noted.
The driver of the Volkswagen Vento was detained under Article 208 of the Criminal Procedure Code of Ukraine. He is charged with violating road safety rules by a person operating a vehicle, if this caused the death of the victim (Part 2 of Article 286 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). The issue of choosing a preventive measure for him is being decided; the prosecutor's office will petition for his unconditional detention. The initiation of a temporary restriction on the use of a special right has also been initiated, specifically, his right to operate a vehicle.
"In addition, according to eyewitness accounts, illegal speed races took place on this section of the road shortly before the tragedy. According to preliminary information, the child was among the spectators," the prosecutor's office reported.
As part of separate criminal proceedings, as stated, "law enforcement officers will establish all those involved in organizing and participating in speed races on the road." "Law enforcement officers have already seized one car used in the race and placed it in a special impound lot. Priority investigative actions are being carried out. The preliminary legal classification in these proceedings is Article 290 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (destruction, forgery or replacement of the numbers of vehicle components and assemblies)," the statement said.
"We draw attention to the fact that speed races on public roads are prohibited. They can turn into a tragedy within seconds. And this concerns not only the participants, but also random people. Law enforcement officers will identify both the participants and the organizers, and based on the established facts, appropriate decisions will be made, including those of a criminal-law nature," the agency emphasized.

====================================================================================================

Spirit Airlines Wants to Sell Its Data to Google. Former Flight Attendants Are Freaked Out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

Spirit Airlines may have declared bankruptcy this spring, but the budget airline is still worth something—to AI giants, at least. In mid-August, Google won a $10 million bid to purchase some 34 years of the airline’s data, from invoices and flight operations information to Wi-Fi sales, employee records, and crew pairings.
In a statement, a Google spokesperson said the data “can be helpful in improving our products and AI models.” The sale would not include customer data, and Google “will not receive any personal information from this dataset,” the spokesperson said. The winning offer, chosen over a competing $7.5 million proposal from AI data and training company Mercor, has to be approved by a judge.
If former Spirit Airlines attendants have their way, that won’t happen easily. Just days after the court announced Google’s winning bid, the labor union representing 5,500 former Spirit Airlines flight attendants filed an objection to the sale. Lawyers for the 55,000-member Association of Flight Attendants (AFA) argue the sale would include an enormous amount of sensitive employee information, and that even Google’s promised safeguards wouldn’t prevent privacy violations of decades of flight attendants who never could have guessed that their data would be sold to train AI systems.
The employee data “has no business being sold,” Sara Nelson, the president of the AFA, said in a written statement to WIRED. “This is outrageous!”
The legal objection opens a potential new front in the AI data wars, as major frontier labs including Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mercor scramble to find new sources of data to help train their products. US laws have contemplated how best to protect consumer data, even after companies go bankrupt and are sold off for parts—laws that have taken on new salience and value in the age of AI.
But the Spirit Airlines’ flight attendants’ legal objection highlights the gap between data protections for consumers and for workers. It also marks the first public tangle between labor unions and corporations over the sale and use of employee data for AI training purposes, legal experts say.
“There is no boundary between the information and data that the employee is producing and their own personal information. The law has not caught up,” says Seema Patel, a law professor at the University of California, College of the Law, San Francisco, who studies labor issues and technology. (California is one of the few states to have explicit worker data protection laws.) "Companies are having a field day with this.”
In the past few months, startups specializing in selling defunct companies’ data—including old Slack messages, GitHub content, and Google Drives—to those training AI have reportedly made millions. Meanwhile, so-called egocentric data collection efforts are on the rise, as companies race to record humans performing work like cooking meals, cleaning kitchens, and operating factory lines, and use that data to train machines to aid and eventually replace them.
The Spirit data sale would, according to a court filing, include more than 1 million time-card records, over 175,000 employee records, nearly 150,000 employee tax forms, employment contracts and litigation files, 80,000 email accounts, 17 million individually owned Microsoft OneDrive items, 20.6 million shared Microsoft SharePoint files, and 500 million Microsoft Teams records.
The court filing describes a process through which the data buyer—Google—would select or OK a third party to strip the data of elements that could be used to link the information with a particular consumer. A hearing related to the data sale has been delayed to September 9.
One former Spirit Airlines flight attendant called the potential data sale “troubling.” “I knew they were going to sell every single part of consumer data. It never crossed my mind that they would be so bold as to sell our private data for AI,” says the flight attendant, who spoke to WIRED under condition of anonymity because they’re still looking for new employment.
The flight attendant says his and other employees’ email accounts and Microsoft files included deeply sensitive personal and medical information shared with the airline as part of their employment and insurance agreements, detailing everything from miscarriages to incidents of domestic violence to union contract negotiations. “There’s this huge consensus of feeling extremely violated by this,” he says.
In its legal objection, AFA argues that “deidentifying” employee data isn’t the same as providing confidentiality, because AI itself makes it much easier to relink private information across datasets, even without specific names. “The privacy architecture of this transaction is consumer-facing; its payload is disproportionately employee-facing,” the union's lawyers wrote. The union argues the bankruptcy court should either exclude all flight-attendant-related data from the sale or guarantee that employee data receives the same protections as consumer information.
Though the flight attendants’ objections are just a small part of the larger Spirit Airlines bankruptcy proceeding, the outcome could have a major effect on how labor unions and companies think about employee data going forward, says Ari Ezra Waldman, a professor of law at the University of California, Irvine, who studies privacy and technology.
“In a world where billions and trillions are being spent on [large language models], anything where words are used is subject to its own profit-making purpose,” he says. “If this goes forward with no limitation, there is no protection for any employee.”
The fact that flight attendants are at the forefront of this labor question, rather than workers who sit at desks and type all day, is a reminder that all employees can create data with market value. “All workers bring an immense amount of knowledge,” Patel says. “Now artificial intelligence has given us the ability to process all different kinds of data.”
More value, meanwhile, is one of the former Spirit Airlines’ flight attendants’ goals. Separately, the union has also intervened in the bankruptcy to demand roughly $68 million in unpaid vacation, health care, and back pay.
“We feel it's another slap in the face that we're waiting for our missing wages while Spirit is going to profit $10 million off our private information,” says the former flight attendant.

Over 20 items planned for CIS Heads of Government Council meeting in Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

MINSK, 25 August (BelTA) - More than 20 items are planned for the agenda of the CIS Heads of Government Council meeting, which will be held in Moscow in December 2026, CIS Secretary General Sergei Lebedev told the media ahead of a meeting of the CIS Plenipotentiaries Council on 25 August, BelTA has learned.
“The main item on today’s meeting of the CIS Plenipotentiaries Council is the coordination of the agenda for the CIS Heads of Government Council meeting, scheduled for December in Moscow. There is enough time for coordination. Nevertheless, more than 20 items have already been put together,” Sergei Lebedev said.
The December meeting agenda includes three concepts proposed for approval, concerning the development of specific industrial sectors. Several action plans covering the period up to 2030–2032 are also included. In addition, nine financial matters will be discussed.
“The agenda for the Heads of Government Council meeting will be packed. We intend to work thoroughly in the time remaining so as not to burden the heads of government with extensive discussions during the meeting. I believe we will succeed,” Sergei Lebedev said.
Also on today’s agenda is the matter of the rules of procedure for the Plenipotentiaries Council.
In addition, a number of issues have been proposed under the “miscellaneous” heading, including a review of the outcomes of the recent elections in Kazakhstan. According to the CIS secretary general, this election campaign is being given significant attention. Today, CIS First Deputy Secretary General Igor Petrishenko, who headed the CIS observation mission, will report on the results of the Kurultai elections.
Members of the CIS Plenipotentiaries Council will also discuss the “CIS Plus” format, which was approved last year at a meeting of the CIS Heads of State Council.
Sergei Lebedev informed that following the approval of this format, he sent letters to several international organizations proposing its consideration. Responses have already been received from some organizations, and there is interest in the format.
“We are currently working with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, which was granted observer status last year. In addition, we usually invite the chairman of the Board of the Eurasian Economic Commission and the secretary general of the CSTO to our meetings. I believe that today’s discussion will encourage their participation,” the CIS secretary general said.
He added that SCO Secretary General Nurlan Yermekbayev has already agreed to participate. Close cooperation is maintained with the organization, and a memorandum has been signed.
In his opening address to the CIS Plenipotentiaries Council, Sergei Lebedev noted that the CIS states are pursuing vital reforms in the economic, social, public, and political sectors. Thanks to their consistent commitment to developing good-neighborly and mutually beneficial ties, the CIS countries have earned well-deserved recognition from the international community and have become active participants in international relations.

Türkiye moves to curb misleading property, car listings on social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:14:37 UTC
18:14:37 KST

The Trade Ministry has stepped up its crackdown on misleading property and vehicle advertisements on social media, imposing 8.2 million Turkish Liras ($171,000) in fines on 82 businesses.
The ministry announced that 42 real estate agencies and 40 vehicle dealerships were fined 100,000 liras each for publishing listings that breached advertising regulations. The crackdown also targets posts featuring phrases such as “DM for price” that hide asking prices from the public.
Under the Electronic Advertisement Verification System (EİDS), identity and authorization checks are mandatory for property and vehicle listings published online, including on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp. Social media posts must include a link to an EİDS-verified listing, while any accompanying photos, videos and descriptions must correspond to the verified property or vehicle.
The ministry said businesses had previously been warned that prices must also be stated in social media posts rather than provided only through private messages.
It also said that Meta will block accounts found violating the rules.

NEW DELHI: Commercial pilots in India could soon be subjected to annual dope tests that may be conducted at random for the surprise factor. This consultation is going on right now. There are multiple ways of approaching this dope test. anne loch magnifies flowers, sheep and mountains at zentrum paul klee in switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:12:54 UTC
18:12:54 KST

Flowers nearly two meters tall, a flock of sheep stretching more than three and a half meters across, and a raven’s head enlarged beyond human scale introduce the monumental dimensions that define much of Anne Loch’s work. Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern brings together around 80 works by the German artist for Anne Loch. Painting: So what?, curated by Amélie Joller and on view through September 20, 2026. The exhibition marks only her second major solo presentation in Switzerland and opens a window onto an extensive body of work that remained largely outside the institutional spotlight for decades.
Loch began her career within Cologne’s increasingly visible art scene of the 1980s, represented early on by Monika Sprüth alongside artists including Rosemarie Trockel, Jenny Holzer and Cindy Sherman. Yet while neo-expressionist gestures were gathering momentum around her, Loch took a markedly different route, painting landscapes, flowers and animals with a cool, constructed precision. Then, in 1988, just as a conventional version of artistic success seemed to be taking shape, she left Cologne behind and withdrew to Thusis in the Swiss canton of Grisons, largely cutting herself off from the art world while continuing to work relentlessly.
Anne Loch in her studio in Thusis, 1989 | image: Estate of Anne Loch | photo: Christoph Guler, Thusis
WHEN FLOWERS GET BIG ENOUGH TO BECOME STRANGE
Across a career of roughly four decades, Loch produced some 1,400 paintings alongside drawings, photographs, texts and video works. Her subjects could hardly be more familiar: mountains, blossoms, sheep, deer, moths and trees. They are motifs with enough decorative baggage to make any contemporary painter slightly nervous. Loch, however, leaned straight into them. Rather than treating their familiarity with irony, she enlarged photographic source material to monumental proportions, turning ostensibly conventional images into something increasingly detached from the things they depict.
That estrangement becomes clearer the closer the viewer gets. From across the room, colors appear saturated and the subjects remain instantly legible; at close range, forms begin to dissolve into lines, surfaces and patches of thinly applied acrylic. Loch carefully planned her compositions through photography before beginning to paint, stripping away the idea of the spontaneous painterly gesture. The result sits somewhere between seduction and distance: a flower may still be a flower, but at 200 centimeters tall it starts behaving rather differently.
AL 235, 1987 | image: Estate of Anne Loch | photo: Dominique Uldry, Bern
PAINTING, WITHOUT THE NEED FOR A GRAND EXPLANATION
Loch was explicit about what she was not trying to do. Her work resisted social commentary, utopian narratives and autobiographical storytelling, focusing instead on color, surface, space and the relationships between lines. As motifs were enlarged, flattened and reconfigured, their original referents became increasingly unstable. Figuration slips toward abstraction, drawing edges into painting, and reality becomes just unreliable enough to keep things interesting. The exhibition’s title, Painting: So what?, feels suitably pointed: instead of offering paintings as containers of hidden messages, it asks what happens when looking itself becomes the subject.
Following her withdrawal from Cologne, Loch continued producing work in relative isolation, first in Switzerland and later back in Germany, with only occasional exhibitions. Her estate, now held in Bern, reveals the scale of a practice that never actually stopped when its public visibility did. At Zentrum Paul Klee, the oversized flowers, animals and landscapes finally get the room — and the audience — they demand. There are no dramatic manifestos waiting behind the petals. Sometimes a raven is a raven, a mountain is a mountain, and painting is allowed to cause enough trouble on its own.
from zucchini ballet flats to shoes covered in flowers and dandelion seed heads, the artist turns fleeting plant materials into playful studies of footwear.
lions, tigers, acrobats and balloons, costumed and created to fit in a suitcase, make up one of alexander calder's foundational works in play and wire.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan has blocked a shipment of Canadian sea urchin roe after border inspections found excessive cadmium, the Food and Drug Administration said Tuesday.
The 17.6-kilogram shipment of refrigerated sea urchin roe imported from Canada by Sushi Express contained 0.6 milligrams of cadmium per kilogram, twice the legal limit of 0.3 milligrams, per Liberty Times. Liu Fang-ming (劉芳銘), director of the FDA’s Northern Center for Regional Administration, said the shipment must be returned or destroyed at the border and will not enter the Taiwanese market.
Sushi Express has had two shipments of Canadian refrigerated sea urchin roe fail inspections within the past six months, including a shipment in April that also exceeded the cadmium limit. The FDA has therefore placed the company’s imports of the product under batch-by-batch inspection while maintaining regular random inspections for other imports of the same product category from Canada.
Separately, 23,500 kilograms of chili flakes imported from China by Global Chilli Foods Co. tested positive for Sudan III dye, per TVBS. The FDA will continue subjecting chili flakes from China to 100% testing for Sudan dyes through Aug. 7, 2027.
An 893-kilogram shipment of frozen beef tongue imported from the US by Shuh Sen Co. tested positive for Sarcocystis parasites, per UDN. The FDA has subjected the company’s imports to enhanced border inspections, with every shipment tested.

China's draft law on farmland protection submitted for 3rd reading
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
17:09:28 CST
18:09:28 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Chinese lawmakers on Tuesday began reviewing a draft law on farmland protection and quality improvement.
The draft was submitted for its third reading to the ongoing session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, the country's top legislature.
Compared with the second-reading draft, the latest version adds provisions on talent, funding and compensation in response to public feedback.
Specifically, the draft calls on higher education institutions and research institutes to strengthen talent cultivation in farmland protection and quality improvement, while prohibiting any organization or individual from embezzling, occupying or diverting funds allocated for high-standard farmland development.
It also stresses the need to improve compensation mechanisms for key grain-producing areas, optimize fiscal transfer payments for major grain-producing regions, and establish a sound interprovincial compensation mechanism between grain-producing and grain-consuming areas.
To further strengthen black soil protection, the draft underscores efforts to preserve the soil's strong productive capacity, aiming to ensure that its total area does not decrease, its functions do not degrade, its quality improves, and its productivity remains sustainable.
For flood-control purposes, land within river and lake management zones should, in principle, not be used as a source of supplementary farmland, the draft says. It also introduces provisions for the comprehensive restoration of sandy, wind-eroded and water-eroded farmland to prevent and control soil erosion.
Farmland protection has remained high on China's agenda due to its importance to food security, as the country steps up efforts to keep its total farmland area above the red line of 1.8 billion mu (about 120 million hectares).
Developing a farmland protection mechanism that integrates quantity, quality and ecology is a key task set out in the outline of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), as part of efforts to safeguard the supply of grain and other key agricultural products. ■

Across China: Mogao Grottoes embrace AI to preserve, share millennia-old heritage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
17:09:20 CST
18:09:20 KST

LANZHOU, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- With a single tap on a smartphone screen, celestial maidens holding lotuses, painted 1,400 years ago, spring to life and glide toward viewers from the ancient murals.
At the millennia-old Mogao Grottoes in Dunhuang, northwest China's Gansu Province, cutting-edge digital immersion is doing more than offering global audiences an unprecedented journey back in time. It is also helping ensure these fragile Silk Road masterpieces survive for generations to come.
Carved into desert cliffs from 366 AD onward, the Mogao Grottoes comprise 735 caves, including 492 sanctuaries featuring Buddhist murals and painted sculptures. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1987, the site is recognized as the world's largest, longest continuously constructed, and most richly endowed Buddhist art repository.
Today, local conservators are employing artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced digital tools not only to preserve these delicate relics but also to transform how the world experiences them.
Through the "Discover Dunhuang" VR exhibition, visitors can enter a high-fidelity 3D reconstruction of Cave 285, where they can view ancient murals up close, explore the space in 360 degrees, and even soar above the ceiling to appreciate the early classic grotto renowned for its Sino-Western fusion and iconic flying apsaras.
Lei Zhengguang, a cultural official at the Dunhuang Academy, said the team achieved a 1:1 high-definition restoration of the caves through digital scanning and 3D reconstruction. Combined with interactive design, the project has greatly enriched the visitor experience.
Behind the scenes, digitalization is quietly revolutionizing heritage conservation.
In Cave 44, where complex wall curvatures pose significant challenges, teams now use automated rail systems to capture images. Ding Xiaosheng, a senior researcher in digital preservation at the Dunhuang Academy, noted that specialized software for error-free stitching of billion-pixel images and multi-source 3D reconstruction has greatly improved processing efficiency and quality.
More notably, AI models trained on tens of thousands of high-resolution images are achieving "pixel-level" disease detection. Wang Wanfu, an official at the Academy, said AI can identify early-stage damage thinner than a human hair. Through spectral analysis, the system can even give early warnings for tiny hollows in the plaster base that are completely invisible to the naked eye.
The digital renaissance is now bringing Dunhuang to the world through the "Digital Library Cave" platform, launched globally by the Dunhuang Academy in 2025. To date, the platform has released digital resources of 11,090 manuscripts and artifacts, along with 72,810 images, attracting more than 250,000 visits from 33 countries and regions.
Dunhuang's pioneering efforts reflect a broader national push in China to safeguard cultural heritage through technology. China has updated its heritage law to encourage digital collection and utilization, while top-level guidelines and comprehensive technical standards further steer digital preservation efforts.
Across the country, institutions are racing to leverage digitalization to strengthen heritage conservation. The Palace Museum has assigned "digital IDs" to over one million artifacts, offering free public access to 150,000 items via its digital relic library. Meanwhile, the National Museum of China has completed 2D imaging for 720,000 relics and 3D modeling for over 7,700, achieving replication-grade precision.
"Next, we will deepen the integration of Dunhuang studies and digital intelligence, build a digital-intelligence research platform for Dunhuangology, and ensure that cultural relics 'remain forever young,'" said Yu Tianxiu, vice president of the Dunhuang Academy. ■

US lawmakers question Health Secretary Kennedy on vaccine settlement disclosures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:08:46 UTC
18:08:46 KST

US lawmakers question Health Secretary Kennedy on vaccine settlement disclosures
Aug 25 - A group of U.S. senators said Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s recent explanation for how he disposed of a financial stake in litigation involving Merck's Gardasil vaccine conflicts with earlier answers he gave in written testimony and federal ethics filings, a letter reviewed by Reuters shows.
The letter, sent on Monday by four Democratic senators, notes that Merck earlier this year agreed to pay $50 million to settle litigation over Gardasil, which prevents cancers caused by the human papillomavirus.
Before becoming health secretary last year, Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist, was an attorney of record in some of the cases. As health secretary, Kennedy oversees multiple health agencies that regulate and pay for vaccines.
After his nomination by Trump, Kennedy initially said he intended to keep a 10% fee of any settlement involving Gardasil cases he referred to the Wisner Baum law firm, which has represented dozens of plaintiffs. Met with concerns from Democratic U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and other lawmakers during the confirmation process, Kennedy then said he would hand over his financial interest in vaccine litigation to a son.
Last month, the senators asked whether Kennedy's son received the health secretary's share of the Gardasil fees, and if so, how much money that represents. They wanted answers to why Kennedy did not commit to recuse himself from U.S. health agency decisions involving Gardasil, or other policymaking around vaccine litigation.
In response, Kennedy said in a social media post earlier this month that neither he nor anyone else in his family have “received a penny” from the Gardasil settlement. Before taking office, Kennedy said he “relinquished any interest in potential Gardasil fees back to the Wisner Baum law firm.”
Kennedy also accused Warren, along with media outlets including Reuters, of “inventing lies” to besmirch him for standing up to the pharmaceutical industry.
In the letter on Monday, Warren and three other lawmakers pointed to Kennedy’s ethics filings and written answers provided to the Senate Finance Committee last year, in which the secretary said he would hand any Gardasil fees to his son. The senators’ staff could find no subsequent filings with different information, the letter said.
Kennedy’s recent statement, the letter said, appears to indicate the information he previously provided “is no longer accurate and suggests that you have either modified your ethics agreement or strayed from it altogether.”
An HHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
When asked last month about the prior letter from lawmakers, an HHS spokesperson initially did not comment and then later pointed to Kennedy's social media posting.
The senators asked Kennedy on Monday to explain why he certified in an ethics form that he would transfer his stake to a family member, if that had not happened.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends Gardasil as a routine immunization for 11- and 12-year-olds to prevent cervical and other HPV-linked cancers.
Earlier this year, the CDC attempted to change its guidance and said U.S. children should receive a single dose of HPV vaccine, rather than the two-dose course marketed by Merck and approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. A federal judge blocked that move. REUTERS

Hong Kong exports jump 50.7% in July, driven by growth in AI-related electronics
Government expects robust demand to continue supporting trade development despite geopolitical risks
Hong Kong exports surged by 50.7 per cent year on year in July, driven by “impressive growth” in AI-related electronic products, with the government expecting the robust demand to continue supporting trade development despite geopolitical risks.
Provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Tuesday showed that the value of exports jumped to a record HK$672.5 billion (US$86.2 billion) last month after a 53.4 per cent rise in June.
A government spokesman attributed July’s strong performance to growth in electronics related to artificial intelligence (AI) and a visible increase in exports to most major markets.
“The value of merchandise exports grew by 50.7 per cent over a year earlier, with exports of AI-related electronic products again registering particularly impressive growth,” he said.
July’s growth rate was the city’s fourth-highest level in recent decades, only surpassed by 53.4 per cent in June this year, as well as 61.6 per cent and 65.1 per cent in March and January 1984, respectively.
The spokesman said global demand for AI-related electronic products was expected to continue to bolster the city’s exports, but warned of geopolitical risks in the Middle East and rising trade protectionism in some advanced economies.

 Listen
China’s muted response to North Korea’s latest missile launch, which came soon after top diplomat Wang Yi’s visit to Seoul, underscores how Beijing is prioritising Pyongyang’s stability over near‑term denuclearisation, according to analysts.
North Korea started launching more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles just hours after Wang concluded his two-day visit on Thursday, the foreign minister’s first official trip to South Korea in nearly five years.
South Korea and Japan condemned the launch as a provocation.
Beijing declined to criticise the barrage fired into the sea east of the peninsula, with China’s foreign ministry saying the following day that it had “noted the reports” and did not have any “new comment”.
The launch highlighted the gap between Beijing’s diplomatic engagement with both Koreas and its ability, or willingness, to restrain North Korea, said Lee Seong‑hyon, a senior fellow at George H.W. Bush Foundation for US-China Relations.
During his meetings in Seoul, Wang urged South Korea to pursue “genuine strategic autonomy”, avoid taking sides between China and the United States and move towards “peaceful coexistence” with its northern neighbour.

“Proper education arouses intellectual curiosity”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

“Proper education arouses intellectual curiosity”
Nathan Ballantyne (ASU) continues his wonderful series of thoughtful, in-depth interviews of philosophers, The Workbench, with a conversation with Paul Gooch (Toronto).
.
The conversation is wide-ranging, with many amusing anecdotes (including one about the role Richard Taylor’s dog played at a dissertation defense), interesting reflections on various aspects of being a philosophy professor, a discussion of what “Canadian Philosophy” is, and thoughts about the limits of philosophy.
Here’s one part of the interview that focused on teaching:
Gooch: As Plato pointed out in the Phaedrus, written texts can’t answer your questions, so the conversation is one-way. (Of course, he made the claim about the inadequacy of the written word in writing.) You talk to yourself when you read. That’s not teaching. I was fortunate to learn very early on that teaching isn’t just about getting my own thoughts in order; it’s an interaction that has to take into account the place the student inhabits. Unsurprisingly, another fifty years on I argued that education is best understood as a kind of conversation involving interlocutors—not a surprising view given my interest in Socrates (who wrote nothing himself).
Ballantyne: How is that different from the so-called Socratic method?
Gooch: It’s certainly different. I don’t mean interrogation to deflate intellectual pretense. Socrates’ victims don’t participate in the dialogue beyond the occasional answer. In fact, I once wrote a poem titled “As I said to Socrates the other day,” which was only a series of Yes, No, Maybe, with ‘Sorry, I’ve got to go now’ as the ending. Proper education arouses intellectual curiosity that asks to know, and the teacher must be open to interrogation as well as the student. I want the conversation to be interrogative in both directions, between teacher and student.
Ballantyne: What have you done to keep your students talking?
Gooch: Early in my career I tried to get my students to do more than tell me what I told them. I often told them not to trust the teacher, but rather the argument. And sometimes I tested them—by going to my Philosophy of Religion class and beginning the lecture by summarizing what I had said the previous week—except that I took my Ancient Philosophy notes and talked from them. I wanted to see if anyone would interrupt…
The full interview is here.
And here’s the poem Gooch mentioned in the foregoing excerpt:

It would be pretty difficult to think that now.

Well, thank you very much, but…
Really, I’d better not keep him waiting.

— Paul Gooch

Details

At her direction, the children handed PVP to buyers and received money for it

Finnish Defence Forces order €14 million in FPV drones
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:57:05 EEST
17:57:05 KST

Finland’s Defence Forces have signed a multi-year agreement worth €14 million with Finnish technology group Insta for domestically produced FPV drones, as the military expands drone training among conscripts.
The agreement includes options as well as training, spare parts and maintenance services. Insta said the first systems have already been delivered to the Defence Forces.
The procurement covers FPV micro-drone systems designed for training and capable of carrying mission-specific payloads. The Defence Forces plans to use the equipment to extend large-scale training with armable micro-drones across Finnish Army brigade-level units.
An FPV, or first-person view, drone transmits live video to its operator, allowing the pilot to control the aircraft through the camera feed.
The systems acquired from Insta have been tested and approved by the Finnish Defence Forces, according to the company.
Insta produces 7-inch and 10-inch FPV drones in Finland. The company said it designs, tests and manufactures the systems domestically for use in Nordic conditions.
The drones use a modular design that allows operators to fit different payloads according to the mission. The wider system includes aircraft, controls, communications, situational-awareness functions, training, maintenance and support.
“Domestic drone production strengthens security of supply and supports the operational readiness of the Finnish Defence Forces,” Juha-Matti Ylitalo, Deputy Director of the Finnish Defence Forces Logistics Command and Brigadier General, said in Insta’s statement.
The Finnish Army started comparable training for conscripts at the Army Academy in autumn 2025. The Defence Forces said training began expanding to other units from the start of 2026.
The latest agreement is intended to take that process across the Army.
The Defence Forces said unmanned systems have taken on a larger role in warfare in recent years and that Finland is developing their use and associated training.
Insta said its development programme has incorporated lessons from the use of drones on current battlefields and changes in the security environment.
“The modern operating environment requires reliable, scalable solutions that can be adapted rapidly, supported by strong expertise in technology and systems development,” Tuure Lehtoranta, Insta’s Senior Vice President for Sales, Marketing and Government Relations, said in the company’s statement.
Lehtoranta said Insta had also drawn on international lessons concerning drone operations and changes in military requirements.
The company has worked with Ukrainian industry on drone technology as well. Insta announced an extended-range version of its Steel Eagle drone system in January 2025, combining an unmanned aircraft with a fragmentation charge.

                    MINSK, 25 August (BelTA) - The Bird of the Year 2027 has been named in Belarus, replacing the black stork, which holds the title for 2026, BelTA learned from the Scientific and Practical Center for Bioresources of the National Academy of Sciences of Belarus.
The voting for the Bird of the Year 2027 has concluded. Participants could vote online for one of four candidates, with a total of 4,172 votes cast.
By a wide margin, the winner is the European bee-eater (in Belarusian: shchurka-pchalayedka), the most colorful of the four bird species presented for selection. It received 2,165 votes and will take the top spot next year, replacing the black stork.
“The European bee-eater, our champion, is a migratory insectivorous bird from the tropical roller family, which nests in burrows and is listed in the Red Book of Belarus. It can be found in all parts of the country, mostly in the south. Its population is not large, but it is gradually increasing due to climate warming, and the species is expanding northward,” the center said.
Second place went to the garganey, which received 946 votes. The center noted that this is a small migratory duck whose population is declining rapidly.
“Bronze” with 533 votes went to the black-headed gull, while the great cormorant rounded out the list with 528 votes.

Nvidia, Supermicro employees charged over export of AI servers to China
Taiwanese authorities indict nine people over alleged chip smuggling scheme.
Taiwanese authorities have indicted nine people, including employees of Nvidia and Super Micro Computer, over their alleged involvement in the illegal export of artificial intelligence servers to China.
Eight of those indicted, including one employee of Nvidia’s Taiwan unit and two employees of Supermicro’s Taiwan unit, were charged with breach of trust and document forgery in connection with the illegal export of high-end AI servers, prosecutors in the port city of Keelung said in a statement on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Two US carrier groups in Middle East strain navy resources
- list 2 of 4Australia’s music charts ban AI-made songs amid backlash over Madonna cover
- list 3 of 4Libya factions draft initial election pact amid lingering mistrust
- list 4 of 4Angel Reese breaks WNBA record with 26 rebounds in Dream’s win over Sparks
Of those servers, 50 were transshipped through Indonesia, eight were sent via Japan and the rest were exported directly to China, according to prosecutors.
An additional 56 servers were seized at Taiwan’s border, the statement said.
Three of the defendants have been charged with embezzlement.
Semiconductor powerhouse Taiwan is the world’s largest producer of advanced chips used in AI applications.
The United States restricts exports to China of the most cutting-edge silicon chips designed by industry leader Nvidia and used to power artificial intelligence systems.
But it is not a criminal offence in Taiwan, a situation lawmakers and experts say needs to change, with Taiwanese prosecutors relying on other laws to go after offenders.
Nvidia said its employees have “every incentive to work diligently with customers to ensure compliance with all applicable laws”, adding it would work with the Taiwan authorities to help them “resolve the allegations as quickly as possible”.
Supermicro said its cooperation with Taiwanese authorities led to the arrests of the indicted individuals, including two former employees of its Taiwan subsidiary.
“The Company continues to cooperate with Taiwan authorities, is not a target of their investigation and has not been accused of any wrongdoing,” it said in a statement.
Prosecutors said they were seeking sentences of up to five years in jail for seven defendants who were “driven by the pursuit of exorbitant profits” to collude in the illegal export of the servers.
“This not only increased corporate compliance costs but also severely damaged the nation’s international image,” the prosecutors said.
They said they were seeking more lenient sentences for the other two defendants who had confessed to all charges and cooperated with the investigation.
Taiwan has tightened export controls in recent years to keep advanced technology and know-how from reaching China, which claims the island as its own territory despite the strong objections of its government.

From Colombia to Venezuela, Palestine is a global litmus test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:49:51 UTC
17:49:51 KST

Breadcrumb
From Colombia to Venezuela, Palestine is a global litmus test
This month, Venezuela revived consular services with Israel after severing diplomatic relations 17 years ago, while Colombia went beyond, recognising Israel’s sovereignty over the Syrian Golan Heights it occupied in 1967 and annexed in 1981. Both moves should be read as declarations of ideological alignment.
Venezuela has not yet restored full diplomatic relations, which the late Hugo Chávez severed in 2009 during Israel’s war on Gaza. The recent channel grew out of Israeli assistance following Venezuela’s earthquake. Yet Israel’s foreign minister immediately celebrated it as a diplomatic success.
Colombia’s decision is more obscene. Until Bogotá’s announcement, only Donald Trump’s United States had recognised Israeli sovereignty over the territory. Gustavo Petro had broken relations with Israel in 2024 over the Gaza genocide. However, only days after the right-wing Abelardo de la Espriella took office, his government restored ties and security cooperation with Israel and recognised Israel’s Golan annexation claim.
His incoming foreign minister had already met Gideon Saar in Washington, where they agreed to appoint ambassadors, eliminate visa requirements and move Colombia’s embassy to Jerusalem. De la Espriella had called for Colombia to acquire advanced weapons, drones and technology from Israel and the United States.
David and Goliath
We have just watched the same play in Slovenia. A centre-left government recognised Palestine, sanctioned Benjamin Netanyahu and two far-right Israeli ministers, banned imports of settlements and imposed an arms embargo. When Janez Janša’s conservative government arrived, it scrapped those measures, removed the Palestinian flag from a government building and reopened the door to Israel.
This shift in domestic power in three states—two in Latin America and one in Europe—produced an immediate policy shift towards Palestine. This is hardly a coincidence. Palestine is a global political litmus test.
Whenever the left is rising, the Palestinian flag is rarely far away. It appears at a small anti-racist protest in an American town, at campaigns challenging the power of money and lobbies in congressional races, and among the progressive ultras of Celtic, who have repeatedly defied their club and UEFA to turn the stands green, white, red and black.
It flew in Tahrir Square, where solidarity with the Palestinian Intifada had helped educate generations of Egyptian activists long before the 2011 revolution.
The flag appears because Palestine condenses the central questions confronting every emancipatory movement. Who is the underdog resisting the powers that be? Who is the little David fighting the giant Goliath? Who is entitled to control the land and decide who lives and who dies?
Any person or political movement struggling to change society with a progressive vision starts drawing parallels with other struggles over similar causes elsewhere and begins to understand how they are connected.
Is it a coincidence that Egyptian striking workers on the eve of the revolution accused the riot police of behaving like Israelis when they suspended by force their sit-in around the parliament? Is it a coincidence that Greta Thunberg began fighting against climate change only to swiftly connect the dots and sail to Gaza?
The reverse pattern is equally visible. When reaction, conservatism and fascism advance, Israel’s flag often follows.
Far-right and Israel
Israeli flags have appeared at Tommy Robinson’s anti-migration mobilisations in Britain, including a 2024 rally where the crowd booed a Palestinian flag. For Germany’s AfD and Europe’s far right—certainly some of the worst antisemites on the planet—support for Israel runs high because the admiration is for walls, militarised borders, demographic engineering, and a state organised around ethnic supremacy.
American white nationalist Richard Spencer made the logic explicit when he called himself a “white Zionist”, presenting Israel as a model for the white ethnostate he desired. The far right sees no contradiction between its hatred toward Jews at home and support for Israel. The latter offers a worldview which embodies the far right’s wildest dreams: minorities separated, migrants expelled, and each population confined to its supposed place.
Latin America has seen first-hand this worldview in action. During the Cold War, Israel armed and assisted right-wing regimes fighting revolutionary dissent, from Somoza’s Nicaragua to the Guatemalan military during its counterinsurgency war. It developed lasting security relationships with governments and armed forces in Colombia, Argentina, and elsewhere.
When the US faced legal constraints, Israel stepped in to supply weapons, training and intelligence to its allies. Such a partnership was natural. Israel and the juntas shared a view of popular movements as enemies to be surveilled, displaced or eliminated.
The same logic is at play today. Washington reasserts its domination over Caracas, and a government born from US intervention opens a channel with Israel. A Colombian administration eager to restore intimacy with Trump restores relations with Israel and endorses Trump’s Golan decree.
Janša, another Trump admirer, takes Slovenia to the right and begins dismantling its Palestine policy. In each case, alignment with the United States carries an Israeli entrance fee.
This is why Palestine is more than just a local conflict in the Middle East. A country at the far end of the world that wishes to identify with US imperial power is expected to make peace with Zionism. It buys Israeli weapons, repeats Israeli security narratives, and treats Palestinian rights as disposable. In so many ways, Israel is the quickest and most important gateway into the reactionary club.
Victories for progressive forces are therefore essential to keeping Israel isolated and making its leaders pay a political price for occupation, apartheid and genocide. Every election that defeats the far right, every successful anti-racist mobilisation and every workplace or university that adopts boycott and divestment helps keep Palestine visible.
Latin America shows what happens when power shifts to the right. But power shifts because people actively push it. Palestine remains the flag that tells us who is pushing, in which direction, and towards what kind of world.
Hossam el-Hamalawy is an Egyptian scholar-activist in Germany, focusing on the military, policing, and labour.

Hong Kong government statistician cleared of loitering charge near girls’ school
Defendant, 59, admits photographing 16-year-old girl, but judge rules loitering charge unsuitable as his conduct did not amount to a threat to the pupil
A Hong Kong court has acquitted a government statistician accused of loitering near a girls’ school and outside a classroom to photograph a pupil, ruling that his conduct did not pose an actual threat despite leaving the girl feeling unsafe.
Eastern Court Magistrate Kestrel Lam Tsz-hong on Tuesday found 59-year-old Patrick Lam Win-hon not guilty of one count of loitering causing concern, despite acknowledging that the defendant had loitered at one of Causeway Bay’s leading girls’ schools on July 5 last year.
The court heard that the statistician entered the school on its open day and spent 14 minutes on the fourth floor, where the classroom of the pupil he allegedly targeted was located.
Other students alerted teachers to the defendant’s suspicious behaviour, including his taking photographs through the classroom window.
The court heard that the target was a 16-year-old girl, who said the defendant had followed her during her daily commute to school for two to three years.
The girl said she first noticed the defendant showing interest in her by smiling and nodding at her on the MTR in late 2022. She said she later spotted the same man in the same carriage while travelling from Olympic to Hong Kong station on her daily commute.

Automated driving comes into view in law update
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:48:51 UTC
17:48:51 KST

China has set a dedicated chapter on autonomous vehicles in its draft revisions to the Road Traffic Safety Law, seeking to strengthen the legal framework for its rapidly developing autonomous driving sector.
The draft defines autonomous vehicles and driver-assistance functions, clarifies the conditions for autonomous vehicles to operate on public roads, sets principles for handling traffic violations, and outlines insurance arrangements for such vehicles.
It specifies that when a road traffic safety violation occurs while an autonomous vehicle's autonomous-driving function is activated, the vehicle's manufacturer or importer shall be responsible for handling the violation.
The draft was submitted for its first reading to the ongoing session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, the country's top legislature, which runs from Tuesday to Friday.
The current Road Traffic Safety Law took effect in 2004, with individual provisions amended in 2007, 2011 and 2021.
The latest draft revisions represent a more substantial revision, aimed at keeping pace with economic and social development, addressing people's needs and enhancing road safety. (Xinhua)
