Death toll from Colombia earthquake rises to 331, over 406,000 affected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
07:15:20 UTC
16:15:20 KST

The death toll from a catastrophic magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia has risen to 331, according to an updated report released on Tuesday by the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD).
The agency said 240 people remain missing, while 4,449 have been injured and 364 people have been rescued alive. In total, 406,273 people from 188,034 families have been officially registered as affected across 494 municipalities in 16 of Colombia's 32 departments.
The earthquake, which struck at 7.34 am local time (1234GMT) on August 10, was the most powerful seismic event to hit Colombia this century. Its epicentre was located near San Jose del Palmar in the Pacific department of Choco at an intermediate depth of roughly 110 kilometers.
The disaster has caused extensive damage to homes and public infrastructure across western Colombia. According to figures provided by the UNGRD on Tuesday, 33,275 homes have been completely destroyed, while 185,889 others have sustained damage.
Health, education and essential services have also been severely affected. The UNGRD reported damage to 376 health centres, 3,819 educational facilities and 4,337 community facilities.
Transport and water infrastructure have suffered significant disruption, with 440 roads, 74 vehicle bridges, 17 pedestrian bridges, five airports and 119 water-supply systems affected.
The earthquake has also taken a toll on animals, with 2,149 affected and 2,949 rescued, according to the latest assessment.
The UNGRD said the figures remain preliminary and are being consolidated by local authorities and operational agencies as emergency response and damage assessments continue.

"I was so nervous I chewed through a pencil while my men were crossing the open ground": Ukraine's six-month advance on the Oleksandrivka front
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
10:15:00 EEST
16:15:00 KST

"I was so nervous I chewed through a pencil while my men were crossing the open ground": Ukraine's six-month advance on the Oleksandrivka front
Dedicated to the reconnaissance troops who cleared wooded areas on the Oleksandrivka front
In late April, some servicemen from the 80th Air Assault Brigade who had spent the previous two years fighting in Sumy Oblast let slip to Ukrainska Pravda that they were being redeployed to a new "secret" front.
At the time, several possible locations were being discussed in military and press circles: Kupiansk, Lyman, and Stepnohirsk in Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
A few days later, UP learned that the "secret" front was in fact the Oleksandrivka front – where Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts meet.
It would be hard to describe this front as "high-profile" or even particularly well-known: it is not centred on a major city such as Pokrovsk or Kramatorsk, and it has also been closed to journalists for the past few months. Yet it played a significant role in the context of Russia's spring-summer offensive campaign this year – an offensive that ultimately failed to materialise – as we will explain below.
In late April, fresh forces, including paratroopers, were being deployed for the defence forces' second offensive operation on this front. The first operation, on the Oleksandrivka and Huliaipole fronts, had taken place at the beginning of the year and enabled the Ukrainian military to breach the Russian defensive line and liberate eight settlements.
The second operation started in early May and was kept secret for a long time. Some said this was because the defence forces had not fully accomplished their mission, others that the operation was still underway and it was therefore worth waiting before announcing it.
A sergeant in the Air Assault Forces whom UP met in Pavlohrad a week before this article was published joked that the Air Assault Forces command would announce the offensive "when we've fallen back to the positions we started from".
What he meant was that the longer the operation went on, the harder it became for his brigade to sustain its pace.
The sergeant summed up the operation: "The overall plan and concept worked, but our forces aren't limitless, and after a month of active fighting, we started to have problems with personnel. Another factor working against us was extensive Russian infiltration: they were wandering around chaotically [remember this part of the quote, as we'll come back to it in the third section – ed.] in areas in our rear."
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy unexpectedly decided to announce the results of both offensive operations on 12 August. In a video he released about the Ukrainian military's work, newly appointed Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi briefs him on the results, with Air Assault Forces Commander Oleh Apostol, who commanded the operation itself, sitting next to him.
The key statistics cited by Drapatyi were as follows: between January and August, the defence forces liberated 26 villages across three oblasts, retaking 745 sq km of territory. That's almost equivalent to the area of Kyiv.
Even allowing for the possibility that the figure may be overstated and doesn't distinguish between territory that was "fully liberated" and territory that was "cleared of infiltrating Russian troops", the scale of the offensive is impressive. Most of UP's sources among company and battalion commanders regard the offensive as a success.
The concept, stages, participants and details of the defence forces' Oleksandrivka offensive have so far remained largely in the shadows.
To remedy that, UP spoke to former commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi and around a dozen commanders and soldiers from four air assault and assault units that took part in the operation.
The operation at a glance
Name: Defence forces offensive on the Oleksandrivka front.
Time and place: January-August 2026 (still ongoing), at the junction of Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.
Initiated by: Oleksandr Syrskyi, Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine from 2024 to 2026.
Commander of the offensive grouping: Air Assault Forces Commander Oleh Apostol.
Main Ukrainian forces: Air Assault Brigades (95th, 82nd, 80th, 79th and 78th) and assault regiments (425th Skelia Regiment and 1st Separate Assault Regiment).
Likely objective: Disrupt the Russian offensive towards Orikhiv and thereby protect the city of Zaporizhzhia; drive Russian forces out of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.
Tactics: mechanised assaults and infiltration.
Result: The Russian offensive towards Orikhiv did not take place. Almost all of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast has been liberated from Russian forces, with the exception of the village of Dachne. Ukraine regained control of 26 villages across three oblasts.
The defence forces' Oleksandrivka offensive was intended to draw Russian troops away from Huliaipole and protect Orikhiv and Zaporizhzhia
Since early 2026, journalists had been closely following the defence forces' offensive actions on the Huliaipole and Oleksandrivka fronts without fully understanding what they were intended to achieve.
The emergency effort to save Huliaipole, the offensive towards Dobropillia-Solodke, the 95th Brigade's initial strike on the Oleksandrivka front and the deployment of fresh forces in May did not appear to form a single, coherent picture.
So UP put the question about the purpose of the Oleksandrivka operation to the man who initiated it – former commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi. It was the defence forces' final offensive operation launched under his command.
In written responses provided to UP, Syrskyi said that in the second half of 2025, he and the General Staff officers working in the combat zone had identified the Russians' plan.
Russian forces intended to advance not only on the Pokrovsk front, but also on the Huliaipole front.
"The enemy's plan was to breach our defences along the Huliaipole-Dobropillia line and subsequently create a threat of encirclement for the Ukrainian grouping near Orikhiv," Syrskyi wrote.
"To thwart these plans, inflict maximum losses on the enemy and at the same time straighten the front line, an offensive operation was planned on the Oleksandrivka front, involving a grouping of Air Assault Forces and assault units supported by units and formations from other branches of the Armed Forces."
Servicemen of various ranks told UP they believe the defence forces could not attack Russian troops on the Huliaipole front head-on because of the high concentration of Russian forces there.
The decision was therefore made to draw some of those forces away to the neighbouring Oleksandrivka front.
Sudden and genuinely secret strikes seem to have been a strong point both for the previous commander-in-chief and for the paratroopers in general.
In response to follow-up questions, Syrskyi said: "This strike [on the Oleksandrivka front] went into the rear of the advancing troops and forced the enemy to redeploy forces from the main axis [towards Orikhiv]. They were even forced to pull some units of the 90th Division back from near Pokrovsk. The objective was to destroy the enemy's assault grouping."
The "Oleksandrivka offensive" actually consisted of two separate operations with a short break between them. The first was centred around Huliaipole, the second around the Komar-Velyka Novosilka area
The first Ukrainian offensive operation began in early 2026, north of Huliaipole, which the Russians had already captured.
The paratroopers and assault troops advanced in two directions – north-west and north-east of the town. It is now clear that the Ukrainian defence forces were attempting to squeeze the Russians from two sides. Both heavy equipment and small infantry groups were used for this.
The Ukrainian defenders advanced 9-11 km into Russian positions as a result.
"It was an infantry operation where everything depended on the soldiers' training," Anton Derliuk, Commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 95th Air Assault Brigade, told UP several months ago.
However, the maximum objective was not achieved.
According to information available to UP, at least one part of the plan envisaged the defence forces advancing another 10+ km deeper and reaching the Russian rear from the direction of the village of Uspenivka.
"We didn't have enough forces for that," one senior participant in the operation told UP.
Although the maximum objective was not achieved, the Ukrainian offensive grouping (as Dmytro "Perun" Filatov, Commander of the 1st Separate Assault Regiment, noted in an interview with UP) blocked the Russians' ability to advance, we now know, towards Orikhiv. It also narrowed the area under Russian control.
The first offensive operation also created the conditions for the next one – the recapture of part of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast that had been seized by the Russians in 2025.
The second offensive operation began on 5 May along an extremely wide stretch of the front line – over 50 km, roughly from Nove Zaporizhzhia in Zaporizhzhia Oblast to Filiia in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. Its aim was to push the Russians as far as possible out of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, most likely towards Komar and Velyka Novosilka.
Velyka Novosilka is a fairly large settlement and a strategically important logistics hub, and its fall 18 months earlier had opened the gateway for the Russians to two neighbouring oblasts at once – Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia.
For the second offensive operation on the Oleksandrivka front, reinforcements arrived from the 78th, 79th and 80th Air Assault Brigades.
A company commander from one of these brigades told UP: "The 95th had slightly run out of steam during the first offensive – they'd taken on a huge amount of work. After that, they needed reinforcements."
Several months later, the same commander would mention this in a conversation with UP, this time talking about his own unit: "The Hospis [medics from the Hospitallers medical battalion] came to us today, but I don't know what they're going to do or who they're going to evacuate. There's no infantry left [this mostly refers to soldiers that were wounded]."
So when the second offensive operation began, Apostol was commanding a large part of the strongest brigades from the 7th and 8th Air Assault Corps. According to UP's information, the 95th Brigade also came under his direct command.
One battalion commander who spoke to UP described Apostol as a competent and understanding commander. Soldiers could always call him and ask for help. He treated even "non-organic" assault units – those that were not directly part of his own formation – reasonably and fairly.
However, it is worth noting that not all assault troops accept the "authority" of the paratroopers. Some believe they can achieve better results if they operate more autonomously.
As usual, the defence forces' casualty rate in the operation has not been disclosed. Some of UP's sources claimed that it was "abnormally low". At least two units operating different types of unmanned systems that UP spoke to did not have a single person killed during the two offensive operations.
Some of our other sources, however, hinted that while the number of deaths was relatively small, the number of soldiers reported missing or AWOL was significant.
During the second offensive operation, the defence forces regained control of more than ten villages stretching along the edges of the three oblasts – Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk and Donetsk. Practically the entire territory of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast was cleared of Russian troops. The operation is still ongoing.
The map produced by DeepState, a Ukrainian group of military analysts, clearly shows how the operation created a huge "protected zone" in front of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. If the defence forces can hold it, it will protect Dnipropetrovsk Oblast from a ground war for some time.
It won't, however, protect it from guided aerial bomb strikes, unfortunately. This is an area where the Russians make particularly intensive use of them. As a result, settlements that are 30-50 km away from the line of contact – which might otherwise seem almost like the rear – are now impossible to live in.
The defence forces' advantages in this offensive were the element of surprise and the infantry's training. Their disadvantages were false information about the actual depth of the Russian advance, difficult terrain, and Russia's numerical superiority in terms of UAVs
In the previous two sections, we mainly presented the views of the military commanders who initiated both offensive operations and were responsible for carrying them out at the highest level. Now we'll look at how the operations were seen by the lower-level commanders and soldiers who directly put the plan into practice with their own feet, rifles and drones.
The first two or three weeks of both offensive operations were "extremely successful". In the initial stages, the Russians (a) didn't yet realise that the defence forces had launched a major offensive, and (b) were afraid to report it to their superiors.
"They saw these servicemen running around wearing the paratroopers' 'mohnatky' [a camouflage covering worn over the head] and spent two days arguing about whose 'mohnatky' they were," one paratrooper company commander told UP, laughing.
"It was only when we reached Myrne [10 km inside the Russian positions] that they realised something was going on. Up until then, they'd been sitting there without any communications or food," his fellow soldier added.
"The early days of the operation were not difficult. We found positions quickly, we could even drive to them, unload the equipment and get to work," explained Maksym Maslivets, commander of a UAV platoon in the Boryviter unmanned systems battalion of the 95th Brigade.
But the main reason why the Russians didn't understand what was happening was down to a tactic the Ukrainian forces were applying – infiltration.
The defence forces literally mirrored the enemy's modus operandi. Instead of carrying out frontal assaults, they quickly and imperceptibly seeped through the Russians' positions in small groups. This was aided by the good training of the Ukrainian paratroopers and assault troops.
"We had to advance as deep as possible without being noticed, bypass the wooded areas held by the enemy, establish a line, cut them off, and then capture those who remained on our side of the line," the paratrooper company commander we mentioned earlier explained.
When using these tactics, a large part of the work falls to traditional reconnaissance troops. They are the ones who later go in to mop up those same wooded areas where Russians cut off from their own remain in the Ukrainian rear, still posing a danger.
Sometimes these Russian forces can be taken out by explosives dropped from bomber drones (still a specific advantage of the Ukrainian military); sometimes they have to be cleared out by hand.
Clearing out enemy troops by hand is one of the most difficult and dangerous tasks in the current war. In the Air Assault Forces, this task is typically carried out by an elite brigade-level reconnaissance unit.
"Everyone ran through the wooded areas – and that was right, because that was how it was supposed to be, but then we had to sweep it all. All that fell on the reconnaissance troops," the commander of one reconnaissance unit told UP. "And we lost a lot of people doing that. Our greatest losses were in these small-arms engagements and from drones. As soon as the enemy detected us, they'd rain everything down on that position. One of our groups was hit by 12 Molniya drones within half an hour."
One of our sources for this article asked UP to mention, in the context of the Oleksandrivka operation, one of his brothers-in-arms, Junior Sergeant Volodymyr Shyshoholik. As part of a reconnaissance group of the 80th Air Assault Brigade, he cleared the wooded areas "that everyone had run through". He was killed with a weapon in his hands, aged 27.
In both the first and the second operation, Russian UAVs kicked in a few weeks into the operation. Rubicon, one of Russia's most effective units, was speedily redeployed to the Oleksandrivka front.
"Within three weeks the enemy realised that something wasn't right here, and both the Russian armies standing opposite us brought in their reserves," explained Andrii Serhiienko, commander of a strike UAV company in the Boryviter unmanned systems battalion of the 95th Brigade.
Service members told UP the Ukrainians had the edge in terms of the quality of the drone crews' work, but the Russians had it in terms of the number of drones.
After the second Ukrainian offensive operation began, the Russians set about intensively mining roads and planting ambush drones at junctions where vehicles would usually slow down.
To counter this, Ukrainian units had to form separate crews that would regularly fly over the roads, monitor them for ambush drones, and drop explosives on them.
Maksym Maslivets, the platoon commander from the 95th Brigade we mentioned before, told UP: "Mid-spring, Rubicon effectively cut off all our logistics routes. My vehicle was attacked by between 30 and 50 drones when it got stuck. And the challenges were compounded by the fact that there was a lot of rain that spring, which turned the field roads we used into mud. Everything got bogged down. There were times when nothing could get through – not Humvees, nor pickups, nor even Urals. And as soon as the enemy spotted that, they'd fire everything at it.
What helped us was that a few weeks into stage two of the operation, we were supplied with better drones that could fly 25-30 km rather than 10-15. This enabled us to reach the enemy further away and to work from a safer place."
Regarding the particular challenges of this offensive, our sources singled out three key aspects.
1. Lies from their own side about the actual depth of the Russians' penetration. Unfortunately, at the start of the second offensive operation Ukrainian troops were faced with the fact that the real line of contact was not the same as the one plotted on the map.
Russian troops had infiltrated 2-10 km deeper than they had been told. So before the main offensive operation started, Ukrainian forces had to finish mopping up their own rear or, worse still, find out that there were Russians in their rear after advancing. This is the "chaotic infiltration" by the Russians that we mentioned in the introduction to this article in the words of the paratrooper sergeant.
One participant in the operation told UP: "As soon as we came in, we were told: 'Everything's fine here, go forward, towards Maliivka.' We take the analysis, we look at where the enemy was last detected, and it was in the Velykomykhailivka Forest [a couple of kilometres into the Ukrainian forces' rear – UP], beyond the crossing – the enemy had crossed the river and was sitting there!"
UP is aware of a similar situation in at least three areas:
- the settlement of Andriivka-Klevtsove (formerly named Iskra) in Donetsk Oblast, which the 80th Brigade passed through. There was up to a platoon of Russians in Iskra;
- Kolomiitsi and Oleksiivka in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, which the 95th passed through. There were also Russian drone pilots in Oleksiivka;
- the forest east of Velykomykhailivka in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, which the Skelia regiment passed through.
2. In some sectors of the offensive, practically all the wooded areas had been cut down or mined, forcing the Ukrainian troops to advance across open terrain for long stretches at enormous risk.
One of UP's sources described his unit's offensive zone as one where "nobody was intending to advance". It was only suitable for static defence.
One commander who took part in the operation told UP: "I was so nervous I chewed through a pencil while my men were crossing the open ground. All the wooded areas had been either mined or cut down for a kill zone. Nobody was intending to advance there, I don't know why they [the Ukrainian units that had previously been holding the sector] did it. It f**ked things up for us so badly. Zaits [commander of the 20th Corps – UP], who arrived when the offensive was already underway, wouldn't have allowed that – he's a very sensible guy."
Incidentally, three of UP's sources in the defence forces said that Sviatoslav Zaits, the commander of the 20th Corps, who comes from the Air Assault Forces, is being considered as a candidate for Commander of the Ground Forces. His place in the 20th Corps may be taken by the current commander of the 141st Brigade and former commander of the 59th Brigade, the young Lieutenant Colonel Bohdan Shevchuk.
3. The advance was complicated by a long logistics chain (more than 10-20 km) and by the rivers that cut across the Oleksandrivka sector in several places at once (particularly the Vovcha River).
Some of the servicemen UP spoke with were convinced that the command had not taken the brigades' logistical capabilities into account – some lacked unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), while others faced such intense enemy activity that bringing anything up to their position was practically impossible.
"In our case, for instance, neither quad bikes nor the armoured vehicles that delivered supplies could drive the distance required. We went on our own two feet, and on UGVs when we had them. The logistics were tough," the paratrooper sergeant told UP.
"My infantry used to walk 20 km, and that was only to the line of contact. And after that you still have to conduct assaults, to work," another battalion commander added.
The servicemen assigned a separate role in this operation to logistics and transport across the river. To cross the water bodies, temporary crossings were set up where possible, and boats were used. In one of the videos passed to UP, two paratroopers can be clearly seen crossing the river, to the sound of explosions, on an inflatable boat with their equipment and moving on further to clear the wooded areas.
There were also those who swam across the river, with dry clothes then dropped to them by drone.
"The crossings, the pontoons, would be destroyed within half an hour of being set up – it wasn't worth it," one of the commanders told UP. "I didn't want to send my men there. So ours swam across. It was wet, but we dropped clothes for them from drones straight afterwards. We tried to look after our people."
***
The operation on the Oleksandrivka front is ongoing. However, the key surges have probably already been made. The Russian offensive on Orikhiv has been thwarted (for now), Dnipropetrovsk Oblast is practically free of Russians, and for the paratroopers and assault troops, new tasks and sectors await.
Olha Kyrylenko, UP
Translated by Myroslava Zavadska, Tetiana Buchkovska and Anastasiia Lipara
Edited by Teresa Pearce

Rohke Debelak: Freedom arrived, but the age of awakening must not end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
07:15:00 UTC
16:15:00 KST

Rohke Debelak: Freedom arrived, but the age of awakening must not end
On August 21, a celebration and concert marking the 35th anniversary of Estonia's restoration of independence was held at the Mere Cultural Center in Tallinn. Among the speakers was Gaute "Rohke Debelak" Kivistik. His full speech is published below.
Circus arrived in Estonia about 35 years ago. It came with a banana, a VCR, a Finnish plastic bag and an Opel brought from Germany. The free world did not enter through a grand parade gate. It seeped in through Finnish television, crossed the border in the trunk of an expat's car and appeared one morning at the market on a stool.
The Soviet economy was precisely planned. That is why no one knew what would be sold in the shop tomorrow. When bananas arrived somewhere, the news spread faster than the internet does today. A queue formed before people even knew what they were queuing for. But they stood anyway. Because if something was being given out, you took it. Later at home you looked at what it was and figured out what to do with it.
In Soviet times, the banana was more legend than fruit. Some had seen one in Moscow, some on Finnish TV, and some knew someone whose brother‑in‑law's coworker had eaten one.
Then we became free.
Freedom did not make us rich overnight. First, it made us consumers. The first hamburger stands appeared, along with the first "hamburgers." They were made like this: a loaf of bread was cut in half, then crosswise into quarters. A three‑to‑four‑centimeter slice of boiled sausage was lifted out of hot water with a fork, placed between two quarters of bread with grated fresh cabbage, and covered with a mix of sour cream and ketchup. A handful of rubles changed hands. The hamburger itself did not really exist yet, but the consumer had already been born.
Suddenly shops had bananas, chewing gum, Coca‑Cola, foreign cigarettes and chocolates whose names we learned to pronounce only after the third purchase. There was so much merchandise that it could no longer be hidden under the counter.
Before, people had money but nothing to buy. Now there was everything to buy, but people had no money. Progress was at least visible.
Foreign plastic bags appeared on the streets — Marlboro, Stockmann, Anttila. These bags were never thrown away. People carried them to work, weddings and, when possible, funerals. If the writing was in a foreign language, the bag was practically diplomatic luggage.
Jeans, sneakers, tracksuits and leather jackets arrived. Some tracksuits had brand names the wearer could not pronounce, but that did not stop them from being the brand's representative for the entire housing district.
Then the expat Estonians arrived. They came with good intentions, proper cars and a pedagogical gaze. They explained how democracy works, how business should be done and why people should wash regularly.
Of course, we washed before too — just not yet using Western methods or under international supervision.
Expats sent us soap, toothpaste, used clothes and, among other necessities, expired Snickers bars. Naturally, we ate them. They were foreign Snickers. If the packaging had English text, the expiration date was more of a suggestion.
Royal spirit arrived in Estonia. In some bars, it was the only thing available. Even the water pipes were frozen. You took a shot of Royal, went outside and ate snow afterward. Today this would be called a Nordic‑concept experience bar.
But Estonians did not want to remain mere recipients of aid. Estonians wanted to be entrepreneurs. The first cooperatives emerged. At one point, entire families reviewed their assets. Grandma had a waffle iron. Aunt Maali had a waffle iron. The neighbor's ex‑wife had a waffle iron.
If five waffle irons were borrowed together, the company was ready. They baked so intensely that the entire neighborhood went dark from overload. But this was no longer a power outage — this was economic growth. Then they took a stool under their arm, stepped into the snowfall and began selling waffles. There was no sales space, no permit, no payment terminal, no health inspection approval. There was a stool, snowfall and belief in the free market. Some got rich. Some got pneumonia. Both gained valuable entrepreneurial experience.
Stalls appeared in cities. They sold everything: cigarettes, vodka, chocolate, batteries, sweatpants and sometimes something even the seller did not know the purpose of. People drove to Poland to bring goods. One person was simultaneously company president, purchasing manager, sales manager, driver and warehouse worker. The warehouse was usually the back seat of the car.
Everyone had business cards. The card said "general director," even if the company had only one employee — the director himself. But "general director" sounded better, especially when the company's assets consisted of a stool, two waffle irons and a plastic bag that said "Thank you."
Foreign cars arrived on the roads. An Opel from Germany was not a used car — it was a Western car. It might have been 20 years old, survived three crashes and two fires, but it came from the free world. Some cars had such long histories that even the car itself no longer remembered all its owners.
Mercedes and BMW became symbols of wealth of questionable origin. In the beginning, wealth without questionable origin hardly existed. If it did, it was especially questionable. The free world sent us clothes, chocolate and used cars. We sent the free world metal.
At one point, half of Estonia was in the metal business. The other half tried to figure out where their fence had gone. Metal was the miracle commodity of the new era. It could be found in factories, warehouses, power lines, along railways and sometimes even still attached to something. The main source was the inexhaustible eastern neighbor.
The Russian army stationed in Estonia sold almost everything for vodka. My childhood friend Toivo bought three air‑to‑air missiles from soldiers at the Tartu airfield and kept them in his garage. Toivo thought he had merchandise. Estonian law enforcement thought he had three air‑to‑air missiles. Both were right, but the state was already stronger than Toivo.
When the missiles were confiscated, Toivo was very sad. Thus ended one promising Estonian garage enterprise before our defense industry had even begun properly.
Video recorders arrived in homes and video rental shops appeared on streets. One and the same man — the world's most famous unknown voice — dubbed every character on the tape: men, women, children and, when necessary, dogs.
Satellite TV, MTV and disco bands arrived. A disco band usually consisted of two men and one synthesizer. One man sang. The other pressed the button at the right moment. Both wore such shiny jackets that the band did not need a lighting rig.
And amid all this colorful world, we had to start building a state. The Estonian kroon arrived. Most people spent their last Soviet money on alcohol and their first Estonian money on alcohol, because Midsummer was approaching. The money was finally truly ours — until it again became theirs, whose it had always been. Soon our own were also the banks, loans and bankruptcies. Banks appeared like mushrooms. Some unfortunately had the lifespan of mushrooms.
Privatization began. Factories, buildings and shops got owners. Sometimes it turned out that those best prepared for the new era were the ones who had stood closest to the old era. Later, many former communists explained how they had been undermining Soviet power from within all along. Some had undermined such a deep cellar that the entire factory's assets fit inside. And when the old system collapsed, they happened to be standing closest to the cash register.
But that time was not funny for everyone. Some got their first passport. Others got their first layoff notice. Some discovered the whole world was open to them. Others discovered that the profession they had practiced all their lives was no longer needed.
Jobs disappeared, savings disappeared, and the old sense of security disappeared. Some found opportunity in freedom. Some lost their footing. Some learned to swim quickly. Some sank before anyone noticed. But the economy was on the right course. The opening of the stock exchange proved it. It took a whole year to reach the first stock market crash.
We wanted freedom of choice and we got it. We could choose a political party, profession, place of residence, car, bank, yogurt — and also which bank loan to use to buy that car. We got the right to succeed. And with it, the right to fail.
Before, there was always someone to blame for our troubles: Moscow, the party, the planning committee or the person who hid the scarce sausage under the counter. In a free country, we eventually had to admit that some decisions were our own. Of course, we have not completely given up blaming others. Some national traditions survived occupation, monetary reform and the market economy.
But deep down we know that freedom is not just the right to choose. Here, together with Ukrainian youth, we know especially clearly that freedom is not a commodity that arrives once across the border and stays forever on the shelf. Freedom did not promise that we would always choose correctly. It gave us something much harder — the right to choose ourselves and the obligation to take responsibility for those choices.
We got our country back. But the country did not become finished. Freedom did not become finished. And we ourselves did not become finished. Because the age of awakening is not one day in history. It is the time when a person understands that no one else will live their life or guard their country. Freedom arrived. But the age of awakening must not end.
--
Editor: Kaspar Viilup, Argo Ideon

Pyongyang has rejected claims that the drills are defensive, describing them as rehearsals for an invasion and warning of intensified countermeasures.

Boeing wins $163 million order for B-52 bomb rack kits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
07:12:48 UTC
16:12:48 KST

- Boeing received a delivery order worth up to $162,966,689 to build Bomb Rack Modernization System kits for the B-52 bomber.
- The sole-source order supports the B-52 Radar Modernization Program and work will be performed in San Antonio through December 2028.
Boeing has been awarded a delivery order worth up to $163 million to build and deliver Bomb Rack Modernization System kits for the B-52 bomber, the Department of War announced. The order supports the broader B-52 Radar Modernization Program and was issued under an existing indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract that dates to 2019.
Work will be performed at Boeing’s facility in San Antonio, Texas, and is expected to be completed by December 20, 2028. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, is managing the order, designated FA8628-26-F-B002. About $35 million in fiscal 2026 aircraft procurement funds were obligated at the time of award, which the Air Force listed as August 21. The action was a sole-source acquisition, and the order combines cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost-plus-fixed-fee, cost-reimbursement and firm-fixed-price elements.
The Bomb Rack Modernization System kits are tied to the same radar upgrade program that centers on installing the AN/APQ-188 active electronically scanned array radar across the B-52H fleet, replacing the aircraft’s Cold War-era mechanically scanned radar. Boeing has said the new radar and associated systems are meant to improve situational awareness, speed up target identification, and enhance aircrew survivability in contested environments. The radar system relies on new mission computers and cockpit displays, including two 8-by-20-inch touchscreens and fighter-style hand controllers for radar operation, along with upgraded liquid cooling to handle the new hardware’s power demands.
Boeing’s San Antonio site, at Port San Antonio, houses one of the largest military aircraft maintenance and modernization complexes in the world, including a hangar capable of holding up to 15 wide-body aircraft at once. The facility has handled ground integration and initial system checks for the B-52 radar program, and Boeing delivered the first B-52 fitted with the new APQ-188 radar to the Air Force’s 412th Test Wing at Edwards Air Force Base in December 2025 for flight testing.
“The new radar will significantly increase B-52 mission effectiveness by improving situational awareness, speeding target prosecution and enhancing aircrew survivability in contested environments,” said Troy Dawson, vice president of Boeing Bombers.
Boeing has continued to add B-52 modernization work at both its San Antonio and Oklahoma City sites over the past year. In December 2025, the Air Force awarded Boeing a $2.04 billion task order to begin hands-on integration and structural modification work on two B-52 aircraft under the separate Commercial Engine Replacement Program, which will fit the bombers with new Rolls-Royce F130 engines. That engine work spans sites in Oklahoma City, San Antonio, Seattle and Indianapolis, with completion scheduled for May 2033.
The radar program itself has faced delays and rising costs in recent years, with flight testing pushed back from fiscal 2024 to fiscal 2026 and the Air Force reviewing program requirements to manage expenses. Data collected during ongoing test flights is expected to inform later phases of the program and the eventual retrofit of all 76 operational B-52 aircraft with the new radar and associated hardware.

Asia-Pacific Community: How modern Chinese builders continue Zheng He's legacy in Indonesia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:12:24 CST
16:12:24 KST

by Xinhua writer Zhang Yisheng
SEMARANG, Indonesia, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Semarang, a major port on Indonesia's Java island, traces its rich history back to the 15th century, when Chinese navigator Zheng He made multiple stops here during his historic maritime voyages.
Historical records show that Zheng's "treasure ships" brought not only thriving trade but also lasting bonds between the two peoples. Local tradition even holds that the city was named in honor of Zheng, with the iconic Sam Poo Kong temple standing today as a timeless testament to his legacy.
Heading north from downtown Semarang, engines roared amidst waves of stifling heat. At the construction site of Indonesia's first dike-highway, Yue Zhenhong, project manager of toll road development of Semarang-Demak 1B built by China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC), navigated the main access route in a hard hat and blue work uniform.
Behind him, bulldozers and road rollers operated in shifts, while over a thousand dump trucks transported materials around the clock, creating a bustling scene filled with the blare of horns.
"We are working 24-hour non-stop shifts to try to complete the basic earthmoving construction before the rainy season arrives," said the 35-year-old, wiping sweat from his forehead.
Both Semarang and Demak are situated on the northern coast of Central Java province. For years, traffic congestion along the existing national highway connecting the two places has been severe. The Indonesian government hopes to ease traffic pressure and solve a long-lasting problem of tidal flooding along the coast through this project.
According to Yue, the project integrates transportation and flood control functions. Once completed, travel time between the two cities will be drastically reduced from 60 minutes during peak traffic to just 10 minutes, significantly lowering logistics costs and injecting fresh momentum into local economic growth.
However, turning the vision into reality requires overcoming formidable challenges. Deep layers of soft mud reaching depths of 30 meters beneath the seabed along the route made construction akin to "building a house on tofu." Enhancing the bearing capacity of the soft foundation while controlling construction stability and post-construction subsidence presented a tough nut to crack for the project team.
"Tailored to local geological conditions and resource availability, we creatively implemented a foundation treatment solution for very soft ground: bamboo piles and mats plus vertical and horizontal drain boards with surcharge preloading," Yue explained.
He noted that the strength of this solution lies in tapping into the local abundance of bamboo. By replacing high-carbon materials like steel and cement with bamboo, the project significantly cuts carbon emissions across its entire life cycle.
For more than 20 years of doing business in Indonesia, the CRBC has built a string of landmark projects across the archipelago country. Those projects have not only accumulated rich expertise for constructing the dike-highway but also cultivated a pool of local engineering talent.
Muhammad Rizky Pradana, a 26-year-old engineer who joined the company a year and a half ago, has developed a profound appreciation for the rigor of Chinese engineering standards.
Rizky admitted that he initially felt considerable pressure facing the project's stringent quality management requirements. However, under the hands-on guidance of his Chinese colleagues, he quickly mastered the know-how.
"The project's strict control over quality has enabled me to learn many new professional skills and management methods. Being able to grow on such a platform makes me feel truly fulfilled," he said.
For 37-year-old Mochamad Zumar Habibi, this year marks his 10th year working with the CRBC, an example of the company's long-term commitment to nurturing local staff.
Habibi said the efficiency and dedication of the Chinese enterprise have continuously inspired him. Working in the CRBC has improved his family's livelihood, making his parents and wife immensely proud of his job. "I hope to stay with the CRBC all the way until retirement."
For local residents, Chinese builders have brought not only technology and skills but also a strong sense of social responsibility.
"In the past, severe sea erosion damaged homes, roads, and fish ponds. Every time high tide came, seawater nearly 1 meter deep poured in, paralyzing the roads," recalled Kumaidi, a local village official, noting that tidal flooding had haunted his village for ages.
Upon learning of the situation, the CRBC project team extended a helping hand by elevating nearly 5 kilometers of surrounding rural roads by about 1 meter, greatly enhancing their flood-prevention capacity.
Kumaidi remarked with gratitude that travel conditions in the village have improved immensely, and residents no longer frequently suffer from being stranded by floods. Furthermore, the team installed streetlights along key sections, illuminating roads that were once pitch-black at night.
"Just like Zheng He's fleet when it arrived here centuries ago," Kumaidi said, "the Chinese builders today have also come bearing friendship and win-win cooperation." ■

Study finds sugar tax could boost Australians' oral health
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:12:16 CST
16:12:16 KST

SYDNEY, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Millions of cases of tooth decay could be prevented if Australia introduced a 20 percent tax on sugar, according to new research from Australia's Griffith University.
The study estimated that such a tax could prevent 3.7 million cases of tooth decay, 191,000 cases of gum disease and 115,000 cases of complete tooth loss, Professor Lennert Veerman from Griffith's School of Medicine and Dentistry said in a statement released Wednesday.
A 20 percent tax would also generate approximately 500,000 health-adjusted life years for Australia's 2019 population over their lifetime, through improvements in dental health and reductions in weight-related illness, according to the findings published in BMJ Public Health.
Oral diseases affect about 3.5 billion people globally, while nearly 32 percent of Australian adults have untreated tooth decay, the study noted.
The research found that males would experience the most health benefits from a sugar tax, as they consume more sugary drinks and have higher baseline levels of some oral diseases. ■

He declined to name any of those leaders when asked by CBS News, and he didn't get into a timeline or other specifics.
Asked whether Chinese banks that finance Iranian oil imports would be among those hit with the punishing financial measures, Bessent said, "no one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions."
Speaking to reporters in Beijing, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said Tuesday that China has "repeatedly stated its firm opposition to illegal unilateral sanctions without the basis of international law and without authorization from the UN Security Council," according to China's state-run Xinhua news agency.
"Economic warfare and extreme pressure do not help solve problems; they only further intensify conflicts, cause risks to spill over, disrupt the global economic and financial order, and harm the legitimate rights and interests of other countries," Lin said, adding that China's cooperation with Iran has "always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be disrupted or undermined."
China "will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own rights and interests," he added.

The most important AI skill leaders can borrow from pilots - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
07:03:07 UTC
16:03:07 KST

A few weeks ago, I was en route to an airport I'd earmarked for landing when I noticed bad weather closing in on it. I checked the alternative, the backup airport I initially planned for, and saw that we'd have to fly through bad weather to get there too. So, I picked a third airport, landed, waited it out for a few hours, and continued safely once the system had passed.
Could we have beaten the weather to the original airport? Maybe. Could we have threaded the patches en route to the alternate? Maybe. But “maybe” is not a risk management strategy. Good risk management doesn't ask whether you can get away with something. It asks whether the risk is worth taking at all. We landed. We waited. We lived to fly another day.
Every pilot learns a simple framework for making this kind of call in the moment. It is clearly laid out in the FAA's Aviation Instructor’s Handbook. It's built for cockpits, but it translates almost line-for-line into how managers decide how fast, and how far, to push AI deployment.
Accept no unnecessary risk
In aviation, the rule isn't “avoid all risk". Flying is impossible without risk. The rule is that risk needs a corresponding return. A new pilot doesn't take a new airplane into low-visibility conditions on day one. There's no benefit that justifies that specific risk, even though the same pilot might accept real risk elsewhere.
Applied to AI, the question managers should be asking isn't “Is this AI system risky?” It’s: What, specifically, are we getting in return for this specific risk, and would we accept it if we wrote it down?
Shipping an unvetted model into a workflow that touches medical records, financial approvals, or safety-critical decisions because it's faster to ship than to test is an unnecessary risk with no commensurate return. If a competitor's speed advantage is the only justification, that's fear dressed up as strategy.
Make risk decisions at the appropriate level
On a single-pilot flight, the pilot decides. Not air traffic control. Not the passengers. The person accepting the risk has to be the person who can actually build and implement the controls that manage it.
This is where a lot of AI governance quietly breaks down inside organizations. Decisions about deploying a customer-facing model or giving an agent write-access to production systems, often get made by whoever is closest to the deadline: a product leader, an engineer under pressure; rather than by the manager who actually owns the downstream consequences.
Ask: “Who in this workflow has the authority to say no, and does that person have full visibility into what's being deployed?” If the answer is “Nobody, really,” the decision is happening at the wrong level, and it needs to be pushed up the chain until it lands with a manager who has both the information and the authority to own it.
Weather is a good analogy here too: A clear day is a far better time to fly an unfamiliar airplane for the first time than a day with deteriorating conditions. Deploying AI is the same. The acceptable risk changes with the environment.
Managers should be asking the equivalent question before every material AI deployment: “Is this the right environment for this risk?” A generative AI pilot in an internal, low-stakes workflow, with a human reviewing every output, is a clear-weather flight.
The same model, wired into an autonomous decision loop with no human check, touching customer money or physical safety, is flying in questionable conditions into weather you haven't checked.
The technology's raw capability doesn't change between those two cases. The acceptable level of risk does.
Integrate risk management into planning at all levels
The earlier a risk gets caught, the cheaper it is to fix. Changing course mid-flight is harder than choosing the right route before takeoff. It's exactly the same with AI systems bolted together in production versus designed with guardrails from the get-go.
Retrofitting oversight, auditability, and kill-switches onto an AI system that's already embedded across a team's workflows is the equivalent of trying to change your destination airport after you've already flown into weather. It's not impossible, but it's expensive, stressful, and far more likely to end badly. Risk management belongs in the design conversation on day one, and not in the incident review six months later.
The diversion wasn't a failure.
Nobody remembers that flight as a bad day. We made the airport, on schedule for what mattered, with nothing more dramatic than a longer layover than planned. That's what good risk management actually looks like - not heroics, not close calls retold as bravado - just a series of unremarkable, disciplined decisions that never had to become a story about what went wrong.
The managers who will deploy AI well over the next few years won't be the ones who moved fastest. They'll be the ones who knew, at every stage, exactly which airport they were headed to, and were willing to divert the moment the weather said otherwise.

Israeli AI trust, safety, and security company Alice today announced the completion of a $140 million financing round led by Apax Digital, with participation from new and existing investors including Samsung, SentinelOne, Maj Invest, MoreTech, Phoenix Insurance, Norwest, CRV, Vintage, Grove and Highland Europe.
Sources inform "Globes" that the financing round, which brings the total amount raised by Alice to $280 million, was completed at a company valuation of $800 million. The company's annual recurring revenue (ARR) is approaching $100 million.
Founded in 2018 as ActiveFence by CEO Noam Schwartz, CTO Iftach Orr, CCO Alon Porat, and president Eyal Dykan. Initially the company developed systems that helped social networks and internet platforms detect violent content, fraud, extremist propaganda, disinformation and coordinated activity. This activity required the company to monitor how hostile actors changed methods and tried to bypass defense mechanisms.
With the launch of ChatGPT in 2022 and the rapid penetration of generative AI into the market, the company realized that the same knowledge could also be used to protect models and the systems based on them. On the one hand, criminal actors began to use AI tools to produce fraud, phishing attacks and misleading content on a larger scale. On the other hand, the companies that developed the models needed a systematic way to examine how they could be misused.
The knowledge gained from the original activity also underlies Rabbit Hole, a repository of attack patterns and harmful content collected from the real world. The database allows the company's researchers to test AI systems against methods already observed online and identify new versions of them. As AI became a larger part of the company's operations, management decided that the name ActiveFence no longer reflected its business, and last January it completed the rebranding to Alice.
Schwartz said, "AI builders should be able to trust their models to do exactly what they were built to do. The only way to earn that trust is to stress test models and agents every day and guard them with defenses built from real attacks. For years, our teams have been embedded with the world's leading platforms and AI labs, finding failures before deployment. Now we are bringing that capability to every AI lab and enterprise launching AI in production."
Alice provides AI safety solutions across the full lifecycle of AI systems. During training, Alice's researchers help frontier labs, including Anthropic, Google, and Nvidia, simulate malicious prompts and agentic tasks to identify and prevent dangerous or unpredictable model behavior, and harden models against jailbreaks and prompt injection attacks.
The company will use the funding to further advance its AI platform, deepening the technology that tests, defends, and monitors AI models across their lifecycle, expanding the team behind Rabbit Hole, its proprietary dataset of real-world adversarial and harmful content, to keep pace with attacks that evolve by the day, and scaling its go-to-market organization serving foundation model labs and enterprises building with AI.
Alice currently has about 400 employees, most of them in Israel, with the rest in offices in New York, London and Hanoi. "Our goal is for organizations to be able to trust their AI systems and know that they will work as designed," said Schwartz "To get there, you need to put experts in front of the models who challenge them every day."

ParaZero wins first US government order for DefendAir counter-drone system

2026-08-26

16:02:56 KST

Israeli defense-tech company ParaZero Technologies has received its first order for its DefendAir counter-drone system from a US federal government entity, marking the company’s first sale of the system to a US government customer.
The order includes DefendAir net launchers, Net Pods, and on-site operator training by ParaZero personnel, the company announced Tuesday.
The Kfar Saba-based company said the deal reflects growing demand among governments and security organizations for counter-unmanned aerial systems (C-UAS) that can provide a physical interception capability against small drones, particularly around sensitive sites and populated areas.
ParaZero’s DefendAir system incorporates patented net-launching technology. The Net pods are engineered by the company for integration across various platforms to deliver precise and effective neutralization of hostile drones.
The technology, which integrates sensors, real‑time monitoring, and automated deployment mechanisms, became a regulatory enabler for commercial drone operators seeking approval for flights over people, as well as other high‑risk operations.
These systems rely on autonomous guidance and net‑based interception rather than kinetic or explosive methods, making them suitable for urban environments, airports, and sensitive facilities where traditional counter‑drone solutions pose unacceptable risks.
The manually operated DefendAir configuration acts as a final layer of defense by allowing security personnel to physically intercept a hostile drone immediately.
The C-UAS system can be operated by individual operators and mobile forces protecting strategic sites.
Tech and training
ParaZero will also provide hands-on training to the US government operators, covering system familiarization, deployment, and practical use. The company said the training component reflects its broader approach to C-UAS, which it describes as providing an operational capability rather than just selling interception hardware.
“Counter-UAS capability is not created when a box arrives. It is created when trained operators can deploy the system confidently and act when seconds matter,” ParaZero CEO Ariel Alon said in a statement released by the company.
“Our approach extends beyond supplying launchers and Net Pods. DefendAir is designed to provide customers with an operational capability supported by training and hands-on preparation. We believe this approach is increasingly important as Counter-UAS solutions move from evaluation to real-world deployment,” he added.
The US order comes as small drones have increasingly become a security concern beyond the battlefield, with government facilities, critical infrastructure, public spaces, and other sensitive locations facing growing exposure to unauthorized or hostile unmanned aircraft.
ParaZero says it has seen growing interest in DefendAir from defense forces, government organizations, security agencies, and defense companies across several international markets.
Earlier this month, the company announced that it received an initial order for its DefendAir Net Pods from a Tier-1 European defense manufacturer.
Alon said that the initial order from the manufacturers points to the fact that there is a growing recognition for net-based interceptors.
“For ParaZero, we believe that integration with established defense manufacturers has the potential to expand the reach of DefendAir beyond individual products and into larger platforms and programs. Each successful integration strengthens our position as an enabling technology provider to the global Counter-UAS market and creates a foundation for broader commercial opportunities as these systems advance,” Alon said.

====================================================================================================

With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael Behr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
07:00:37 UTC
16:00:37 KST

Now is the twilight of Donald Trump’s supremacy. The US is still the richest and most heavily armed nation on Earth. That status is secure. The current president, contemptuous of law and indulged in lawlessness by a supine Congress, enjoys even greater power than the constitution allows.
With those advantages it takes a special talent for incompetence to look as thwarted and impotent as Trump does with more than two years of his second term still to run.
History will record the war against Iran as a turning point in the fortunes of the current US administration and a grievous wound to national prestige.
Pumped with hubris after the audacious military operation to kidnap Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, Trump believed an equally brisk triumph was available in the Middle East. The Tehran regime would be decapitated. The country’s hydrocarbon resources would then be available for US exploitation.
Six months later, Iran is controlled by a new generation of hardliners. Emboldened by resilience under US and Israeli bombardment, they demand financial concessions from Washington as the price for peace – reparations and a right to toll the strait of Hormuz.
The war is not over, it has just turned cold. Trump believes Iran’s fragile economy is close to collapse. He threatens to push it over the brink with “D-day” sanctions. The metaphor of second world war amphibious assault is supposed to make yet another round of financial coercion succeed where past embargos have failed.
It is true that ordinary Iranians are suffering terrible privations, but repression limits their capacity to translate discontent into demands for political change. By contrast, US consumers, aggrieved by the inflationary consequences of the war, and confused about its purpose, get to express their unhappiness in midterm elections in November.
The calculation in Tehran is that American tolerance for economic pain is low enough that Trump will be forced to blink first. It is a reasonable assumption: the need to declare mission accomplished to a domestic audience – even on terms that amount to defeat by any objective measure – drive an impatient president’s actions more than long-term strategy.
If sanctions fail, diplomatic climbdown is the only remaining move. The Pentagon couldn’t revert to the all-out military option even if Trump ordered it, because Operation Epic Fury burned too much of the national munitions stockpile.
This is where an asymmetry of cost and capability comes into play. Iran can frighten ships out of the Gulf with a few mines. It can harry neighbouring states with drones knocked together for less than $50,000 and dispatched from mobile launchers that are hard to target. The Patriot interceptors that protect US forces and their allies in the region cost $4-5m apiece. (More than 1,500 Patriots are thought have been fired in the war so far, leaving fewer than 830 in the US inventory.)
That depletion has global repercussions, most pressingly in Ukraine where top-end US interceptors are essential for shielding civilians from Russia’s most sophisticated ballistic missiles.
Trump’s attitude to that conflict has evolved from craven pro-Kremlin partisanship and an assumption of inevitable Russian victory to grudging respect for Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s fortitude and ingenuity in proving that assumption wrong. But the shift is not stable. It depends on undertakings by Nato’s European members to cover the cost of arming Kyiv.
If Trump had used normal diplomacy to cajole European democracies into financing the defence of their eastern flank, it would count as a foreign policy success – rebalancing the relationship to both sides’ benefit. But he did it with credulous admiration for Vladimir Putin and deranged demands for territory in Greenland. As a result, the European drive to autonomy looks less like burden-sharing and more like a hedge against American perfidy.
It isn’t just Europe where US allies feel burned. Gulf states that found themselves on the frontline of Iranian retaliation in a war they didn’t start or want, expected a more reliable umbrella of protection. They feel unrewarded for their decades of service, hosting US military bases and functioning as proxies for American interests in the region.
Last week Trump abruptly cut short a joint military exercise with South Korea – a loyal Asian partner to the US. A rational explanation, and the one preferred by Seoul, was that US forces were overstretched by their Middle Eastern entanglement. Trump framed it instead as an amicable gesture towards North Korean tyrant Kim Jong-un, whose regime he judged to be “unthreatening and respectful”.
Such civility, lavished on a monstrous dictatorship, is withheld from Canada, a benign democracy. Trump dismisses his northern neighbour as an economic freeloader, barely even a proper country; a mislabelled territory that should be the 51st US state.
Unsurprisingly, that attitude sours relations. Canadian prime minister Mark Carney pulled out of trade talks last weekend, citing unreasonable last-minute demands from US negotiators. Trump responded with punitive tariffs, to which the Canadians promise “dollar-for-dollar” retaliation.
The smaller economy is likely to suffer more from a trade war. But for Carney the cost in reduced commerce had to be weighed against the political damage he may incur if seen to capitulate to Trump’s bullying. He knows the US president takes concessions as an invitation to come back with yet more demands. He also knows that November’s midterm elections are likely to flip the House of Representatives to Democratic party control, and possibly the Senate too.
Trump cannot be chastened by unwelcome election results. He would rather deny their validity. But irrefutable evidence of failure at the ballot box may at least stir some Republicans out of stupefied obedience to a commander-in-chief whose way of governing has made their party less popular and left their country friendless.
Even if the constitutional mechanisms that are supposed to keep a president in check are only partly rehabilitated, the spell of impunity is broken. The cult of personality that once made Trump look like an irrepressible force of nature has shrunk to a sycophantic sect. An administration that styled itself as a national revolution looks more like a kleptocratic junta, using the privileges of office to pilfer what it can as the clock runs down.
The president still has followers across the country. A hard core bring unshakable devotion to the cause. But even some of them can surely sense the decay of purpose and whiff of panic in a man running out of ammunition.
Trump’s reign is far from over. With his hands on the levers of American power he can still do a lot of damage. But the rest of the world has learned to read his lurches, anticipate his spasms, manoeuvre around him. The phase of deference is past. Now is the time of planning for whatever comes next in the dimming light of a waning star.
- 
  Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

U.S. Navy awards Castelion $90 million for hypersonic weapon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
06:46:54 UTC
15:46:54 KST

- The Navy awarded Castelion $89,997,162 to advance the Blackbeard hypersonic weapon to Early Operational Capability, funding 50 weapons.
- The order supports Blackbeard's transition to a Navy Program of Record and includes work to speed potential exports to allies.
The U.S. Navy awarded Castelion Corp. nearly $90 million to advance its Blackbeard hypersonic strike weapon toward Early Operational Capability, the company announced August 25.
The order funds engineering, technical, logistics and manufacturing work supporting 50 early operational capability weapons and the missile’s transition to a formal Navy Program of Record.
The contract also funds Defense Exportability Features, design modifications intended to speed up potential sales to U.S. allies and partners. Work will be performed in Torrance, California, and is expected to be completed by August 2028.
The order falls under a Small Business Innovation Research Phase III effort tied to the topic “Low Cost Highly Manufacturable Long Range Strike Weapon Production.” Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division in Lakehurst, New Jersey, is the contracting activity, and the action was not competitively bid. Funding includes $50 million in fiscal 2026 defense-wide research funds, roughly $15.8 million in fiscal 2026 Navy research funds, and about $24.2 million in fiscal 2025 Navy research funds, the last of which expires at the end of the current fiscal year.
Blackbeard is designed to fly faster than Mach 5 while maneuvering within the atmosphere, built for both air launch from aircraft such as the F/A-18 and a parallel ground-launched variant compatible with HIMARS. The Navy selected Blackbeard in February as the first weapon candidate under its Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector program, known as MACE, which aims to field large quantities of lower-cost, longer-range strike weapons rather than relying solely on smaller numbers of expensive, exquisite systems. The Navy confirmed that link in April, tying the missile to a rapid prototyping effort structured within the fiscal 2026 Navy research budget as part of its Precision Strike Weapons Development Program.
Castelion has received a rapid sequence of expanding Navy contracts for Blackbeard over the past year, each building on the last. Following initial integration awards from the Army and Navy in October 2025, the Navy awarded the company nearly $50 million in February 2026 to fund full-scale prototypes and flight testing at Point Mugu Sea Range. That was followed in April by a $105 million contract modification to integrate the missile onto the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and support live-fire testing in the Indo-Pacific Command area of responsibility, with work expected to run through January 2028. In June, the Navy ordered 50 early operational capability pre-production prototypes and 50 storage and shipping containers under a $23.4 million contract, the first production-style delivery order for a low-cost hypersonic weapon of its kind. Roughly three-quarters of that work went to Castelion’s Project Ranger manufacturing campus, a 1,000-acre hypersonic production site in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, with the remainder handled at the company’s Torrance headquarters.
Castelion was founded in 2022 by Bryon Hargis, Sean Pitt and Andrew Kreitz, all of whom previously worked at SpaceX. The company describes Blackbeard as the first U.S. hypersonic system engineered from inception for industrial-rate output and commercial-style unit costs, built around continuous flight test iteration rather than the long, singular test campaigns typical of legacy hypersonic programs. Castelion has said its longer-term ambition includes multi-year procurement of 500 weapons annually, a production rate intended to shift the program from a development effort into fielded capability at scale. The company operates manufacturing sites in New Mexico, Texas and California, along with offices in Washington, D.C.
Congress increased MACE program funding by more than $140 million in the fiscal 2026 defense appropriations act, more than doubling the program’s base funding, though lawmakers did not specify how the additional money should be spent. Early budget documents for fiscal 2027 show continued funding growth planned for the broader Precision Strike Weapons Development Program that houses MACE.

Ukraine Uncovers Russia’s Secret Fleet of Unmanned Sea Vessels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
06:44:43 UTC
15:44:43 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Uncovers Russia’s Secret Fleet of Unmanned Sea Vessels
Ukrainian defense intelligence has released details on Russia’s uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) on its official website on August 18. The update revealed platforms capable of carrying up to 1 metric ton of payload.
These maritime drones can operate at ranges reaching 500 kilometers and attain speeds of up to 55 knots.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The catalog of unmanned platforms ranges from early reconnaissance and hydrographic craft to multi-purpose combat platforms designed for coastal attacks, anti-ship strikes, and serving as motherships for FPV drones.
Early Russian projects include the Skanda, an uncrewed vessel tested on Lake Ladoga in 2014 and in occupied Sevastopol in 2019, which offers a range of up to 150 km at speeds of at least 20 knots.
Subsequent developments include the Iskatel, capable of carrying 600 kg at 25 knots with up to seven days of endurance, and the Farvater, a planing catamaran featuring an operational range of at least 250 km and speeds up to 32 knots. Additionally, the 8.6-meter Trezubets delivers speeds up to 30 knots via twin 320-horsepower engines.
Russia's combat-oriented platforms feature significant payload capacities and specialized features. The Vizir-700 carries up to 600 kg at speeds up to 80 km/h, equipped with a bow weapon station for machine guns and rocket launchers, alongside a newer Vizir-2M variant.
The Zefir/Orkan system provides an operating range of up to 400 km, speeds up to 35 knots, and a 400 kg payload capacity. Heavyweight models include the BEK-1000, which carries up to 1 ton of payload across distances over 500 km at 40 knots, and the Katran, designed to launch FPV drones over ranges of 100 to 200 km.
Other specialized models include the Murena-300s, which features a 500 km range, a tethered aerial drone that ascends up to 100 meters, and options for torpedoes or FPV deployment.
Defense intelligence reiterated that all production facilities manufacturing these Russian vessels represent legitimate military targets during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
During the Ukrainian Youth Forum on August 12, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine and its partner nations had established a joint action plan aimed at ending Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
He stressed the necessity of expanding domestic pressure against the invading power, stating, "We need to bring the war back to the territory of Russia," so that Russian society would feel the consequences and exert pressure on its authorities.
At the same time, the Ukrainian leader urged international partners to strengthen defense support, specifically regarding air defense systems, as Moscow was preparing a new wave of autumn mobilization following pseudo-parliamentary elections.

2026-08-26
06:43:07 UTC
15:43:07 KST

Türkiye’s Treasury and Finance Ministry has completed preliminary work on a plan to tax so-called “hot money” flowing into money market funds, Bloomberg HT reported.
Under the proposal, gains earned by domestic and foreign institutional investors from money market funds would be subject to a 10 percent withholding tax, according to the report.
The planned measure would apply equally to resident corporations and non-resident corporations in Türkiye, with no distinction between the two categories, Bloomberg HT said.
Currently, gains generated by resident corporations from such funds are not subject to withholding tax. Instead, those earnings are taxed through provisional tax returns filed every three months.
If the regulation is enacted in line with the draft work, resident corporate taxpayers would be able to offset the withholding tax paid against their declared provisional tax liabilities, the report said.
For foreign corporations, the 10 percent withholding tax would be treated as a final tax, according to Bloomberg HT.
The report also said no changes are envisaged to withholding tax rates on gains earned by domestic and foreign individual investors.

Turkish investors’ overseas real estate investments reached $2.6 billion in the second quarter of 2026, exceeding the average level of the past five years by tenfold, according to TEPAV’s Direct Investments Bulletin.
The report said that longer payback periods in the domestic property market and the search for foreign-currency-denominated returns continued to drive Turkish investors toward overseas real estate assets.
Financial and regulatory incentives, including “Golden Visa” schemes in European countries and tax advantages offered in Dubai, also supported demand for overseas property investments, according to the report.
Real estate maintained its dominant position in Türkiye’s outward foreign direct investments during the second quarter, with its share in total investments increasing over the period.
In the second quarter of 2026, 44.8 percent of overseas investments were directed to the real estate sector, while 14.2 percent were invested in the construction sector, the report said.
According to TEPAV, Türkiye recorded a net direct investment outflow of $0.9 billion in the second quarter of 2026, compared with a net inflow of $0.9 billion in the same period a year earlier.
During the quarter, direct investment inflows totaled $1.6 billion, while outward direct investments reached $2.5 billion.
Foreign home sales in Türkiye fell 3.8 percent year-on-year to 4,918 units in the second quarter. Istanbul accounted for 43 percent of the transactions, followed by Antalya with 32 percent.
Russian citizens bought 912 homes during the period, while Iranian and Ukrainian citizens purchased 395 and 347 homes, respectively.

US pauses immigrant visa applications worldwide: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
06:28:16 UTC
15:28:16 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
The Trump administration has paused immigrant visa applications worldwide to accommodate “in-depth training” for consular officers, as it seeks to screen out applicants deemed likely to need US assistance, the Financial Times reported Tuesday.
Applicants with scheduled interviews at US embassies and consulates have received emails saying their appointments were being rescheduled and that they would receive notice of new dates and times.
“A more prosperous America means ensuring that visa applicants are not likely to become a public charge, as defined under US law and regulation, and not likely to become dependent on US public benefits reserved for qualified Americans in need,” a State Department spokesperson told the FT.
The department this month launched “a global training initiative” to “ensure all consular officers are fully equipped to evaluate every visa applicant comprehensively and consistently,” the spokesperson said.
The pause comes as President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to tighten US immigration policies, including imposing new limits on visas and green cards and ending nearly all refugee resettlement.
Brian Simmons, an attorney at immigration law firm Fragomen in Washington, said many affected applicants had “already spent thousands of dollars and disrupted their lives to attend scheduled interviews, only to have their appointments cancelled at the last minute”.
The State Department did not say when appointments would resume, saying: “To accommodate this in-depth training, appointments for visa services will be adjusted.”
The move follows a federal judge’s ruling last week striking down Trump’s pause on immigration applications from 75 mostly poorer countries whose nationals the administration believes could need assistance.

CANBERRA, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- The state of South Australia (SA) on Wednesday reported a suspected case of the H5N1 bird flu strain in a red fox, marking the country's first suspected case in a land mammal.
The SA Department of Primary Industries and Regions reported five new suspected H5N1 bird flu events on Wednesday, including the fox that was found in the northern suburbs of the state capital of Adelaide.

Panama declares nationwide emergency over El Nino risks
