Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:20:11 CST
15:20:11 KST

PANAMA CITY, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Panama's government on Tuesday declared a nationwide state of emergency over the climate impacts of El Nino, citing risks of drought, floods and possible effects on Panama Canal shipping, agriculture and energy supply.
In a statement, the government said the Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology of Panama (IMHPA) forecast that El Nino would strengthen from October this year through March 2027, with below-average rainfall expected in some areas and its impacts likely to last until May.
High temperatures and reduced rainfall could strain water resources and hurt agricultural production, the statement said.
The government warned that drought could lower water levels in rivers, lakes and reservoirs, potentially threatening vessel transits through the Panama Canal and the water supply needed for canal operations. Hydropower generation could also be affected.
Luz Graciela de Calzadilla, director of IMHPA, said 11 watersheds in Panama were already under water stress, with low river levels creating difficulties for hydropower plants and drinking water treatment facilities.
Omar Smith, director-general of Panama's National Civil Protection System, said El Nino had affected more than 10,000 people nationwide since January this year.
The government said the emergency declaration is intended to strengthen the ability of state institutions to respond to extreme weather and prepare for risks, including floods and landslides in some areas and drought in others. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: After UNESCO listing, Jingdezhen seeks lasting momentum for its living heritage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:20:01 CST
15:20:01 KST

NANCHANG, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- One month after the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, a symposium was held on Tuesday to explore how to turn the status into lasting momentum for urban development.
Themed "Preserving Cultural Heritage: Advancing the Inheritance and Innovation of Ceramic Culture," the event gathered experts, scholars and craft artisans in Jingdezhen, the ancient "porcelain capital" in east China's Jiangxi Province.
On July 25, with its UNESCO inscription, the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites became China's 61st World Heritage site. As symposium participants noted, this was not an endpoint but the beginning of a new chapter, with the focus now shifting to how the city's living heritage can be protected, passed on and revitalized.
Wang Tongmao, deputy secretary-general of the Jingdezhen Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, said ensuring effective post-inscription efforts hinges on concrete actions that integrate conservation, utilization and industrial development, allowing heritage protection to generate broader cultural and economic benefits.
He pointed to Taoxichuan, a former state-owned porcelain factory, as an example. The site has been transformed into a cultural and creative district, where 22 historic factory buildings and industrial facilities have been preserved and repurposed. It received 12.59 million visits in 2025, generating revenue of 1.31 billion yuan (about 193 million U.S. dollars).
Wang also stressed broader public participation. He said the city is exploring mechanisms to encourage community involvement, allowing local residents to not only benefit from heritage protection but also to play an active role in safeguarding it.
Jingpiao, a community of young artists and artisans who choose to live and pursue their dreams in this porcelain capital, is among those helping keep the city's ceramic culture alive. At times, as many as 5,000 foreign creators work and live in Jingdezhen.
Among them is Yann Colleu, a French ceramic artist who first came to the city in 2017 for what was meant to be a three-month academic exchange. Drawn by Jingdezhen's open and vibrant ceramic community, he later returned to pursue a doctoral degree at Jingdezhen Ceramic University.
"I felt that I had entered a city where ceramic history was still being practiced," he said. "People help and respect each other, exchange techniques, collaborate and continuously push one another to improve, and I believe this is one reason why Jingdezhen's ceramic ecosystem remains so dynamic."
Yet keeping this ecosystem alive requires more than attracting new talent. It also depends on preserving and passing on traditional skills.
Fu Changmin, a national-level inheritor of traditional famille-rose porcelain-making techniques, said Jingdezhen's value lies not only in its surviving historic sites, but also in its living craftsmanship.
"What we are safeguarding is not just the bricks and kilns of the past, but also the living heritage carried through generations of artisans," Fu noted.
The UNESCO inscription, she added, should serve as a starting point for bringing traditional craftsmanship to a wider audience and helping more people see the contemporary vitality of the millennia-old porcelain capital.
Beyond safeguarding craftsmanship at home, the city's experience also offers insights into how Chinese cultural heritage can be presented to the world.
Lyu Zhou, director of the National Heritage Center at Tsinghua University, said Jingdezhen's successful inscription demonstrated how the historical and cultural value of Chinese heritage can be integrated into an internationally recognized framework, offering a distinctive Chinese approach to heritage communication.
Participants said that for Jingdezhen, the inscription has thus opened a new chapter in which protection, inheritance and innovation will continue to shape the future of the millennia-old porcelain capital. ■

06:19:24 UTC
15:19:24 KST

Fire has destroyed the Kherson apartment of Mariano García Calatayud, the Spanish volunteer, who was abducted by Russian forces during the occupation of the city in 2022. His partner, Tetiana Marina, told ZMINA she received two videos from neighbors that morning, the first showing her apartment alight and the second showing the fire spreading through the building.
Calatayud is one case in a system of civilian captivity that Russia does not acknowledge. Ukraine's ombudsman estimates Russia holds up to 20,000 Ukrainian civilians, with confirmed identities for only a fraction. Russia has never charged Calatayud with a crime, never allowed him a lawyer or contact with his family, and for more than three and a half years has declined to confirm it holds him at all.
The building stands at the start of Yevropeiska Street, formerly Suvorova, roughly 500 to 700 meters from the Dnipro, Marina said. Police have recorded the damage. She does not know what caused the fire and suspects a Russian drone.
The videos showed the fire spreading
"In the first, I saw clearly that only my apartment was engulfed. In the second, I saw that all the apartments in the video had burned," Marina said.
She is still trying to reach a neighbor, Iryna, who had been sleeping in a bomb shelter because of the shelling.
- "I still do not know what happened, but everything burned. It does look like a drone," she said.
A moral debt brought him to Ukraine
Calatayud ran the road construction department at Valencia city hall before retiring. He moved to Ukraine in 2014, collected humanitarian aid from several countries and delivered it to Marinka and Krasnohorivka in Donetsk Oblast, and worked with orphanages.
Marina explained his reason to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. Under Franco, many children of repressed Spaniards were sent to Ukraine, to Odesa. His mother's family was among the repressed.
"That is why he went to Ukraine in 2014, to, as he put it, repay a debt to Ukraine," she said.
When Russian forces took Kherson, he stayed. He could have left for Spain, but did not.
Russia stopped acknowledging him
On 19 March 2022, Calatayud attended a pro-Ukrainian rally. Two men in balaclavas seized him at his own entrance, handcuffed him, put him in a dark blue minibus, and drove him to the occupation administration, Marina said.
He was held in Simferopol pre-trial detention center No. 2. According to other civilian hostages, he was beaten and subjected to electric shocks while in detention. They also described inhumane conditions and a lack of proper medical care. He suffered a heart attack in custody.
In December 2023, Russia reported Calatayud's transfer to Kherson Oblast, the Media Initiative for Human Rights reported. Spain proposed exchanging him for a Russian prisoner of war, and Russia refused. The Red Cross is searching for him in penal colonies, including in Siberia.
Russian military bloggers listed him in a database of foreign fighters, claiming he had joined Kherson's territorial defense. He never carried a weapon in the city, his wife said.

Amid heatwaves in Europe, at least 35,000 additional deaths recorded
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
08:58:01 EEST
14:58:01 KST

Amid heatwaves in Europe, at least 35,000 additional deaths recorded
Kyiv • UNN
This summer, heat claimed at least 35,000 lives in Europe. The highest number of deaths was recorded in Germany, France and Spain.
At least 35,000 more people than normally expected died in Europe this summer during four record-breaking heatwaves in a row, according to incomplete data obtained from almost half of the continent, The Guardian reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to preliminary data, excess mortality in just the three largest EU countries — Germany, France and Spain — has already exceeded 25,000, and experts say the death toll will rise significantly after the overall data for August are compiled.
Successive heatwaves in Western Europe have broken historical temperature records at hundreds of weather stations since May, while France recorded the hottest day averaged across the country in the entire history of observations.
Records were broken for three consecutive days in Germany at the end of June, when temperatures exceeded 40°C at 46 stations, while Spain experienced sustained highs above 42°C. Scientists say that human-caused global warming is making such extreme events more frequent and intense.
The highest number of deaths has been recorded in Germany, where approximately 14,000 heat-related deaths from 6 April to 9 August were reported at the end of last week. The health agency of the Robert Koch Institute (RKI) reported that 9,600 people died in just one week, from 22 to 28 June.
Systematically collected excess-mortality data across the EU, available since 2008, show that the only other summer week when a higher level of additional deaths was recorded was July 2022, when Covid-19 was still active.
This summer was the worst on record in Germany for the number of heat-related deaths since records began. The previous high in the EU's most populous country was 8,900 in 2018. According to the RKI, the number of heat-related deaths during a typical summer is often below 2,000.
Data from the Carlos III Health Institute's mortality-monitoring system indicate that 4947 deaths in Spain can be attributed to heat from May through this week, making 2026 Spain's worst year on record for heat-related deaths, surpassing the 4520 deaths recorded in 2022.
A final determination of the cause of death can take weeks or even months, and many countries have not yet released data even for the beginning of August. Karl Lauterbach, Germany's former health minister, said last week that the data published so far would probably prove to be underestimates.
In France, where more than 500 weather stations recorded temperatures above 40°C and, at one point, 98% of the country was under a heat alert, the national health agency said last week that the number of excess deaths "from all causes" from the end of May to 22 July was 7300. August data were not yet available, and the initial figures were based on electronic death certificates, which account for only 80% of total mortality, the statement said.
In Italy, modelling shows that 2700 more people than usual died between 22 and 28 June alone, while epidemiologists said that the total number of heat-related deaths in the country would probably be between 5000 and 8000 by the time they were officially registered.
Other European countries that have already reported excess deaths include the United Kingdom, where the health agency said in July that its modelling showed that the heatwaves in May and June had caused 2877 heat-related deaths in England.
Belgium said its preliminary data showed that mortality rose by 39% between 18 and 29 June, equivalent to 1222 additional deaths, while the Netherlands said that at least 900 more people than usual died between 22 June and 5 July.
According to rapid modeling cited by the European Commission, 1,070 more people than usual died in Poland during the heatwave at the end of June, while data from the Swiss health authority indicate 220 cases of excess mortality linked to the heat during the same week.
Preliminary data from Luxembourg, Greece, Romania, Bulgaria and Denmark indicate approximately 40 cases of excess mortality in each of these countries. Agence France-Presse calculated that temperatures exceeded 40°C this summer in areas where more than 80 million Europeans live.
The World Health Organization said in May that heat-related mortality in the European region had increased by more than 30% over the past 20 years and was highly likely to rise significantly as a result of the climate crisis and an aging population.

Islamabad’s Chief Commissioner Sohail Ashraf said an emergency fire call was made just before 7 a.m. local time on Aug. 26, adding that rescue teams and firefighters rushed to the scene.
The fire was brought under control, according to a statement made by Islamabad’s Chief Commissioner via X. The Capital Development Authority (CDA) wrote, "Six fire brigade units and four ambulances were deployed. The fire was brought under control promptly. Rescued children were shifted to the ICU for immediate treatment."
The post added, "The exact figures of casualties and injuries are being verified by the AC, SP and Rescue Teams along with hospital administration."
"A committee headed by the ADCG, ICT, has also been constituted to investigate the cause of the fire, assess the rescue response and examine the effectiveness of fire-safety measures at the hospital."

The United States will refrain from striking Iran "for the time being," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told several foreign counterparts, Axios reported Tuesday, citing a US official and a second source familiar with the matter.
According to the sources, the US instead intends to pressure Tehran through other means, including the recently announced Operation Economic Outcast, though the official did not rule out a return to strikes should Iran attack the US first.
Another US official said that the US Navy's clearing of mines from the Strait of Hormuz is a "watershed moment in the war," which removes one of Iran's main points of leverage in the war.
"The Iranians have lost control over the strait. Now the US controls it," Axios quoted one US official as saying.
Rubio outlined the Trump administration's current policy on Iran to his counterparts, Axios reported, including the intention to avoid military action against Iran for the time being, increasing economic pressure on Tehran, and transporting as much oil as possible through the Strait of Hormuz.
The policy is expected to last until after the US midterm elections on November 3, according to a second US official, after which a new military offensive might return to the table.
"The Iranian economy is in free fall, and the regime's military has been decimated," US State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott told Axios, "and we are cutting off every financial lifeline the regime has remaining."
"The president has been clear that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, and that he will use the tools necessary to ensure that objective is accomplished."
US launches Operation Economic Outcast
Operation Economic Outcast was announced on Monday by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, following earlier threats of an "economic D-Day" against the regime.
"Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," said Bessent.
Bessent described the operation as "a sustained campaign to collapse every last option for Iran," saying that those involved in "any" economic cooperation with Tehran would expose themselves to "the full reach of American power."
He added that Iran faces a "very clear choice," saying the regime can either accept "complete global isolation" or a path to normalcy.
Bessent described the operation's methods as actions that will "tighten the noose" around Iran's funding sources, leaving it "no breathing space."
He listed five Iranian "vital lifelines" that the operation would initially target: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping.
Aaron Glick, Esther Davis, and Reuters contributed to this report.

More than 50 children die in diphtheria outbreak in northwestern Nigeria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:50:32 UTC
14:50:32 KST

Kabir Adeniyi
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
More than 50 children have died from a diphtheria outbreak in Rano Local Government Area of Nigeria’s northwestern Kano state, a state lawmaker said Tuesday, urging authorities to step up efforts to contain the disease.
 
Ibrahim Malami, who represents Rano Constituency in the Kano State House of Assembly, raised the alarm during a motion of urgent public importance, saying the outbreak had severely affected communities in Rurum Ward, including Rurum A, Rurum B and Sabuwar Kaura.
He said the local government’s medical department had launched emergency measures, while his office had provided medicines to support the response.
 
Malami called on Kano Gov. Abba Kabir Yusuf and state health authorities to deploy additional medical personnel, medicines and other emergency assistance to the affected communities.
 
“We want to inform the Governor and the Commissioner for Health to send further emergency aid to the region because the disease has spread heavily in that area,” Malami said. 
 
Another lawmaker, Usman Abubakar Tasiu, representing Kiru Constituency, warned that the outbreak had spread beyond Rano, with cases also reported in Kwanar Dangora, Garin Dangora and Yelwa communities in neighboring Kiru Local Government Area.
 
The state Assembly subsequently adopted a resolution urging immediate government intervention and tasked its health committee with coordinating with the state Health Ministry to ensure emergency measures are implemented in the affected areas.
 
Diphtheria is a highly contagious bacterial infection that can cause severe illness and death, particularly among unvaccinated children. Nigeria’s Centre for Disease Control and Prevention advises parents to ensure children receive the recommended three doses of the pentavalent vaccine, which protects against diphtheria, at 6, 10 and 14 weeks of age.
Nigeria has faced recurring diphtheria outbreaks in recent years, with Kano among the states hardest hit. The World Health Organization said Kano accounted for the majority of suspected cases during a major nationwide outbreak in 2023.
The latest deaths underscore ongoing challenges in vaccination coverage, disease surveillance and access to timely treatment as Nigerian authorities work to contain diphtheria outbreaks.

China Focus: China's cotton know-how takes root in Central Asia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:39 CST
14:30:39 KST

URUMQI, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Several hundred kilometers from Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan, cotton plants in a 1,000-mu (about 66.67 hectares) demonstration field are approaching one meter in height, each bearing 8 to 10 bolls.
For Song Meizhen, chief scientist of a high-quality cotton research team at the Institute of Western Agriculture under the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, the crop is developing as expected.
"Given the current growth and field management, the field is well on track to exceed the target of 550 kilograms of seed cotton per mu this year," Song said.
This high-standard cotton seed breeding demonstration field is jointly operated by Xinjiang Huaxing Investment Group and the institute. From surveying the land and selecting varieties before spring planting to designing cultivation methods and setting technical standards for sowing and field management, Chinese researchers have been involved throughout the process.
They have also provided regular video guidance and remote technical support.
The project combines high-quality cotton varieties with a range of techniques already widely used in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, including drip irrigation under plastic film, denser planting designed to improve light use, and mechanized harvesting.
Song said the cooperation endeavor is aimed at introducing a package of Chinese cotton-growing technologies and management practices to Uzbekistan.
Xinjiang is China's largest cotton-producing region. In 2025, it produced 6.17 million tonnes of cotton, accounting for 92.8 percent of the national total. The region's cotton sector is already among the world's most mechanized, with an overall mechanization rate for cultivation and harvesting surpassing 97 percent.
At a smart cotton field jointly developed by the Xinjiang Changji National Agricultural High-tech Industry Demonstration Zone and the institute, weather stations and soil-moisture sensors collect field data around the clock, helping growers manage irrigation, fertilizer and other field operations more precisely.
According to the institute, the system can save more than 10 percent of water and nearly 20 percent of fertilizer per mu while increasing yields by over 10 percent.
Similarities in climate, water and soil conditions between Xinjiang and Central Asian countries have laid the groundwork for cross-border adoption of improved cotton varieties, cultivation techniques and agricultural machinery.
Shadman Namazov, an academician of the Uzbek Academy of Sciences who has visited the Changji demonstration zone several times, said Chinese cotton-growing techniques have brought improvements in planting density, water use, yields and quality compared with traditional local practices.
He cited precision irrigation and fertilizer use, mechanized operations and modern field management, saying these technologies were scientifically grounded and could be replicated on a wider scale.
Namazov added that the use of Chinese techniques in Uzbekistan has helped raise cotton yields while reducing production costs, contributing to higher incomes for local growers.
These cooperation efforts are also translating into stronger demand for Chinese cotton seeds and agricultural machinery in Central Asia.
Hilltide, a Xinjiang-based seed industry company, sells cotton seeds and provides related technical services in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan. Company executive Lu Yang said its cotton seed exports to Central Asia rose from 800 tonnes during the sales season from late 2024 to early 2025 to 1,500 tonnes during the season from late 2025 to early 2026.
Lu revealed that the company's cotton seeds have maintained a market share of more than 70 percent in its Central Asian markets, attributing the growth to high-yield, stress-resistant varieties and technical services provided in addition to the seeds.
Chinese cotton pickers are gaining ground in Central Asia as well.
The Xinjiang branch of China Railway Construction Heavy Industry Co., Ltd. dispatched a batch of new four-row box-type cotton pickers to Central Asia in early July. The company said its cotton pickers have been developed to suit planting patterns and harvesting conditions in Central Asia, and orders from the region account for more than 70 percent of its production capacity this year.
At Xinjiang Boshiran Intelligent Agricultural Machinery Co., Ltd., Vice President Feng Guang said Chinese high-end cotton pickers can match leading international products in harvesting efficiency while costing about half as much as comparable European and U.S. machines.
Feng said a high level of domestically produced components, shorter delivery times and more timely after-sales service have also helped Chinese machines meet demand in Central Asian markets. The company has seen a sharp increase in overseas orders since last year, he added.
Alongside business exchanges, research cooperation has also deepened. Since 2023, Chinese institutions have worked with agricultural research institutes across all five Central Asian countries on joint research and technical training in cotton breeding, high-yield cultivation and water-saving irrigation, while promoting standardized technical guidelines in English and Russian.
The Uzbek demonstration field is one place where the results of this cooperation can be seen in the crop itself. Across Central Asia, Chinese cotton expertise is increasingly arriving not as a single product, but as a combination of seeds, farming techniques and machinery. ■

Across China: "China can set an example": U.S. delegation seeks lessons on aging, healthcare reform
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:36 CST
14:30:36 KST

Members of the exchange program "Harvard Healthcare China Trek 2026" pose for photos while visiting Peking University in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 19, 2026. (Xinhua)
BEIJING, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- China can set an example for the world in confronting demographic change, a U.S. public health scholar said, as a 25-member American delegation tours the country to learn from its healthcare reform, biotech innovation and artificial intelligence application.
David Crumpacker, assistant professor at Texas A&M University and a master of public health graduate from Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, stressed the importance of learning from Chinese experience, such as primary care infrastructure, and efforts to manage the intersection of economic development with population health.
"These are insights that are not fully reflected in global health literature. We want to understand those insights from the people who generate them," he said.
The delegation, comprising scholars, medical professionals and students from Harvard University and other leading U.S. institutions, has been in China since Aug. 16.
They have visited the National Healthcare Security Administration and a national artificial intelligence medical pilot base in Beijing, as well as hospitals in Shanghai. They are also scheduled to tour health companies in Shenzhen, a global tech hub in southern Guangdong Province, and the Boao Lecheng International Medical Tourism Pilot Zone -- the country's sole medical special zone -- in Hainan Province.
China is racing to upgrade its healthcare system to meet the needs of an aging society. With more than 300 million people aged 60 and above, it has the largest elderly population of any country in the world.
By the end of 2025, the national basic medical insurance program covered 1.331 billion people, with the participation rate remaining stable at over 95 percent.
"Over one billion people means over one billion patients," said Jennifer Miles-Thomas, vice chair of integration and innovation at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago.
She said China and the United States are "very aligned" in the goal of delivering the highest quality care, but the U.S. faces challenges with expensive healthcare and incomplete insurance coverage. "I'm here to observe and to receive information and ideas about what we can do better," she said.
The exchange program, "Harvard Healthcare China Trek 2026," is hosted by the China Center for International People-to-People Exchange under the Ministry of Education, with support from Peking University Health Science Center and Fudan University Shanghai Medical College. It is part of a broader initiative to invite 50,000 young Americans to China over five years for study, research and dialogue.
During a visit to the BioPark in Beijing, Khaoula Belahsen, a 28-year-old master's student at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and an AI researcher at Harvard Medical School, was impressed by the scale and speed of the pharmaceutical and biotechnology hub. First announced in October 2025, the BioPark has drawn nearly 5,000 medical and healthcare companies, including global leaders Eli Lilly, Pfizer, Bayer, AstraZeneca and Medtronic.
"I've always dreamed of coming to China. The country has so much history, but also so much progress economically and scientifically," Belahsen said.
Morgan Moncada, 35, a Harvard graduate and founder of an AI digital health company, said strong incentives exist for medical companies to engage with the Chinese market, citing lower costs and vast reach. "China is open to collaboration, and that is really exciting," he said.
China is pushing artificial intelligence deeper into healthcare, with a roadmap to bring AI-assisted diagnosis to all primary-care clinics by 2030. Major hospitals are already using AI for imaging analysis and treatment planning.
Noting that his company uses AI agents to help people manage chronic diseases such as sleep apnea and diabetes, Moncada expressed his hope to introduce the technology they're building in the U.S. to China and adapt it for the Chinese population.
"I think something that we're really interested in is how we can contribute to China's healthcare system and how we can learn from China's healthcare system to improve healthcare in the United States and other countries around the globe," Moncada added.
In the Boao Lecheng pilot zone, patients can access innovative drugs and medical devices not yet approved on the mainland -- a policy that has benefited nearly 280,000 people and spared many costly overseas medical trips. The zone also uses real-world patient data to accelerate regulatory approvals, helping more products reach the wider Chinese market faster.
"We're very interested in seeing how this special zone actually helps, and how all those incredible medical technologies take effect," said Ze'ev Drukker, a 26-year-old bioengineering graduate from Tufts University who is applying for a master's program at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
As the delegation explores China's healthcare landscape, they are also building bridges of understanding between the younger generation of U.S. and Chinese health professionals, paving the way for joint efforts to advance global public health.
"What I like about healthcare is that it's something shared between all people, and across all countries. We all face the same challenges, and all want to integrate innovation to save people's lives and reduce burdens," Belahsen said. "It's really inspiring to come to China and see what innovation looks like here." ■

Syria's Kurdish-led group announces dissolution
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:34 CST
14:30:34 KST

DAMASCUS, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Mazloum Abdi, commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), announced Tuesday the dissolution of the force following the completion of its integration into Syrian state institutions, ending a decade-long chapter in which the U.S.-backed group controlled large parts of northern and northeastern Syria.
"Today, we announce the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces, and we responsibly announce its dissolution as a military force," Abdi said at a press conference at the People's Palace in Damascus, according to Syria's state-run Al-Ikhbariya TV.
Abdi also announced the dissolution of the Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration and affiliated military and civilian formations, following their full integration into state institutions.
He described the move as the beginning of a new chapter focused on peace, stability and rebuilding Syria after years of conflict.
The transition should mark a genuine shift "from the battlefields to the fields of construction," said Abdi, calling for the building of a unified country encompassing Syria's different communities.
He also raised the issue of Kurdish cultural and linguistic rights, saying he had sought an open position from Syrian interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa regarding the right to education in one's mother tongue.
Tuesday's announcement caps months of difficult negotiations and intermittent military confrontation between Damascus and the SDF over the future of northeastern Syria and the shape of the country's post-war state.
The two sides initially agreed in early 2025 to integrate the SDF and the Kurdish-led administration's civilian institutions into the Syrian state. Implementation, however, became bogged down amid disagreements over the structure of the integration, military command arrangements and the degree of autonomy Kurdish authorities would retain.
Tensions subsequently escalated, including clashes in Kurdish-held neighborhoods of Aleppo, before developing into a broader military confrontation in January this year.
Government forces advanced into SDF-held territory in northern and eastern Syria, substantially reducing the territory controlled by the Kurdish-led force.
On Jan. 18, Damascus and the SDF reached a ceasefire and integration agreement providing for an immediate halt to fighting, the withdrawal of SDF formations to areas east of the Euphrates River and the transfer of administrative and military authority in Raqqa and Deir al-Zour provinces to the central government.
A more comprehensive agreement followed later that month, setting out the phased integration of the SDF's military and administrative structures.
The arrangements included the deployment of Interior Ministry security forces in Hasakah and Qamishli and the incorporation of SDF fighters into formations operating within the Syrian military structure.
Implementation continued over the following months. Damascus assumed control over key state institutions and facilities in the northeast, including Qamishli airport and major oil fields, while government security forces entered Hasakah and Qamishli.
Yet disagreements persisted over the SDF's ultimate status, particularly whether it could retain a distinct command structure within the Syrian military. As recently as early August, dissolution remained a key issue under negotiation between Abdi and al-Sharaa.
Abdi announced on Aug. 20 that the integration of the Kurdish administration's military, security and civilian institutions into the Syrian state had been completed, paving the way for Tuesday's formal dissolution.
Tuesday's announcement also came one day after Washington formally removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, ending a designation that had lasted since 1979.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the decision was part of Washington's effort to give Syria a path toward prosperity.
Washington also revoked the designation of Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), a former al-Qaida-linked rebel group that played a dominant role in the formation of Syria's new government, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization.
Since its formation in 2015, the SDF had been backed primarily by the United States and served as Washington's main local partner in the fight against Islamic State militants.
But following the fall of the former Syrian government in December 2024, Washington increasingly supported efforts to bring Syria's institutions and armed groups under a unified state framework while building closer ties with the new authorities in Damascus. ■

Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Aug 25 that those responsible for hybrid attacks “will pay the price” after an explosive-laden drone was discovered at an airport in Leipzig near a Ukrainian cargo plane, raising speculation that Moscow was involved in an attempted strike.
European officials have been anticipating for months that Russia may escalate its aggressive campaign against the continent.
But the bloc has yet to change its fundamentally defensive posture, according to people familiar with how the institutions gauge outside threats, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
That has likely encouraged Moscow to probe how far it can go in trying to intimidate and wear down Western allies as it remains locked in a war of attrition with Ukraine.
“NATO, European and national responses have largely been reactive and defensive,” said Agnia Grigas, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council in Vilnius.
“They have focused on detecting and countering individual provocations, but have not built a record of effective deterrence by consistently dissuading Moscow from continuing or escalating them.”
That lack of preparedness comes as Europe has taken on the primary role in supporting Ukraine, with the US shifting away from the continent.
While NATO’s mutual defence clause commits member states to help one another in case of an attack, Russia’s alleged actions have so far fallen short of what would become a trigger for such a response.
Moscow has increasingly relied on recruitment via social media to carry out arson or other sabotage attacks after large-scale expulsions of its diplomats following the invasion of Ukraine.

 Listen
South Korea said on Wednesday it had scrambled fighter jets in response to Russian military aircraft entering its air defence zone, the second such incursion in weeks.
The relationship between the countries has worsened since South Korea joined Western sanctions following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and since Moscow built stronger ties with North Korea.
Seoul’s defence ministry said multiple Russian aircraft had entered and then left its air defence identification zone over the East Sea, also called the Sea of Japan.
“South Korea’s military detected the Russian aircraft before they entered the zone and deployed Air Force fighter jets to prepare for any contingency,” it said, without giving details.
The Russian aircraft did not violate South Korean airspace, it said.
An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area where countries require foreign aircraft to identify themselves for security purposes.

35 on 35 – Independent Ukraine Through the Eyes of a Ukrainian Woman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:27:00 UTC
14:27:00 KST

Yana Oller was born in a small village in Ukraine’s Vinnytsia region on May 4, 1991. Three months and 20 days later, Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada adopted the country’s Act of Declaration of Independence.
“I still have a birth certificate that says in Russian, in a Soviet Union paper, that I was born this and this, in the Russian language,” she tells Kyiv Post.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
As the country slowly built its identity over the past 35 years, Ukrainians such as Oller, like their nation, have also been forging a path of their own.
A small village in Vinnytsia region
Oller was born into a Ukrainian-speaking family from the village of Dzhulynka, in central Ukraine’s Vinnytsia region.
It was the 1990s, and the whole family lived in a house built by her grandfather – not particularly Soviet, she says, but not exactly modern either.
Like most former Soviet Republics in the 1990s, the newfound freedom also came with a crippled economy inherited from the fallen Soviet empire – between 1991-96, the Ukrainian economy contracted between 9.7 and 22.7 percent annually, compounded by hyperinflation, according to a 2012 study by think tank Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
Life, according to Oller, was far from abundant.
“My family was extremely poor, like so poor that we couldn’t afford to buy meat, or to bake something,” she explains. “I remember that we always ate soup. It was just potatoes, carrots, and nothing else.”
From Soviet Republic to EU Applicant: Ukraine’s Identity Shift
The Ukrainian revival of the 1990s
Childhood at Dzhulynka is a vague memory for Oller, but the visible changes, or rather, audible ones, came in the form of music.
“I guess what changed was mostly what we watched… or what we listened to. Like the culture was changing. The music, the movies, the shows,” she continues.
And long before the Ukrainian language law was passed in the Verkhovna Rada in 2019, the 1990s already saw a small revival of the Ukrainian language in media.
“Probably everything was in Russian… and then in 1998, and later, we began watching Ukrainian channels,” she says.
And for young Oller, the surge in Ukrainian language in media wasn’t just a sense of familiarity – it represented something exciting.
“I don’t know why but I always wanted to watch something in Ukrainian… all the Western movies that started coming, they were all translated into Ukrainian. I loved Western stuff, and it was so nice to hear,” she says.
At some point, young Oller would come to the TV just to wait for the end credits to play from one particular show because the song was sung by Okean Elzy, one of the most famous Ukrainian bands.
“I was always waiting for the titles just to hear that song,” Oller recalls.
2000s and the Orange Revolution
After nine years in Dzhulynka, Oller moved to a nearby town because her father, a Protestant church pastor, started a new church.
“I don’t know how, [but] we bought an apartment in town on the third floor. It was my first apartment… I really loved it because I always wanted to live in the big city,” she says.
The highlight for young Oller? The cinema in town.
“We had one movie theater. A movie theater! You don’t have such things in a village,” she says.
But just a few years later, the Orange Revolution would begin – the first test of democracy in independent Ukraine, where electoral fraud claims against presidential candidate Viktor Yanukovych (who later became president in 2010 and was ousted in 2014) led to a popular revolution, which brought reformist leader Viktor Yushchenko to victory.
But for Oller and her family, far from Kyiv, the revolution remained a topic spoken of between adults, now more of a distant memory for Oller.
“It was discussed by parents. It was discussed by adults… You don’t really watch news because you’re a kid,” she says.
“One thing I always remember… during the Orange Revolution, my dad would always complain about it,” she recalls. “He would say everybody’s bad, politicians are bad, everything is horrible, and everybody will go to hell. That’s all I remember.”
She did remember wearing orange – but that doesn’t mean she understood what any of it meant.
“I think we were wearing something orange just because everybody was doing it. Did I understand what it meant? No,” she says.
Moving to the big city
Oller moved to Kyiv in 2008 to study philology at university – and moving to the capital was both an exciting and difficult ordeal.
At the time, the exchange rate to the US dollar had fallen to around 1 to 5, partly in the wake of the US financial crisis, and with little prospect of improvement, according to then-National Bank supervisory board chairman Petro Poroshenko – the same man who would become Ukraine’s president in 2014 in the wake of Euromaidan.
But while the world dealt with the fallout of the crisis, that was the last thing on young Oller’s mind.
“When I came to Kyiv, the news was the last thing I wanted to hear about. I was not aware of anything going on then,” she says.
Ordinary students from outside Kyiv would typically stay in a dormitory, which cost Hr. 600 (around $120) per semester – but since it was overcrowded, Oller had to pay Hr.700 (around $140) for a private room per month, bunking with her flat mate in the same room, on the same bed.
Oller’s memory of university years was mostly of hours of strenuous study, as it also meant a Hr. 500 (about $100 at the time) scholarship to supplement her family’s meager income – but the system did not work in her favor.
“I received a scholarship because I was a good student. But it only lasted, like, the first year or something. Then they failed you,” she says. “In my university, they would fail your last exam on purpose, just to avoid paying you.”
While the issue might not necessarily be attributed to corruption, many Ukrainians have had a similar taste of Soviet-style bureaucracy in different aspects of life – a system that many are still fighting against to this day.
“And even Hr. 500 seemed like, ‘Wow, I can actually buy food.’ Basic food, like pasta and grains,” she adds.
Graduation and the Euromaidan
Oller graduated in 2012 and soon found herself a job teaching English in Kyiv – by then, the exchange rate to the US dollar had fallen to around 1 to 8.
Her first full-time job was teaching at the American English Center in Kyiv, where she first worked as a tutor for around Hr. 20 ($2.5) per hour, or around Hr. 4,000 ($500) per month, before they made her a teacher with higher pay.
“It was enough,” she says, adding that rent per month for a room was about Hr.1,000 ($125) per month at the time.
It was also at work where she met her future husband Jeff, a US citizen who was teaching at the same center, though the two wouldn’t start dating until a few years later.
Then came late 2013, when the Euromaidan – also known as the Revolution of Dignity – would erupt in Kyiv into early 2014, and bring about unprecedented changes for the country.
At the time, protesters rallied against former President Yanukovych’s decision to backtrack on a trade deal with the EU he personally promised in 2010 after meetings with Russia. The protest later grew into a wider mandate against Russian influence and corruption.
Thousands gathered. Then shots were fired. When the smoke was clear, over a hundred were shot dead by Yanukovych’s government near the capital’s central Maidan square, and Yanukovych himself fled to Russia.
But for Oller, while the protests raged on near the central square, the city was relatively calm on the left bank, where she worked – but not for her future husband Jeff, who had to go to work near Maidan.
“I was already friends with Jeff, and he worked there… And he had to go through this, and there were blockposts. Every time, you had to show your documents, especially if you were a foreigner,” she recalls.
“It was hard every day… It was really affecting people here, but I remember that all the time I just didn’t go to Maidan,” she continued. “I love spending my weekend here on Khreshatyk, you know, I love this place. But when it was the revolution, I was scared.”
When Russia later annexed Crimea and started waging a war in eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region, the ripples also came to Oller as she began to notice a change in some people.
A question of national identity
“At the time, one of my best friends was from Sevastopol in Crimea,” Oller says.
“We met at work, and we were had a great time. She was living with a boyfriend who was from Kyiv… and they often went to Crimea before 2014 to visit her mom,” she added.
While Oller says she “was not very aware of what exactly [was] happening,” she began noticing strange comments from her friend as the events unfolded in Crimea.
“I remember loving this friend, but at the same time, she said some weird things,” Oller continues.
“I remember she said, ‘But you know, it’s crazy what’s happening in Crimea, but you know, they’re promising them better life. My mom will get either a better job or hospitals will be modernized; they’re going to pay better salaries because people in Crimea are struggling,’” Oller recalls.
Eventually, her friend moved to Moscow with her family, and they severed all contact.
“She was not one of those people who would do propaganda or tell you that Russia is better,” she added. “She just moved to Russia because they were worried about her mom or something.”
“I remember this – I was listening to it, but I didn’t understand it, or I didn’t want to understand it,” she says.
Calm before the storm
The exchange rate plummeted to around Hr.22-27 per US dollar in the years that followed, as Russia’s 2014 invasion of Ukraine continued in the ensuing years and the country was still reeling from the revolution.
That same year, Poroshenko became Ukraine’s first post-revolution president, and for Oller and many others, things were slowly getting better despite the turmoil.
In 2014, she also moved to a new flat with a private room all to herself, and with a balcony as the cherry on top.
“There were three rooms, three girls, and I chose the best room because it was with the balcony,” she says. “It wasn’t like a super fancy room. But I was so happy and everything seemed great to me.”
She also took vacations from work for the first time to travel abroad.
“This was the year when I first traveled abroad twice a year,” Oller recalls. “On the first trip I went to Egypt because Egypt was the one place that people could afford. It was with my roommate and her friend.”
Then the next trip was to Paris.
“We couldn’t afford flying, I think. Package tours were very popular around Europe as bus tours,” she says. “So we visited three countries, and it was really great.”
She would also start dating her future husband, and life was going well despite small hiccups during COVID-19.
“I didn’t want to teach online, but we had no choice,” she explains. “And then they let us go home. And that’s when we enjoyed it.”
But later came Feb. 24, 2022 – a day that Ukrainians would never forget.
Russia’s full-scale invasion
In the early hours of Feb. 24, 2022, Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Tanks began marching across the border, and missiles began raining down across Ukraine as gunshots echoed through the streets.
“We woke up at 9 a.m. without an alarm because it was a Thursday,” she says. “I remember this very well because work started at 12 that day.”
Like many Ukrainians, while different countries warned of an impending Russian invasion, life went on as usual until it didn’t.
“Of course, the war was in the air before that, and everybody was expecting something,” she says. “The first thing that we were thinking about is like run to the windows
See what’s happening… And I just remember that the lessons were canceled.”
That night, Oller and her husband – like many Ukrainians – spent the night at the shelter.
Eventually, Oller’s mother said she found them a driver, and after hours of driving through dark streets and avoiding the highway, they found their way to the village of Dzhulynka.
There, they spent a week with her parents before deciding that it was best to leave the country.
Moldova was their next destination, but they were also stuck for a week because the airport was closed. Then they went to Romania, and eventually to the US – home to around half a million displaced Ukrainians by 2026.
But Oller says she never wanted to stay in the US.
“I never wanted to live there. I never thought of doing the protection program there. It’s just temporary,” she says. “I never wanted to live in another country. I always liked living in Kyiv.”
“This is the city where I want to live forever.”
According to Oller, she and her husband wanted to return to Ukraine, but the blackouts in Kyiv at the time stopped them in their tracks as they had to work online.
Eventually, after their brief six-month stay in the US, they found themselves briefly in Sweden, then Slovakia – before they heard that a friend had returned in 2023, and the decision was made.
“Somebody said, ‘Let’s do Shashlik in Rusanivka,’ and we’re like, that’s it,” she says, referring to their old district in Kyiv where they would do barbeques (shashlik) by the Dnipro river.
“I texted the landlord and we decided in five minutes that we were going back to Ukraine,” she says.
“It was the best decision I have made in my life,” she continues. “It doesn’t matter how bad this war is; the moment we arrived, I wanted to kiss the asphalt.”
On Aug. 24, 2026, as Ukraine marks its 35th independence anniversary, Oller says she decided to make borscht – Ukraine’s national dish – for dinner after a long working day while listening to Okean Elzy, the same band little Oller was looking toward at the end of the TV show, back in the village of Dzhulynka.
Asked about what she looks forward to should the war end soon, she has a simple and humble wish – to stay in the big city she always dreamed of living in, without the fear of war.
“I want to continue living in this beautiful city and this beautiful country, without ever fearing any threat.”

Cyclone from Balkans and anticyclone from Scandinavia affect weather - forecast for August 26
Kyiv • UNN
On August 26, rain and thunderstorms are expected in some regions of Ukraine, while the rest of the country will remain dry. Temperatures will reach 30°C during the day.
The weather in Ukraine on August 26 will be influenced by a cyclone from the Balkans and an anticyclone from Scandinavia; it will be rainy in some places and dry in others, while daytime temperatures will reach 30 degrees Celsius, the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center reported, writes UNN.
On August 26, an atmospheric front from the cyclone over the Balkans will bring unsettled weather to the central regions, Zakarpattia, Chernivtsi, and, during the day, most southern regions, while also affecting the southern districts of Kyiv region. Weather without precipitation in the rest of the country will be determined by a high-pressure field from an anticyclone centered over southern Scandinavia. Moderate northeastern winds will prevail, bringing cool air to Ukraine; its influence will be most noticeable in the northern part, especially at night
According to the forecast, today will be partly cloudy.
In the central regions, Zakarpattia, Chernivtsi, during the day also in most southern regions and in Kyiv region, there will be moderate, locally heavy rain and thunderstorms; elsewhere, no precipitation.
The wind will be predominantly northeastern, 5–10 m/s.
Temperatures will be 14–19° at night, 8–13° in the northern part; 21–26° during the day, and 25–30° in the southeast of the country.

Iceland to vote on reopening EU membership talks in close referendum

Iceland to vote on reopening EU membership talks in close referendum
Icelanders will vote in a referendum on Saturday whether to resume entry talks with the European Union amid growing global insecurity. Voters are not being asked to decide just yet if they want to join the 27-member bloc – only whether they want their government to negotiate possible terms.
Icelanders are to vote Saturday on whether to resume entry talks with the European Union amid growing global insecurity, in a referendum seen as going down to the wire.
Icelanders are not being asked to decide just yet if they want to join the 27-member bloc – only whether they want their government to negotiate possible terms, including on the highly sensitive fishing issue.
"This is an opportunity, it's not a final decision," Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir told AFP, arguing that the referendum paved the way for a "risk-reducing 'Yes'".
"This way you get a deal on the table, you're able to see all the questions, the answers to all the questions we get here," she said.
She was speaking to AFP after a "listening meeting" in Selfoss, one of the many small towns the Social Democratic leader has visited to hear Icelanders' questions and concerns on the issue.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
On Saturday, voters will be asked to answer "Yes" or "No" to the question: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"
Implied is the question of whether the country of 400,000 inhabitants ultimately thinks it best to remain the captain of its own ship, or hitch its cart to the EU.
If the "Yes" side wins, an accession agreement negotiated with Brussels would be put to a new referendum and likely require a change to Iceland's constitution, as well as ratification by EU member states.
The north Atlantic island applied to join the bloc in 2009, a year after the 2008 financial crisis led to the collapse of its banks and economy.
Membership negotiations began in 2010 but were suspended in 2013 after a eurosceptic government came to power.
The world has changed radically since then.
Read moreIceland to hold EU referendum 'in the coming months', PM says
"The EU is looking around, it's finishing deals with India, with Mercosur. We're seeing changes in the global climate when it comes to how people are using tariffs as weapons," Frostadottir noted.
Divisive question
While Iceland's economy is flourishing again – albeit with a volatile currency – households are struggling with rising inflation and soaring interest rates, with the central bank raising rates three times so far this year to eight percent. This makes the euro an attractive option to indebted households.
On the global stage, the return of war in Europe with Russia's invasion of Ukraine has shaken established security doctrines.
US President Donald Trump's threats to take over neighbouring Greenland have added to Icelanders' concerns. Their island is strategically located in the sub-Arctic, has no military and depends on NATO and a 1951 bilateral agreement with the United States for its defence.
"The geopolitical upheaval that we have seen recently is not the root cause of this referendum. But obviously, those concerns are impacting the debate," Bifrost University professor Eirikur Bergmann told AFP.
"Mainly the aggression towards Greenland has caused great concern in Iceland and caused many people here to pause and reassess where Iceland belongs."
Opinion polls suggest Icelanders are deeply divided on the EU question.
Office worker Vilborg Inga Magnusdottir said she saw no reason to change the status quo.
"Why would we want to enter the European Union? What would we benefit from it when things are already good?" the 33-year-old told AFP.
Unlike her, Hrafnkell Gudnason plans to vote "Yes".
"It's getting more dangerous for a small country to stand outside the EU," the 59-year-old consultant and horse-breeder said.
"I think it's safer to be a part of a bigger family."
Compromise on fishing?
In a country where seafood products account for around 40 percent of exports of goods, fishing – an integral part of Iceland's national identity – would inevitably be the key issue in EU negotiations.
Half a century after the last "Cod Wars" with Britain, many Icelanders are reluctant to yield even the tiniest bit of control of their hard-won national waters to Brussels.
Even Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir, a staunch europhile, has made it clear that in any future negotiations Reykjavik would insist on retaining "sovereign control over all fisheries".
That would be difficult to reconcile with the EU's current Common Fisheries Policy.
Brussels has stayed out of the fray ahead of the referendum, but has sent positive signals, even on the sensitive fisheries issue.
For the EU, the prospect of welcoming a wealthy, stable country already largely integrated in the single market through its membership in the European Economic Area would provide a strong showcase for its enlargement policy and strengthen its presence in a coveted region.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Partial lunar eclipse on Friday: Where to see it in Spain, Italy, France, Portugal and Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:14:07 UTC
14:14:07 KST

At maximum eclipse on 27–28 August, Earth’s dark umbral shadow will cover 96% of the Moon’s face - an almost total eclipse.
Europeans will be treated to a “very deep” partial lunar eclipse in the early hours of Friday (28 August) morning, just before dawn.
A partial eclipse always happens about two weeks before or after a solar eclipse, so this one follows the total solar eclipse that captivated Europeans earlier this month.
During a partial eclipse, an imperfect alignment of the Sun, Earth and Moon means a Full Moon passes through only part of Earth’s shadow in space. The shadow grows and then recedes without ever entirely covering the Moon, creating a rare celestial phenomenon.
Friday’s is a Full Sturgeon Moon, named after North America’s largest fish. The moon could turn a rusty red as it gets 96.2 per cent covered by Earth’s dark inner shadow. The change of colour is caused by Earth: “the edge of Earth’s shadow in space has a reddish glow that comes from sunlight streaming through the atmosphere that surrounds our planet”, according to timeanddate.
You won’t need the special glasses that were necessary to safely view the total solar eclipse earlier this month. Looking directly at the moon during a partial eclipse is totally safe.
If you happen to have binoculars or a telescope, they will make the shadow clearer to see.
Location and weather will determine where in Europe that will get the best view of the eclipse. The places facing west with the least cloud cover will get the most spectacular experience.
If you won’t be able to see the eclipse in person, it will be streamed during a live show by timeanddate on YouTube.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Spain
Just like with the solar eclipse, Spain will get the best views. The lunar eclipse will be visible from anywhere in the Iberian Peninsula, the Balearic Islands, the Canary Islands, Ceuta and Melilla, provided the skies remain clear with no clouds.
There will be a difference in viewing time, however. In central and eastern Spain, the Balearic Islands, as well as Melilla, the moon will set before the partial eclipse has finished, whereas in the rest of the country, including the Canaries and Ceuta, you will be able to see the whole process of the eclipse.
The moon will rise in Spain at 9.01pm on 27 August and set at 7.47am on 28 August. The partial phase of the eclipse will begin at 4.34am and end at 7.52am – one hour earlier in the Canary Islands.
The peak of the eclipse, which is when Earth’s shadow covers the largest percentage of the moon, will occur at approximately 6.12am, just before sunrise. At that moment, Earth’s shadow will be projected onto 93 percent of the lunar disk.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Italy
Based on current weather forecasts, some of Italy’s biggest cities are set to have the best views: Naples, Rome and Venice are forecast to have the least cloud cover, meaning they should see a 93 per cent eclipse. Bologna is one of the next best, followed by Turin. Genoa and Milan will also have 93 per cent coverage but they are forecast to be very cloudy.
The partial eclipse will start at 03.23am in Italy, it will be at best coverage at 06.12am and it will end at 09.01am.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in France
Current weather forecasts are predicting a lot of cloud and some rain for Friday morning in France so it may not be the best place for a viewing.
The moon will not begin crossing into Earth’s shadow until around 03.20am, with the colouration effects seen around 04.34am. The peak of the event – when the majority of the moon is in the Earth’s shadow and the red colour its deepest – will take place at around 06.13am. At this point however, the moon will be only around 8° above the horizon, and early morning sunshine may interfere.
Marseille and Strasbourg currently have the best chance at a viewing as they’ll have low cloud cover, though there may be heavy rain or lightning.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Portugal
Anyone in Portugal wanting to catch the partial lunar eclipse from the start will be in for an early start - it begins at 02.23am local time and ends at 08.01am.
Lisbon and Amadora currently have the clearest skies forecast, with Braga and Coimbra also in with a good chance.
Partial lunar eclipse: Where to see it in Germany
As with the rest of the Central European Summer Time time zone, the eclipse will be at its best at 06.13am in Germany. This is after the Moon has set and the Sun has risen in eastern Germany. It begins at 04.33am.
In the far west of the country, however, the rise and set times for the Sun and Moon are delayed by a little more than half an hour, so that more of the eclipse will be visible. The Moon’s exit from the umbra at 7:53am will, in any case, occur long after sunrise and moonset as seen from Germany, according to the Haus der Astronomie.

Nicotine e-cigarettes are more effective than other alternatives for quitting smoking, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:12:10 UTC
14:12:10 KST

A major analysis found that vaping outperforms patches, gum and other conventional aids in helping people give up cigarettes.
Nicotine electronic cigarettes can help people stop smoking, working better than other replacement therapies such as patches or gum, a new review has found.
The Cochrane review analysed 80 studies, involving a total of 29,861 adults who smoked, comparing nicotine vapes with other options offered to help people quit.
“There is clear evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase smoking cessation rates at six months or longer compared to nicotine replacement therapy,” Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, senior author of the review at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, told reporters during a press briefing presenting the report, adding that nicotine vapes increase cessation rates by about 60%.
“Our certainty in that evidence is high, which means we do not think future studies are likely to meaningfully change these conclusions,” she added.
The review found that more people were able to quit smoking and remain smoke-free for at least six months with e-cigarettes than with nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), such as patches, gum and sprays.
“In our study population, we might expect six people per 100 to quit with nicotine replacement therapy. If they were given nicotine e-cigarettes, we might expect that number to increase to around 10 per 100,” Hartmann-Boyce said.
NRTs help smokers stop by supplying nicotine as a substitute, easing withdrawal symptoms, though even with this support, long-term quit rates remain low.
Meanwhile, people may also be more likely to stop smoking with nicotine vapes than with non-nicotine alternatives or behavioural support only, the study found.
Not all vapes are the same
Despite the evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes can be a useful alternative for smokers wanting to quit, the researchers warn that not all products are alike.
“The harms that we often hear about are overwhelmingly from unregulated vaping devices that contain ingredients that are known to be harmful for human health. They may contain psychoactive substances other than nicotine — for example, THC (the main chemical compound in cannabis,” Hartmann-Boyce noted.
She added that the products included in the review are part of controlled trials and regulated for sale on the market, which can differ from other products people encounter in everyday use.
The researchers also warned that more evidence is needed on the effects of newer types of vaping devices.
Towards quitting smoking
Tobacco dependence is caused not only by the effects of nicotine but also through broader social and behavioural aspects, the researchers noted.
Quitting tobacco is associated with substantial health benefits. However, despite most people who smoke wanting to quit, many find it difficult to succeed in the long term, the researchers added.
Almost half of the smokers who try to stop without support do not manage to stop for even a week, and fewer than 5% remain smoke-free a year after quitting.
In light of this, the researchers noted that there is a need for more research into alternatives.
“There is interest in developing smoking cessation products that not only help relieve the unpleasant effects of nicotine withdrawal, but that also act as effective substitutes for smoking behaviour and the rituals and sensations that accompany smoking, without the health risks associated with the inhalation of tobacco smoke,” they wrote.

Armenia plans EU bid, rules out renewed role in Russia-led bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:11:23 UTC
14:11:23 KST

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said his government plans to begin work on a formal application for European Union membership and will not resume active participation in the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) over the next five years.
Addressing parliament on Aug. 24 during debate on his government’s 2026-2031 program, Pashinyan said the CSTO had not addressed the security concerns raised by Yerevan.
“It is clearly stated in our program that we have no plans to return to the CSTO over the next five years. I can say with certainty that we will not step up our activities in the CSTO,” he said.
Pashinyan said discussions were underway within the alliance about potentially expelling Armenia and that he would welcome such an outcome.
“I would be very happy if the organization decided to expel Armenia from the CSTO. It would free us from the dilemma of whether or not to withdraw,” he said.
Armenia froze its participation in the six-member security alliance in early 2024 but remains a formal member.
Turning to the country’s European ambitions, Pashinyan said Yerevan must first submit an official application before determining whether EU membership is achievable.
“Armenia must first submit an official application for EU membership,” he said, adding that preparations would probably begin “in the near future.”
Pashinyan said Yerevan would assess Brussels’ response and prepare an accession road map before putting the issue to a referendum. Armenia’s parliament adopted legislation in 2025 launching the EU accession process, but the country has yet to file a formal application.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Armenia was free to leave the CSTO if it no longer considered membership necessary.
On the proposed EU application, Peskov pointed to Türkiye and other countries whose accession processes have continued for decades.
He also said aligning Armenian legislation with EU trade, customs and food safety rules would create conflicts with the standards of the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union, of which Armenia remains a member.
Pashinyan’s Civil Contract party won 49.7 percent of the vote in Armenia’s June 7 parliamentary election and retained its majority, allowing it to form a government alone.
Russia imposed restrictions on a range of Armenian agricultural products and beverages before the vote, citing sanitary and phytosanitary violations.
The European Union described the measures as “economic coercion,” while Moscow denied that they were politically motivated.
Separately, former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan and his eldest son, Sedrak, were detained on Aug. 25 as part of a corruption investigation, the Prosecutor General’s Office said.
Four other people were also detained.
Prosecutors opened proceedings against Kocharyan on suspicion of abuse of authority, bribery and large-scale money laundering. Investigators are examining allegations that state-owned buildings and land were sold below market value to private companies during his presidency from 1998 to 2008.
Kocharyan, who leads the opposition Armenia Alliance, has denied wrongdoing. His allies described the investigation as politically motivated.

Scientists turn plastic bottles into protein-rich cookies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:03:30 UTC
14:03:30 KST

Scientists turn plastic bottles into protein-rich cookies
Scientists at Southern Illinois University Carbondale (SIU) have developed a way to make 3D-printed cookies using genetically engineered yeast to produce protein and nutrients from plastic and agricultural waste.
The project aims to tackle two of the planet’s crises: plastic waste accumulation and food insecurity.
The team first set out to develop ways to make use of waste plastics, Lahiru Jayakody, an associate professor of microbiology at Southern Illinois University said in an interview with the American Chemical Society (ACS) published on Monday.
“We thought, why not focus on making food? Because plastic is carbon and food is carbon,” he said.
The process starts by breaking down plastic and plant waste with water and oxygen under high temperature and pressure. Genetically engineered yeasts then consume the resulting compounds and produce proteins, fats, and acids. With the addition of fiber, starch, and sweetener, the resulting mix is fed into a 3D printer which molds the paste into any desired shape.
With this technology, the scientists created small protein-rich cookies they dubbed “µBites” or “microbites.” They are waiting for the safety go-ahead from their university to actually taste-test them, however.
The novel technology could be useful in hostile environments, according to Jayakody.
“If you want to produce food in a very extreme environment using the resource you have, carbon resource waste like Arctic, or the desert, and potentially one day in the Mars or the lunar surface, microbeids can do that job,” he told Reuters.
SIU researchers have been developing the technology since 2021, when their µBites concept was selected for NASA’s Deep Space Food Challenge.
The news comes as scientists are paying closer attention to how plastic already unintentionally enters the human food chain.
Researchers have reported microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics in human tissues. A 2025 study published in Nature Medicine detected them in the liver, kidneys, and brain, while a 2026 review published last month said particles had also been found in blood, placenta, and heart tissue.
The particles could pose health risks, with studies linking exposure to inflammation, oxidative stress, cell death, and disruptions to metabolism and immune function. However, researchers say more evidence is needed to determine the effects of long-term exposure in humans.
