====================================================================================================

"The response seems very timid": where does ecology fit in the presidential race?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

After a summer of extreme weather, can France's political parties rise up to the challenge of climate change?
Massive wildfires in Gironde, the Landes and the Var. Back to back heatwaves across the country. Severe drought seriously affecting agriculture. This summer, the impacts of human-caused climate change have well and truly come to France.
With only a few months to go before the presidential election, environmental issues are expected to take an unprecedented place in the political debate. Historically championed by the left, the topic has become inescapable, forcing the right and the far right to take it up.
Because today, "given the delays and the seriousness of the situation, France no longer has a choice: it must adapt, and fast", warns the Climate Action Network (Réseau Action Climat), which challenges recent governments, saying they "have not taken the necessary measures to adapt the country to the effects of climate change".
Yet the warnings have been sounding for several years. As early as 2013, the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) stated that "warming of the climate system is unequivocal and, since the 1950s, many of the observed changes are unprecedented over decades to millennia".
"The years 1983 to 2012 are probably the warmest 30-year period the Northern Hemisphere has experienced in at least 1,400 years", the report also noted.
Are French politicians out of touch?
In a survey published on 24 August, Ipsos revealed that 64 per cent of French people felt "anxiety or fear" for the health of their loved ones and 48 per cent for their own health during the summer of 2026.
The polling institute also reports that French people "expect above all solutions from the public authorities": 79 per cent of respondents want government measures to help the population cope with heatwaves.
A study by the French Environment and Energy Management Agency (Ademe) published last year reported that 6.3 million French people were moderately eco-anxious. "2.1 million are thought to be highly eco-anxious, with intense, chronic symptoms" and "420,000 of them have mental health that is genuinely at risk", the study noted.
The problem is that they are not necessarily being heard by political leaders. "Most parties and presidential candidates seem out of touch with the realities of everyday life for French people who have been badly affected" by these events, says Anne Bringault, programme director at the Climate Action Network, speaking to Euronews.
"Faced with an unprecedented challenge for humanity and biodiversity, with the many deaths caused by heatwaves, the economic losses, particularly for farmers, homes destroyed by wildfires and nature dried out, the political response seems very timid and not at all commensurate with what French people expect or with their perception of the concrete impacts of climate change", she says.
Appearing on France Inter this Tuesday, Jean-Marc Jancovici, founder and president of the climate-transition think tank The Shift Project, was even more scathing, claiming that the political class is "in a form of denial" about climate change.
Politicians do not grasp the root causes of climate-driven disasters
A view shared by Eva Morel, secretary-general of the association QuotaClimat. "We have the feeling that elections are moments when ecology really struggles to find a way through", she laments to Euronews, before trying to explain the reason for this lack of interest. "In fact, they themselves are not encouraged to understand the issue and make ambitious proposals on it, because the media reception of their statements on the subject is generally quite favourable."
She goes even further. "Above all, we cannot hope for a constructive debate on the subject if, when climate disasters occur, we talk only about what is happening and do not try to understand the underlying factors – both the causes and the structural solutions that would allow us to address them", stresses Eva Morel.
She cites the events of the summer of 2026, which sparked discussions focused "mainly on observations and not necessarily on explanations". "So, for example, we talked more about climate, which was almost unavoidable. But we talked less about fossil energy", she regrets. "From there, we cannot really expect the proposals of the various candidates to be convincing when it comes to addressing the root of the problem", the expert continues.
What are French political parties saying on ecology?
"Which of the candidates puts at the centre of their programme the fact that the world is going to change? None of them", snaps Jean-Marc Jancovici. In his view, the programmes of potential or declared candidates for the next presidential election are stripped of coherent environmental measures. "You find inconsistencies everywhere", says The Shift Project's president.
For Eva Morel, this situation is explained in particular by how hard it is, in "a political system that rewards demagoguery, to ask candidates to confront a crisis that profoundly destabilises citizens' ways of life and still come up with a desirable project".
On the right, climate issues struggle to break through against traditionally popular themes like immigration or the law. "Right-wing and centrist parties stay in their lane, like Édouard Philippe who chose to highlight immigration issues during his trip to Mayotte", says Anne Bringault. Eva Morel agrees: "Even just on adaptation, the right as a political family still considers that it is not a political question."
In his manifesto, the former prime minister uses the word "ecology" only once. "We believe that this ambition requires the introduction of an effective policy to decarbonise our economy, preserve biodiversity and increase investment in the excellence of French energy and agricultural sectors", he writes, without providing further detail.
For his rival in the centrist bloc, Gabriel Attal, ecology for now seems framed more in terms of competitiveness and innovation than constraint. The Renaissance candidate advocates an energy mix combining nuclear and renewables and wants to turn climate transition into a driver of investment and growth. In early August, Attal also said he refused to leave the water crisis "to the left and the far left around Jean-Luc Mélenchon", promising to create a "ministry for water" if elected.
As for the left, "electoral opportunism, in a context of competition to harvest the green vote, seems to play a significant role", Anne Bringault continues. This competition is all the stronger as ecologists are struggling to appear united and to impose their line in the run-up to 2027, while the La France insoumise candidate seeks to occupy this space by putting forward proposals such as "eco-regions" or enshrining in the Constitution the principle of the "green rule", under which we do not take more from nature than it is able to regenerate.
"What we see is that, today, the environmental programmes of parties on the left are still more substantiated than those on the right, and that has been the case for several years", continues Eva Morel. "What we find interesting is the extent to which political discourse mirrors scientific discourse. And today, that seems to be happening more on the left than elsewhere."
National Rally are 'purely opportunistic'
On the other side of the political spectrum, the National Rally strongly rejects so-called "punitive" environmental policies and opposes wind power, instead making nuclear energy a pillar of decarbonisation.
The far-right party "is trying in haste to dress itself up in green by advocating simplistic solutions that are barely realistic financially or technically, such as widespread air conditioning", claims Anne Bringault.
"In fact, they focus on hot-button issues. And since climate is now one of those hot topics, they focus on it. It is purely opportunistic", adds Eva Morel, who acknowledges that the National Rally has rowed back on its statements questioning the IPCC's credibility or the reality of global warming, even if that "is not enough". "The problem is that their political software has not integrated the environmental question at all. They have no proposals that genuinely protect us from the consequences, let alone address the causes."
She also accuses the party led by Jordan Bardella of circulating, in her view, misleading information. "These are narratives that are deliberately orchestrated because they work with public opinion, instrumentalising moments that attract a great deal of attention. [...] It has been shown that this is an obstruction strategy that works. It blocks the implementation of public policies that are supposed to be effective", the expert explains, citing the example of low-emission zones.
"And what we fear is that, alongside this obstruction, there is an effort to disqualify political opponents and environmental defenders by demonising them. And by doing that, they push solutions away from the problem, even though the problem is highly visible", concludes Eva Morel.

Asia-Pacific Community: Chinese-built wastewater plant revives Mongolian capital's green lifeline
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
12:40:52 CST
13:40:52 KST

Staff members monitor the operating status of wastewater treatment equipment at the Ulan Bator central sewage treatment plant in Ulan Bator, Mongolia, July 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Yao Qilin)
ULAN BATOR, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Ulan Bator's Tuul River, long choked by untreated sewage and plagued by acrid odors, has seen a remarkable environmental turnaround thanks to a landmark Chinese-Mongolian wastewater treatment facility, with local staff like Urnaa devoting years to preparing for its full handover to local operators.
Urnaa works as the chief translator at the Ulan Bator central sewage treatment plant, the nation's largest and most advanced sewage plant that began construction in early 2019 and was inaugurated on June 15 this year.
Every working day, she shuttles across the sprawling facility's workshops, providing real-time interpretation for Mongolian technical teams and compiling operation and maintenance manuals to smooth the handover process to the local team. Over the past year, she has watched how the plant, built entirely to Chinese standards and using Chinese technology by China Railway No. 4 Engineering Group Co., Ltd., has evolved from early construction to full operation.
Standing on the rooftop on the fourth floor of the plant's comprehensive service building, eight massive secondary sedimentation tanks stretch outward like polished mirrors, their clear treated water reflecting Mongolia's boundless blue skies and white clouds.
Covering a total area of 178,000 square meters with 55 standalone buildings, the plant boasts a daily treatment capacity of 250,000 cubic meters. It can process nearly all residential and industrial wastewater produced in Ulan Bator, serving roughly half of Mongolia's entire population.
Two side-by-side display boards in the facility's lobby lay bare the capital's decades-long sewage crisis, drawing a stark contrast between this modern, recycling-focused new plant and its outdated predecessor.
Constructed back in the 1960s and expanded three times over the years, the aging plant only handled 160,000 to 170,000 cubic meters of wastewater each day. As the capital's population exploded, sewage output surged, triggering equipment malfunctions.
For years, vast volumes of inadequately treated wastewater were discharged directly into the Tuul, Ulan Bator's mother river -- a foul reality Urnaa remembers all too clearly from her early career. Ten years ago, while working on a Mongolian disabled children's rehabilitation project run by the same Chinese contractor, the stench from the polluted river lingered constantly around the work compound. Today, stable operation of the new treatment plant has delivered visible improvements to surrounding air quality and the river's water clarity.
Lyu Haiyun, project manager from China Railway No. 4 Engineering Group Co., Ltd, noted that the plant's value stretches far beyond simply producing clean discharged water, as it delivers a complete low-carbon circular development concept tailored for Mongolia. Its integrated design unifies wastewater treatment, clean energy production and resource recycling.
Design teams took full account of Mongolia's sludge, which contains high organic matter, installing four large medium-temperature anaerobic reactors on-site to ferment sludge into biogas for power and heating. Once fully operational, the biogas system will meet 25 to 30 percent of the plant's electricity and heating demands, slashing long-term operating expenses.
Beyond filling Mongolia's critical domestic sewage treatment technology gap, the project prioritizes cultivating independent local operational capacity through systematic training. Starting in 2023, around 70 Mongolian operation and maintenance technicians have traveled to China for specialized training courses. In July, Urnaa accompanied local regulatory officials to Beijing to attend training sessions on biogas power generation.
"Many Mongolian engineers have learned so much through this project," Urnaa said. "For me personally, all the training and on-site practice have given me full confidence to work for similar infrastructure projects in the future." ■

UK concerned about possible changes to backpacker visa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:39:32 UTC
13:39:32 KST

PM rules out British backpackers being forced to work in regions
In short:
The government was considering imposing regional work requirements on British backpackers to make the scheme less attractive in a bid to bring down migration numbers.
The prime minister has publicly poured cold water on that idea, heading off a diplomatic stoush.
What's next?
No date has been set for the government to unveil its changes in migration policy after Tony Burke postponed a National Press Club address earlier this month.
The prime minister has vowed not to make British backpackers work in regional areas as part of a looming migration overhaul, defusing a potential diplomatic stoush with the United Kingdom.
British citizens on Working Holiday Maker, or backpacker, visas are allowed to live in Australia for up to three years without any specific work requirements under a free trade deal which came into force in 2023.
Working holiday makers from all other countries must work in regional or remote areas to have their visas extended beyond a year.
The favourable treatment has led to a steep increase in the number of UK backpackers coming to Australia, up from 47,238 in 2023/24 to 79,412 in 2024/25 according to Home Affairs data.
Under pressure to clamp down on temporary visas and reduce overseas arrivals, the government was considering a plan to impose regional work requirements on British backpackers to make the scheme less attractive.
But some in the government were concerned that would clearly breach the free trade agreement between Australia and the United Kingdom at a time when the government had positioned itself as an international champion for trade rules.
Anthony Albanese quashed the proposal on Wednesday afternoon, ruling out any changes to the deal.
"The UK situation is a separate agreement as a result of the UK free trade agreement which we are certainly honouring," Mr Albanese said.
He intervened not long after UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke on the sidelines of a Five Eyes meeting in Sydney.
After that meeting, Mr Burke did not deny the issue had been canvassed.
"We talk regularly about all migration issues, about the issues we are managing in each of our countries," Mr Burke told reporters in Sydney.
"In terms of anything coming forward, as to any changes we'd made to the migration program, those are decisions that would be made by the Australian cabinet."
The possible change to UK arrangements was one of several under consideration as part of a wider crackdown on immigration which Mr Burke was due to announce three weeks ago before being forced to postpone.
No new date has been set for the policy announcement, which is designed to ensure Labor meets its own target of cutting net overseas migration (NOM) from the current 300,000 to 225,000 by 2028.
Backpackers are a significant contributor to the NOM with a record 321,116 visas being issued last year, up from 234,556 the year before.
Mr Burke last month paused the processing of applications from 24 countries including Argentina, Chile, Spain, Poland, Thailand and Malaysia, and pushed workers applying for overseas skilled visas to the back of the queue.
"The processing of backpacker visas across the entire program is happening more slowly than it was," Mr Burke said.
"And similarly there are changes we've made to the permanent program in preferencing, at the moment, onshore positions rather than offshore."
The far-reaching directive is designed to stop, or dramatically slow, the number of overseas arrivals but has created an enormous amount of confusion and concern within the business, hospitality and tourism sectors which rely on migrant workers.
As one business figure told the ABC, "everything has ground to a halt".
One Nation and the Coalition are promising dramatic cuts to migration, but both have ruled out any cuts to backpacker visas given their popularity in regional areas.

Ming dynasty work shows how Chinese understood the world in the 1600s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:00:05 UTC
13:00:05 KST

Ming dynasty work shows how Chinese understood the world in the 1600s
Scholar Zhang Huang set out to document heaven, Earth and humanity in vast compendium described as a ‘visual summary of Chinese culture’
The result was an encyclopaedia spanning 127 volumes known as the Tushu Bian, or Compendium of Illustrations and Texts.
The work – published in 1613 – was compiled by Neo-Confucian scholar Zhang Huang and drew on more than 200 printed sources across several decades to document the concepts of heaven, Earth and humanity.
“His goal was to gather all the illustrations and texts an educated person needed to understand the world,” information designer Paul Kahn, who analysed the encyclopaedia, wrote in his book Mapping Knowledge Across Time: Seven Books That Visualised the World.
“The result was too costly to print during his lifetime. It was eventually carved on woodblocks and printed after his death,” Kahn wrote.
Kahn compared the Tushu Bian with six other books that described the world from the perspective of Euro-Mediterranean culture.

An Architecture of Attention: Inside Syn Architects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

As Saudi Arabia's cities expand through increasingly ambitious cultural projects, Syn Architects has spent much of its practice looking at what predates that transformation. The practice's participation in the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale grew out of years spent documenting Najdi architecture, disappearing urban fabric, local materials and inherited forms of knowledge. For Syn, heritage becomes useful when it can be documented, tested and brought back into use.
This approach can be traced back to Shamalat Cultural Center, a 615-square-metre intervention on the outskirts of Diriyah. Originally an old mud house acquired and converted into a cultural hub by Saudi artist Maha Malluh, the project was developed through two distinct phases: restoration and addition. Parts of the earthen structure were retained, while a new volume was inserted within the footprint of the former yard and organised around remnants of the original adobe fence. Riyadh stone forms a deliberately contemporary backdrop to the textured mud walls. What matters at Shamalat is what the two phases allow the building to accommodate. The restored structure and new addition accommodate galleries, an artist residency, a darkroom and workshops, allowing the building to remain useful rather than becoming a static historical object.

It maintained an upward trend for 24 straight months since July 2024.
For the first six months of 2026, a total of 145,804 babies were born, up 15.4 percent compared to the same period of 2025.
The total fertility rate, or the average number of children a woman is expected to bear during life, gained 0.11 over the year to 0.88 in June, but it stayed far below the replacement rate of 2.1 births per woman to maintain a stable population.
The number of marriages jumped 14.0 percent to 21,075 in the cited month, and the number of divorces advanced 13.5 percent to 7,688.
The number of deaths rose 2.0 percent to 27,794 in June compared to the same month of last year.
Affected by still-low births and high deaths, the natural population decline stood at 4,683 in the month. ■

2026-08-26
11:53:26 CST
12:53:26 KST

SEOUL, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- South Korean banks' lending rate turned downward last month due to lower corporate borrowing costs that offset a gain for household loans, central bank data showed Wednesday.
The weighted average rate for new bank loans dipped 0.04 percentage points from a month earlier to an annualized rate of 4.27 percent in July, shifting downward from an increase of 0.12 percentage points in the previous month, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The rate for banks' new corporate loans declined 0.07 percentage points to 4.20 percent in July on a monthly basis.
The lending rate for large companies ticked up 0.01 percentage point to 4.18 percent, driven by a growth in short-term market interest rates, while the rate for small and medium enterprises tumbled 0.16 percentage points to 4.22 percent.
Amid rising inflationary pressure, the BOK raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent in July, turning toward monetary tightening in about three and a half years since January 2023.
The rate for fresh bank loans to households surged 0.14 percentage points over the month to 4.64 percent in July.
Mortgage loan rate for households swelled 0.12 percentage points to 4.48 percent, and credit loan rate soared 0.25 percentage points to 5.97 percent.
The weighted average rate for new bank deposits was up 0.13 percentage points over the month to an annualized 3.21 percent in July. ■

12:25:22 KST

Iran and Oman held talks in Tehran to discuss the management of traffic passing through the Strait of Hormuz, as well as a joint mine-clearing project. Further negotiations are expected to discuss a permanent solution.
Iran and Oman's foreign ministers met in Tehran on Tuesday to discuss a phased approach to managing ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a criticial waterway that remains effectively closed since the war in Iran started in February.
Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi and his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi "discussed a phased framework that could provide a practical and implementable basis for moving forward," a joint statement said.
The proposed framework includes a "joint temporary navigational corridor" through the strait and a mine-clearing project in the waterway.
Further negotiations will establish a "permanent navigational corridor and future administration of the Strait, as well as a mechanism for information-sharing, traffic management, and the provision of relevant navigational and security services", the statement added.
"I am hopeful we will soon announce a temporary corridor for the Strait of Hormuz," Albusaidi wrote on X, adding that the countries will work towards a permanent solution, as well as an agreement on who will administer the strait.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told state television that the temporary route for marine traffic enterting the Persian Gulf from the Gulf of Oman would pass entirely through Iranian waters, while the outbound route would pass through both Iranian waters and Omani waters.
Iran and Oman will hold further talks over 30 to 60 days, Gharibabadi added.
The talks come a week after US President Donald Trump threatened to launch strikes against Oman if it "gets in the way" of talks between Washington and Tehran over the Strait of Hormuz.
"If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the s--- out of them, Trump said in an interview with Fox News on Monday, as June's US-Iran memorandum of understanding expired.

Unknown

Iran has agreed with Oman to establish a temporary seven-mile-wide transit route through the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Tuesday, while stressing that the arrangement does not amount to reopening the strategic waterway.
Speaking in an interview with Iranian television, Gharibabadi said the agreed route would run through Iranian territorial waters on entry, with part of the exit route also passing through Iranian waters.
“The agreed-upon width of the transit route with Oman in the Strait of Hormuz is seven miles,” Gharibabadi said, describing the route as a temporary arrangement.
He said Iran and Oman would hold further negotiations, which are expected to last between 30 and 60 days, to determine a permanent route and future arrangements for managing passage through the strait.
Gharibabadi emphasized that the agreement with Oman should not be interpreted as the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and we have complete control over it,” he said, dismissing claims that ships were already passing through the waterway.
According to Gharibabadi, activating the joint route agreed with Oman would also mean closing the southern passage. He said the two countries had agreed to begin technical negotiations on an alternative to the historical route.
Gharibabadi said Iran considered the strait a matter of national security and had the right to take measures it deemed necessary to protect its interests.
The official also said Iran did not trust Washington and that any return to diplomacy would require the United States to first fulfill its commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.
"Before any action to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the US must fully implement all of its violated commitments," he said.
"The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz will only take place in exchange for an end to the war on all fronts, the lifting of the blockade, and a resolution of Yemen's status."
Gharibabadi said Pakistani Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir had conveyed the same message during his recent visit to Tehran, telling Iranian officials that reopening the strait depended on Washington fulfilling its commitments.
'No one except Iran knows the location of these mines'
Gharibabadi also rejected reports that US forces had cleared mines in the waterway or were preparing to send mine-sweeping vessels into the area.
“If the United States claims that the mines have been completely cleared, why doesn't a US ship pass through?” he said. “If they have cleared them, why don't they pass? No one except Iran knows the location of these mines.”
He warned that US mine-sweeping vessels entering the area would be considered targets.
“If US mine-sweepers enter the region, they will become targets for us,” Gharibabadi said, adding that US President Donald Trump’s comments about mine clearance were intended only to calm markets.
Earlier, Trump said that all mines have been successfully removed or detonated in the international waters of the Strait of Hormuz.
“Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed,” he wrote on his social media platform Truth Social.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch delivers her speech on the final day of the 2025 Conservative party conference in Manchester, a performance that marked the beginning of her transformation as party leader. | Ian Forsyth/Getty Images
LONDON — Kemi Badenoch’s Conservative Party used to discuss who would replace her. Now they want her secret sauce.
Almost two years after taking the helm of the Tory party in the wake of its 2024 general election battering, Badenoch’s personal ratings are soaring. YouGov polling, conducted last month, found 38 percent of Brits think Badenoch is doing well as Conservative Party leader — up 23 points from last October. Some 43 percent of Brits see her as decisive, with 40 percent regarding her as competent.
But with just one in five Britons believing her Conservative Party is ready to govern again — and the party now facing a more popular adversary in No. 10 Downing Street in Andy Burnham — strategists are eyeing an autumn blitz putting Badenoch to the fore.
Advertisement
“Kemi is popular. We are trying to promote the rest of the shadow Cabinet to make sure that popularity rubs off on the rest of the party,” said one Badenoch staffer, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record.
So far, it hasn’t worked.
“Badenoch’s success has still failed to translate into any meaningful movement in the polls for her party,” said Scarlett Maguire, founder of independent polling firm Merlin Strategy. “The Conservatives’ mediocre polling numbers, still worse than when they lost the 2024 election, shows the extent to which they have lost trust in their brand.”
New look conference
The party’s first big set piece moment this autumn will come when the Conservative Party meets for its annual conference in Birmingham at the beginning of October.
Badenoch’s performance at last year’s gathering marked the beginning of her transformation as party leader, and her team is hoping to repeat the trick by making this year’s conference more Badenoch-focused.
There will be less policy this year, according to one shadow minister familiar with the plans and also granted anonymity to speak freely.
Advertisement
“Last year was a bit scattergun. There was a bit too much policy, trying to prove we had something to say. This will be about putting Kemi forward as an alternative to Andy Burnham,” this person said.
“People see Burnham as someone who blows with the wind a bit, so [we] want to push forward the theme that Kemi is someone who doesn’t change her mind, is guided by a strong set of principles and isn’t going to change just to be popular,” the same shadow minister added.
Viral economics
Hot on the heels of party conference season will be the Burnham administration’s first budget, currently penciled in for Oct. 28.
Strategists hope it will give them a chance to promote the party’s “sound” economic vision.
Badenoch’s response to last year’s budget went “viral” — and is seen as a key moment when the public started to see the Tory leader differently.
It is Badenoch and not Shadow Chancellor Mel Stride who is “calling the shots” on economic strategy, according to another member of the shadow Cabinet.
Advertisement
“The economic direction of the party has to come from her, not from Mel,” they said.
Badenoch discussed how to shape a right-wing economic vision — in particular the challenge of keeping wealthy people from leaving the country — with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Monday, according to the Times.
Though shadow ministers and advisors agree long-serving Conservatives like Stride will help give Badenoch credibility within the business community.
“We need to get to a point where we’ve got a real economic narrative. That’s what Kemi’s team are hoping will be the transformative thing,” said the same shadow Cabinet minister quoted above.
Reform, interrupted
The mood in Tory ranks has also been bolstered by a difficult few months for Reform’s Farage, who has faced questions over whether he properly declared donations.
MPs and strategists were delighted Farage spent his summer tied up in the Clacton by-election triggered by his own resignation in July, leaving Badenoch clear to be the main critic of the newly crowned Burnham.
Advertisement
Tory MPs gleefully claim those who defected from their party to Reform are starting to look differently at the Reform UK leader.
“The change in the Conservatives has been substantial, but there has also been a big change in Reform as well,” the shadow Cabinet member quoted above said, pointing to reported splits in Reform over how to approach Farage and and policy areas such as welfare spending.
Badenoch’s sharp remark that a pact with Reform would be “monstrous” points firmly to the Tory leader wanting to stand her ground against the threat from the right.

Trump sends Saudi civil nuclear agreement to Congress for review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
03:17:31 UTC
12:17:31 KST

Trump sends Saudi civil nuclear agreement to Congress for review
US President Donald Trump has submitted a civilian nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia to Congress for review, an administration official said. The classified pact, sent to Capitol Hill on Monday, is aimed at bolstering Riyadh’s nuclear programme but remains contingent on Saudi Arabia normalising relations with Israel.
President Donald Trump has submitted to Congress for review an agreement with Saudi Arabia aimed at bolstering the kingdom's civilian nuclear program, but continues to insist that it won't move forward if Saudi Arabia doesn't normalise relations with Israel, according to a Trump administration official.
The classified document was submitted to Capitol Hill on Monday as required by the Atomic Energy Act, according to the administration official, a congressional aide, and two others familiar with the matter. All four spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly on the classified matter.
The agreement was signedlast month in Washington by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and his Saudi counterpart. But the next day, Trump announced he was requiring the Saudis to normalise relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords as part of the pact — raising doubts that the agreement would come to fruition.
Neither the administration official nor the others familiar with the matter would comment on whether Trump's call for the Saudis to join the accords is detailed in the classified document submitted for the congressional review.
Read moreSaudi Arabia to invest €6 billion in theme parks near Paris, Macron says
Under law, Congress has 90 days while in session to review the agreement. Unless Congress passes a joint resolution rejecting the agreement during the review period, the agreement can take effect without a vote by either chamber.
It is unusual for the entire contents of such agreements to be classified at such a high level. Previous civil nuclear pacts with other countries — known as 123 agreements — have been made public, although some of them have contained classified annexes that were not released.
The Saudi embassy in Washington did not have any immediate comment on the matter.
But Trump's continued insistence on the Saudis joining the accords could complicate the path to final approval. The accords approved in 2020 expanded the number of Arab and Muslim-majority nations with diplomatic ties with Israel.
Read moreWhy is Saudi Arabia spending billions to become a global Esports power?
The Saudis were taken by surprise by Trump’s announcement that the completion of the civil nuclear deal would hinge on Riyadh’s agreement to join the accords.
Trump faced fierce criticism from some lawmakers, including some who are concerned it could potentially help the Saudis fulfill their long-standing desire to enrich their own uranium and, in the process, spur new rounds of nuclear proliferation and competition.
The Saudis, meanwhile, have made clear that normalising relations with Israel would first require the establishment of a clear path for Palestinian statehood. And Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the idea of Palestinian statehood as being untenable for his country’s security.
The deal, if approved, is expected to last 30 years and is also expected to involve US firms in developing the program following a joint US-Saudi study.
The formal submission of the agreement to Congress for review was reported earlier Tuesday by The Wall Street Journal.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

‘I want to survive’: Malaysian commando adrift in South China Sea for 15 hours
The seaman was the last of six navy special forces personnel to be rescued after they missed their landing site and ended up in the sea
“I want to survive.” That was uppermost in Senior Seaman Michael Coccon Johen’s mind while he was drifting in the South China Sea, hours after a free-fall parachute training exercise went wrong.
It happened during the drill’s second jump at 4.30pm, when a sudden change in weather severely affected visibility.
“We were about 10km (six miles) away from the island when we jumped from the helicopter. From 9,000 to 4,000 feet (2,700 to 1,200 metres), we were still moving towards the island,” Johen told the media at state Deputy Transport Minister Henry Harry Jinep’s service centre in Bau, Sarawak, on Tuesday.
“But from that point on, our parachutes stopped moving forward because the wind changed suddenly. So we landed in the sea at about 5pm.”
Thanks to his training, he did not panic but waited for help from the navy’s safety vessels. However, the vessels could not reach them because the waves were too high.

Meta, US states have discussed settling teen social media case

Meta, US states have discussed settling teen social media case
- Meta and 29 US states are discussing a possible mid-trial settlement over claims that Facebook and Instagram addict teens and violate privacy laws.
- The case alleges Meta designed features to encourage prolonged teen use and misled users about safety, risking penalties up to US$1.4 trillion.
- This lawsuit is part of a broader backlash against social media firms for harming young users, with courts becoming key to regulatory efforts in the US.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Meta Platforms and state attorneys-general have discussed a possible mid-trial settlement of a blockbuster case accusing the company of deliberately designing Facebook and Instagram to addict teens, people familiar with the matter said.
The trial, now in its second week in federal court in Oakland, California, poses an enormous risk for Meta as the top legal officers of 29 states are seeking both massive financial penalties on behalf of the public and mandatory changes to how the platforms operate.
The people familiar with settlement talks asked not to be identified due to their sensitivity.
A spokesperson for Meta had no immediate comment.
A representative of the attorney-general’s office in California declined to comment.
Representatives of the other three states leading the case, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The states have alleged violations of state consumer protection and federal privacy laws, which carry fines that add up quickly when multiplied by millions of young Instagram and Facebook users.
Meta has denied the states’ allegations and accused the attorneys-general of seeking unreasonable design changes and an “outlandish payout”.
By Meta’s own calculations, a loss at trial could saddle it with penalties of as much as US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion), an amount close to its market capitalisation and unheard of in the annals of legal history.
A settlement would likely amount to a far smaller sum.
During the first week of testimony at the trial, jurors heard from Instagram head Adam Mosseri and a collection of current and former Meta employees who helped design its social media platforms and study how teen users interact with tools designed to cut down on problematic use.
Lawyers have said they also expect to call Meta founder and chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg to testify.
The four attorneys-general spearheading the case alleged under their separate state laws that Meta knowingly designed features that encouraged compulsive and prolonged use of its platforms by young people, while simultaneously misleading consumers about safety features.
The broader bipartisan group of 29 states accused the company of collecting data from users under 13 years old in violation of the federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act.
Social media companies are facing a global backlash over concerns that they profit at the expense of young users, for whom a growing body of research shows that excessive screen time is dangerously unhealthy.
While authorities from Australia to Europe have enacted or proposed outright bans for youths in the last year, legislative crackdowns in the US have had limited success, turning the courts into a pivotal battleground.
Meta, Alphabet’s Google, Snap and TikTok all face billions of dollars in potential exposure from more than 3,000 personal injury claims by individuals and families in the US, and about 1,300 more lawsuits by public school districts across the nation. BLOOMBERG

Online demand for services, such as travel, food delivery and e-coupon purchase, surged 17.5 percent, while offline sales of foreign luxury brands soared 28.9 percent.
Online sales of home appliances increased 11.4 percent, propelled by high demand for air conditioners and cooling equipment. ■

Economists from the Commonwealth Bank of Australia had forecast that CPI growth would fall to 3.2 percent in July and the trimmed mean would ease to 3.5 percent.
The ABS said that housing prices were the biggest driver of headline inflation in the 12 months to July, rising by 5.0 percent, followed by a 3.2 percent rise in food and non-alcoholic beverage prices.
Rachael McCririck, head of price statistics at the ABS, said that new dwelling prices rose by 5.7 percent in the year to July as builders passed on higher costs for materials and labor.
She said that automotive fuel prices were 7.5 percent higher in July than in June due to higher global oil prices and the federal government winding down fuel tax relief measures.
The latest forecasts from the RBA projected that annual trimmed mean inflation would drop to 3.3 percent in December before falling within the central bank's 2-3 percent target range in 2027. ■

It should make promoting political solutions to conflicts a priority, actively engage in mediation and good offices, encourage the parties to resolve their differences through dialogue, and work for an early and lasting ceasefire to create the basic conditions for restoring agricultural production," he said.
International humanitarian law is a fundamental baseline that must be respected, Fu said, stressing that hunger must never be used as a weapon of war.
Parties to conflict should always put the protection of life first, protect agricultural infrastructure, avoid disrupting agricultural activities, and ensure the unimpeded delivery of humanitarian assistance, including food aid, he said.
In the context of economic globalization, food production and supply are closely linked to the international situation, particularly the global logistics and transportation system. In the face of intensifying geopolitical rivalry and regional conflicts, the international community should ensure the safe and unobstructed operation of land and sea trade routes and the normal flow of essential goods such as food and fertilizer, Fu said.
China welcomes the UN initiative to establish a time-bound mechanism for the Strait of Hormuz and supports a greater role for the United Nations, he said.
At the same time, all parties should further uphold open and transparent market policies, deepen international cooperation on food supply, and promote the rational allocation of food resources globally, he said.
Food security governance is a global issue that requires coordinated action and a collective response from all countries. It cannot be dictated by a handful of countries or interest groups, Fu said.
All parties should firmly support the United Nations in playing a central role, while the representation and voice of emerging market economies and developing countries in international organizations dealing with food-related issues should be effectively enhanced, he said.
"We should uphold the principles of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, promote a more equitable, reasonable, inclusive and effective global food security governance system, and safeguard the common interests of all countries," Fu said.
As the world's largest grain producer, China feeds more than 1.4 billion people with less than 9 percent of the world's arable land. Through its own efforts, China has achieved basic self-sufficiency in grain supply and absolute security of staple food, Fu said.
"This is not only a great achievement in China's development, but also a major contribution to safeguarding global food security," he said.
China has always been committed to strengthening international cooperation, helping improve global food security and contributing to global poverty reduction, Fu said.
China stands ready to continue upholding the vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity, work with all parties, and make greater contributions to the complete eradication of global hunger and to world peace, security, development and prosperity, he added. ■

Writing the rulebook? China to steer world’s first solid-state battery standards
As next-gen EV tech accelerates, the global standard agency’s nod could allow Beijing to export its domestic testing benchmarks worldwide
A Chinese-proposed international standard for automotive solid-state batteries has been approved as a new work item by the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) – marking the first of its kind for the advanced power systems and the nation’s latest effort to shape rules in emerging industries.
Led by China, with input from technical experts in France, Japan, South Korea and other countries, the proposal outlined application guidelines, items and conditions for testing rechargeable lithium-ion solid-state batteries used in electric vehicles (EVs), according to an official statement by the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR).
The governmental agency said the framework would draw on domestic research and development benchmarks to standardise testing specifications for solid-state batteries, which are widely viewed as the next frontier for EV power systems.
Announced by the SAMR last week, the China-led proposal comes amid intensifying global competition in advanced technologies, as major economies increasingly leverage standard-setting to secure long-term industrial influence.
“When Chinese products go to an overseas market, they will more easily meet the requirements – there will be few major changes in parameters, production processes and so on,” said a veteran Chinese researcher on international standardisation, who spoke on condition of anonymity. This would place China in the position of setting benchmarks that others followed, she noted.

Taiwan wholesale revenue hits record NT$1.76 trillion in July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:21:46 UTC
11:21:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's wholesale revenue reached a record NT$1.7573 trillion (US$55.16 billion) in July, surging 56.4% from a year earlier, according to a Ministry of Economic Affairs press release on Tuesday.
The July total was the highest monthly wholesale revenue on record and marked the 18th consecutive month of year-on-year growth. Demand for AI, high-performance computing, and cloud services drove shipments across related supply chains.
Wholesale revenue for the first seven months rose to NT$10.7905 trillion, up 36.2% from the same period last year and a record for the first seven months. At the current pace, wholesale revenue could surpass the annual record set in 2025 as early as September, according to MOEA Department of Statistics Deputy Director-General Chen Yu-fang (陳玉芳).
Retail revenue also reached a record for July, totaling NT$418.3 billion, up 7.7% year on year. Revenue for the first seven months reached NT$2.881 trillion, up 4.6% from the same period last year and a record for the January-July period.
The automotive and motorized two-wheel vehicle sector grew 12.6% year on year, while department stores rose 9.6% and information and communications technology and home appliance retailers increased 12.5%. Hypermarkets and convenience stores also posted gains of 10.3% and 4.2%, respectively.
Chen said the automotive and motorized two-wheel vehicle market benefited from summer promotional campaigns and the introduction of new models, contributing to growth for a second consecutive month. However, she cautioned that major purchases typically slow during Ghost Month, which falls in August this year.
Food services revenue reached NT$88.7 billion in July, up 2.5% from a year earlier and the highest July figure on record. Revenue for the first seven months totaled NT$642.2 billion, up 3.9% year on year and also a record for the period.
Restaurant revenue increased 0.8%, while beverage shops posted a 9.7% increase as summer vacation boosted dining out and group meals. Catering and group meal contracting services rose 7.7%, supported by continued cross-border travel and increased demand for in-flight catering.
Chen said the number of days affected by typhoons in July was greater than expected, weighing on retail and food-service revenue growth. While supermarkets and hypermarkets benefited from increased demand for supplies ahead of storms, some businesses were hurt by typhoon-related closures and cancellations.
Regarding the impact of the Central Union Oil food-safety incident on July retail and food-service sales, Chen said the availability of substitute products meant the overall impact was not significant. The ministry attributed the weaker-than-expected growth primarily to typhoons.
Looking ahead, the ministry expects retail sales in August to benefit from Father's Day and Chinese Valentine's Day promotions, while food services are expected to receive support from summer travel, dining out, festive gatherings, and demand for cold beverages amid high temperatures.

Productivity Commission slams political attacks on integrity after GST report
In short:
WA Premier Roger Cook called the Productivity Commission "east coast clowns" over its interim findings on GST, with a senior federal minister casting doubt over the report's validity.
The interim report recommended changing the current GST arrangements, saying they were a "costly mistake" and the only state better off was WA.
What's next?
Angela Jackson told the ABC the commission welcomed debate ahead of their final report, which she stressed would not be influenced by politics.
The Productivity Commission says the WA premier "crossed a line" with his criticisms of the body's interim report on GST, adding that political commentary from federal government ministers undermines the commission's integrity.
The report, released earlier this month, was tasked with looking at GST distribution reforms put in place in 2018. It described those arrangements as a "costly mistake" that had forced Australian taxpayers to foot the bill of almost $23 billion, and the only state better off was WA.
WA Premier Roger Cook lashed the report authors as "east coast clowns" and described the commission's proposals for change as "dodgy, deceitful, and quite frankly dumb".
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese labelled the findings as an "economic rationalist" position, while Resources Minister Madeleine King sympathised with the WA premier's comments and cast doubt on the report's methodology.
Within days of the interim report's release, Mr Albanese stood with Mr Cook in Perth, pledging not to unwind any deal for WA while he was prime minister.
Productivity commissioner and economist Angela Jackson, who co-authored the report, said the body welcomed public debate, but the WA premier's remarks went too far.
"Our view is that a line was crossed in terms of the nature of those comments," she told ABC Radio National.
"To undermine and, I guess, attack our integrity, I think, is an additional bridge too far.
"We want to call this out as being unacceptable as a result. But that said, in doing that, we welcome ongoing dialogue with Western Australia."
Mr Albanese this week distanced his party from the commission's report, pointing out the previous Morrison government commissioned it.
"This report was commissioned by the Morrison government, not us," he said.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who wrote the terms of reference for the report, said today the Productivity Commission is "full of really good people ... publicly-spirited people".
"I want them to know just how much I value their work," he said.
"I don't consider what the PM said to be inappropriate, but I think some of the other commentary around it has been unfortunate," Mr Chalmers said.
"I think you can disagree with the conclusions of the Productivity Commission without denigrating them."
Commission says it is 'above politics'
Dr Jackson said the prime minister's comments were "disappointing" but added that most economists would take being described as "economic rationalists" as a "badge of honour".
She said the findings were part of an interim report and were subject to consultation and change.
The productivity commission was independent and would not be swayed by politicians' views, she added.
"We often refine our recommendations. We may well change our recommendations in some instances, depending on the feedback we receive," she said.
"It's important for us to indicate that that process will not be influenced by the prime minister's comments,"
"We are above politics."
Dr Jackson's comments come after her co-author, Alex Robson, told The Australian Financial Review (AFR) he was disappointed by senior Labor member's comments, which he called inappropriate.
"I totally reject those comments and the language used. It doesn't advance the policy debate at all," he told the AFR.
Other government ministers have declined to condemn Mr Cook's remarks.
Industry Minister Tim Ayres today told the ABC his "east coast clowns" comment was "colourful language" but insisted Labor welcomed debate and MPs did not have a "glass jaw".
Ms King, who hails from WA, said Mr Cook's comments were "fair enough", although she would not use that language herself.
"I don't actually quite agree that it [the Productivity Commission] has gone through it as methodically as it might have," she told ABC's Radio National on Tuesday.
"I respect the work of the commissioners. And I also note there are no Western Australians on the Productivity Commission."
The Productivity Commission is the independent research and advisory body for the Australian government, undertaking research in areas like housing supply, childcare subsidies and hospital funding and carrying out ongoing work on Closing the Gap.

The trade war came too soon for Mark Carney’s middle powers alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:16:48 UTC
11:16:48 KST

The trade war came too soon for Mark Carney’s middle powers alliance
The Canadian prime minister called for pro-trade democracies to resist great-power coercion together. Seven months later, he is largely fighting Trump alone.
At the start of the year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called on the world’s middle powers to band together against Donald Trump. But a new trade war with the U.S. came before they were ready.
Seven months after Carney called in a landmark speech in Davos on fellow democracies and supporters of free trade to join together and resist economic coercion, they have largely left him to do battle with Trump alone.
The U.S. president’s 50 percent tariffs imposed on $20 billion in Canadian goods last week should be a wake-up call to Ottawa’s allies, said one Canadian official with knowledge of the trade talks.
Advertisement
Other countries have tried to appease Trump, the official said. But Canada, which has the most to lose since it’s so economically and geographically intertwined with the U.S., has “put out our chest.”
After Carney walked away from a deal that in his view threatened Canada’s sovereignty, he vowed to fight back. Ottawa would match Trump’s new duties “dollar-for-dollar,” he said — only for the U.S. president to menace Canada with more sweeping tariffs of 50 percent on cars, trucks and auto parts from January.
“Frankly, I think other countries are watching Canada’s response and we hope, I hope, will be following along. At some point, the rest of the world will say enough,” said British Columbia Premier David Eby.
On Tuesday, Ottawa announced a suite of retaliatory tariffs and domestic support measures meant to protect Canadian sectors caught in the crosshairs of the trade war. The dollar-for-dollar Canadian counter-tariffs target U.S. steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
The tariffs take effect on Sept. 8. Meanwhile, Canada’s government is rolling out C$7.5 billion in financing, liquidity and income support to sectors hit by tariffs.
Yet so far, Canada’s allies have left it in the lurch.
Advertisement
Gondor calls for aid
For more than a year, the EU, Canada, the United Kingdom and other economies have talked up plans to deepen ties between the EU and an Asia-Pacific trade bloc called the CPTPP — which includes Canada, Australia, Japan and the U.K. — to counter Trump’s trade coercion.
Since Ursula von der Leyen floated the idea at a summit of EU leaders in June 2025, progress on bringing the EU and the 12-nation CPTPP together has been glacial.
“The mechanisms for responding collectively to economic coercion are still at an early stage,” said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft — a new Canadian foreign policy think tank.
Ursula von der Leyen speaks at a press conference in Brussels on March 18, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/Getty Images
“I would describe the progress as meaningful, but incomplete: the political alignment is increasingly there; the institutions and instruments now need to catch up,” Nadjibulla said. “There needs to be much greater coordination among Canada, Europe and democratic partners in Asia on economic security.”
The European Union, the U.K. and allies like Japan are now keeping their heads down as they digest the lessons from Carney’s lonely stand against Trump.
Advertisement
Bernd Lange, the chair of the EU Parliament’s trade committee, was quick to express solidarity with Canada. But the European Commission, EU leaders and the U.K. have avoided taking sides publicly. Behind the scenes, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke with Carney on Monday.
When asked if the EU would stand by Canada’s side following Trump’s tariff threats, deputy chief spokesperson Arianna Podestà said on Tuesday that “the U.S. and Canada are both important trade partners for the European Union, and we of course continue to work closely with both, aiming to maintain stability and predictability in transatlantic as well as in global trade.”
“We are opposed to tariffs as they are taxes which end up being paid by importers and consumers,” she added.
Since Trump’s return to the White House, EU institutions and governments have been determined to keep him onside and avoid escalation. That approach resulted in a trade truce that was seen as one-sided until the European Parliament pushed hard to strengthen its guardrails following Trump’s threats at the start of this year to take over Greenland, a Danish territory.
“The Europeans will push back to defend their own interests when they have to, but they are also trying to accommodate Trump because they still need America,” said Tom Wright, a foreign policy analyst at the Brookings Institution who was a senior director at the National Security Council during the Biden administration. “Europe is politically close to Canada, but coordinating a collective pushback against Washington would feel like a significant escalation.”
The U.K. isn’t likely to join a collective pushback against Trump, either.
Advertisement
Both the U.S. and Canada are “among the very top trade and investment partners for the U.K.,” said William Bain, head of trade policy at the British Chambers of Commerce, noting “there are no winners from the escalation of this trade dispute.”
British firms, Bain said, “value” the Economic Prosperity Deal struck with the Trump administration last year, which halved the White House’s steel tariffs and lowered automotive tariffs. The BCC also wants to see the U.K.-U.S. Technology Prosperity Deal “implemented in full through continuing negotiations between both governments,” Bain added, after parts of the pact were frozen last year.
Trump’s threats to levy further tariffs on the U.K. over its Digital Services Tax have also prompted Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government to say it’s “open to discussing U.S. concerns” about the revenues it collects from U.S. tech firms.
Andy Burnham engages with local community members in Stevenage, England, on Aug. 12, 2026. | Ben Montgomery/Getty Images
The world as it is
The latest clash with Washington has led Carney to step up his outreach toward the EU.
“This fall we will begin intense discussions with the European Union, the world’s second-largest economy, to build a much stronger and deeper economic and security partnership,” Carney said on Monday. “We can build such unparalleled access, because we can be trusted.”
Brussels has a lot riding on Carney’s gambit. Like the EU a year ago, Canada balked at U.S. requests it saw as encroaching on its sovereignty. In Canada’s case, they relate to Canada’s French-language and cultural protections — enshrined in its constitution — and demands that would have compromised Ottawa’s ability to strike trade deals with other partners.
Advertisement
Washington has similarly been pushing Brussels to cut back its green and tech rulebooks, doubling down on those demands over the summer. The EU executive insists its rulebooks aren’t up for negotiation. If Carney prevails, that could help Brussels hold the line.
Canada is also confronting a weaker Trump than Brussels did a year ago. His original tariffs have since been struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court, while the November midterm elections could further weaken his hand.
“There was also a political calculation from Canada that trying to reach a deal now was not a good idea and that it was actually better to stay firm, with the expectation that after the midterms, if anything, the United States administration may be in a weaker position,” said Ignacio García Bercero, the European Commission’s former top official on U.S. trade.
An EU-Canada summit is due to take place at the end of October, when the two sides will look to cement their partnership.
London and Ottawa are also working toward striking a new strategic partnership this year that would deepen trade ties.
“We are continuing to deepen these ties through the CPTPP and the Economic and Trade Working Group,” a U.K. government spokesperson said of Britain’s economic relations with Canada.
Advertisement
But diversifying away from the world’s biggest economy and building a coalition capable of resisting U.S. pressure could still take years, particularly while potential allies remain wary of confronting Trump.
“The middle powers tend to be the ones most committed to the multilateral trading system. But let’s be frank: Without the U.S. and China, it’s gonna have a hollow ring to it. For the moment, we have to be patient,” said Keith Rockwell, a former WTO spokesperson who is now a senior research fellow at the Hinrich Foundation.
Camille Gijs and Kathryn Carlson reported from Brussels, Graham Lanktree reported from London, and Stefanie Bolzen from Washington. Additional reporting by Nick Taylor-Vaisey in Ottawa.

Transgender former CIA officer Curlee opens up, over a year after leaving agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:15:00 UTC
11:15:00 KST

Transgender former CIA officer Curlee opens up, over a year after leaving agency
WASHINGTON – When US President Donald Trump returned to power in 2025, Julia Curlee, a long-time Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) analyst and transgender woman, opted to continue serving as a senior official at the White House despite right-wing attacks on trans issues.
But after a far-right influencer publicised her transgender identity online, the White House immediately dismissed her.
“They needed me. They asked me to stay” when Trump succeeded Joe Biden in the presidency, Curlee told AFP in an interview, over a year after she was fired.
“But the moment (my gender identity) became public and a political problem with their supporters, that’s when they got rid of me.”
Curlee, who has since resigned from the CIA after 20 years of service, recently shared her experience in a first-person essay published by The Atlantic magazine.
In her view, she was the victim of hypocrisy by Trump’s Republican Party.
Trump himself promised to end “transgender madness”, after campaigning on an agenda that included banning trans people from competing in sports, serving in the military and using bathrooms different from their birth sex.
“To live up to the hatred that they say they have, they had to fire me,” Curlee said.
‘It wasn’t ever an issue’
Now in her mid-40s, Curlee in 2013 became the first CIA officer to transition while working at the agency.
In 2017, during Trump’s first term, she successfully made it onto the National Security Council (NSC), the White House’s top advisory body on issues of national security, the military and foreign policy.
For a year, she gave daily intelligence briefings to then vice-president Mike Pence, a staunch conservative with a history of opposing LGBTQ rights.
Despite her close proximity to Pence as a trans woman, Curlee noted that his views did not impact her work.
“He never made it a problem. Everyone in his staff knew that I was transgender, but it wasn’t ever an issue,” she said.
It made her think working under a second Trump administration would be possible, she added. “Obviously, I was wrong.”
‘Humiliating’ return to CIA
Although Curlee decided to continue working for the White House after Trump won re-election in 2024 following an openly anti-trans political campaign, she lived with constant fear of being fired.
Three days after Trump’s return to office, many NSC staff were let go, but she was asked to stay.
“It was just being a handful of people, and it was complete chaos,” Curlee recalled of those initial months.
For about 10 weeks Curlee continued her White House work, despite administration officials’ public attacks against the transgender community.
“Senior staff at the new Trump administration, they all treated me very well,” she told AFP.
But on a Saturday afternoon that March, while eating barbecue with family, she got a call from her new boss. “‘You’ve been fired, but I can’t tell – I don’t know why,’” she remembered him saying.
Earlier that day, prominent far-right influencer Laura Loomer posted on X: “SCOOP: A transgender, Biden holdover who hates President Trump is still working in the NSC intel office.”
In response to an AFP inquiry on Curlee’s dismissal, a White House spokesperson said: “Anyone who writes a 3,000-word op-ed bragging about themselves while attacking the President clearly doesn’t belong in public service,” referring to The Atlantic essay.
Pence spoke warmly of Curlee on Aug 23.
“My wife and I believe in treating others the way that we’d like to be treated, with decency and respect,” Pence, a devout Christian, told CNN. “And I was heartened to hear Julia reflect that that was the experience that took place in our office.”
Curlee returned to the CIA for less than a year, finding going back to her old employer “impossible” for several reasons.
“I would spend my days walking across the CIA compound to the... unisex or family bathroom, which I could use, and it was humiliating having to do that,” she described.
Now a fellow at Lawfare, a nonprofit publication covering national security, Curlee said she hoped her story broke the transgender “caricature” fuelled by the American right to convince voters to back “an extremist agenda based on fear”. AFP

Five ways the US-Iran conflict is shifting - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:11:57 UTC
11:11:57 KST

The confrontation between the United States and Iran has entered a new phase. The military conflict that dominated headlines earlier this year is increasingly giving way to a broader contest of economic pressure, maritime security, diplomacy, and great-power competition. This is part of the changing world order, as the conflict accelerates new trends around the world.
The Trump administration has made it clear that it believes the next stage of the campaign will rely less on airstrikes and more on isolating Iran economically while maintaining military deterrence. Tehran, meanwhile, is seeking to mobilize its remaining allies and show it still has leverage.
Here are five ways the US-Iran conflict is changing.
1. The Strait of Hormuz may be shifting from a battlefield to a shipping corridor
One of the clearest signs of the transition came today, when President Donald Trump announced that the US Navy had successfully cleared naval mines from the Strait of Hormuz. "All mines have been removed and/or detonated from within the International Waters of the Strait of Hormuz," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The message was about more than mines. It was intended to demonstrate that Washington intends to guarantee freedom of navigation despite months of Iranian attempts to disrupt maritime traffic. Trump also warned that Iran had been informed that any vessel attempting to lay additional mines would be "immediately and systematically destroyed." The US has backed freedom of navigation as policy since the Woodrow Wilson administration more than 100 years ago.
For decades, Iran has viewed the Strait of Hormuz as one of its strategic anchors. Around one-fifth of global oil shipments traditionally transited the waterway. The ability to threaten shipping has provided Tehran with leverage during periods of crisis. It did this in 2019, mining ships. The US objective now appears to be removing that leverage while reassuring global energy markets that international shipping can continue.
2. Economic pressure has become Washington's primary weapon. The Trump administration has also signaled that economic pressure will now become the centerpiece of US strategy
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the launch of Operation Economic Outcast, describing it as an unprecedented whole-of-government campaign to isolate Iran financially. "In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions," Bessent said. "Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe."
The Treasury Department indicates it has mapped Iranian financial networks, oil smuggling operations, sanctions evasion mechanisms, and funding channels linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The goal is to sever what Washington describes as every remaining economic lifeline supporting the regime.
Unlike previous sanctions campaigns, this initiative appears designed as an open-ended global effort rather than a series of individual sanctions packages. Washington is also framing the campaign as a choice for third countries: align with the United States or risk becoming economically isolated alongside Iran. It remains to be seen if this will work.
3. China is slowly expressing its concern about the conflict as it inches its way into the region
The new American strategy immediately highlighted another reality: the growing importance of China. Beijing criticized the new sanctions, warning that they would "only further intensify tensions" and arguing that China's legitimate cooperation with Iran should not be disrupted. Chinese officials again opposed what they described as unilateral American sanctions. China has a 25-year economic deal with Iran. China also benefits from the US being tied up in fights with Iran.
Iranian officials have emphasized that China remains one of Tehran's most important partners. Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh argued that both China and Russia have shown no indication that they intend to fully comply with Washington's new campaign.
This reflects a broader geopolitical competition. For years, Iran has looked eastward as relations with Western countries deteriorated. China has purchased Iranian oil, invested in infrastructure to a limited extent, and expanded political ties. Russia has likewise deepened military and strategic cooperation with Tehran. Iran expects more from China. China has shown it is cautious and pragmatic.
As a result, the US-Iran confrontation is becoming inseparable from wider competition among major powers as the world order shifts toward a multipolar world. The effectiveness of Operation Economic Outcast may depend not only on American enforcement but also on whether Beijing and Moscow decide to reduce their engagement with Tehran.
4. Iran is responding with economic measures and attempts at deterrence
Iran's response illustrates that Tehran increasingly views economic pressure as another form of warfare. Madanizadeh described the new sanctions as an "economic terrorist attack" and warned that Washington should "expect an attack" in response. "We know how to play the game too," he said during an interview broadcast on Iranian state television.
Although the precise meaning of those comments remains unclear, Iranian leaders have sought to respond to economic pressure through so-called asymmetric means. Previous periods of sanctions have coincided with responses that included cyber attacks, threats by Iranian-backed proxy groups, maritime attacks, and efforts to disrupt regional energy infrastructure. The fact that the US has been successful against mines may show Iran can’t control the tempo any longer.
5. Regional diplomacy is continuing alongside confrontation
Diplomacy has not evaporated. On August 25, Oman and Iran issued a joint statement following consultations between Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr bin Hamad Albusaidi and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. They posted about the new initiative on the social media platform X/Twitter.
The discussions focused on restoring safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz while respecting sovereignty. Both governments said they discussed a phased framework that could provide a practical basis for moving forward following the recent conflict.
Oman has long played a key role in regional diplomacy. The Sultanate has maintained relations with both Washington and Tehran and has frequently served as a discreet channel for negotiations. Previous US-Iran nuclear talks also benefited from Omani mediation. This has led to US threats against Oman.
Iran is seeking to demonstrate resilience while preserving diplomatic options through partners such as Oman. Regional states are attempting to prevent another escalation that could once again threaten global energy markets. Oman’s outreach follows Pakistani officials' visit to Tehran.
