TEHRAN - Long queues formed at petrol stations in Tehran on Aug 25 after the United States announced fresh sanctions aimed at pressuring Iran into submission.
Washington has turned to pulling economic levers six months into a war on Iran that has ground to a stalemate, with peace talks stalled and most traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz blocked.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Aug 24 laid out plans for the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, saying the “objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime”.
Though Iran’s leaders have shrugged off the tough talk, having already endured sanctions for decades, some residents of the capital feared that they would feel the pinch.
“People are being hurt, both those who are financially well-off and those who are financially weak,” said realtor Mehdi Yazdian, 55, who urged the authorities to control prices. “Yes, these sanctions are having an effect, but naturally, our people are resilient.”
Iran had already been grappling with sky-high inflation before the war, which fuelled an anti-government protest movement that peaked in January. The authorities met the movement with a crackdown that foreign rights groups said killed thousands of people.
The government has attributed the violence to “terrorist acts” orchestrated by the United States and Israel.
English teacher Kia Farahani, 45, said similar unrest could lie ahead. “I personally am not afraid of war at all because this is our land,” he said. “But I think that this war will be more economic and will cause people to feel a lot of pressure, and now maybe there will be protests again.”
Iran has carried out a spate of executions related to the winter protests, drawing outrage from US President Donald Trump, who said it was “killing protesters, even when they are not protesting, at levels not seen before”. He said on Truth Social: “It is a humanitarian crisis of epic proportions, and must be stopped, NOW.”
‘Another defeat’
AFP images showed lines of cars snaking out of petrol stations on Aug 25 after the Iranian president’s chief of staff said that petrol quotas would be reviewed. “What is certain is that the quotas will be reduced without changing the price, but anyone who wants to buy more petrol than the quota will have a higher price,” Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei told state TV.
Announcing the new sanctions, Bessent said countries that did not support the US economic campaign would “share in the isolation” of Iran. The Treasury Department said expanded secondary sanctions would target Iran’s digital assets and its technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors.
The measures hit entities around the world, including in the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, China, Singapore and Europe.
China, a key customer for Iranian oil, said on Aug 25 that it opposed the sanctions and vowed to “take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own rights and interests”. Bessent did not rule out the possibility of Chinese banks being targeted.
Iran, however, was dismissive of the moves and predicted “another defeat” for Washington. “We’ve been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events,” said Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh.
Hormuz talks
Saeed Laylaz, Tehran-based economic expert, told AFP that the new US measures were in line with Trump’s “maximum pressure” approach, which he has pursued for years. “The United States of America has nothing that it can do that (it) had not done before,” Laylaz said, noting years of isolation had made Iran’s economy more self-sufficient. “But I have doubts about the internal governance of the Iranian economy” and the authorities’ ability to take concrete measures like fighting inflation, he added.
Oil prices, meanwhile, slipped for a second day on Aug 25 as traders judged the risk of renewed strikes on Iran to have receded, falling around three per cent to below US$90 a barrel for international benchmark Brent.
Crude prices had shot up after Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz early in the war, and it and fellow coastal state Oman have been hammering out plans for the crucial waterway, whose closure has rattled the global economy.
The two countries’ foreign ministers met in Tehran on Aug 25, later saying they had discussed “the establishment of a joint temporary navigational corridor through the Strait of Hormuz and an agreement to implement a joint project to clear the Strait of mines”. AFP

Instagram CEO denies company hid low use of teen safety feature in Meta trial

2026-08-26

09:07:11 KST

Instagram’s CEO disputed allegations by US prosecutors that his company hid negative information from the public while testifying during a blockbuster social media trial.
“I am not trying to encourage my team to hide anything,” the CEO, Adam Mosseri, told a California courtroom on Tuesday.
Mosseri is the first top executive from Meta, which owns both Instagram and Facebook, to testify in a historic lawsuit brought by 29 US states. His testimony began toward the end of the day on Tuesday and is slated to continue on Wednesday.
When the executive was posed with multiple questions about not disclosing low user numbers for Instagram’s features geared toward teen safety, he brushed them aside, saying: “We don’t publish every single stat.”
Jason Slothouber, a prosecutor for the state of Colorado, asked specifically about a tool called Take a Break, meant to encourage teens to close Instagram if they’d been scrolling for a while. Slothouber pointed out that just 1.8% of teens signed up for the feature, and that while Mosseri had touted the tool, he never publicly disclosed that number.
“I’ve definitely said publicly that the opt-in rates are low,” Mosseri responded. “I don’t know if I’ve said numbers.”
The jury trial, taking place in federal court in Oakland, California, began with opening statements last week. The lawsuit centers on the states’ allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. The states additionally claim the social media company regularly collected data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws.
If found liable, Meta could be forced to pay damages as high as $200bn and change the design of its products to make them safer for kids. Legal experts say the outcome of this trial could fundamentally change the way social media apps function for young people.
Meta has denied all allegations, saying the states are chasing an “outlandish payout”. A spokesperson said Tuesday that Meta’s safety teams strive to be industry-leading and that Mosseri’s testimony showed the company does research to find ways to improve user experience.
Mosseri became the head of Instagram in 2018 and over the years has faced scrutiny about whether he may have dismissed internal warnings about the platform’s addictive design and negative effects on young people. He was called to testify before a Senate committee in December 2021 and as a witness in other trials about the alleged harm of social media to children.
On Tuesday, Slothouber asked Mosseri about a blog post he had published just one day before his Senate testimony. The post was titled “raising the standard for protecting teens and supporting parents online” and included the announcement of the Take a Break tool. Slothouber questioned Mosseri about the timing of his post.
“We had made progress, and we wanted to get the progress out, so we could talk about the progress,” Mosseri responded.
Slothouber then asked the CEO whether he was aware of the phrase “drumbeat messaging”, the idea of saying something repeatedly until it’s drummed into people’s heads. Mosseri said he had and that it’s necessary when dealing with parents and safety features. “We need to repeat it to raise awareness of those tools,” Mosseri testified.
Over the last week, jurors also heard from Arturo Béjar, a former Meta safety engineer turned whistleblower, who testified that the company has a “don’t ask, don’t tell” strategy when it comes to the safety of children on its platforms. They also heard from a psychologist and other former and current company employees.
The trial is expected to last through September with several other witnesses, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

United States of Dolly: How a country queen bridged America’s divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26

09:00:00 KST

United States of Dolly: How a country queen bridged America’s divide
WASHINGTON – The death of country music icon Dolly Parton, who kept her distance from the political debates gripping America, offered a rare moment of unity to a divided nation on Aug 25.
Affording her the sort of honour given to major state figures, US President Donald Trump ordered flags across the country to be lowered for a week to mark what he called a “true loss for millions of people”.
Trump spared the legendary singer – who like him was 80 – the kinds of barbs he has levelled at other figures, including former Federal Bureau of Investigation chief Robert Mueller and director Rob Reiner after their deaths.
Reactions to the death of the Jolene star were the same on the other side of the political divide.
“Dolly Parton was a true American icon,” said Kamala Harris, Trump’s Democratic rival in the 2024 US presidential election and the first female and black US vice-president.
Worried about its future and often nostalgic for an idealised past, it is fair to say that much of the US saw itself in Parton.
Perhaps it was because the child who grew up in a cabin without running water or electricity in Tennessee, and became a global, successful businesswoman and generous philanthropist, reflected a flattering image back to the world’s leading power.
The queen of country music never got involved in politics, rising above the fact that the scene has frequently leaned conservative.
Parton repeatedly insisted that her songs said all she had to say.
“Everybody knows I don’t do politics,” she told Fox And Friends in 2017. “My mother was a Democrat and my daddy was a Republican, so I’m a hypocrite,” she quipped.
Parton also said she had fans on both side of the aisle, “and I don’t want to make any of them mad at me”.
‘All for gals’
A devout Christian, she also became a supporter of gay rights.
“We are all God’s children,” she said in an interview with Larry King in 2016.
In that same year, she also declined to say whether she would support either Democrat Hillary Clinton or Republican Trump in the presidential election.
Parton told The New York Times that “a woman would do a great job”, but added that: “I think no matter if it’s Hillary or Donald Trump, we’re gonna be plagued with PMS either way – presidential mood swings!”
During the Covid-19 pandemic, Parton waded into another politically charged area by funding vaccine research and encouraging Americans to get vaccinated. She even sang a parody version of her hit song Jolene, renamed Vaccine, while filming a video of her first injection.
But Parton, whose hit 9 To 5 was a feminist anthem, declined to describe herself as such despite shaking up the male dominated country music industry.
“I’m just all for gals,” she told The Guardian in 2019.
The result was a moment of almost unheard-of unity for a country split over everything from the Iran war to the culture wars.
While Trump did not mention it in his Truth Social post, there was widespread praise from both parties for her Imagination Library programme, which gave away millions of free books to children.
“She always believed in giving back, especially in her efforts to promote literacy,” said Democratic former president Bill Clinton.
Trump’s Education Secretary Linda McMahon concurred, saying Parton “placed millions of books into the hands of young children and helped spark a lifelong love of reading”.
The Democrats, however, could not resist pointing out that Trump’s Republicans had tried to reduce funding for Parton’s signature programme. AFP

TIME and Statista have launched the 2026 list of Best Employers, based on independent employee surveys conducted in countries around the world. These surveys asked open-ended questions about employees’ willingness to recommend their own employer and their willingness to recommend other employers in the same industry. The top 500 employers, ranked based on these results, were named Brazil's Best Employers 2026.
Microsoft, like in 2025, is once again the country’s top employer. The company has had a decades-long presence in the country and invested billions in AI infrastructure and related skills training in Brazil, the leading economy in Latin America. This year, the top four employers in Brazil are all U.S. tech companies, including SAP, Alphabet, and IBM. In the past year or so, Brazil has drawn interest from a growing number of global tech companies as it positions itself as a hub for sustainable data centers, with national policies offering tax breaks and clean energy for powering these facilities. In fact, the government, along with Brazil’s largest banks, has been shaping the tech sector in Brazil for the last decade by spending billions on digital services like software licensing and cybersecurity from foreign companies, according to a 2025 study by researchers at the University of São Paulo, the University of Brasília, and Fundação Getúlio Vargas—a move some critics say undermines Brazil’s tech sovereignty and diverts investment from domestic solutions. At the same time, many of these tech companies, like Microsoft and IBM, have been providing accessible professional certificate programs to workers across the globe in hopes of closing the skills gap.
The top-ranked Brazil-based employer is accounting firm Contabilizei (no. 5), which specializes in helping small businesses and entrepreneurs with financial services from managing expenses and invoices to taxes. As the number of new small businesses in the country continues to grow, and more people flock to digital banks, innovative fintechs like Contabilizei have an opportunity to become a key part of that domestic economic ecosystem.

Netanyahu, facing tight elections in October, earlier in August rejected the latest stage in the Gaza peace plan after Hamas said it had agreed to disarm.

In response to Netanyahu, the Board of Peace backtracked and assured him that Israeli troops need not leave Gaza until a complete demilitarisation of Hamas.

China, India hold border talks in Beijing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
23:21:59 UTC
08:21:59 KST

China and India agreed on Tuesday to continue dialogue and seek a "fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable settlement" of their border issue after talks between senior diplomats in Beijing.
The world's two most populous nations share a roughly 3,800-km, largely undemarcated and disputed border in the Himalayas.
Foreign Minister Wang Yi and India's National Security Advisor Ajit Doval had "comprehensive, in-depth, friendly and candid" discussions on border affairs and bilateral ties, the foreign ministry said in a statement.
Wang said China-India relations were no longer only of bilateral importance but carried global and strategic significance, saying the two neighbours should strengthen communication and reduce their differences.
"China is ready to work with India to develop bilateral relations from a strategic and long-term perspective, be good neighbours and friends as well as partners that help each other succeed, and realise the "Dragon-Elephant Tango," Wang said.
Xinhua News Agency reported that Doval said India is willing to further enhance strategic communication with China, effectively manage border areas, explore solutions to the border question, and promote the accelerated improvement and development of India-China relations.
Ties between Beijing and New Delhi have gradually improved in recent years following a deadly 2020 border clash, which led to a four-year military standoff before a disengagement agreement was reached in October 2024.
Last year Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited China for the first time in seven years, in a sign of a thaw in relations. More recently, a fresh border-related dispute triggered sharp diplomatic exchanges between the two rivals.
"Both sides should learn from historical experience, place the border issue in an appropriate position in bilateral relations, and move forward without stagnation, regression, or deviation,"  Wang was quoted as telling Doval at Tuesday's meeting.
The two countries have agreed to hold the next round of border talks in India in 2027, the Chinese statement added. (Xinhua/Reuters)

How Dolly Parton fostered child literacy as a tribute to her dad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
23:18:45 UTC
08:18:45 KST

Dolly Parton leaves a legacy to children's literacy with her Imagination Library
While Dolly Parton was known as the Queen of Country, her work improving child literacy rates will be another of her lasting legacies.
Parton, who died this week aged 80, grew up in extreme poverty in the Great Smoky Mountains of East Tennessee, the fourth of 12 children to her parents Robert Lee and Avie Lee Parton.
Parton adored her dad, describing him as "the smartest man I've ever known" with a good head for numbers.
However, he never learned to read or write after leaving school at a young age to work to help support his family.
"I knew in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from seeing all his dreams come true," Parton said on social media.
"Inspiring kids to love to read became my mission."
Her tribute to her dad became the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, which she established in1995, initially to help underprivileged kids in her rural home county.
"When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee I knew my dreams would come true," Parton wrote on the organisation's website.
"I know there are children in your community with their own dreams. They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer.
"The seeds of these dreams are often found in books and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world."
It has now been operating for 31 years, expanding across the US, the UK, Ireland, Canada and Australia, where it was established in 2013.
How does it work?
Every month the Imagination Library sends an age-appropriate book to all registered children at no cost to their family.
Kids can register from birth, and receive a monthly book until the age of five.
The program has so far gifted 332 million books to children around the world.
More than 2 million of those books have gone to kids in Australia.
Australia's selection committee, which is run by United Way Australia and is comprised of early education and literacy experts, picks titles specific to the region, and includes Indigenous writers and publishing organisations.
Previous book selections have included the board book Australian Babies, With Sky Country by Annette Sax, Backyard Footy by Carl Merrison and Pamela Allen's Who Sank the Boat?
The program has been embraced by public libraries around the country.
Loading...
Its effect on literacy
The Imagination Library's impact has been far-reaching and affirmed in an international study led by United Way Australia's head of research, statistician Claire Galea, in 2025.
The study, which is the largest dataset in the world on shared book reading, collected data from 86,000 families with children in the program.
It found in all countries, the program significantly helped prevent early literacy gaps that often persisted in primary school.
Children enrolled in Imagination Library were also nine times more likely to be read to four or more days per week compared to those not in the program.
In Australia, the number one benefit reported by caregivers was seeing their children develop a strong love of books and reading.
Dr Galea's thesis specifically looked at the impact of the program in Tamworth, finding children in this local government area were read to more often, for longer, and had more books in the home than the average Australian child.
The Imagination Library team posted a tribute to Parton on social media, saying they were "heartbroken at the loss of our founder".
"The work ahead has never felt more meaningful, and we will carry it forward as she lifts us all up. Dolly, we will always love you."

Morales, who served as deputy minister under Jose Gabriel Espinoza, takes over after lawmakers last week censured and removed Espinoza in a blow to Paz.

He also called on Congress to quickly pass an investment bill that the government sees as crucial to unlocking domestic and foreign investment by providing clearer rules and stronger legal certainty.
Morales, meanwhile, said he would deepen the administration's existing policies.
"Our commitment will be to preserve stability, strengthen public finances, generate conditions for investment, production and employment, and continue recovering confidence in our economy," Morales said. REUTERS

Mark Carney, the former central banker who said ‘no’ to Trump
- Mark Carney, now Canadian Prime Minister, boldly opposed US President Trump by halting trade talks and imposing counter-tariffs, gaining 76% public support.
- Carney transformed quickly from banker to politician, winning leadership in 2025 and promoting Canada as a united middle power on the global stage.
- Facing a tougher phase, Carney seeks new trade partners, plans a Pacific oil pipeline, and strengthens EU ties to reduce dependence on the US market.
AI generated
MONTREAL – Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is more seasoned as a banker than a politician but has shown a confident touch in standing up to US President Donald Trump and navigating a trade war that threatens his nation’s economy.
“We are masters in our own house,” the prime minister said on Aug 22, just hours after breaking off trade talks with the US and ordering his negotiators back to Ottawa.
Despite the risks this decision poses to Canada, which is heavily dependent on exports to the US, Carney can boast of broad support, with 76 per cent of the public praising his stance towards Washington, according to a weekend poll.
“Mark Carney has the means to achieve his ambitions because the country is behind him,” says Genevieve Tellier, a professor of political science at the University of Ottawa.
After Washington slapped Canada with 50-per-cent duties, Canada on Aug 25 announced counter-tariffs of its own.
The former head of Canada’s central bank, Carney, 61, was not known for his charisma – unlike his flamboyant predecessor Justin Trudeau, from the same Liberal Party – but has nevertheless managed to kindle a patriotic flame among Canadians weary of American attacks.
It was trade tension with the US that propelled him to power – two months after Trump began his second term – as Canadians saw him as a protector of their economy.
Replacing Trudeau as leader of his party and the government in March 2025, he won a general election a month later, to everyone’s surprise.
“He transformed into a politician quite quickly; it was a surprise,” said Tellier.
The Davos turning point
A blunt speech Carney gave at January’s World Economic Forum marked a turning point for him on the international stage.
Declaring that the world was in the midst of a “rupture in the world order”, he called on middle powers like Canada to unite.
“If we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu,” he said.
The speech sent a message that Carney was positioning himself “as an international leader with a different, credible vision”, Tellier said.
After studying at Harvard and Oxford, Mark Carney made his fortune as an investment banker at Goldman Sachs in New York, London, Tokyo and Toronto.
In 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis, he was appointed governor of the Bank of Canada by a conservative prime minister, Stephen Harper.
Five years later, he was chosen by a conservative British prime minister, David Cameron, to head the Bank of England, becoming the first foreigner to lead the institution.
In this role, he would face the economic turmoil caused by Brexit, after the UK decided to leave the European Union.
‘Difficult phase’
Declaring on Aug 24 that “America has changed”, the Canadian leader is moving forward with determination: seeking new trading partners, launching major projects and boosting military spending.
Carney has notably forged closer ties with the EU and is set to discuss soon the strengthening of that partnership.
In Armenia in May, he emphasised that the EU and Canada were not “doomed” to submit to a “brutal” international order.
Carney was born in Fort Smith, a remote town in Canada’s Northwest Territories, and was raised in Edmonton, Alberta, a province rich in hydrocarbons.
He wants to construct a new pipeline to the Pacific in order to export Canadian oil to Asia and thus reduce the need to sell to the American market.
But by “putting his foot down” with Trump, Frederic Boily, a political science professor at the University of Alberta, Carney “will now enter a somewhat more difficult phase” where he will have to manage the impact on Canada’s economy and his popularity. AFP

NEW YORK, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks ended higher on Tuesday as a rebound in technology and semiconductor equities allowed investors to look past escalating cross-border trade tensions following Canada's announcement of retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 160.24 points, or 0.3 percent, to 53,577.4. The S&P 500 added 24.42 points, or 0.32 percent, to 7,677.28. The Nasdaq Composite Index increased by 171.11 points, or 0.66 percent, to 26,151.3.

North American trade friction escalated after the Canadian government announced retaliatory tariffs targeting approximately 20 billion U.S. dollars in annual imports from the United States, alongside financial relief measures for affected domestic businesses and workers. The countermeasures, set to take effect on Sept. 8, levy duties of 15 percent, 25 percent, and 50 percent across more than 700 U.S. product categories to match recent trade measures imposed by Washington.
On the macroeconomic front, the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index for the United States decreased by 0.8 points to 89.4 in August, the lowest level in seven months, down from July's reading of 90.2.
U.S. housing data also pointed to cooling demand. Joint figures released Tuesday by the U.S. Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development showed that the median sales price of new single-family homes fell 2.3 percent month-on-month to 393,800 dollars in July. Concurrently, new home sales tumbled 10.5 percent from June to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 607,000 units, marking a 6.3 percent decrease compared to the same period last year and indicating that price reductions have yet to revive broad buyer activity.
In corporate developments, shares of DICK'S Sporting Goods plummeted more than 30 percent after the athletic apparel retailer missed second-quarter earnings estimates and slashed its full-year outlook, citing softening consumer demand across the sports retail sector.
Semiconductor shares spearheaded the advance on the tech-heavy Nasdaq. Graphics processing unit leader Nvidia rose 2.19 percent ahead of its highly anticipated second-quarter earnings report on Wednesday, while peers Advanced Micro Devices and Micron Technology gained nearly 5 percent and 2.5 percent, respectively.
Market participants now turn their focus to the release of the U.S. Personal Consumption Expenditures price index for July on Wednesday for further clues about the trajectory of domestic inflation. ■

U.S. works to revoke nonimmigrant visas from foreigners who apply for asylum

WASHINGTON, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. State Department is working with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who apply for asylum, State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said Tuesday.
"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," Pigott said in a statement.
"These types of visas are issued with the clear understanding that they are for those who intend to return home. Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud -- which is grounds for visa revocation," he continued.
Pigott's remarks came shortly after multiple U.S. media outlets reported that the Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States.
The move is expected to apply to those granted B1 and B2 visas between 2016 and 2026 who have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to a report by The Washington Post.
In the Tuesday statement, Pigott did not confirm how many visas could be revoked in the upcoming action, saying that the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, his administration has tightened immigration policies, cracking down on undocumented immigrants and increasing scrutiny of U.S. visa holders.
On Aug. 10, the State Department announced that it had revoked more than 175,000 visas since January 2025, when Trump began his second term.
On Monday, the DHS proposed a 103,265-U.S.-dollar fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions, marking the agency's newest move to restrict the visa program on new grounds. This came after previous efforts to charge 100,000 dollars for the visa were struck down by the courts. ■

Here's why markets are starting to care about the 2026 election 10 weeks out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
22:43:08 UTC
07:43:08 KST

Markets are starting to care about the 2026 midterm elections, which loom 10 weeks away and could rip full control of Congress from President Donald Trump and the Republican Party.
Democrats are favored to win at least one chamber of Congress come November, leading the generic ballot by roughly 6 percentage points according to FiftyPlusOne, a website that tracks poll results. A divided Washington would likely block lawmakers from passing any major non-bipartisan measures while turning the legislative branch's most basic tasks into a drawn-out negotiation.
Analysts detailed to CNBC how a full or partial shift in power from Republicans to Democrats in Congress could affect the country's capital markets. Potential outcomes include a lengthy standoff over raising the debt ceiling, more whipsawing executive actions and potential volatility if there's a protracted wait for election results.
A more volatile executive
While divided government tends to temper federal government actions, that's not always the case with President Donald Trump in the White House for the two years of the next Congress.
"One of the things you often hear is the market loves a divided government, and that usually means the extreme positions don't get enacted," said Ed Mills, managing director of Washington policy at Raymond James. "But what we have been cautioning is the biggest market moves from a policy perspective of the last two years have come from executive action."
"After the midterms, if Democrats have a majority at least in the House, do you think that President Trump is going to work with Democrats more? Or is it more likely he's going to get more aggressive on executive action? My bet's on more executive action," Mills said.
The most prominent of Trump's market-moving executive actions is his tariff campaign, which drew on untested emergency authority to impose sweeping levies on a swath of countries. Although the Supreme Court eventually ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorize Trump to impose tariffs, they remained on the books for over a year and weighed heavily on markets. And Trump has been replacing the tariffs that were rebuffed with new ones using different executive authority.
Trump often touts stock market performance, with the S&P 500 most recently reaching a record high close on Aug. 13. JPMorgan noted in a June report that dating back to 1950, the S&P 500 has performed better under a divided Congress than with single-party control. The firm also noted that even if Democrats gain control of the Senate, Trump will remain in the White House and would prevent Democrats from advancing tax, climate or healthcare legislation.
The debt ceiling
Most financial institutions believe the U.S. will reach its debt ceiling of $41.1 trillion in midyear 2027, requiring Congress to raise or suspend the debt limit so Treasury can continue borrowing to meet obligations. If Congress does not, the U.S. would be unable to borrow to pay its obligations and could default on its debt.
Congress last raised the debt ceiling in 2025 as part of Republicans' massive party-line tax cut and spending package known as the "one big beautiful bill act." If Democrats win at least one chamber of Congress, most analysts agree it won't be so easy to do it again because Democrats could use their opposition as leverage to get policy changes.
"Split government can make the process of raising or suspending the ceiling especially contentious, though a blue wave could make the process less tricky," said one recent report from TD Securities, referring to the prospect of Democrats winning both congressional chambers. "While we ultimately expect the ceiling to be raised, we look for negotiations to go down to the wire."
The scenario played out in the inverse in 2023, when Republicans captured the House while Democrats controlled the Senate and the White House. The House GOP, then led by Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., demanded spending cuts in exchange for raising the debt ceiling and brought the U.S. to the brink of default.
A debt ceiling standoff can affect the market by increasing volatility and raising rates on Treasurys, said Molly Brooks, one of the authors of the TD Securities report. That volatility intensifies the closer the U.S. gets to the "X-date," or the point at which the Treasury Department would no longer be able to pay its obligations.
"I'm expecting it to be raised at some point. It's just a question of when and how much volatility it increases in the near term while we get towards that," Brooks said. "Treasury bills that will be maturing in that year will be at higher rates because these investors are requiring a higher premium on that debt, just because there's some scenario or some odds that they think that they may not get their principal back if the government defaults at that exact point in time."
Mills said he is also keeping an eye out for unusual market moves during a debt ceiling fight, such as a bond sell-off.
"There's been a perverse incentive at times that the worse the fight got, the better the yields on U.S. Treasurys were, like the very instrument that could default actually benefited ... the traditional playbook around the debt limit is you don't really have to worry about the Treasury market because it's a flight to safety," Mills said. "We're always asking how it would be different this time, and it would be if the bond market sells off in anticipation of a debt ceiling fight, the market would pay much more attention to this one than it has the last several ones."
A contested or delayed election result
Another outcome investors are watching for is a potentially contested or delayed election call, which could keep markets guessing over who will be in charge of Washington for the next two years.
Election night has grown especially contentious in the U.S. over the last several cycles, especially after Trump's efforts to discredit his loss to former President Joe Biden in 2020. The president has also attempted to add new voter-ID requirements to vote this year, moves his opponents say are a pretext to undermine election results and restrict voter access.
While investors have largely not weighed in on the president's efforts specifically, they have been loud and clear that a delay in declaring a victor could disrupt the market.
"Independent of the final outcome, one scenario that could become problematic for markets is the potential for election chaos," the TD report read. "Recent Supreme Court decisions have reinforced states' ability to count votes after Election Day and given that much of the swing in House seats may come in California, markets may not know the definitive winner for some time."
"Generally, higher volatility would weigh on risky assets such as equities, and it could actually lead to slightly lower rates if you're seeing a flight to quality move where people are reacting to more uncertainty and then putting their money into a safer government debt," Brooks said.
Investors would much rather see a decisive victory for one side or another as soon as possible after votes are counted, Mills said.
"There is no desire to replay 2020," he said, noting how control of the Senate that election took until Jan. 5, 2021, to be decided. "Even in the 2024 election, what I heard consistently from investors was their number one goal was for a clear outcome on election night."
Corrections: This story has been revised to reflect that the U.S. debt ceiling is $41.1 trillion. A previous version misstated the amount of the statutory debt limit. In addition, the recent report in the midterms and the markets was from TD Securities. A previous version of this story misstated the source of the report.

Instagram chief Adam Mosseri testified on Tuesday during a social media addiction trial that he doesn't direct employees to withhold information from him that could pose potential legal liabilities.
"I'm not trying to encourage my team to hide anything," Mosseri said, in his first day of testimony at a federal courthouse in Oakland, California. He was responding to questioning from trial attorney Jason Slothouber with the Colorado Attorney General's office.
Slothouber asked Mosseri if he was aware that Meta attorneys may have asked the company's internal staff not to share information related to safety research for kids under 13 and teen mental health concerns. Mosseri said he "wouldn't be surprised" if Meta lawyers reviewed child-related safety research for complicated legal and policy reasons, but would be taken aback if the motivations for doing so were to provide cover in case of potential litigation and to mislead the public.
Opening arguments started last week in the landmark trial against Meta that's being co-led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the AGs from Colorado, New Jersey and Kentucky. They represent a bipartisan group of 29 AGs in a combined case.
The AG coalition alleges that Meta violated the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA, and consumer protection statutes, and are seeking penalties that could reach $200 billion. Central to their claims are allegations that Meta executives like Mosseri and CEO Mark Zuckerberg publicly misrepresented certain child-safety features and related internal research to the public. Meta has denied the allegations.
During Mosseri's testimony, which kicked off late in the day, the Instagram head acknowledged that the company curbed the number of employees who could access certain internal research following whistleblower Frances Haugen's 2021 leaking of corporate documents related to children and teen mental health. 
Mosseri said Meta made the policy changes because "we don't want anything to be taken out of context," similar to what executives say happened with the leaked documents, published by the Wall Street Journal as part of The Facebook Files series. 
Mosseri said the plaintiff lawyers are incorrect in suggesting that Meta also reduced the number of researchers studying youth mental health harms after Haugen's leaks.
"I disagree with that characterization," Mosseri said. "I don't think the team was smaller, it was just centralized."
Mosseri's testimony will continue on Wednesday.

Dozens of rights and advocacy groups are galvanising supporters to oppose an event scheduled to take place at Madison Square Garden in New York on Saturday, headlined by Mohan Bhagwat, the boss of the Indian Hindu paramilitary organisation Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).
Bhagwat arrived in New York on Tuesday on the first leg of a three-nation outreach tour to the US, Canada, and the UK at the invitation of overseas Hindu groups to mark the centenary of the RSS, whose affiliates Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP) and Bajrang Dal were described by CIA as "militant religious organisations".
Saturday's event is being organised by the non-profit American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, which heaped praises on Bhagwat in a statement for frequently addressing "social harmony, family and community relationships, environmental responsibility, volunteerism, and dialogue among different sections of society."
The RSS — founded in 1925 with the declared goal of strengthening the Hindu community — remained outside mainstream politics for decades.
It was historically tainted by the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi, and has been known for inciting hostility against religious minorities amid recurring communal unrest across India.
While the group with five million members views Indian civilisation as intrinsically linked to Hinduism, critics argue its foundational ideology is rooted in Hindu supremacy.
Today, the RSS maintains an extensive network of affiliate groups spanning student and trade bodies, non-profit entities, and vigilante groups frequently linked to incidents of violence, especially against minority Muslims and Christians.
The organisation's political prominence is heavily reinforced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which originated from the RSS.
'Bhagwat does not speak for all Hindus'
Meanwhile, on Tuesday, opposition groups — including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council, the Interfaith Center of New York, and various other Hindu, Muslim, interfaith, and civil rights organisations — staged a demonstration against Bhagwat's arrival in New York.
During a press briefing on the steps of New York City Hall, representatives called on Madison Square Garden to cancel the gathering and spoke out against the promotion of Hindu nationalism in the US.
"The RSS is a century-old Hindu nationalist organisation with a documented history of religious supremacy, anti-minority violence, and attacks on India's pluralistic foundations.
Bhagwat’s event, promoted as a celebration of 'Universal Oneness', attempts to spiritually sanitise that history and expand the RSS's influence in the United States," Hindus for Human Rights said in a statement.
Sravya Tadepalli, deputy executive director of the advocacy group, noted that Bhagwat does not speak for all Hindus and leads a movement that has fostered division and insecurity for minority communities.
"New York should not provide the RSS with a stage on which religious nationalism can be repackaged as unity. We will gather at City Hall to defend a genuinely pluralistic vision of an India where no faith is used to determine who belongs or who holds power."
Organisations that have denounced Bhagwat's visit include 18 Million Rising, the Arab Resource & Organizing Center, CodePink, the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Dalit Solidarity Forum, the American Council for Judaism, the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, and the Muslim Public Affairs Council.
In May, the RSS — which has been banned three times in India's post-independence history — stated that it organised international visits, including to the US, to counter allegations regarding its conduct and structure.
'Country of Particular Concern'
The outreach followed a report by the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), which stated that the RSS has engaged in severe intolerance and actions targeting minority communities over several decades.
USCIRF is an independent, bipartisan US federal government body that monitors religious freedom globally and submits policy recommendations to the US President, the Secretary of State, and Congress.
USCIRF also highlighted Prime Minister Modi's RSS background and recommended that the US State Department designate India as a "Country of Particular Concern".
International human rights monitors, including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, have documented increasing civil rights pressures faced by India's estimated 200 million Muslims, pointing to punitive demolitions of properties without due process and the use of security legislation against civil society figures.
Modi has already delivered on two key agenda items for the RSS: building a temple to the Hindu deity Ram on the site of a some 400-year-old mosque razed by Hindu zealots in 1992, and annexing the Muslim-majority India-administered Kashmir in 2019.
RSS is often described as the Indian version of the Ku Klux Klan — a notorious US white supremacist group, established in 1865, and known for using terrorist tactics — violence, intimidation, and murder — to enforce racial hierarchy and oppose civil rights in America.
Indian opposition leaders, notably Rahul Gandhi of the Indian National Congress, have consistently argued that majoritarian narratives undermine India's constitutional secularism.
While the RSS does not operate under its official name in the US, its activities and outreach are primarily conducted through the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh USA (HSS USA), which manages roughly 267 branches across 33 US states.
Earlier this year, public records and lobbying disclosures revealed that payments totalling $330,000 were made to the US lobbying firm Squire Patton Boggs — which was also linked to Pakistan, India’s nuclear-armed arch-rival — to represent interests linked to the organisation before the US Senate and House of Representatives

Oil prices fall for second day as US shifts from Iran strikes to sanctions

Oil prices fell for a second day on Tuesday as traders judged the risk of renewed military strikes on Iran to have receded, after the United States instead threatened broader economic sanctions.
Although Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the White House was declaring an "economic D-Day" against Iran and its trade partners, the US gave no timeline for its new sanctions and did not name any other countries it would punish.
The measures were softer than analysts had expected and were accompanied by renewed shuttle diplomacy, with key Pakistani mediators reporting positive talks with Iran's president on Monday.
Pakistan Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi reported "a very positive and productive meeting," saying on X he believes the "momentum will help pave the way for further progress and lasting peace in the region."
Read moreUS economic D-Day sanctions: 'Repeated bombing attacks across Iran failed to change the calculus'
The news helped calm oil markets, with prices falling more than three percent and the international benchmark Brent back below $90 a barrel, following weeks of rising prices caused by deadlock in talks to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Wall Street stocks finished solidly higher, with the broad-based S&P 500 advancing 0.3 percent.
But FHN Financial's Chris Low warned that markets seemed to be shrugging off the US-Canada trade war, with Canada unveiling counter-tariffs on US goods ranging between 15 and 50 percent.
"There may be a mistaken belief that because there were already tariffs in place, that it won't make much difference," Low said. "But that is a mistake because the tariffs imposed over the weekend are much broader and much bigger than the tariffs that were there before."
Major European markets closed higher, aside from Paris, which slipped back slightly in late trading.
"European stock markets rebounded early Tuesday with some relief evident from the lack of any material increase in the economic pressure on Iran," said Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo UK.
Markets were also boosted by German data showing the country's second-quarter growth was stronger than previously estimated.
Read moreIran discovers major new gas reserves amid war-hit energy sector
Investors are looking ahead to earnings Wednesday from artificial intelligence pace setter Nvidia.
The chipmaker's performance has become a key test of the AI boom, with concerns growing over whether the sector can match lofty expectations.
"The most actively traded stocks in the US right now are all the major AI names," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB trading group.
She added that Nvidia's results "will be a key driver of price action, and potential volatility later this week".
Investors are also looking to the annual Jackson Hole gathering of central bankers, economists and finance chiefs beginning Thursday, where Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh is due to speak.
His comments will be parsed for clues about monetary policy, with US inflation still stubbornly high and after Bessent said the Treasury would buy back more of its own bonds to push down borrowing costs after the 30-year yield hit a 19-year high.

====================================================================================================

Canadian student wins water prize for AI plastic-cleaning robot
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:47:18 CST
06:47:18 KST

HELSINKI, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- A Canadian student has won the 2026 Stockholm Junior Water Prize for developing an autonomous robot that uses artificial intelligence (AI) and magnetic technology to remove plastic from water while minimizing harm to aquatic life.
Moroti Adegboyega of Canada, selected from national winners representing more than 40 countries and regions, received the award from Sweden's Crown Princess Victoria at a ceremony on Tuesday evening in Stockholm.
Adegboyega's project, Ecoferroquatics, combines AI, robotics and a specially developed ferrofluid-based magnetic suspension to detect and collect plastic particles from water.
According to the Stockholm Water Foundation, which hosts the annual competition, the project offers an alternative to existing cleanup methods such as nets, trawlers and filters, which can be labor-intensive and may harm marine organisms.
Tests showed the system outperformed a simple sieve in collecting small particles, including microplastics that can pass through conventional screening methods.
Plastic debris can break down into smaller particles, be ingested by wildlife and carry harmful chemicals through the food chain, the foundation said.
The jury also awarded its Diploma of Excellence to Laura Ivanka of Hungary for DIVE&CLEAN, a project using specially designed underwater bins along recreational diving routes to collect plastic waste before it breaks down into microplastics.
The People's Choice Award went to Basmala Diab of Egypt, whose project uses activated carbon made from rice and corn straw to improve microbial fuel cells that treat wastewater while generating electricity.
Held annually since 1997, the Stockholm Junior Water Prize is an international competition for young people working on water-related research and innovation, with national competitions involving tens of thousands of students worldwide. ■

ABUJA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- At least 50 children have been killed and several others hospitalized in an outbreak of diphtheria in Nigeria's northwestern state of Kano, the state legislature said Tuesday, calling for swift emergency measures to assist affected communities.
The Kano State House of Assembly called on the government to invoke the state's Health Protection Law to contain the outbreak and directed its committee on health to engage relevant authorities on the public health issue affecting several local government areas.
Ibrahim Muhammad, a state lawmaker representing Rano, one of the affected local government areas, said during plenary on Tuesday that the outbreak was particularly severe in Ridin and Sabuwar Kaura communities, where most of the deaths were reported.
He said limited emergency measures had been taken so far, including the provision of medication and deployment of health workers, but more needed to be done to contain the disease.
Other lawmakers at the plenary said the outbreak had spread to other communities and towns across six local government areas, including Rano, Tudun Wada, Kibiya, Bunkure, Bebeji and Kiru.
Diphtheria is a disease caused by a bacterium that affects the upper respiratory tract, and sometimes the skin. It also produces a toxin that damages the heart and the nerves.
According to a 2025 report by the World Health Organization, at least 884 diphtheria-related deaths were reported in an outbreak that affected about 240 local government areas across 30 of Nigeria's 36 states.
The global health body had previously urged Nigeria to increase vaccination coverage to at least 80 percent to ensure community protection and prevent future outbreaks in the country.
In Nigeria more than 2 million children are under-immunized, including those with zero-doses, highlighting the high risk of further spread. ■

Elected officials recently launched a congressional investigation into the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) practice.
Aviles’s son, Joshua, posted on Facebook on Tuesday that his father had been released from federal immigration custody. An immigration judge dismissed Aviles’s case on Monday, just hours after he was booked into an immigration detention center in Miami, according to Department of Justice records.
The DHS didn’t offer comment to clarify why Luis Manuel Aviles was arrested – or subsequently released.
Margaret Stock, an immigration attorney for military families, called the rapid succession of filed and dismissed charges “super unusual”.
Joshua said in a Facebook post on Saturday that he had been working 12-hour days without a break since the USS Abraham Lincoln left US shores in November. The US navy confirmed that Aviles is enlisted and serves onboard the Lincoln, where his physically demanding duties include moving aircraft on the ship.

Ottawa's new tariffs encompass more than 700 U.S. goods and are worth about $20 billion, mirroring the size of Trump's latest import taxes on Canadian wine, cement, hockey sticks and more.
The counter tariffs range from 15% to 50% and target a wide array of Canadian imports from the U.S., including dairy, seafood, appliances, wood and paper products, and clothes.
Among the most significant are 50% tariffs on American steel and aluminum, doubling the current rate. The duties on metals and wood were chosen to respond to previously imposed U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum, lumber and other products.
The new tariffs are set to take effect Sept. 8. Canada also unveiled an additional $7.5 billion package to support businesses and workers being harmed by the U.S. tariffs.
"When the United States of America asked too much and offered too little, we made a choice. We chose Canada," said Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne at a news conference Tuesday morning.
The new duties would have been averted if the two sides struck a trade deal before they took effect on Saturday. Trump had claimed earlier that week that a deal was all but complete — but Canada suspended negotiations on Friday evening, contending that the U.S. made unreasonable demands and "last-minute changes." The Trump administration has likewise accused Ottawa of blowing up the talks by seeking last-minute changes to the deal.
Trump, asked in a call with CNN about Canada's claim that the U.S. made eleventh-hour demands, said, "That sounds like me."
When pressed to clarify that he does not deny Canada's account of the collapse in trade talks, Trump said, "No, no, I don't deny anything," CNN reported Tuesday afternoon
"So no, they have to pay a fair amount. And if they don't pay a fair amount, we won't make a deal. That's fine," Trump said, according to CNN.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on CNN's report.
The collapse of the negotiations has opened a bitter new chapter in the top allies' trade war, raising tensions that were already inflamed by Trump's heavy use of tariffs and inflammatory comments toward Canada.
The new tit-for-tat tariffs could also exacerbate widespread concerns about high costs, as businesses warn they will cause major uncertainty and could make it prohibitively expensive for some sellers to trade across the border.
Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a speech following the failed trade talks, acknowledged that the decision to retaliate "will raise costs and reduce choice for Canadians."
Carney, who became prime minister last year after previously leading the Bank of Canada, has expressed a desire to diversify his country's economy in order to reduce dependence on the U.S., which he says has "changed" under Trump.
Trump has placed tariffs at the center of his agenda throughout his second term in the White House, though his use of the economic tool has faced some major legal setbacks and stoked heated pushback from other countries.
Trump lashed out at Canada on Tuesday morning, suggesting on Truth Social that the U.S. would halt business with Ontario, and repeatedly floating the prospect of renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America."
In more Truth Social posts, Trump accused Canada of targeting U.S. farmers, and complained about America's trade deficit with Canada — though that is primarily due to the U.S. making heavy purchases of Canadian crude oil.
"I deal with many countries, and Canada is easily the most difficult and unreasonable," Trump wrote in one post.
Canada's trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" earlier Tuesday morning that Ottawa did not want to abandon trade talks with the U.S.
"Our preference was to find a deal that benefits both countries," he said. "We still believe that's possible. But in the meantime, we're not waiting by the phone."

— 1776Girl (@sipjack1776) August 24, 2026
Sorties of that length are within the design endurance of the type but sit at the upper end of what is routinely observed. The RQ-4D is NATO’s variant of the Global Hawk Block 40, capable of remaining airborne for more than 30 hours at altitudes above 50,000 feet, and the airframe is built around persistence rather than speed.
The Phoenix fleet forms the Alliance Ground Surveillance force, one of the few capabilities NATO owns and operates directly rather than relying on contributions from individual members, alongside the airborne early warning fleet at Geilenkirchen. The aircraft are based at Sigonella and flown by a multinational unit, having reached initial operating capability in 2021.
Their sensor is the Multi-Platform Radar Technology Insertion Program radar, which combines synthetic aperture imaging with a ground moving target indicator mode. In practice that allows the aircraft to build a radar picture of terrain and structures and to detect vehicles and formations moving across it, from a standoff distance and without entering the airspace it is watching.
Since 2022 the fleet has flown extensively along NATO’s eastern flank, with regular missions over the Black Sea, Romania, Poland and the Baltic states, and over the eastern Mediterranean. Flights are frequently visible on public tracking, which is a deliberate feature of the way NATO conducts much of its surveillance, though aircraft do periodically operate without broadcasting.
As we reported on Tuesday, a United States Air Force C-17A Globemaster III, serial 07-7191 and using the callsign REACH 4555, flew from Riga to Moscow Vnukovo, arriving mid-morning. The aircraft had routed from Joint Base Andrews to Latvia two days earlier. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was aboard for meetings in the Russian capital, according to CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs, in what appears to be his first known trip to Russia since taking the post.
Neither Washington nor the Kremlin explained the flight while it was in the air, and military aircraft generally require approval before entering another country’s airspace, which is what made the Riga to Moscow leg notable.
NATO does not comment on individual intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance sorties, and no link between the two movements has been established. Alliance Ground Surveillance aircraft fly routinely over the Black Sea, the eastern flank and the eastern Mediterranean, and a long mission on any given day is not in itself unusual for the type.
Alliance Ground Surveillance sits under Allied Air Command and delivers its product into NATO’s intelligence structures rather than to any single nation. The programme was funded by fifteen member states, with Britain not among the original contributors, though the United Kingdom operates its own strategic ISR fleet including the RC-135W Rivet Joint from RAF Waddington, which flies missions along the same frontier.
One of those aircraft flew a patrol around Kaliningrad on 7 August, and a substantial allied air package including a NATO E-3A Sentry operated over the Baltic region on 18 August, with further flights on the two days following.

Expert witnesses challenge claim that Lindsay Clancy experienced psychosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
21:23:43 UTC
06:23:43 KST

One more day of rebuttal testimony was expected this week in the trial against Lindsay Clancy, followed by closing statements likely on Thursday.
The jury, which will likely begin deliberations on Friday, will decide whether the Massachusetts mother was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed her three children in January 2023.
On Tuesday, prosecutors put two expert witnesses on the stand who challenged the arguments made by Clancy’s defense team – specifically, that Clancy committed the acts while suffering from postpartum psychosis – a mental illness that can cause hallucinations, mood swings, delusions and more, and was hearing a voice compelling her to do it. Her attorney Kevin Reddington has also claimed Clancy had bipolar disorder and was overmedicated.
Tuesday’s testimonies capped off more than a month of testimony in a trial that has largely depended on opposing views from experts about Clancy’s mental health and her ability to understand the gravity of what she was doing. 
 It’s not disputed that she strangled the children – Callan, 8 months, Dawson, three years old, and Cora, five years old, before she allegedly jumped from a second-floor window, which left her paralyzed from the waist down. But the outcome of the trial hinges on questions surrounding Clancy’s mental state at the time of the children’s deaths. The burden of proof is on the prosecution to show Clancy was not suffering from “a mental disease or defect” and that she had enough capacity to understand “the wrongfulness or criminality of her conduct”.
Kirk Heilbrun, a forensic psychologist hired by prosecutors, initially took the stand on Friday and continued his testimony on Tuesday morning. He told the court he “did his best to have an open mind”, when he evaluated Clancy in April and that he believed she was “criminally responsible” for the deaths.
“She retained an awareness of the illegality of killing others, including her children,” he said. “Her moral awareness of this killing was influenced by her strong desire to die and, if she was dead, not to leave her children behind.”
Over nearly three days of testimony, the prosecution also focused on the timeline of events during the killings, asking Heilbrun to identify whether each step Clancy took was a decision – including her action to take the children down to the basement – in an attempt to convince the jury that these were planned murders. For each, he answered that they did.
Under cross-examination, Heilbrun’s told the court he had been paid roughly $54,000 for the 180 hours he has worked on the case on behalf of the state, and that he will likely be paid more as the trial goes on. He also told Reddington that he didn’t have experience with postpartum mental health conditions.
A recess was called at one point, after several heated exchanges between Heilbrun and Reddington during which Clancy’s attorney accused the psychologist of not reading her medical reports.
Heilbrun’s testimony on Monday prompted a request for a mistrial from Reddington after the psychologist mentioned Clancy’s Catholic faith. The request was denied, but Judge William Sullivan admonished Heilbrun for the comment and instructed the jury to disregard the reference to “the religion that the defendant was raised with”, calling it “an absolutely inappropriate area of testimony”.
After Heilbrun left the stand on Tuesday afternoon, prosecutors called forensic psychiatrist Gregory Saathoff, who is affiliated with the FBI and University of Virginia. Unlike Heilbrun, he claimed he was not paid for his testimony and had treated several women who have killed their children.
Saathoff told the court that it was unusual that Clancy hadn’t reported hearing voices before the killings and that the voices ceased afterwards. He also said he found several inconsistencies in Clancy’s account of what happened.
It is well documented that Clancy needed treatment for a mental health condition, and admitted herself to McLean, a psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts, a few weeks before the murders. Testimony from expert witnesses who were called by the defense had very different conclusions about her mental state.
Dr Phillip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist and expert in filicide, testified on Friday that Clancy was “clearly psychotic” on the day she killed her children and was not in control of her actions.
“It was almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings,” he said.
That echoed another defense witness, Paul Zeizel, the psychologist who concluded Clancy “had no appreciation for the wrongfulness of her act”.
Before the court adjourned for the day on Tuesday, Judge Sullivan told the jury that the presentation of evidence would conclude on Wednesday and that closing arguments would likely follow on Thursday. Deliberations are expected to begin on Friday. He encouraged jurors not to form their own conclusions until the very end.
“You’ve heard a lot of evidence, but you haven’t heard all of it, right? And like I said before, you haven’t heard the closing arguments of the attorneys,” Sullivan said. “You haven’t heard the law that you’re going to have to apply to this. So you still have to keep an open mind.”

20:53:39 UTC
05:53:39 KST

France is pushing to limit the duration of exemptions allowing Ukraine to buy non-European defense equipment with money from the EU’s €90 billion (roughly $105 billion) Ukraine Support Loan.
Under the exemptions, Kyiv is allowed to procure Chinese drone components and urgently needed US-made Patriot interceptors to deter Russian ballistic missiles. The rules, however, require most defense spending under the program to go to suppliers in the EU or European Economic Area, according to Euronews on Tuesday, Aug. 25.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We continue to stress that the swift approval of product schedules is crucial, including through the pragmatic use of the derogation for the purchase of materiel produced by third countries,” defense ministers from nine EU countries wrote in a July letter to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius – advocating for Ukraine to continue having maximum flexibility in procuring equipment in needs to defend itself.
France pushes for EU procurement
The package includes €30 billion ($35 billion) in economic support and €60 billion ($70 billion) in military assistance, and it was approved by EU member states in April for 2026-27.
Initially, the EU released €3.9 billion ($4.6 billion) for drones in June, followed by €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) for defense procurement earlier in August, Euronews reported.
Under the program, defense purchases Ukraine makes using the EU funds cannot have more than 35% of their total cost sourced outside the bloc.
KADORR Group’s Ruslan Kivan Receives State Award From Zelensky
Ukraine can, however, seek an exemption when EU-made alternatives cannot meet its operational needs, such as cost, production volume or delivery times.
France is now seeking to limit these exemptions, aiming to shift the procurement more toward European manufacturers. According to Euronews, Paris has one of Europe’s largest defense industries and is involved in producing the Franco-Italian SAMP/T air defense systems, often described as Europe’s closest alternative to the Patriot interceptors.
Kyiv seeks flexibility
For each exemption, Ukraine must submit detailed procurement information, including contracts identifying the equipment, supplier and delivery timetable, which the EU commission reviews before releasing the funds.
Exemptions must also be renewed whenever Ukraine requests a new payment. If an EU producer can later match a foreign supplier’s production capacity, cost and delivery terms, Brussels could decline the exemption and require Ukraine to procure the item from European suppliers, according to Euronews.
For Chinese suppliers, given China’s role as one of Russia’s most important wartime partners alongside North Korea, the EU commission must additionally verify that the companies are not subject to EU sanctions connected to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
The nine countries advocating for Ukraine’s flexibility regarding the matter are Sweden, Germany, Denmark, Estonia, Poland, Latvia, Finland, Lithuania and the Netherlands.

Dolly Parton’s Enduring Gift of Books
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
20:52:53 UTC
05:52:53 KST

Dolly Parton, who rose from poverty to become the nation’s most beloved country music legend and a unifying literacy hero, died today at her home in Nashville, according to a family statement.
Thirty years ago, in honor of her father, Robert Lee Parton, who could neither read nor write, she launched Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library in Sevier County, Tennessee, the Appalachian community where she grew up. The goal was simple: put carefully selected, age-appropriate books into children’s homes before kindergarten, every month, at no cost to families.
Three decades later, that local initiative has become an international program to promote early literacy that mails free books to children from birth to age five through partnerships with the Dollywood Foundation, local program partners, states, communities, and donors. It operates in English-predominant countries—the US, Canada, the UK, Australia, and the Republic of Ireland, but it has expanded its reach to include bilingual Spanish-English options in some states, as well as audio and Braille books.
Recent program reports count more than 300 million books gifted and more than 3 million books mailed each month.
Parton’s philosophy was to treat literacy as a birthright for everyone. A child enrolled from birth can receive a home library of up to 60 books, each arriving in the child’s name.
Learn more at https://imaginationlibrary.com/. Supporters can contribute directly at https://donate.imaginationlibrary.com, where gifts help local partners keep books moving from shelves to doorsteps.

Air Force Plans Support Contract That Could Keep RQ-4s Flying Into 2030s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
20:34:07 UTC
05:34:07 KST

The Air Force is planning to award Northrop Grumman a contract that could allow the RQ-4 Global Hawk to keep flying into 2033.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center posted a presolicitation notice Aug. 17 saying it plans to award Northrop a sole-source contract for development, modernization, retrofit, and sustainment of the surveillance drone.
Those support activities include program management, hardware and software upgrades and sustainment, engineering and onsite support, logistics, training development and administration, and other test and integration activities.
In its 2026 defense policy bill, Congress barred the Air Force from retiring any of its remaining nine RQ-4s until the end of fiscal 2030. This new notice suggests the service could be planning to fly them longer than that.
This contract will last for as long as five and a half years, beginning in January 2028 and potentially running until the end of June 2033. It will include a one-year base period and four one-year ordering periods, taking the contract through the end of 2032, as well as an option to extend the deal up to six more months.
The notice did not say how much the contract might be worth. An Air Force spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that cost information was not available for release. AFLCMC said in the notice that it plans to issue a solicitation in September, with responses expected by February 2027.
The RQ-4, which is made by Northrop Grumman, is a strategic long-endurance, high-altitude intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance unmanned aircraft. It can capture imagery or signals intelligence or conduct ground moving target indication.
The Air Force at one point had 33 RQ-4s, some of which were forward deployed to places like Yokota Air Base, Japan; Andersen Air Force Base, Guam; or installations in the Middle East. But the Global Hawk fleet started shrinking in earnest in the early 2020s as the Air Force sought to divest older models.
In 2022, the service announced plans to retire the entire fleet by 2027. Congress intervened, however, and has extended its prohibition on retirements several times, most recently through 2030.
An Air Force spokesperson said in a statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine the service no longer has a projected retirement date for the RQ-4.
“To ensure operational continuity, this contract is structured with a one-year base period of performance followed by individual, one-year option periods,” the spokesperson said. “This structure grants Air Force leadership the flexibility to sustain the fleet as needed up to 2032, without committing to the full duration up front.”
