Syrian Democratic Forces commander lands in Damascus for national unification talks - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
17:18:35 UTC
02:18:35 KST

Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) commander Mazloum Abdi arrived in Damascus for important talks on August 25.
The talks come at a key time for Syria. The US rescinded sanctions on Syria on August 24, and on August 23, reports say Syrian and Israeli officials met in Amman in a meeting backed by the US.
The SDF was the key force that helped defeat ISIS. It was backed by the US. Now it is integrating into the new Syrian security forces.
As such, the Abdi meetings in Damascus are a symbol of the success of integration in Syria and also unification of the country.
Six months ago, it was unclear how the SDF-controlled areas would integrate into Damascus rule. There was a lot of fear among Kurds and others about the process. There were clashes. Some worried that the US would walk away and leave the SDF isolated.
Damascus leadership rooted in al-Qaeda, SDF rooted in Kurdish leftism
They feared Damascus would seize the moment and conquer eastern Syria rather than pursue a process in which both sides gained positions, with respect and power-sharing.
The leadership in Damascus mostly comes from Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, which is a conservative Islamic and right-leaning movement that once had roots in al-Qaeda.
By contrast, the leadership of the SDF is far-left and has roots in the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). The movements are very different. One is Arabic, one is Kurdish.
One where most of the women wear hijab or veils, and another where women are fighters and serve as co-leaders in many positions. Both are deeply ideological groups. However, they know they must work together after years of war in Syria.
Asharq al-Awsat noted on August 25 that Abdi and top SDF official Ilham Ahmed held talks with Syrian government officials in Damascus on Monday as the two sides seek to complete integration measures by the end of the month.
The report said, “sources in Damascus told Asharq Al-Awsat that education was the main issue discussed at the meeting, which was held under a media blackout.”
This report added that “the talks came about 20 days after Abdi and Ahmed met President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus. Sources said that meeting failed to produce agreement on several disputed issues despite both sides’ commitment to implementing their January 29 accord.”
It’s worth noting that the new developments come a week after another announcement by Abdi that civil and military integration with Damascus was largely complete.
"I want to say that the phase of integrating military, security and administrative institutions into national state institutions is complete and finished," Abdi said at the time, according to France 24. "From now on, we begin a new phase," he added.
Meanwhile, Asharq reported that “Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said on August 18 that several issues remained unresolved, including how to integrate the Women’s Protection Units and Kurdish-language education.”
Rudaw also reported that Abdi was heading to Damascus. This comes after Abdi gave a long interview recently about what comes next in Syria.
Some SDF members had sought to boycott Syrian elections and other Syrian initiatives. The SDF has been tied to civilian organizations such as the AANES that ran eastern Syria over the last decade, as well as the PYD and other groups.
These groups have largely been unwilling to actively participate in Damascus’ new civilian rule. However, some SDF members have chosen to work with Damascus. Besides Abdi, this also includes Sipan Hamo, who has taken a role in the defense ministry.
Kurdish education, language a priority in government talks
Rudaw noted, regarding Abdi’s agenda today, that “Abdi also said that Kurdish education has been a priority in talks with Damascus, reiterating that they will not accept Kurdish as an optional language in Rojava but want it to remain the main language of instruction.
He said they were open to Arabic being taught alongside Kurdish in the region, as proposed by the government.” Abdi is seeking to move from being a military commander to working on Kurdish civil rights issues and domestic policy.
“Kurdish officials want school curricula translated into Kurdish, while Damascus proposed offering Kurdish language as an optional subject, arguing that separate curricula could prompt similar demands from other Syrian communities,” Asharq noted.
Elham Ahmed, a key Kurdish official, also went to Damascus with Abdi, the reports said. She wrote on X/Twitter that “Mother-tongue education is a fundamental right of every people. Languages are creations of the Merciful God; they must not be banned, nor should their sanctity be diminished.”
She added, “We believe that by recognizing these fundamental rights, Syria can become a model of justice, stability, and peace in the region.”
Asharq’s report noted that Syria’s president Al-Sharaa “issued Decree No. 13 on January 16, recognizing Syrian Kurdish citizens as an ‘essential and integral part of the Syrian people’ and their cultural and linguistic identity as part of Syria’s national identity.”
This came amidst clashes with Kurds in Aleppo. Weeks later, the Syrian government swept into eastern Syria, and it was clear the SDF would need to accommodate and work with Damascus.
Syria’s work with the Kurdish leadership is important. Several Kurds are in the new parliament in Damascus. Many come from the ENKS or KNC Kurdish political background, which is very different than the SDF and PYD background of officials from the AANES.
Although this seems like a lot of groups to keep track of, it’s not as complex as it seems. Kurds are largely divided into groups on the far left that have historical links to the PKK, or they are more centrist nationalists, often linked to groups that have alliances with the Kurdistan Democratic Party.
There are also smaller Kurdish religious parties and the PUK in the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq. Kurds, like all groups, have their own internal political differences.
This has played out in Syria. When the SDF and AANES were in power in eastern Syria from 2015 to early 2026, they mostly sidelined the KNC and ENKS.
Now that Damascus is unifying Syria, it has preferred to invite the Kurdish opposition groups to parliament. This reduces tensions with Turkey, which has opposed any PKK-linked officials in the past.
However, Damascus knows that those like Abdi and Elham Ahmad have support in Syria, and there is recognition on all sides that they should play a future role. What that role will be is unclear.
Sipan Hamo, the SDF commander, has settled into his role as a deputy minister of defense for eastern Syria.

Ukraine at 35: The view from Russia
Thirty-five years after Ukraine declared independence, the anniversary offers little cause for celebration from Moscow’s perspective. Russian officials and commentators argue that a country which inherited one of the Soviet Union’s strongest industrial bases has spent the ensuing decades squandering that legacy, surrendering its real sovereignty to the West, and building a national identity around hostility toward Russia and rejection of the two nations’ shared past.
RT gathered comments from Russian diplomats, politicians, and analysts on what – if anything – remains of that independence and where the country’s chosen path is ultimately leading.
Vassily Nebenzia, Russia’s representative to the United Nations:
Ukraine is marking the 35th anniversary of its so-called “independence” with great fanfare. But is there really anything to celebrate? Over the past three and a half decades, successive governments have run the country into the ground. Those who shouted the loudest about Ukraine’s independence and bright future have, whether knowingly or not, been the very ones destroying it. Its current dictator – the self-proclaimed “president of peace,” whose term has long since expired – has been particularly successful in this regard.
With the active involvement of the collective West – whose countries claim to embody “civilization” and “democracy” – Ukraine has been turned into a “Zelensky concentration camp.” All dissent and political opposition have been outlawed, while those brave enough to voice an alternative point of view are imprisoned without trial or due process – or physically eliminated. The unprecedented persecution of the canonical Orthodox Church has been accompanied by brutal attacks on clergy and parishioners. Meanwhile, history is being rewritten wholesale: the Soviet legacy is repudiated, while Hitler’s accomplices and collaborators – responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Russians, Jews, Poles, and Ukrainians during World War II – are glorified.
It is not only the Russian language that is under attack. Everything associated with our shared past is being systematically erased. The Kiev authorities display a truly primitive form of Russophobia and xenophobia – directed, in practice, even against their own citizens, many of whom are Russian not only by ancestry but also by cultural identity.
Perhaps nowhere is the wretchedness of Kiev’s rulers more evident than in one seemingly absurd example. Ukraine has even imposed sanctions on the Russian animated series Masha and the Bear, claiming that it promotes Russian militaristic narratives.
Having failed to achieve the desired results on the battlefield, the Kiev regime has now descended into outright terrorism against Russia’s civilian population. At the same time, Zelensky continues begging his Western patrons for more weapons and ammunition, which are then used to strike Russian cities, residential neighborhoods, and civilian infrastructure. The calculation is obvious: to frighten the public, sow chaos, and destabilize the situation inside Russia. Terrorism has become Kiev’s last resort in its attempt to reverse a situation that is increasingly turning against it.
Sergey Poletaev, analyst, CFDP member, co-founder and editor of the Vatfor Project:
Ukraine marks its 35th anniversary as more than just a failed state. It has become a country reduced to a single function, whose only reason for existing is to wage war against Russia. It is not fighting for its own interests, since everyone understands that Ukraine’s only chance of surviving in any form is to make peace with Russia immediately.
Whatever the ultimate outcome of the war, Ukraine has already perished in it. Its population has been cut in half, it has lost one-fifth of its territory, its industrial base and energy sector have been destroyed, and, most recently, its agricultural exports have been severed. Countries do not recover from something like this.
And all of it has been sacrificed for the interests of Ukraine’s Western masters. The country is now dying to give France, Britain, and Germany a chance to establish themselves in a post-American world. But Ukrainians spent 35 years consciously pursuing this path, and now they are getting exactly what they worked so hard to achieve.
Happy Dependence Day, neighbors.
Dmitry Rodionov, Director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies at the Institute for Intonational Development (IID):
The document that laid the foundation for Ukrainian “statehood” was adopted by the Supreme Soviet of the Ukrainian SSR exactly 35 years ago.
Ukraine marked the occasion with its customary pomp, despite the ongoing hostilities. After all, the “dignity” and “unbreakable spirit” of the “Ukrainian nation” must be emphasized at every opportunity. Yet much of this pageantry stems from the architects of Ukrainian “statehood” recognizing just how artificial and fraudulent their creation really is – hence their determination to make it appear as real as possible.
Frankly, they have done a poor job of it throughout the past 35 years, although the leaders of the Kiev regime have bent over backward trying. But no amount of whitewashing can change the facts, and the history of “independent Ukraine” contains far too many dark chapters for the country ever to establish itself as a viable state.
The declaration of Ukrainian independence was riddled with legal inconsistencies. These became a kind of foundational birth defect that predetermined the future of the Ukrainian “state,” which ultimately turned into a textbook failed state. Its historic collapse was baked in from the beginning, but regrettably, the process has dragged on for years and continues to claim more and more lives.
There are more than enough such inconsistencies to declare Ukraine a nonexistent state and withdraw its recognition as an entity under international law. But what would be the point? Ukraine’s fate is now being decided on the battlefield. Kiev still has a chance to preserve at least some form of statehood, yet it stubbornly refuses to do so, clinging instead to historical phantoms such as the “1991 borders.”
History will therefore put everything in its proper place and bury the temporary geopolitical aberration known as “Ukraine” once and for all.
Anatoly Viktorov, Russian Ambassador to Israel:
On August 24, 1991, Ukraine adopted its Act of Declaration of Independence. The 35 years that have passed since then provide an opportunity to look back and acknowledge with regret that Ukraine cannot claim any genuine autonomy in either its foreign or domestic policy.
Western countries have completely stripped Ukraine of its international legal personality, placing it under direct foreign control and turning the country into a staging ground for threats to Russia’s security.
Ukraine once inherited a unique legacy from the Soviet Union: advanced industry, infrastructure, and agriculture. Regrettably, instead of developing as an independent democracy, pursuing national progress, and building a society that respected the legitimate rights and interests of people of every nationality and faith, the Kiev authorities began persecuting the Russian language, culture, traditions, religion, and our shared historical memory.

Russia’s achievement of all the objectives of its special military operation would not only serve our vital interests in security and the protection of human rights, but also help curb modern Ukraine’s unchecked and destructive influence on the very foundations of international relations.

Before becoming part of the Russian Empire, Ukraine was dependent on other states, particularly Poland. After 1991, that dependence merely changed direction: Ukraine became dependent on Western countries – above all the United States, Poland, and Britain. It possesses neither political nor economic sovereignty, so there is no reason for it to celebrate Independence Day.

Türkiye will stay on path of development despite regional conflicts: President Erdogan

Gizem Nisa Çebi Demir
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Türkiye will continue pursuing development and prosperity despite conflicts in the region, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Tuesday.
“Türkiye is on the right path, God willing. Its direction is clear, and sooner or later it will reach its destination,” Erdogan said in an address following a Cabinet meeting in Ahlat, Bitlis.
“Türkiye is safe. The trust entrusted to safe hands, representing 86 million people, is secure. We will under no circumstances allow this sacred trust to be cast into shadow,” he added.
The Cabinet met under Erdogan’s chairmanship at the Ahlat Presidential Complex.
Erdogan said the meeting addressed issues including foreign policy, trade, security and the government’s “Terror-Free Türkiye” process.
He said regional economic crises were affecting Türkiye but the government would remain committed to its goals in employment, exports, agriculture and tourism.
On the economic impact of tensions between Iran and the US, Erdogan said: “As the shockwave caused by the Iran-America tensions in the global economy gradually loses its effect over time, we will have the opportunity to clearly see its repercussions on daily life.” 
‘Terror-Free Türkiye’ process
Turning to the “Terror-Free Türkiye” process, Erdogan highlighted a law recently approved by parliament with 467 votes, calling it a historic consensus and saying it had strengthened the process.
“The Turkish democracy has the maturity to resolve any problem when it acts with an understanding that puts the country and the nation at the center rather than daily political calculations,” he said.
Erdogan called on people from all political views to contribute to the process, describing it as a matter concerning the entire state and its 86 million people, rather than only the government and its alliance.
“Come, let us fulfill our debt of gratitude to our martyrs and veterans properly by ridding Türkiye of terrorism,” Erdogan said.
He warned that any initiative that complicates, sabotages or provokes the process, or stands against it, would be held responsible before history.
Erdogan also called on civil society organizations and opinion leaders in the region to contribute more to the process.
Regional conflicts and peace
Turning to regional conflicts, Erdogan reiterated Türkiye’s efforts to promote peace.
“As Türkiye seeks peace for everyone in its region, together with its citizens, the plans of criminal networks built on blood and conflict are being disrupted,” he said.
“We see what bloody scenarios are being devised for our region. God willing, we will not allow them to be carried out.”
“We will not refrain from working to establish peace in our region because some do not want it, are concerned about it or see their plans disrupted,” Erdogan added.
He said Türkiye would continue supporting its neighbors’ recovery despite opposition from what he described as “criminal networks with the blood of innocent people on their hands.”
“We have no hidden agenda or intentions, contrary to what some claim. Our aim is for an atmosphere of peace to prevail around us,” Erdogan said.

Hackers published a ‘Sberbank memo’ war-gaming eight endings to the war in Ukraine. One source in Russia’s financial market thinks a chatbot wrote it.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
17:09:37 UTC
02:09:37 KST

Hackers published a ‘Sberbank memo’ war-gaming eight endings to the war in Ukraine. One source in Russia’s financial market thinks a chatbot wrote it.
The hacker group Black Mirror has published screenshots of a purported Sberbank analytical memo that lists eight scenarios for ending the full-scale war between Russia and Ukraine. The document is dated April 2026, meaning it was prepared before Ukrainian forces stepped up strikes on oil refineries and logistics sites. According to the hackers, the memo came from correspondence between Sberbank board chairman German Gref and an unnamed correspondent. The authenticity of the screenshots has not been confirmed, and it is not known who wrote the memo. Sberbank has not commented on the reported leak of the correspondence. Meduza runs through the scenarios outlined in the document.
Update: A source in Russia’s financial sector told Meduza that they had not seen the original of the “memo” but suspected the material was generated by an AI chatbot. That theory is backed up by Pangram, an AI-detection service, which found that 83% of the document’s English-language text was machine-generated.
1. Russia’s decisive military advantage
Probability: 7%
This scenario envisions Russia gaining full control over the four “new constituent entities” — the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic (“DPR”), the self-proclaimed Luhansk People’s Republic (“LPR”), Zaporizhzhia region, and Kherson region — within their administrative borders. The document also mentions Kharkiv region as a kind of “political symbol.” It does not contemplate taking Kyiv, but Russia would have to force Ukraine into talks “from a position of absolute military dominance.”
The document says Russia cannot carry this out without a second wave of mobilization — 300,000 to 500,000 people. Under current conditions, contract soldiers are enough to replace Russia’s monthly losses of 20,000 to 25,000 troops, but not enough to build new strike groups. The country would also need to fix its rear-area air defenses, since Ukrainian strikes on oil and military facilities — including strikes with “Flamingo” missiles — could make the cost of an offensive “unacceptable” for Russia.
Analysts also point to the need to increase air support several times over and to field autonomous drone swarms coordinated by artificial intelligence. The document says Western software could help Ukraine do this faster.
Another important point:
- Analysts at the Russian state bank Sberbank put Vladimir Putin’s real approval rating at 55% to 65%. Mobilization could cut that by another 10 to 15 percentage points, and only a guaranteed successful offensive would offset the decline.
2. ‘Exhaustion of the West’: peace on Russia’s terms
Probability: 12%
In this scenario, Ukraine loses political — and with it, financial — support from its Western allies. That would require three factors to coincide: U.S. support for Ukraine falling below 30%, an energy crisis in Europe this coming winter, and a domestic political crisis in Ukraine itself.
Russia could then secure the lifting of some sanctions and guarantees that Ukraine will not join NATO. Analysts consider each of these three factors likely on its own but doubt all three will occur at once.
The conflict would be frozen without a formal treaty, and Ukraine could still join the European Union. The document draws a comparison to Cyprus, which does not control all of its own territory: Northern Cyprus is under Turkish control and recognized by no country other than Turkey, yet the Republic of Cyprus remains an EU member.
Another important point:
- Sberbank estimates that, as of April 2026, Russia’s economy can hold out for another 12 to 18 months under current conditions. Analysts say time favors Russia, since every month that passes weakens the Western coalition.
3. ‘Trump’s deal’: a frozen conflict with partial sanctions relief
Probability: 32%
This scenario resembles the previous one but, in Sberbank’s view, is more likely. The conflict freezes, most likely without a formal peace treaty; Ukraine does not join NATO; and some sanctions are lifted. The United States accepts Russian control over the four regions while still legally recognizing Ukraine’s 1991 borders. The EU does not recognize the new borders.
Analysts put the scenario’s probability high because they expect Donald Trump to want a deal closed before the November 2026 midterm elections, which would push him to pressure both sides. He would threaten Russia with lifting all restrictions on arming Ukraine, and Ukraine with cutting off support entirely. A successful deal would let Trump stake a claim to the Nobel Peace Prize.
The problem: neither side trusts Trump’s long-term guarantees, and any change in the U.S. administration could reignite the conflict. A durable deal would require a multilateral format, but Trump shuns such arrangements, and European countries would oppose the deal.
Another important point:
- For Russia, this scenario would amount to neither victory nor defeat. The document says the Kremlin could sell the deal at home as “forcing NATO to retreat,” which would boost its approval rating. But an unfinished war could also fuel opposition sentiment.
4. A ‘Korean freeze’: without a formal agreement
Probability: 22%
This scenario would play out if neither side could achieve a decisive breakthrough. The conflict fades without a formal agreement, the front line stabilizes, and the intensity of fighting declines — though the drone war continues.
Analysts say this is possible if Trump loses interest in Ukraine and turns his attention to another country or to domestic politics. The EU would then shoulder the bulk of support for Ukraine and speed up the country’s accession to the union.
For Russia, this would mean not just a “normalization of the war” but an economic respite as well. Sberbank says the risks to those in power are relatively low: the ruling party United Russia’s low approval rating — 31% — points to war fatigue, but analysts see no revolutionary potential in it.
Another important point:
- Both sides could use the pause to rearm on a large scale over the following three to five years. The next stage of the conflict would be a technologically different war altogether.
5. A protracted war (another two to three years)
Probability: 15%
The conflict grinds on without a freeze or breakthroughs, with Russian losses and front-line advances holding at current levels. This scenario would mean a total failure of diplomacy.
Ukraine would face a humanitarian catastrophe and demographic collapse. Russia would be forced to fight “at the outer limit of what its economy can bear,” though analysts do not expect significant protests at first. Birth rates would continue to fall, and skilled workers would keep leaving the country, while Putin’s real approval rating would fall below 50%.
At some point, the Russian public might break its silence — something that would happen if living standards fell noticeably, as they did during perestroika from 1986 to 1991.
Another important point:
- This scenario implies a further tightening of sanctions. Russia’s isolation would continue to grow, though it would not reach the level of Iran or North Korea, since the country would still be trading with China, India, and others.
6. Peace on compromise terms
Probability: 5%
Significant political change on one side of the conflict could lead to a full-fledged peace treaty with mutual concessions. Analysts doubt, though, that Putin’s position will weaken substantially — they are more inclined to bet on a change of power in Ukraine or on outside pressure on both sides, including from China on Russia.
Under this scenario, Russia could return part of the occupied territory to Ukraine — Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions in part, or all previously captured territories — in exchange for recognition of Russian control over Crimea and part of the Donbas. Ukraine would get security guarantees and the possibility of joining the EU and even NATO, though not sooner than 15 to 25 years from now.
This would be the most difficult scenario for both sides. Ukraine would effectively be forced into capitulation, while Russia would have to explain to its own population what the war — which cost hundreds of thousands of lives — was actually for.
Another important point:
- Russia would also have to overhaul its current narrative. It has written the “four new constituent entities” into its constitution, which would make returning any of that territory politically very difficult.
7. Peace on Ukraine’s and Europe’s terms
Probability: 2%
Sberbank rates this the least likely scenario of all: Russia withdraws to the 2014 or 1991 borders and pays reparations, while Ukraine joins NATO. Crimea would either be returned to Ukraine or become the subject of negotiations.
Such an outcome could follow from an economic collapse in Russia (GDP falling by more than 15%, hyperinflation), a catastrophic military defeat, or regime change. Analysts consider all three unlikely.
Another important point:
- The document says this outcome would require the eighth and final scenario to unfold — and analysts currently see no preconditions for that.
8. The ‘wild card’: black swans
Probability: 5% (combined for all sub-variants)
Here, Sberbank considers unlikely events that could radically alter the course of the conflict. None of the possibilities below can be forecast using standard analytical methods.
Nuclear escalation: Russia’s use of tactical nuclear weapons. This would bring instant and total isolation, cutting Russia off from Chinese and Indian support — and could also draw a NATO response.
“A new Chernobyl”: a Russian strike on a nuclear facility such as the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant or the Chernobyl sarcophagus. Such a strike would set off a humanitarian catastrophe on a scale that would eclipse either side’s war aims, and international pressure would force an immediate ceasefire.
A direct NATO–Russia clash: a provocation — in the Baltic Sea, for example — or an incident involving a missile or drone on NATO territory. A series of such incidents or a deliberate strike would escalate into direct conflict.
Regime change: Putin’s removal from power by the security services in order to make peace, or Ukraine’s military leadership putting forward an alternative to Volodymyr Zelensky. The document says a change of power in Russia is unlikely: “Prigozhin has been eliminated, Shoigu has been transferred, Surkov has been removed.”
An Iranian cascade: a new round of conflict in the Middle East involving the United States, Iran, Israel, and other countries. It would sharply increase Russia’s oil revenues, trigger an energy crisis in Europe, and push Ukraine further down the Western agenda.
A technological surprise: a breakthrough in AI-assisted drone swarm control, or a cyberattack on critical infrastructure in Russia or Ukraine. The first would hand one side an absolute tactical advantage; the second would strip its target of the ability to wage war.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. U.K. estate used as Wayne Manor in "Batman Begins" must be surveyed for bats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
17:09:06 UTC
02:09:06 KST

Historic U.K. estate used as Wayne Manor in "Batman Begins" must be surveyed for bats, officials say
A British estate used as a filming location in Christopher Nolan's "Batman Begins" may be taken from its owners if repair work, including bat surveys, does not commence, according to local council notices.
The stately home was built between 1852 and 1854 in Buckinghamshire, a region in southeast England. It stood in for Wayne Manor in the 2005 superhero blockbuster, which starred Christian Bale and Katie Holmes.
Buckinghamshire Council served the company that owns the estate with a formal listed-buildings repair notice amid reports of deteriorating conditions at the property. CBS News partner BBC News reported that the notice was dated Aug. 4.
The building could be placed on the market – unless the owners show evidence that a licensed bat ecologist has been appointed to conduct surveys. The owners have one month to begin the process and provide evidence, council deputy leader Peter Strachan told CBS News. If the notice is not dealt with, the council could seek government approval to acquire the mansion, though this would be subject to further legal action, according to the BBC.
Mentmore Towers is considered a Grade I heritage building, which means it must have a special architectural or historical interest. Around 2.5% of buildings in the United Kingdom, including Buckingham Palace and the Tower of London, are among the Grade I-listed buildings that have been preserved.
The property has been owned by Mentmore Towers Limited since 1999. That company is owned by Simon Halabi, a Syrian-British property developer. In 2007, Halabi was named Britain's 14th richest man, according to The Times. However, in 2010, the tycoon was declared bankrupt over a $76 million loan he received from a failed Icelandic bank.
In addition to being used in "Batman Begins," Mentmore Towers was also featured in other films, including "The Mummy Returns" and "Johnny English." It was also used as a filming location in the Spice Girls' music video for the 1998 song "Goodbye." Before appearing onscreen, it was home to the Rothschild family. But despite its famous past, the building has "fallen into an increasingly worsening state of disrepair over recent years," the council told CBS News.
Historic England, a public body responsible for advising the government on protecting historic sites, lists the building as being in "very bad" condition and at risk of "further rapid deterioration." The organization noted that Mentmore Towers is on its Heritage at Risk register, "which identifies sites most at risk of being lost through neglect, decay or inappropriate development."
The BBC describes the building as having deteriorating roofs, chimneys, rooflights, roof lanterns and leadwork. According to Save Britain's Heritage, an independent charity that works to protect and restore historic buildings in England, permissions to repair the roof were granted in 2016, but the work was not completed.
The ecological survey is the first step of the repair work. By August 2027, the property owners must have conducted three such surveys, as well as acquired any essential historical licenses to undertake the necessary repairs.
The BBC reported that the owners must demonstrate that they are taking steps to appoint a contractor with appropriate experience for repairing listed buildings and roofs that are of similar size and historic appearance. Once repair work begins, Buckinghamshire Council and Historic England officers must be allowed to inspect it weekly, the BBC reported.
"We welcome this action taken by Buckinghamshire Council requiring the current owner to carry out urgent and overdue repairs to this great house," said Henrietta Billings, the director of Save Britain's Heritage. "We urge the owners, who have owned the building for over 25 years, to step up and undertake immediate repairs. This exceptional landmark has been neglected for too long."

Canada hits US with counter-tariffs targeting hundreds of products

Canada hits US with counter-tariffs on more than 700 products
Canada imposes tariffs on US goods worth $19.9bn goods which will take effect on September 8 as trade talks with Washington collapse.
Canada has announced retaliatory tariffs against the United States as the trade war between Washington and Ottawa escalates, impacting hundreds of products.
On Tuesday, the Canadian government said it would impose tariffs on 27.6 billion Canadian dollars, or $19.9bn, worth of US goods, matching “dollar for dollar” the new US duties that Trump imposed. It also announced a new plan for financial support for businesses caught in the trade war.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Nvidia, Supermicro employees charged over export of AI servers to China
- list 2 of 4Who are Iran’s top trading partners US would need to target to isolate it?
- list 3 of 4How can a heavily indebted football club afford Mo Salah?
- list 4 of 4China says will safeguard its own interests as US expands Iran sanctions
The counter-tariffs will impact more than 700 products, the government said in a statement, and will target the steel and aluminium, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, plastics and electronics sectors.
The tariffs will range from 15 percent to 50 percent and take effect on September 8.
The Canadian government also announced a new 7.5 billion-Canadian-dollar ($5.42bn) funding package to help small- and medium-sized businesses mitigate financial risks caused by the new tariffs.
Negotiations deteriorate
The new tariffs come after US President Donald Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on Canadian products on Saturday, impacting $20bn worth of Canadian goods, only days after announcing a deal.
On Monday, Trump announced new tariffs on Canadian autos, which would double existing tariffs to 50 percent from January 1.
Trump has also hurled insults at Canada in recent days. On Tuesday, Trump said that he was considering renaming Lake Ontario – the easternmost of the Great Lakes, which borders the Canadian province of Ontario – “Lake America”. The US president also referred to Prime Minister Mark Carney as “Governor Carney”, echoing longstanding remarks about annexing Canada as the “51st state”.
On Tuesday, Trump claimed in a post on Truth Social that the US lost $60bn to Canada annually for the last decade.
But Canada maintains a trade surplus with the US of 9.9 billion Canadian dollars ($7.1bn), according to Statistics Canada. Al Jazeera reached out to the White House for clarification but did not receive a response.
US consumers feel the pinch
The impact of US tariffs is expected to be felt by US businesses and consumers. Cars and auto parts have been exempt from the tariffs that were imposed on Saturday, but have been a point of contention between Washington and Ottawa.
Canada is the largest purchaser of US-made cars, which could put pressure on American carmakers who rely on Canadian demand.
Meanwhile, US households could face higher prices on 550 consumer goods imported from Canada because of Trump’s 50 percent tariff. Those products include ice skates, toilet paper, some alcoholic beverages and paint.
That could drastically affect Americans, according to a report from the Kiel Institute for the World Economy, an economic think tank, which found that US importers and consumers absorb 96 percent of the tariff burden.
Markets react
The price of gold, which is largely considered a safe investment in times of economic uncertainty, is trending upwards after falling nearly 1 percent earlier on Tuesday. It remains largely flat, down only 0.03 percent at $4,696 per ounce.
The US dollar has remained fairly stable, down 0.04 percent on Tuesday to 98.96, while the Canadian dollar index has risen comparably by 0.04 percent to 72.27.
On Wall Street, the Nasdaq is up 0.5 percent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average is flat, and the S&P 500 is up 0.2 percent.
In Toronto, the S&P/TSX Composite Index is up 0.6 percent.

Iran army ground forces commander: “borders are our red line”
TEHRAN- Brigadier General Ali Jahanshahi, commander of Iran’s army ground Forces, has warned Takfiri terrorist groups and other hostile elements operating beyond Iran’s borders that any attempt to create insecurity or carry out attacks near the country’s territory would trigger a “decisive and crushing” response.
Jahanshahi issued the warning during a visit to Iran’s northeastern border areas, where he assessed the combat readiness, defensive capabilities and deployment of army ground units stationed along the frontier.
 
 “Any movement, hostile act or action against the borders of the Islamic Republic will be met with a firm and crushing response,” Jahanshahi said, stressing that Iran’s borders constitute a red line for the country’s Armed Forces.
Drone and artillery capabilities within reach
The commander said the ground forces had the capability to respond effectively against positions and bases belonging to groups that threaten Iran’s security.
“In the event of any aggression or violation, all positions and bases of those threatening the country’s security will be within range of the army ground forces’ drone and artillery capabilities,” he said, adding that the Armed Forces’ response to any threat would be “swift, precise and deterrent.”
Jahanshahi said the ground forces were operating at their highest level of combat readiness and had developed specific operational plans for confronting different types of threats. He also highlighted the deployment of new weapons and military equipment as part of efforts to strengthen the force’s defensive and operational capabilities.
He warned that any incursion or aggression against Iranian territory would result in a stronger response, saying the ground forces would not allow hostile elements to compromise the security of Iran or its border communities.
24 hour surveillance along the borders
Jahanshahi said the ground forces maintained continuous surveillance of developments along the country’s frontiers, supported by 'a comprehensive intelligence command.'
He said Iranian forces monitor and track hostile movements across the borders around the clock, allowing them to identify and neutralize ground-combat operational plans before they can be implemented and prevent hostile groups from achieving their objectives near Iranian territory.
The commander also pointed to the deployment of mobile assault and rapid-reaction units along the northeastern borders. He said the combination of these units, continuous intelligence monitoring and the broader readiness of Iran’s Armed Forces had created an effective deterrent against potential threats.
“Today, the entire capacity and capabilities of the ground forces units deployed along the borders are dedicated to ensuring security, safeguarding the borders and confronting any threat,” Jahanshahi said. “We will not allow any enemy to undermine the security of our people, including our border residents.”
Jahanshahi also referred to the ground forces’ performance during the latest round of what Iranian officials describe as unprovoked US-Israeli aggression against Iran, from February 28 to April 7. He praised the force’s use of its drone capabilities, including precision strikes against US positions in the region, as part of Iran’s military response.
The remarks underscore Tehran’s continued emphasis on border security and rapid-response capabilities amid concerns over militant groups and other hostile elements operating in areas adjacent to Iran’s frontiers.

Six bodies of migrants recovered in southeast Libya, security directorate says
TRIPOLI, Aug 25 - Libya's security authorities recovered the bodies of at least six migrants in the southeast of the country after their vehicle broke down in the desert, the Alwahat Security Directorate said in a statement on Tuesday.
The Directorate said the bodies were recovered in a desert area about 200 km (124 miles) northwest of the town of Jalu.
Libya has become a transit route for migrants fleeing conflict and poverty to Europe via dangerous routes across the desert and over the Mediterranean since the toppling of former leader Muammar Gaddafi in a NATO-backed uprising in 2011.
Two bodies were found inside the broken-down vehicle, three more were found about four km (2.5 miles) away from the vehicle, and one body was found about 10 km (six miles) away, after tracking their footprints, the Directorate said.
According to the vehicle documents, its owner was from Chad, the Directorate said.
It added that in the same incident 19 migrants were rescued on Sunday, although it did not say where they were rescued.
According to the brother of the vehicle's owner, who was one of the 19 rescued migrants, there was another vehicle with them that took the fuel from the broken-down vehicle and continued the journey, the Directorate said.
Pictures that the Directorate posted showed security staff accompanied by members of the Fifth Battalion of the 129th Brigade recovering the bodies in a desert area and placing them in black plastic bags. REUTERS

More than 20 Marvel universe actors join campaign for release of Palestinian politician Marwan Barghouti

More than 20 Marvel universe actors join campaign for release of Palestinian politician Marwan Barghouti
- Mark Ruffalo, Benedict Cumberbatch, Ian McKellen and other featured Marvel actors sign international appeal calling for Barghouti's release from Israeli prison
Yasin Yorgancı
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
ANKARA
More than 20 actors who have appeared in Marvel universe films and TV series have joined an international campaign calling for the release of Palestinian politician Marwan Barghouti, who has been held by Israel and, according to the campaign, kept in solitary confinement since 2023.
"We express our grave concern at the continuing imprisonment of Marwan Barghouti, his violent mistreatment and denial of legal rights whilst imprisoned," the campaign, known as "Free Marwan Now," said on Instagram last week.
The campaign was launched by Barghouti's family and supporters and has attracted the backing of more than 200 figures from film, music, literature, and other cultural fields.
"We call upon the United Nations and the Governments of the World to actively seek the release of Marwan Barghouti from Israeli prison," the statement added.
Among the signatories are actors with prominent Marvel contributions, including Ian McKellen, who played Magneto in the X-Men series, plus Rebecca Hall, Riz Ahmed, Jason Flemyng, Elliot Page, Hugo Weaving (famed from the Matrix films), Zawe Ashton, Emma Corrin, May Calamawy, Brian Cox, Dan Stevens, Rob Delaney, and Kingsley Ben-Adir.
The campaign also includes Marvel Cinematic Universe stars Mark Ruffalo, who played Bruce Banner/the Hulk; Benedict Cumberbatch, who played Doctor Strange; and Don Cheadle, who played James Rhodes/War Machine. Cate Blanchett, who portrayed Hela in Thor: Ragnarok; Tilda Swinton, who played the Ancient One, Tatiana Maslany, who starred in She-Hulk, and Daniel Bruhl, known for his role as Zemo, are also among the signatories.
Who is Marwan Barghouti?
Barghouti was born on June 6, 1958, in the village of Kobar, northwest of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank. He joined the Fatah movement at the age of 15.
He was arrested by Israel in 1976, when he was 18, and spent a period in prison, where he learned Hebrew. During his university years, he was detained several times. In 1985, he was again placed in administrative detention and was later confined to house arrest.
Barghouti became one of the prominent figures of the First Intifada, which began in the Palestinian territories in 1987. Israel subsequently deported him to Jordan, where he remained for seven years.
He returned to the West Bank in 1994 under the Oslo Accords signed between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization.
In 1996, Barghouti was elected to the Palestinian Legislative Council representing Fatah in the Ramallah and Al-Bireh area. He subsequently rose rapidly within Fatah and became the movement's secretary-general.
In 2002, Israeli forces arrested Barghouti at his home in Ramallah. An Israeli court later convicted him on charges including murder and attempted murder and sentenced him to five life terms plus 40 years in prison.
Contemporary reporting says the sentence followed his conviction in connection with attacks during the Second Intifada that killed five people.
Barghouti studied political science at Birzeit University, earning a bachelor's degree in history and political science and a master's degree in international relations. He completed a doctorate while in prison.
He has also written books including The Promise, Resistance to Arrest, and One Thousand Days in a Solitary Confinement Cell.
In February 2024, Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir ordered Barghouti transferred from Ofer Military Prison to Ramon Prison, where he was placed in solitary confinement.
Israeli authorities said the move followed the alleged acquisition of intelligence concerning plans for an uprising in the West Bank. The decision prompted increased concern among Palestinians about Barghouti's safety.
The current campaign says its appeal is aimed at securing his release and urging international institutions and governments to intervene on his behalf.

Brazil fines TikTok owner over mishandling of children's data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:52:23 UTC
01:52:23 KST

According to a report by Brazil's National Data Protection Authority (ANPD), the social network failed to block under-16s and mishandled personal data.
Brazil's National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) said on Tuesday that it had imposed a fine of 153.7 million reais (€25.57 million) on ByteDance, owner of the social network TikTok, for "irregularities in the processing of data belonging to children and adolescents".
In addition to the fine, the Chinese platform will be required to delete data collected irregularly and, according to the statement, "ByteDance has also committed to implementing a compliance plan to improve the protection of children and adolescents on TikTok".
The platform will have to automatically apply stricter privacy settings to accounts belonging to children under 16, strengthen systems for parental supervision and introduce tighter content filters.
The Brazilian oversight and regulatory authority identified practices by the Chinese company that were not in line with the country's General Data Protection Law (LGPD) in two modes of access to the platform, specifically in relation to the feed for users with and without an account.
ANPD said it had found that the mechanisms adopted by TikTok "were not sufficient to prevent, from the outset, the improper processing of personal data of children and adolescents".
The company behind TikTok will have to strengthen parental control systems and introduce stricter content filters.
In the version without user registration, for example, TikTok will have to suspend advertising across Brazil, restrict the experience to content suitable for all ages and cut screen time to 12 hours.
In the no-login version, users will also not be able to post or watch live broadcasts.
Earlier this month, ANPD also ordered popular streaming platform Discord to suspend live broadcasts and video calls after a teenage girl was allegedly encouraged to take her own life during a stream.
The agency told AFP that an appeal lodged by Discord on Monday against the suspension is currently under review.
In recent years, Brazil has taken a tougher line in regulating social media platforms.
A recent law requires platforms to link accounts held by users under 16 to their parents' accounts and to verify the user's age.
In 2024, the platform X was blocked in Brazil for 40 days, until the social network owned by the world's richest man, Elon Musk, complied with Supreme Court orders to remove accounts spreading disinformation.

EVA Air, partners sign sustainable fuel deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:06 UTC
01:41:06 KST

EVA Airways and AIT Worldwide Logistics yesterday signed an agreement to promote the airline’s Green Transportation Program, which is expected to help Microsoft reduce its carbon emissions by 15,000 tonnes in the first year.
The four-way partnership — comprising EVA Air, AIT Worldwide Logistics, Formosa Petrochemical Corp (FPC) and Microsoft — aims to accelerate the adoption of sustainable aviation fuel and decrease carbon emissions across the supply chains in the aviation, technology, transportation and energy sectors.
EVA Air president Clay Sun (孫嘉明) said at a ceremony in Taipei that the airline is committed to increasing the use of sustainable fuel, produced by FPC from used cooking oil, as part of its goal of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050.
Photo: Huang Yi-ching, Taipei Times
“The civil aviation industry’s transition to the zero-carbon model requires collective efforts of airlines, aviation fuel suppliers as well as logistics service providers and their corporate customers,” Sun said.
The partnership can enable Microsoft, an important corporate customer of AIT Worldwide, to reduce its carbon footprint generated by cloud equipment transportation by approximately 15,000 tonnes of Scope 3 emissions.
No company can solve aviation’s decarbonization challenge alone, AIT Worldwide chief strategy officer Greg Weigel said, adding that sustainable fuel adoption requires both supply and demand.
Aside from airlines, corporate customers such as Microsoft can help create demand, he said.
“The more important thing is that it [the partnership] sets a foundation for the future,” Weigel said, adding that AIT Worldwide hopes that the initiative would encourage more airlines, fuel suppliers, freight forwarders and corporate customers across Asia-Pacific to participate.
FPC president Lin Ke-yen (林克彥) said that sustainable aviation fuel serves as an important means for the aviation industry to reduce carbon emissions.
However, the supply is limited, and the cost is relatively high, he said.
The partnership helps transform the need for corporations to reduce carbon emissions to a market demand for sustainable fuel, Lin said.
Increased use of sustainable fuel would help expand FPC’s production and lower operational costs, he added.
Vincent Shih (施立成), general manager of corporate, external and legal affairs at Microsoft Taiwan, said that Microsoft has set the goal of achieving carbon negative, water positive and zero waste by 2030.
The partnership helps the technology giant resolve the problems with Scope 3 emissions, which refers to carbon emitted at the logistics’ end, Shih said.
Civil Aviation Administration Director-General Ho Shu-ping (何淑萍) said that Taiwan last year launched the sustainable fuel demonstration project in the civil aviation industry.
Taiwan is capable of producing 6,500 tonnes of sustainable aviation fuel in a year, Ho said.
Microsoft’s goal for zero carbon emissions can serve as an important force to propel the further development of the market for sustainable aviation fuel, she added.
American Institute in Taiwan commercial deputy chief Eric Crowley said that Taiwan is the US’ fourth-largest trading partner, and the US has become Taiwan’s largest export market.
During the first five months of this year, Taiwan was the 18th-largest source of international visitors to the US, up 15 percent year on year, Crowley said.
About 170 passenger flights are dispatched between Taiwan and the US each week, while air-cargo demand between the two countries continues to grow rapidly, he added.
“This agreement represents a critical step forward in decarbonizing modern supply chains. The cross-industry partnership shows that economic growth and environmental protection can coexist, and serves as an example of how the US and Taiwan can promote green and sustainable trade together,” Crowley said.
The airline said that sustainable aviation fuel accounts for only 0.5 percent of its total aviation fuel consumption due to limited supply, and about two-thirds of sustainable fuel it uses is procured from other countries.
Sustainable aviation fuel costs about three to five times higher than regular aviation fuel, it added.

The CWA issued a warning today for torrential or extremely torrential rain in Tainan, Kaohsiung, Pingtung County and Taitung County, and for extremely heavy to torrential rain in Chiayi County, Hualien County and on the Hengchun Peninsula (恆春半島). Families of detained Chinese Christians cling to faith in legal limbo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:05 UTC
01:41:05 KST

Clasping her hands together in prayer, four-year-old Huanle tells God she misses her mum, whom she hasn’t seen since Chinese authorities raided their home last year in a crackdown on their unregistered church.
Huanle’s mother Wang Cong is a pastor at Zion Church, one of China’s largest “underground” churches where some Christians choose to worship instead of government-regulated ones.
Chinese authorities detained more than 20 of Zion’s members last October, including 43-year-old Wang — one of a series of similar recent clampdowns across the country.
Photo: AFP
“My child saw everything, she cried,” said Ren Zhong, Huanle’s father, as he described how seven unidentified officers had entered their home in Beijing that night before he was held down. “She was in her mother’s arms, and they ripped her away.”
Wang was taken along with many of her books, and her family have not spoken to her directly since.
China’s constitution guarantees citizens religious freedom. However, the ruling Communist Party, which requires its members to be atheist, has historically regarded organized religion with suspicion. It recognizes Protestantism and Catholicism as official religions, but practicing organizations must register with the government — something many Christians feel yields an unacceptable amount of control over church affairs and teachings.
Scrutiny of the country’s many unofficial groups has tightened since President Xi Jinping (習近平) came to power, though enforcement can vary. Zion was forced to close in 2018, but flourished online during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Authorities detained its founding pastor Ezra Jin during the October crackdown but he was released in July, weeks after US President Donald Trump raised his case with Xi.
Wang and seven others are set to be tried in the southern Chinese coastal city of Beihai — where Jin lived — for fraud and illegally operating a business, criminal charges their families dispute.
“After I heard the news (of Jin’s release), I was shocked and afraid to believe it,” said 36-year-old Ren, also a preacher.
“But after joy came worry, worry for my wife, because she was still inside, suffering.”
Asked about the detentions, China’s foreign ministry said Beijing “manages religious affairs in accordance with the law.”
The Beihai public security bureau and local detention facilities said they said they would not accept interviews.
HARD TO JUSTIFY’
A single suitcase lay open on the floor at Ren’s temporary residence in Beihai.
Ren had initially hoped Jin’s release might mean his wife’s would soon follow.
Instead, legal proceedings quickened. Authorities indicted Wang and the others two weeks after Jin was reunited with his family in the US.
A trial was set for the middle of this month, but later postponed.
Relatives of the detainees argue they should no longer be held now that Jin is free.
“It shouldn’t be that the head pastor is fine, but people below him... are in trouble,” said Gao Guangjun, the father of detained pastor Gao Yingjia.
“It’s a little hard to justify,” the elder Gao, 76, said.
According to legal documents described by Ren, the basis for Wang’s detention is that her collection of church offerings was fraudulent because Zion is not registered.
Authorities say she gathered around 660,000 yuan (US$98,000) between 2019 and last year.
Ren insisted that financial giving — used partly to pay pastors — is part of Biblical teaching practiced by Christian churches.
“If it’s because of this that my wife has been charged with fraud, then I think this is actually not an accusation against my wife,” he said.
“It is a denial of the Christian faith as a whole.”
COSTLY CONVICTION
Jin has been recuperating in the US and spending time with his family, who relocated there as Zion came under pressure from authorities in 2018.
He said he feels “deep pain” knowing that colleagues were left behind.
“I am deeply conflicted, truly torn. I am free, yet in reality, I am not,” the pastor said.
The 57-year-old was visibly emotional as he described urging the eight detainees to have courage, in a text he had drafted for their lawyers the previous day.
“I hope that one day (their) children will understand that their parents’ separation from them — and their current detention — is a source of honor,” he said. “For the sake of a higher conviction, they are paying a price.”
At Ren’s Beihai flat, Huanle danced around to imaginary music, seemingly carefree.
But Ren said there are nights when his daughter refuses to sleep and tells him she’s scared.
‘NOT FORGOTTEN’
Having stopped full-time work in May, Ren spends his days caring for Huanle and advocating for his wife — posting case updates to an X account with a few hundred followers.
He said worry for his wife has faded, even though people convicted of fraud can face 10 years in jail.
“I believe God is just,” he said. “I know God has not forgotten about these eight people.”
Gao, also a Christian, hopes authorities will release his son, but acknowledged the outcome is beyond the families’ control.
“It’s for leaders to decide,” he said. “It’s not something ordinary citizens can influence.”

Father-son spy duo resentenced

In a retrial by the High Court, former major Lee Hai-peng (李海鵬) and his son Sergeant Lee Chu-hsiang (李楚庠) yesterday were sentenced to 11 years and six months and 16 years in prison respectively for passing confidential information to China
The two were sentenced under the Anti-Corruption Act (貪污治罪條例) and the Criminal Code of the Armed Forces (陸海空軍刑法). The ruling may be appealed.
According to the ruling, Lee Hai-peng started working in tourism decades ago after retiring from the military and was recruited by Chinese intelligence officers during one of his trips to China.
Photo: Taipei Times
He enlisted the aid of his two sons, Captain Lee Yu-sheng (李輿聖) and Lee Chu-hsiang, as well as former acquaintance Lee Wen-sheng (李文生) to obtain military secrets for about six years before discovery, the court said.
The Investigation Bureau verified that the intelligence the defendants gave to China was genuine with the Ministry of National Defense, the court said.
In the first High Court trial, Lee Wen-sheng was given three years and two months, while Lee Yu-sheng and Lee Chu-hsiang received two years and two months and two years and four months respectively.
During a retrial, Lee Wen-sheng’s sentence was increased from three years and two months to 15 years, while Lee Yu-sheng was sentenced to two years and one month, a month shorter than the initial sentence.
Lee Chu-hsiang was sentenced to 10 years and six months, a large increase from the initial sentence of two years and four months.
The first retrial ruling stated that the defendants’ crimes were severe, and that they became Chinese spies despite the nation’s support and training, the court said.
The 15-year sentence for Lee Wen-sheng and two year, one month sentence for Lee Yu-sheng were finalized by the Supreme Court in December last year after their appeals were rejected.

Kiribati detains Chinese ship over banned shark fin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

Kiribati, a tiny Pacific neighbor to Hawaii that has grown ties with Beijing, detained a Chinese vessel this month for illegally harvesting shark fins, its maritime police said.
The practice of cutting fins off live sharks and throwing the carcasses back into the sea is banned in much of the Pacific Ocean, but persists due to demand in East and Southeast Asia.
The Chinese ship was among four vessels detained in a surveillance crackdown by 11 Pacific island nations from Aug. 3 to 14, assisted by the US Coast Guard in some areas and an Australian military aircraft. Kiribati, however, operates its own patrol boat.
Photo: Reuters
The vessel was licensed to ply Kiribati’s waters, but was detained by the maritime police after inspectors found shark fins on board, commander Tom Redfern said.
“It was escorted back to Christmas Island for further investigation,” he said, referring to a large atoll belonging to Kiribati and located south of Hawaii.
Kiribati has an exclusive economic zone spanning 3.5 million square kilometers of ocean, and has drawn interest from Chinese state companies since switching diplomatic ties from Taiwan in 2019.
It also hosts Chinese police, a decision the US has said risks fueling regional tensions.
“A Kiribati Police maritime boarding officer, not under a shiprider agreement, boarded and inspected it, finding that the vessel was breaching its condition of licence by keeping and retaining shark fins onboard,” Redfern said.
Kiribati has recently strengthened cooperation with France, with French military personnel due to arrive next month on Christmas Island to rebuild local police stations.
The practice of removing shark fins is banned across the region.
Andrew Chin, a fisheries researcher at Australia’s James Cook University, said finning had led to “massive declines” in shark numbers, prompting stringent controls in the Pacific.
“Because it is now illegal, if people are doing it, it is going to be hidden and really hard to detect,” he said.
Research on the DNA of thousands of shark fins sold in Hong Kong markets pointed to its origins in the region.
“We have seen evidence of illegal trade from the western and eastern sides of the Pacific,” said Demian Chapman, who conducted the research as director of the Sharks and Rays Conservation Research Program at Mote Marine Laboratory in Florida.
There have been other cases of Chinese vessels breaking the finning ban, he said.
Reduced demand in China for shark fin soup, including a ban on serving it at government functions, had contributed to a fall in the amount of fins being traded in Hong Kong, he added.

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

When summer temperatures soar, humans reach for fans and air conditioning. But wild animals lack these luxuries, so they have evolved remarkable strategies to prevent overheating. From desert foxes to African giraffes, nature has engineered some surprisingly clever cooling systems.
One of the most iconic examples involves unusually large ears. Fennec foxes and jackrabbits, both inhabitants of hot desert environments, possess ears that function as natural cooling devices. Blood vessels close to the surface of the ears release heat into the air, helping lower these animals’ body temperature. When the weather becomes extremely hot, more blood flows through their ears, allowing heat to escape efficiently. This process works much like a radiator in an engine.
Some animals rely on their outer covering rather than their body shape to stay cool. Saharan silver ants, for example, are coated in tiny hairs that reflect sunlight away from their bodies. These hairs also help release built-up heat rapidly, allowing the ants to survive in temperatures that would be fatal to most other creatures. Without this protective coat, they would overheat within seconds of stepping onto the burning sand.
Photo: Freepik / 照片：Freepik
Perhaps the most visually striking mechanism belongs to the giraffe. Scientists believe that the giraffe’s distinctive spots help regulate temperature. Beneath each dark patch lies a network of blood vessels. Warm blood flows into these areas, where heat can dissipate through the skin. In this way, the pattern on a giraffe’s body may serve as a natural cooling system.
Not all cooling solutions rely on radiation, though. The Cape ground squirrel of southern Africa takes a more hands-on approach: it flips its bushy tail over its head like a portable shade. By raising its tail over its body like an umbrella, the squirrel reduces direct exposure to sunlight and keeps its body cooler while searching for food.
These creative solutions show that animals have developed diverse ways to cope with heat. By studying such natural designs, scientists may even discover new ideas for cooling technologies for everyday human use.
當夏季氣溫飆升時，人類會使用電風扇和空調。然而，野生動物沒有這些奢侈品，因此牠們演化出各種非凡的策略來避免過熱。從沙漠狐狸到非洲長頸鹿，大自然設計出一些出乎意料的巧妙降溫系統。
其中一個最具代表性的例子與異常巨大的耳朵有關。同為沙漠環境居民的耳廓狐和傑克兔都有能作為天然散熱裝置的耳朵。靠近耳朵表面的血管能將熱量釋放到空氣中，幫助降低這些動物的體溫。當天氣變得極端炎熱時，流經耳朵的血液會增加，使熱量能更有效地散逸。這個過程的運作原理就如同引擎中的散熱器。
有些動物則依靠外層覆蓋物而非體型來保持涼爽。例如，撒哈拉銀蟻的身體覆蓋著細小的毛，能將陽光從身上反射出去。這些細毛也有助於迅速釋放積聚的熱量，使牠們能在對其他大多數生物而言致命的高溫中存活。如果沒有這層保護外衣，牠們一踏上灼熱的沙地，幾秒內就會過熱。
或許最引人注目的降溫機制屬於長頸鹿。科學家認為，長頸鹿身上獨特的斑紋有助於調節體溫。每一塊深色斑紋下方都有一個血管網絡。溫熱的血液流入這些區域後，熱量可透過皮膚散發出去。如此一來，長頸鹿身上的斑紋可能可以充當一種天然的降溫系統。
不過，並非所有降溫方式都依賴散熱。生活在非洲南部的南非地松鼠採取更手動的方法：牠會把蓬鬆的尾巴翻到頭上，像一把可攜式的遮陽傘。透過將尾巴像傘一樣舉在身體上方，牠在覓食時能減少陽光直射並讓身體保持涼爽。
這些充滿創意的解決方案顯示，動物已發展出多樣的策略來應付高溫。藉由研究這些自然的設計，科學家甚至可能發現新的靈感來應用在人類日常使用的降溫技術上。
KEY VOCABULARY
1. luxury n. 奢侈（品）
Jeff only has an average salary, so he can’t afford luxuries such as a sports car.
傑夫的薪資不過一般，所以他買不起跑車之類的奢侈品。
2. remarkable adj. 非凡的；引人注目的
The latest space mission to Mars is considered a remarkable achievement.
前往火星的最新一起太空任務被視為非凡成就。
3. involve v. 包含；涉及
International diplomacy involves conducting negotiations between nations.
國際外交包含進行國家間的協商。
4. fatal adj. 致命的
The factory worker sustained a fatal injury while using dangerous machinery.
那名工廠工人在使用危險機械時受到致命傷。
5. regulate v. 調節；規範
Air conditioners can regulate humidity as well as temperature during hot summer days.
空調在炎熱夏天不僅可以調節溫度，也能調節濕度。
6. patch n. 一小塊；斑塊
The dog had a white patch on its fur, making it look very cute.
那隻狗的毛上有一塊白色斑點，看起來非常可愛。
7. radiation n. 散熱；輻射（能）
Proper ventilation helps improve radiation in rooms during hot summer days.
適當的通風能改善房間在炎熱夏天的散熱效果。
8. flip v. 翻轉；擲
Jay can flip a pancake perfectly without spilling any batter on the stove.
杰可以完美地翻煎餅，爐子上完全不會灑到麵糊。
9. cope with 應付；處理
Maria does yoga to cope with the stress stemming from her job.
瑪麗亞做瑜珈來應付工作造成的壓力。

built-up adj. 積聚的

China upgrades Antelope Reef
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

Located in the southwestern Paracel Islands (Xisha Islands, 西沙群島), Antelope Reef (Lingyang Reef, 羚羊礁) holds a significant advantage over China’s outposts in the Spratly Islands (Nansha Islands, 南沙群島) due to its proximity to Hainan and the Chinese mainland. That position makes resupply, reinforcement and force protection easier.
China had dredged and filled about 6.03km2 at Antelope Reef as of March, according to the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, making it one of Beijing’s largest land reclamation projects in the South China Sea. Satellite imagery reveals a 680m pier, a deep-water harbor, a helipad and more than 50 structures under construction. The northwestern shoreline, which runs more than 3km, could also provide enough space for a runway. Initial signs of excavation for a potential runway were also detected this month.
Given these developments, Antelope Reef is expected to become a multipurpose military outpost supporting surveillance and the deployment of aircraft and warships. Some assessments suggest that Beijing could eventually station anti-ship missile systems there, such as the YJ-12B and YJ-18. With an estimated 400km to 500km range, these systems can threaten naval operations and targets moving from the South China Sea to Taiwan.
Outposts such as Antelope Reef can also serve as forward sensing and attrition nodes in a potential conflict over the Taiwan Strait. They can play a role in detecting, tracking, weakening and slowing intervention forces before they reach the battlefield.
This development presents a troubling prospect for Taiwan and its allies. US forces approaching Taiwan from the South China Sea would have to deal with anti-ship missiles, air defenses, electronic warfare and anti-submarine capabilities from Chinese outposts. They might also be forced to take alternative routes. A dense network of these outposts could produce a 48-to-72-hour delay, which would favor Beijing during an amphibious assault or maritime blockade of Taiwan.
Antelope Reef could additionally figure into the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) effort to build bastions in the South China Sea, which are tightly controlled zones meant to shield its strategic submarine fleet from US surveillance and anti-submarine operations. Only about 300km from the PLA South Sea Fleet submarine base in Sanya, Antelope Reef serves as a transit point.
Beijing is gradually transforming its scattered outposts into a network capable of creating strategic depth for the PLA. This network could help China better control southern access routes, force the US and its allies to disperse their resources and extend the time needed for adversaries to enter the operational area.
While countering China’s expansion in the South China Sea is challenging, Taiwan has viable options. First, it should develop multiple contingency scenarios, with response levels corresponding to different threat levels.
The base layer should be equipped with radar, surveillance systems, and radio communications for early detection, identification and warning. Then, uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) can track lower-risk targets, and fighter jets should only be deployed once a genuine threat emerges. Even when jets need to launch, Taiwan should choose the appropriate aircraft for each situation and avoid using high-end fighters for routine missions.
For this to work well, Taiwan must carefully manage its combat endurance. Rotating units, tightening maintenance cycles and expanding the use of high-fidelity flight simulation would sustain pilot and ground crew readiness.
Second, publicizing China’s coercive actions carries diplomatic value, although transparency alone cannot deter “gray zone” tactics. Exposing Chinese behavior must be paired with robust defense capabilities to impose costs and complicate Beijing’s operational objectives.
Taiwan needs to push harder on asymmetric, mobile and survivable defense capabilities. Priority should be given to mobile air defenses, anti-ship missiles, tactical UAVs, dispersed radar networks and command centers that can keep functioning under strike conditions. Taiwan’s ultimate objective should be a dispersed, resilient defense network that can raise the cost of any coercive action or kinetic attack.
Additionally, Taiwan needs a systematic mechanism to document and publicize Chinese “gray zone” incursions. Data gathered from radar, UAVs and other assets should be combined with analysis from research institutions to build an objective record of the frequency, scale and operational patterns of PLA operations. Sharing this data with international partners, think tanks and foreign media could help Taiwan push back against China’s efforts to normalize coercion.
Third, strengthening collaboration with other Indo-Pacific countries and the US can be achieved through military training exchanges, officer education, intelligence sharing and combat-experience sharing. Compared with large-scale military exercises, such low-profile programs are less provocative, yet they still provide Taiwan with vital expertise, enhance interoperability and foster shared operational approaches.
Finally, Taiwan must advance a whole-of-society approach to defense, which raises public awareness, encourages business and local government participation, and strengthens non-partisan institutions. Empowering the Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Committee is necessary.
The economic dimension is equally important. Taiwan must continue reducing its excessive dependence on China by diversifying trade, investment and supply chains, while using the New Southbound Policy+ to expand ties with Southeast Asian countries, India and Australia. Upgrading high-tech industries, increasing research-and-development investment and building alternative supply chains would all help limit China’s capacity to use economic dependence as a tool of coercion.
Truong Tuan Kiet is a master’s student at the Taipei School of Economics and Political Science at National Tsing Hua University, and a columnist at the Vietnam Strategic Forum. Huynh Tam Sang is founder and editor-in-chief of the Vietnam Strategic Forum and a doctoral student at the Taipei School of Economics and Political Science at National Tsing Hua University.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Taiwan cannot become a bigger wolf than China, but it can ensure that

Manufacturing confidence rises: TIER
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:41:01 UTC
01:41:01 KST

Taiwan’s manufacturing confidence rose to a more than four-year high last month as the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom continued to drive orders for chips and related hardware, providing momentum for the export-reliant economy, the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research (TIER, 台灣經濟研究院) said yesterday.
The manufacturing climate index rose 2.48 points to 101.09 from the previous month, hitting the highest level in more than four years, the institute said in its monthly survey.
“Demand for AI, high-performance computing and new smartphone models boosted semiconductor shipments,” TIER Economic Forecasting Center director Gordon Sun (孫明德) told a news conference in Taipei.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research
Exports and overseas orders also improved from the previous month, prompting more manufacturers to expect business conditions to improve, while the share anticipating deterioration declined, Sun said.
Electronics and machinery companies continued to benefit from global demand for AI chips and infrastructure, as well as preparations for new smartphone launches, he said.
Capacity utilization was high at advanced-process fabs, advanced-packaging facilities and high-end testing operations, Sun said.
Demand was also improving for power-management chips, high-speed transmission components, memory and silicon photonics, supporting mature-node manufacturing as well as testing and packaging businesses, he said.
The survey showed that more than 40 percent of electronics and machinery firms were optimistic about their outlook, he said.
Chemical producers also expect conditions to improve, helped by higher oil prices, inventory restocking by downstream customers and the resumption of some production lines, Sun said.
The improvement in the manufacturing sector contrasted with weaker sentiment in the services sector, with the services climate index falling 1.29 points to 98.2, ending a four-month run of gains.
Financial market volatility was a major drag on the sector, Sun said.
Securities firms were hurt by corrections in stock markets and trading volumes, while banks remained relatively steady as lending, wealth-management and credit-card businesses held up, he said.
Retailers provided some offset, benefiting from travel, hot weather and demand for daily necessities ahead of typhoons, he added.
The climate index for the construction sector rose 2.96 points to 110.55, extending its advance to a fourth consecutive month despite higher costs for construction waste disposal and building materials, the survey showed.
Demand from AI and information and communications technology companies continued to bolster the sector, TIER Taiwan Industry Economics Database director Arisa Liu (劉佩真) said.
“The overall momentum is strong,” Liu said, adding that construction activity is expected to continue growing over the next six months.
