Israeli forces raid UNRWA training centre in occupied East Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:59:32 UTC
21:59:32 KST

Israeli forces raid UNRWA training centre in occupied East Jerusalem
Israeli forces raid and seize the Qalandiya Training Centre, a key facility operated by UNRWA, in the Kafr Aqab neighbourhood.
Israeli forces have raided the Qalandiya Training Centre, a key facility operated by the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) in the neighbourhood of Kafr Aqab in occupied East Jerusalem.
Before the raid on Tuesday, which UNRWA condemned, Israeli forces closed the nearby Qalandiya checkpoint, the primary Israeli checkpoint between East Jerusalem and the northern West Bank.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Palestinian factions explore broad alliance for November elections
- list 2 of 3Who was Hind Rajab and why is Israel investigating her killing?
- list 3 of 3Over 100 ex-diplomats urge France, UK to sanction Israel over Palestine
Heavy military deployments spread throughout the surrounding neighbourhoods and the adjacent Qalandiya refugee camp in the occupied West Bank. Soldiers forcibly expelled all UNRWA employees from the site, telling them not to return. Five Palestinians were injured by Israeli gunfire near the training site in Qalandiya, according to the Jerusalem governorate.
Far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir participated in the raid. Speaking from the site, Ben-Gvir praised the operation, stating that authorities had begun an “operation to evacuate the building” and asserting that “there is no place for the agency in Jerusalem and Israel.” He also posted on X that “UNRWA in our hands.”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the incursion was lawful. In a post on X, he said: “In accordance with my directive and following the law we passed, the evacuation of the UNRWA compound in Kafr Aqab, Jerusalem, began today.”
After the raid, the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced that the Jerusalem Municipality had already commenced work to transform the property into a new educational and community complex.
The ministry claimed the project would serve thousands of Palestinian residents in Kafr Aqab with facilities including schools, a mosque, sports grounds and health centres.
‘Deeply concerning incursion’
UNRWA released a statement to “unequivocally condemn” what it described as an “unauthorised and deeply concerning incursion”.
“The entry of armed security forces into a United Nations facility, without the authorisation or consent of the United Nations, is unacceptable,” it said. “The KTC [Qalandiya Training Centre] is a United Nations facility protected by the privileges and immunities afforded to the Organisation under international law. Its inviolability must be fully respected.”
UNRWA also called on the international community to act immediately and condemn the violation.
“The international community must ensure that United Nations premises are protected from unauthorised entry and seizure, and that UNRWA can continue delivering essential services to Palestine Refugee communities without intimidation, obstruction or interference,” UNRWA said.
“The integrity and inviolability of United Nations premises cannot be conditional. They must be respected, upheld and protected.”
Speaking to Al Jazeera, the director of UNRWA affairs in the West Bank, Roland Friedrich, said the break-in was a “very concerning development” and “not just a violation of the privileges and communities of the United Nations” but also a “violation of the right of young Palestinians to quality education”.
Israeli officials alleged that the site had been owned by the Jewish National Fund since 1937 and had been allocated to the Jerusalem Municipality for the educational and community project, arguing that UNRWA had fenced off the land for decades without legal ownership rights. The Foreign Ministry directly cited anti-UNRWA legislation passed by the Israeli Knesset in October 2024, banning the agency’s activities in Israel, to justify the takeover.
UNRWA, however, firmly rejected the claims, maintaining that the Qalandiya Training Centre is a UN facility and is protected under international law.
The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs has also condemned the Israeli raid. In a statement, the ministry called the seizure “a flagrant violation of international law and the inviolability, immunities, and privileges of UN facilities”, adding that it constitutes “a dangerous escalation”.
Similarly, the Palestinian National Liberation Movement, or Fatah, condemned the forced displacement of UNRWA’s facilities.
“Targeting UNRWA is a direct attack on the Palestinian refugee issue and a blatant attempt to undermine one of the most important international organisations,” said a statement by the party, which is led by Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas.
‘Clear violation of international law’
Reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, journalist Sarah Abu Alrob highlighted the severe human impact of the decision. She noted that the centre provided vital services to 16,000 Palestinian refugees who are either in the Qalandiya refugee camp or who visit from across the West Bank.
She said the raid follows a similar operation months ago when Israeli forces raided the UNRWA headquarters in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of occupied East Jerusalem, where they evacuated the premises and demolished part of the building.
“This comes within a larger campaign where the Israeli government has been calling to dismantle the UNRWA organisation that provides educational, medical and social services to Palestinian refugees who are still in the occupied West Bank,” Abu Alrob said.
Human rights advocates and legal experts have condemned the action. Mohammad Dahleh, a lawyer and human rights advocate from East Jerusalem, described the takeover as a direct breach of international law.
“It’s a clear violation of international law, and it’s a clear violation of the advisory opinion rendered by the International Court of Justice, the highest court in the world, just in December 2025,” Dahleh told Al Jazeera.
“Israel doesn’t care about international law, doesn’t care about the ruling or the advisory opinion of the [UN] International Court of Justice or about the criticism that many countries have against these actions, especially in a period where Palestinian refugees are so vulnerable.”
Dahleh emphasised the critical role that UNRWA has played on the ground during this crisis.
“Palestinian refugees are in a period where they need the assistance that UNRWA is providing the most, whether it’s in occupied Gaza or the occupied West Bank.”

Taiwan to unveil 10-year circular economy roadmap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:41:06 UTC
21:41:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will unveil a 10-year circular economy roadmap in 2027 as waste volumes and treatment costs continue to rise, Environment Minister Peng Chi-ming (彭啓明) said Tuesday.
Speaking at a net-zero investment forum, Peng said economic growth has produced more waste. He said the circular economy is not only an environmental issue but is also important for Taiwan’s resource security, CNA reported.
Taiwan has limited land and a dense population, making waste treatment facilities difficult to build because they often face local opposition, Peng said. He added that the costs of handling commercial food waste, household waste, hazardous waste, and landfill disposal are rising.
Peng said Taiwan needs better ways to turn waste into usable resources and energy. He said the global circular economy market is currently worth about NT$8.1 trillion (US$251 billion) and is expected to nearly double to NT$16.2 trillion by 2034.
Peng said about 69 listed and over-the-counter Taiwanese companies have potential in circular economy-related sectors and employ more than 100,000 people. However, their share prices and employee salaries tend to rank relatively low, making it harder to attract young workers and investor attention.
Peng outlined four measures to develop the sector. The government will work with the economics ministry to establish regular dialogue among government agencies, businesses, universities, and researchers to address regulatory and business obstacles.
The government also plans to raise the profile of promising companies among the public, investors, and venture capital firms. It will work with securities and financial institutions to develop financial products linked to the circular economy.
Peng said the ministry will gather public and industry views through forums before releasing a circular economy policy white paper in 2027. The document will set development goals and a roadmap for the following 10 years.

'We have to further curb climate change,' said German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at the start of a cabinet retreat (AFP photo)
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Aug. 25 sought to assuage critics who accuse his government of doing too little against climate change after a brutal summer of heatwaves and drought.
"We have to further curb climate change and at the same time better adapt to the consequences," Merz said at the start of a two-day retreat outside Berlin with members of the cabinet.
Germany had to "draw the long-term lessons from extreme situations such as this summer of heat," he said, adding that the biggest EU economy had suffered "significant damage" over recent months.
A heatwave in late June saw Germany break its all-time temperature record three days in a row, topping 42 degrees, and official data shows that the country has registered a record of around 14,000 heat-related deaths this year.
The country has seen wildfires and serious impacts to harvests, as well as rivers falling to levels which have restricted crucial navigation routes.
Merz's center-right CDU/CSU alliance has until now emphasized the need to "balance" climate action against efforts to revive Germany's stuttering economy.
It also faces pressure from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is leading in the polls and which denies the scientific consensus of man-made climate change.
The Greens party and environmental activists argue the government, a coalition of the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democrats, is not acting with the urgency the climate crisis deserves.
Social Democrat politicians have suggested further measures to enshrine climate protection in the constitution, which has been met with a frosty reception by the CDU/CSU.
"After weeks of silence and playing the issue down, the government is finally talking about climate protection and adaptation," Greens party leader Felix Banaszak said on Aug. 25.
"This will only be credible if Merz and his government fundamentally change course," he told the Rheinische Post newspaper, saying particular action was needed on the green energy transition.
An expert commission in May forecast that Germany would miss its 2030 greenhouse gas emissions targets, which are anchored in law.
A Greenpeace study this week estimated that the economic costs of the extreme summer of 2026 — from productivity losses and health costs to poor harvests and throttled river traffic — amount to at least 36 billion euros for Germany.
Outside the venue of the cabinet retreat in Neuhardenberg, Brandenburg state, Greenpeace activists set up a fire engine with a large banner that read "Merz, extinguish the fire".

The process began in late 2024 after Bahçeli called for a new initiative to resolve the PKK issue. It reached a major turning point in February 2025, when jailed PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan called on the terror group to end its armed campaign and dissolve itself.
PKK subsequently announced in June 2025 that it would disarm and disband. A month later, members of the group held a symbolic weapon-burning ceremony in northern Iraq.
Türkiye regards the PKK as a terrorist organization, as do the United States and the European Union.
The Manzikert commemoration comes during “Victory Week,” when Türkiye also marks the start of the 1922 Great Offensive against occupying forces and celebrates Victory Day on Aug. 30.

Third drone and suspected military explosives found near Leipzig airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:37:24 UTC
21:37:24 KST

German investigators uncovered a third drone and suspected military explosives thought to be connected to an attempted attack on Leipzig airport, local media have reported.
The drone was discovered in Kabelsketal, just to the west of the airport, along with about 50g (1.8oz) of a suspected military explosive on 14 August, 10 days after the unsuccessful sabotage. Leipzig airport is a cargo and military logistics hub used by Nato and Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines for transporting military supplies.
The office of the prosecutor general, which is leading the investigation, declined to comment on Tuesday. But the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said the government would soon provide information about who it believed was behind the drone attacks.
“They will pay for this,” Merz said, stopping short of naming a suspect, before a cabinet meeting in Brandenburg. He added that the government was “working intensively on this together with the security authorities and we will present our findings and comment on them shortly”.
Intelligence sources cited by the broadcasters NDR and WDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung said they suspected the involvement of Russian intelligence in the attempted attack. Moscow has denied involvement.
The German government has so far avoided expressing a clear position as to whether it thinks Russia, or an actor close to it, is responsible.
Merz said the attempted attack showed that Germany was increasingly becoming a target. “Attackers are increasingly ruthlessly accepting even serious property damage, and even injuries and deaths,” he said on Tuesday.
A drone carrying explosives was found on 4 August near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used for military supplies. According to investigators, the drone was apparently intended to land on the wings of the aircraft, which was filled with kerosene, but the explosive device did not detonate.
Investigators say that about 20 minutes after the discovery of the first drone, a second drone possibly collided with a DHL cargo plane, which was forced to abort its landing manoeuvre and was diverted to Marseille.
According to the latest media reports, an inspection of the DHL aircraft revealed damage to the tail section, suggesting a collision with an object. However, the drone has not yet been found. Investigators believe it could have been sucked into the engines after the collision and shredded into small pieces.
The third drone was found in a field in a municipality that directly borders the western edge of Leipzig airport. Forensic technicians from the federal criminal police office found residues of a substance that initial assessments indicated could have been the highly explosive substance hexogen. This explosive also failed to detonate, but the investigators’ report, according to the media reports, stated: “The perpetrators may have had a far larger attack in mind than previously known to the public.”
Other suspicious traces and components were also discovered close to the airport, the report said. In Kursdorf, investigators found an antenna attached to a tree, and other electronic parts, which may have been used to control the drones. Close by and near where witnesses reported hearing a loud bang on the day of the incident, investigators discovered a burnt patch and charred metal parts.
If the drones had exploded, they could have caused a catastrophe, German officials said.

Vatican foreign minister, in Moscow, says Ukraine war must end
MOSCOW, Aug 25 - A senior Vatican official urged an end to the Ukraine war after meeting in Moscow on Tuesday with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in the first in-person talks between Vatican and Russian officials in five years.
Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican's foreign minister, said every day that the four-year Russia-Ukraine war continues, it "creates new victims ... and renders future reconciliation ever more difficult."

Rwanda accuses DR Congo of supporting an armed group on its soil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:17:56 UTC
21:17:56 KST

Rwanda accuses DR Congo of supporting an armed group on its soil
Rwanda says FDLR threat justifies its continued involvement in eastern DRC, as efforts to verify a ceasefire advance.
Rwandan President Paul Kagame has again blamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for the continuing conflict in the country’s east, linking Rwanda’s involvement in the conflict to the continued presence of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), a Rwandan Hutu armed group, on Congolese territory. He said Rwanda would continue to take whatever measures it considers necessary to protect its security.
Speaking at a news conference in Kigali, Kagame reiterated that the FDLR’s presence in the DRC is Rwanda’s main concern, adding that “if this problem is not resolved, it is natural for Rwanda to remain involved” in the conflict.
Old accusations, renewed claims
Kigali accuses the FDLR, which was formed from remnants of the Rwandan army accused of involvement in the genocide against the Tutsi, of threatening Rwanda’s security from Congolese territory.
Kagame said Rwanda has information that Congolese authorities “are arming the FDLR and integrating its members into their own forces”.
Kinshasa, meanwhile, accuses Kigali of supporting the M23 movement, an armed group in eastern DRC, and of sending Rwandan troops into Congolese territory. Rwanda denies the allegations.
Kagame told reporters that Kigali’s evidence includes testimony from former FDLR members. Some returned voluntarily to Rwanda, while others were captured. He said they all “tell the same story” about the support the FDLR receives from Congolese authorities.
The Rwandan president said United States and European missions, as well as United Nations missions, had visited the Mutobo centre and heard testimony from the fighters themselves.
The Mutobo Demobilisation and Reintegration Centre is located near Musanze in northern Rwanda and operates under the supervision of Rwanda’s Demobilisation and Reintegration Commission.
The centre’s task is to disarm former fighters from armed groups arriving from eastern DRC, particularly the FDLR, and prepare them to return to civilian life through training and financial support.
Kagame also criticised calls for Rwanda to stay out of the crisis in eastern DRC, saying those making such calls should first address the armed group.
“Remove this problem, and then see whether Rwanda is using it as an excuse or not,” he said.
Fighting for peace
Kagame stressed that protecting Rwanda’s security remains a non-negotiable priority.
“The right thing to do is to protect ourselves, and we will do so without fear, day or night and at any time,” he said.
Kagame also said Rwanda seeks to work with countries in the region to achieve peace, adding that Rwanda is “ready to fight for it” and wants to work with others to that end.
Peace tracks
On March 18, 2025, Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani brought Kagame and DRC President Felix Tshisekedi together in a meeting described as historic, paving the way for two peace tracks: One between Rwanda and the DRC and another between the parties to the conflict in the DRC.
On June 27, 2025, Rwanda and the DRC signed a peace agreement in Washington that included provisions to end support for armed groups, respect sovereignty, and coordinate security efforts, as well as plans for regional economic integration.
Alongside the Washington track, Qatar hosted a series of talks between the parties to the conflict in the DRC that resulted in the signing of the Doha Framework Agreement for Peace on November 15, 2025, between the DRC government and the M23 movement.
The agreement contains eight implementation protocols aimed at protecting civilians, restoring state authority, and strengthening national reconciliation and economic and social development, with Qatar, the US and the African Union overseeing implementation.
Ceasefire verification
In a joint statement, representatives of the DRC government and the Congo River Alliance-M23, along with Qatar, the US, Togo, Switzerland and the AU Commission, welcomed the field mission on August 20, conducted with logistical support from MONUSCO in preparation for the first mission to verify the ceasefire.
On the evening of August 24, local sources told Al Jazeera that a delegation from the joint mechanism tasked with verifying the parties’ compliance with the ceasefire under the Doha peace agreement had arrived in South Kivu province in eastern DRC.
The delegation arrived with logistical support from MONUSCO.

Rohingya refugees demand justice, dignity at Cox’s Bazar protest
The United Council of Rohingya refugee group says it organised the protest to highlight ‘ongoing humanitarian crisis’.
Tens of thousands of Rohingya refugees have rallied to protest against conditions at overcrowded camps in Bangladesh, demanding more international assistance to improve conditions.
The United Council of Rohingya refugee group said it organised the protest on Tuesday to “remember the atrocities committed” and highlight the “ongoing humanitarian crisis” on the ninth anniversary of the exodus from Myanmar.

More than 1.2 million Rohingya people, many of whom fled the 2017 military crackdown in their home country, live in about 30 camps in the world’s largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar.
Conditions in the camps have deteriorated amid a funding reduction, limited rations and cuts in services, aid groups say.

One in three Rohingya refugees is expected to face “crisis” hunger levels or worse between September and December, according to the rights group Save the Children.
Bangladeshi authorities say they are already overstretched and have called for the dignified return of the Rohingya to their homeland.
The 2017 Myanmar crackdown, which saw Rohingya villages burned and civilians killed, is the subject of a genocide case at the United Nations’ top court in The Hague.
A joint statement issued by 16 diplomatic missions in Bangladesh, including those of the European Union, the United Kingdom and Canada, said conditions in Myanmar did not allow for the safe repatriation of refugees.
“Rohingya refugees have a right to return to their homes in Myanmar,” it said.
“Regrettably, conflict is escalating across Rakhine and humanitarian need is rising. Deepening insecurity, airstrikes on civilian infrastructure and the Myanmar authorities’ blockades on aid and trade are worsening the humanitarian crisis.”
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called for “renewed global attention and action” for the Rohingya.
“Rohingya people in Myanmar, Bangladesh and across the region face deepening insecurity, shrinking protection space and diminishing prospects for durable solutions, exacerbated by funding cuts impacting life-saving assistance,” the UN chief’s spokesman, Stephane Dujarric, said in a statement.

The humanoid robot ‘Olympics’ is as ridiculous as it is impressive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:14:59 UTC
21:14:59 KST

The World Humanoid Robot Games is back for a second year, and the bots are just as unsettling and impressive as they are ridiculous and unwieldy. On the first day of the Games, two humanoid robots beat Usain Bolt’s world record for the 100-meter dash—before crashing into a padded wall. Still, this five-day extravaganza showcases how far and how rapidly humanoid robots have come in even the 12 months since last year’s Games.
The Games are taking place in Beijing and feature 51 events, including kickboxing, table tennis and soccer. Chinese companies produce the majority of humanoid robots, but machines representing 16 countries are participating in the Games this year, including Germany, Japan and the U.S.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In theory, the robots’ superhuman feats are super cool. In practice, a black-and-white hunk of metal sprinting into a wall looks silly. But companies such as X-Humanoid, which created one of the robots that broke Bolt’s record (and got the best time overall), along with another that beat the human record for a standing high jump, are proving that they can achieve extraordinary feats of athleticism. Similar robots, especially those built for such specific purposes, however, may crash and burn (literally) when faced with the unexpectedness of human life—even in tasks as basic as folding laundry.
When a humanoid robot beat the human half-marathon record this April, Rodney Brooks, an emeritus professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told Scientific American that it’s important to recognize these robots aren’t actually interacting with the real world.
“When you see a performance of an [artificial intelligence] system or a robot on one thing,” he said, “that fools us into thinking that it has the same general competence as a human. And that’s a mistake people make.”
Indeed, most of the robots that ran the 100-meter dash on Saturday crashed into the padded wall at the end. One even caught fire. Another humanoid robot in the weight lifting event crashed into the judges’ table. These machines are far from having the agility, balance and mobility of a human athlete, even if they are faster or stronger in the moment.
Still, they are catching up. One humanoid robot managed to successfully play tennis against a human, anticipating unpredictable moves and showing an ability to adapt in a real-world setting. We may not expect robots at the actual Olympics anytime soon, but they sure are fast—and gaining.

Ceuta migration sparks nearly 9,600 hate posts on social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:14:32 UTC
21:14:32 KST

The Spanish Observatory on Racism and Xenophobia logged 9,590 hate messages in two days tied to a July influx of some 80,000 migrants into Ceuta.
The latest incident in Ceuta sent hate speech on social media soaring, with 9,590 posts detected by the Spanish Observatory on Racism and Xenophobia (OBERAXE) in just two days, coinciding with the mass arrival of migrants on 30 and 31 July, which the government put at around 80,000 people.
The Ministry of Inclusion, Social Security and Migration says this spike pushed the number of hate-content items recorded in July to 57,406, up from 40,800 in June.
The monthly report notes that people from North Africa remain the main target of hate speech on social media, accounting for 68% of the content detected in July. Messages targeting immigrants made up 19% of the total, followed by those directed at Muslims (16%), people of African descent (10%) and Latin Americans (7%).
Public safety fears and the World Cup drove hate speech in July
Public safety was the main focus of hate speech in July, accounting for 48% of the content analysed, much of it broadly linking migration with crime.
Sport accounted for another 34% of the posts, in a context shaped by the Football World Cup, which fuelled racist, xenophobic and Islamophobic content targeting players, national teams and fans. Migration policies were the focus of 17% of the content, followed by posts about sexual assaults (5%), terrorism (4%) and the arrival of boats (1%).
OBERAXE, which reports to the State Secretariat for Migration, notes that four in ten posts dehumanise or seriously degrade the groups targeted. Some 38% contain threats, while 15% call for their expulsion and 4% incite violence. A further 2% seek to discredit them and 1% praise those who attack them.
Platforms improve removal of hate content
The report says that 60% of the content used openly aggressive language, with insults, threats and slurs. Some 34% relied on irony or sarcasm, while 33% used images, videos, memes or coded language, tools that facilitate its spread and make automatic detection harder.
The OBERAXE report highlights an improvement in platforms' removal of hate content, with platforms deleting 12% of user-reported posts, up from 10% in June.
Some 9% was taken down within the first 24 hours, while another 3% disappeared over the following week. The role of the "trusted flagger", which literally means 'trusted reporter', enabled the removal of 58% of reported content, seven points higher than the previous month.
By platform, X led takedowns with 93%, followed by TikTok (88%), Facebook (74%) and Instagram (71%). YouTube lagged well behind at 14%, although Instagram stood out by more than doubling its removal rate compared with June.

'Bombed by nature': French village deals with aftermath of rare tornado
A rare tornado that swept through the Aude department in southern France devastated the tiny village of Pomas, the mayor said on Tuesday, destroying homes, the town hall and a local school and leaving residents feeling like they are living through "a wartime situation".
A tornado of rare intensity devastated a village in southern France, causing widespread destruction and leaving residents in shock on Tuesday, with the mayor describing the aftermath as resembling "wartime".
The tornado, which swept through the Aude department late Monday afternoon, hit the small village of Pomas hardest, bringing down walls, tearing off roofs, and uprooting trees.
Thirty-nine people were injured, including two severely, and 17 people were hospitalised.
Herve Gine, the mayor of Pomas, which is home to around a thousand people, said he had the feeling of living through "a wartime situation".
"We were bombed by nature," he said. "People are in shock... [some] have lost everything".
He said the nursery school was lost to the storm, adding, "We no longer have a school, we no longer have a town hall."
Gine said it was a "miracle" that no one had died, estimating there could have been several dozen fatalities.
The village's narrow streets testified to the tornado's violence, with debris everywhere, cars overturned, and homes left with shattered windows and torn-off shutters.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
'Rare intensity'
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on X that the tornado was "of rare intensity", while Marie-Helene Bouissac, the regional deputy prefect, said it was "an exceptional and highly traumatic event".
Of the village's 476 homes, around 300 were damaged, said the mayor, adding that the extent of the destruction was so severe that much of the village would require reconstruction.
By early Tuesday, 7,250 households across the Languedoc-Roussillon region were without power including 1,600 in Aude, said grid operator Enedis.
Under clear skies, roofs ripped apart by the storm had been covered with blue and green plastic tarpaulins, an AFP journalist witnessed.
Nearby fields and vineyards were littered with broken deckchairs, scraps of fibreglass insulation and pieces of wire fencing ripped apart by the fierce winds.
Emergency crews worked throughout the night while local residents tried to salvage what they could. Meanwhile firefighters, assisted by a canine search unit, searched the site for possible victims.
"Search and inspection operations are still under way, involving 75 firefighters supported by specialist reinforcement teams," the prefecture said.
'Kids are traumatised'
Overnight, some locals took refuge in the community hall, which had been converted into a temporary shelter. Others stayed with friends and relatives, officials said.
At a police checkpoint, relatives waited for permission to enter the affected area, bringing supplies or offering assistance.
Jose Gomes, a resident of the nearby village of Trebes, said a friend's house had collapsed.
"He was inside, he suffered a head injury and broke three or four ribs... He got out of hospital this morning."
Abdallah Wakkas, the grandfather of two children aged 13 and 17, said the teenagers were shaken.
"Nothing happened at their house, but the kids are a bit traumatised because their grandmother's roof was torn off," he said.
France sees several dozen tornadoes of varying intensity each year, according to weather agency Meteo-France.
This summer France has endured three heatwaves, registering a record 52 days of heat intensified by climate change. The intense weather conditions have sparked droughts, wildfires and a record number of rockfalls in the Alps.

Less sugar early in life might decrease dementia risk
People who had sugar rationed early in life around World War II had lower dementia risk
Parents of toddlers know too well what sugary treats can do. Kids can buzz with energy initially, only to crash or have mood swings later. Now a new study provides more evidence that excess sugar in early life could also pose health problems much later.
Eating too much sugar during the first 1,000 days of life may be associated with a higher risk of developing dementia decades later, scientists report in the Aug. 25 Neurology.
“The first 1,000 days are critical for brain development,” says epidemiologist Jiazhen Zheng of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in Guangzhou, China. During that period, the brain undergoes exceptionally rapid growth and neuronal development, he says.
Data already suggest that high sugar intake early in life may lead to health problems, including diabetes and high blood pressure. Zheng had previously studied the effects of sugar on the cardiovascular system and wondered if it might also influence brain health.
He and his colleagues pored over health records of nearly 65,000 people in the U.K. Biobank who were in utero, infants or toddlers between July 1942 and June 1954. During those years, they would have been subject to a British government policy that set a daily limit on the amount of sugar a person could purchase. This policy, an austerity measure for World War II, allowed each person 41 grams of sugar a day — roughly the amount of sugar in a 12-ounce can of Coke today.
After adjusting for lifestyle, socioeconomic status and other conditions, the team found that those who lived their first two years of life with sugar rationing had a 23 percent lower risk of developing dementia and a 28 percent lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease than those born after the policy ended. There was a similar reduction in risk among those who lived under rationing for the first year of life. Among those who did develop either condition, their disease developed almost three years later, on average, than those who were never subject to rationing.
Other factors beyond sugar consumption may have also played a role, Zheng says, so he can’t say how much sugar is safe to consume to reduce risk.
Still, given, the data, what families should do is limit added sugars in their children’s diets, he says. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans, for instance, don’t recommend any added sugars under 11 years old. “That’s one of the best things they can do, a sensible step for children’s overall health,” he says.

One million Afghan children suffering 'life-threatening' malnutrition, UNICEF says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:59:30 UTC
20:59:30 KST

Afghanistan has endured repeated periods of widespread hunger in recent decades as it has struggled through civil war and other crises.
One million children in Afghanistan are suffering from life-threatening malnutrition in a worsening new crisis hitting the country, the United Nations warned on Tuesday.
Across Afghanistan, 3.7 million children suffer from wasting, meaning they are acutely malnourished, the UN children's agency UNICEF said.
Among that number are "one million children who are suffering from life-threatening severe acute malnutrition," UNICEF's Afghanistan country representative Tajudeen Oyewale said.
"If there is no treatment and we are not able to act fast, that one million number are at risk of dying," he told a media briefing in Geneva from Kabul.
Afghanistan has endured repeated periods of widespread hunger in recent decades as it has struggled through civil war and other crises.
An economic collapse followed the Taliban government's return to power after US-led forces withdrew in 2021.
He said that nearly 40% of children admitted to hospitals with severe wasting and medical complications were babies under the age of six months old.
Meanwhile children under two years old make up more than 80% of severe acute malnutrition cases in Afghanistan.
"Malnutrition plays a central role" in the growing numbers of deaths of very young children, Oyewale said.
He described a "worsening nutrition crisis" across the country, with more than half a million children admitted to hospital so far this year for high risk, moderate and severe wasting.
In July 2025, around 6,000 cases were recorded; in July this year, the numbers went above 8,000, a third higher.
"In parts of southern Afghanistan, some hospitals are now seeing three or four severe malnourished children for every available bed," he warned.

Iran Vows Retaliation After U.S. Widens ‘Economic D-Day’ Sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:54:05 UTC
20:54:05 KST

Iran has pledged to “attack” the U.S. financially after Washington unveiled a sweeping set of sanctions as part of ‘Economic D-Day', an attempt to further isolate Tehran and curb its access to the global financial system as the war between the two countries drags on.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled the measures as part of President Donald Trump’s announcement of the "most crushing economic operation" against Tehran, labeled “Operation Economic Outcast.”
"D-Day marked a historic campaign with our allies,” Bessent said Monday. “Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe."
After the measures were announced, Tehran’s Economy Minister Seyed Ali Madanizadeh said the government was prepared to counter the newly-unveiled U.S. sanctions.
“They want to launch an economic terrorist attack against us. We also have our own tools, and we know the rules of this game,” he said in response to Bessent’s announcement during a televised interview with Iranian state media Monday.
“This time, they shouldn't think that our approach is purely defensive; they should also expect an attack from us.”
Although the Iranian minister did not elaborate on what such an attack would entail, he said the country had developed plans in preparation for the economic threats.
“Plans have been developed for various scenarios, including what actions should be taken if they attempt to cause damage in the financial sector or in the country's financial relations,” he said, adding that “the global financial system is not structured in a way that allows anyone to claim they can cut off” Iran’s economy.
During the announcement, Bessent stopped short of immediately imposing secondary sanctions on countries that trade heavily with Iran, instead favoring an approach that would give them time to decouple from that trade.
When asked why he was waiting to impose those sanctions, Bessent responded: "Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?"
“We believe that it is important to level set and give people a cure period, but they should know that that will move very quickly, and that we are serious,” he added.
Bessent did not name any countries that could face sanctions, but said "they know who they are."
China, one of Iran's biggest trading partners and the primary buyer of Iranian oil exports, has already pushed back against the threat.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said China-Iran cooperation "should not be disrupted or undermined," noting that it had been conducted in accordance with international law.
“China has made clear on many occasions its firm opposition to illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorization of the U.N. Security Council. Economic warfare and maximum pressure provide no solution,” Jian said during a press conference Tuesday.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has sanctioned nearly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels connected to Iran’s regime, while also gaining powers to impose additional sanctions on any person operating within the digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping sectors of the Iranian economy.
Iranian leaders had previously dismissed the impact of extensive economic sanctions on the country and instead sought to highlight struggles within the U.S. economy.
Trump, meanwhile, claimed Monday that Iran is "completely collapsing,” without elaborating on what he based the claim.
Strait of Hormuz attack raises stakes after sanctions announcement
Following Bessent's economic announcement, an oil tanker was hit by a projectile off the coast of Oman in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a report by U.K. Maritime Trade Operations.
The incident highlights the continued danger for shipping companies attempting to transit the key waterway, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply passed before the war. The closure of the Strait has rattled energy markets and thrown the global economy into disarray.
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi had previously threatened heavy blows against vital U.S. interests and energy chokepoints if Iran’s economy was targeted with sanctions.
"The U.S. President says that he ordered an economic war and launched the most severe economic campaign against Iran,” he said, as reported by Iranian state media Sunday. “We have repeatedly announced that we have scenarios in place for any hostile action by the enemy. One of the enemy’s hostile actions is economic measures and warfare.”
The attack came as a high-level delegation from Pakistan, which has been a key mediator between the United States and Iran, was wrapping up meetings in Tehran aimed, once again, at bringing a return to negotiations and an end to the nearly six-month-old war.
The cease-fire established under the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between Washington and Tehran expired on Aug. 17, but the agreement had already deteriorated after each side presented differing interpretations of its terms.
Both parties had vied for control of the Strait of Hormuz, eventually leading to tit-for-tat strikes, the reimposition of the American blockade on Iranian ports, and minimal dialogue between Washington and Tehran.
Iran has since released a comprehensive list of demands for the U.S. to meet, which Trump immediately rejected. Both sides have since shown little sign of progress in negotiations, despite relatively limited fighting in recent weeks.

Kazakhstan’s Election Brings a New Parliament — and More Pressure on Journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:54:00 UTC
20:54:00 KST

Reported by
Kazakhstan’s first election to a new unicameral Parliament on Sunday gave a commanding victory to the newly formed, pro-presidential Adilet, or “Justice,” party, in a vote that press-freedom advocates said was held amid mounting pressure on independent journalists.
Adilet won 71.17 percent of the vote, or about 6.5 million ballots, while turnout was 74 percent, according to results released Tuesday by Kazakhstan’s Central Election Commission. Four other parties cleared the five-percent threshold.
None of the seven parties that took part in the election could be seen as opposing President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s policies, according to international observers.
The new 145-seat legislative body is elected entirely through a proportional representation system based on party lists.
The new unicameral Parliament, called the Kurultai, was established earlier this year following constitutional reforms promoted by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. It replaced Kazakhstan’s former two-chamber parliament, abolishing the upper house and the mixed electoral system under which voters could also choose candidates directly, rather than only from party lists.
“I pin great hopes on the election of Kurultai and believe that it will give a major impetus to the development of our country. New faces have appeared, and new ideas have emerged,” Tokayev said on Sunday after casting his vote.
But independent observers said the groundwork for the election had been laid in advance through the “cleansing of the information landscape” of the country’s most vocal critics and journalists.
Nazira Darimbet, head of the human rights organization Adil Soz, said these were the first elections in her memory to have “passed in grave silence, as quietly as a graveyard,” without independent journalists able to document violations.
“All this is connected with unprecedented pressure on journalists, which will most likely only intensify,” Darimbet told OCCRP.
Five days before the election, former editor-in-chief of Orda, Gulnara Bazhkenova, was sentenced to eight years in prison for embezzlement, illegal business activities and disseminating false information. Her sentence was deferred for two years because she has a minor child.
She was also banned from working as a journalist or holding leadership positions for five years. Bazhkenova denied the allegations.
“Yes, the fact that I paid part of the salaries in cash is a violation, but I did not steal anything. Accusing a person of something they didn’t do is a terrible sin. There is a Heavens (Higher) Court, and I know it is on my side,” she said in her final statement to the court.
Journalist and political observer Azamat Omarov, who runs the YouTube channel “Akhual Segodnya” (“Today’s Situation”), was arrested in July for allegedly “inciting social, national, racial, or religious discord.”
“Omarov made a satirical video about the new Constitution and elections as well as critical remarks about the authorities and President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev,” said Darimbet.
Omarov’s channel is currently unavailable.
Journalists Lukpan Akhmedyarov and Dinara Yegeubayeva have both been banned from traveling abroad.
Akhmedyarov was charged with spreading “false information.” Colleagues and activists believe the charges relate to his posting information he found on a Ukrainian government website that claimed Kazakh citizens were fighting in Ukraine on the Russian side.
“Why are they going to try him for false information if he took it from an official website?” Darimbet wondered.
In Yegeubayeva’s case, a cyclist crashed into her car, after which a criminal case was opened against her. The cyclist is demanding around $6,400 in damages.
“All of these sentences and cases lead to the main goal of the authorities: self-censorship and intimidation of journalists and the media,” said the head of Adil Soz.
Diana Okremova, head of the Legal Media Center, an organization that protects journalists, expressed similar concerns.
“By election day, everyone was simply afraid to say or do anything out of line,” she told OCCRP.
Okremova said activists and journalists faced not only legal pressure but also attempts to block their social media accounts.
“The online space was practically the only opportunity to express their opinions. But after a series of attacks, it has been practically destroyed,” she said.
Her own Facebook profile is currently unavailable due to “copyright infringement” after she published details about an access-to-information case the Legal Media Center filed against the Ministry of Culture.
The parliamentary election was part of constitutional changes introduced earlier this year that effectively reset Tokayev’s current presidential term, allowing him to run again in 2029 for another seven-year term.
Tokayev said it was too early to speculate on whether he would run again in 2029.
“We are literally walking along the edge of a cliff, yet we have managed to ensure peaceful domestic conditions that allowed us to develop. So let us meet again — perhaps next year I will give you a more specific answer,” he told a Vlast reporter.

El Nino drives up corn futures to highest in 3 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:13:13 UTC
20:13:13 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu, Emir Yildirim
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Corn prices rose to $5.2425 per bushel in global markets, reaching their highest level in three years amid the El Nino weather event, dry conditions and geopolitical risks due to the Russia-Ukraine war.  
Price movements in grains came to the fore due to El Nino, with sharp hikes in corn prices.
Corn previously reached $5.2450 on July 31, 2023.
Corn rose more than 11% compared with the end of July and increased more than 17% compared with the end of December 2025.
The bushel price of corn later stabilized at around $5.18.
Growing concerns over crop yields in the US fuel expectations of tighter supplies and drive up corn prices, while rising US corn exports contribute to the price increase.
Hot and dry weather in some corn-producing regions of the US, adverse weather in Europe and ongoing grain shipment disruptions in Ukraine fuel concerns over the global corn supply.
The corn harvest in the American Midwest came in lower than expected, while Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's shipping routes halted grain exports.
While weather conditions threaten production, geopolitical disruptions pose risks to crop deliveries, and given the already high energy and fertilizer costs, the margin for offsetting additional supply shocks narrows.
Waning expectations of Fed rate hikes and falling demand for the US dollar also continue to drive up commodity prices.
Zafer Ergezen, a futures and commodities expert, told Anadolu that El Nino’s effects began to be seen in June, especially in South America, Southeast Asia and Australia, and to a somewhat lesser extent in the US and Europe.
“We’re seeing a serious impact of the weather phenomenon in West Africa,” he said. “There were concerns over a decline in corn yields, especially in Brazil, the US, and Southeast Asia.”
Ergezen stated that oil prices also contributed to the rise in corn prices as demand for corn used in biodiesel production climbs when oil prices rise, while around 60% of the corn produced across the globe is used for industrial purposes.
The combined effects of El Nino and high oil prices were instrumental in raising corn prices.
“El Nino will continue until the beginning of next year, and if oil remains at these levels, we may see even more upward movements in corn,” he said.
“As long as oil prices don’t decline and there isn’t a lasting peace deal between the US and Iran, I don’t expect a deep pullback in corn prices,” he added.

A car phone mount is no longer an option—it's a necessity. Nearly every US state restricts cell phone use while driving (we see you, Montana!), and most require full hands-free operation. The best car phone mounts offer an easy view of your phone's screen without blocking your view of the road, hold your phone securely, and keep vibration to a minimum.
I've spent weeks and hundreds of miles testing car phone holders for iPhones and Android alike, on busy freeways and on potholed city roads. What I found is that the best car phone mounts aren't necessarily expensive or name brands: They're just smartly designed.
The best car phone mount for an iPhone is almost always a secure MagSafe mount. The one I keep in my car when I'm not testing other mounts is a sturdy, compact Andery suction mount ($36) that holds preternaturally fast to both my phone and dash but can also be mounted to a window. My favorite mechanical car phone holder for Android phones is a sturdy, versatile, ball-joint mount from Andobil ($30) that affixes tightly to a car's dash, windshield, or air vents.
Here are the best car phone mounts for each car and phone type. See also WIRED's guides to the Best USB Car Chargers, Best Portable Jump Starters, Best iPhone Cases and Accessories, Best MagSafe Accessories, and Best Wireless Phone Chargers.
Best Car Phone Mount for iPhones and Qi2 Phones
The world is full of bulky phone mounts that block your view of the road, inflexible phone mounts that only allow for horizontal or vertical mounting, weak suction cups, and kinda mid MagSafe attachments. And then there's this innovatively designed, wonderfully compact dash and window mount from Andery.
On flat surfaces, the nano-gel suction cup holds fast like Hodor at the door. The 22-magnet MagSafe ring allows airflow to avoid overheating, but it also holds stronger than most comparable Qi2 magnets. And unlike bulky plastic mounts, the Andery's aluminum-arm, stainless steel ring keeps a low profile and interferes minimally with one's line of sight. In fact, when affixed to my dash, this device doesn't block my view of the road at all. The ring rotates 360 degrees. The two-joint arm can either fold tightly to the mount or extend outward. No other mount I've tested combines all of these virtues.
But note you'll need a relatively flat surface to get a good bond with the suction cup. I've also seen some reports that the suction cup can lose adhesion over time if repeatedly re-mounted (and it's cussedly difficult to remove in the first place, though it leaves no residue when you do). Non-Qi2-compatible Android phones will need a MagSafe case to be compatible with this car phone holder. But if your phone has a magnet or a magnetic case, this is the simplest and most effective car phone mount I know, and it performs leagues better than other similarly designed car mounts like this one from Acer.
Note also that Andery offers a Qi2-compatible phone charger version at the expense of airflow. I haven't tested this variant yet.
Best Universal Car Phone Mount
Mechanical mounts like this one from Andobil—with holders that can be slid in sideways to securely grip the phone—are flexible for a broad range of phones and don't require MagSafe technology. But they're also mostly bulky, making them a less preferred option as a windshield or dashboard mount because this will block your field of vision.
Among all similar devices I've tested, this one from newer Chinese company Andobil is the most compact I've tested when not in use, while still offering a lot of flexibility. The nanogel suction cup on its dash mount is one of the most stable I've tested (almost aggressively stuck on, to be honest). And the extendable arm, while plastic, feels less cheap and breakable than other models. The kit also comes with an air vent mount, whose three-point design makes it among the most stable vent mounts I've tested and allows you to maneuver the phone so it does not block the vent.
This mechanical car phone holder is hard to call aesthetic. It's essentially a pad with a gripper on the side. But the grips extend to accommodate even larger phones and are able to keep the phone in place even during vigorous shaking. (If you're wondering whether I place phones in these phone mounts, and then come at them like they're a shake weight? I do.) The release button's a little awkwardly placed, and Andobil's marketing about “military standards” is a little silly on a low-cost device made with thermoplastics. But after I watched other suction cups wilt in summer heat, this Andobil's still going strong.
★ A Great, Low-Cost Air Vent Mount: If you're mounting only to your air vent, the Vanva air vent phone mount ($13) is among the cheapest mounts of any kind that I've tested, while ranking among the most secure mechanical mounts. (Actually, I like the mechanical phone holder a bit better than Andobil's.) The lockable clamp affixes easily and securely to most vertical or horizontal-slatted vents—and unlike hook-based vent mounts, it's easy to install and remove. The multi-joint ball arm can be maneuvered so you don't lose airflow from the vent, and the adjustable grips that lock in your phone can be released with a simple button press. This Vanva is a relatively flimsy plastic device, so I don't rule out that it might break someday. But its inexpensive replacement cost makes this an acceptable risk.
Best Car Phone Mount With Charger
Look, I'll be honest: I have mixed feelings about chargers on car phone mounts. The mount will have to be plugged into a car charger anyway—and at that point, I might as well just plug in the phone directly, which will usually lead to faster charging.
But convenience is in the eye of the beholder, and many people prefer to just leave the car mount plugged permanently into a car charger so they never have to worry about their phone draining while navigating on a mapping app. For y'all, here's the car mount from ESR, which offers decently fast 15-watt charging and a cooling fan to mitigate phone overheating.
The suction was effective when attached to both my window and dash, and the device is compact enough to not much hinder my field of view. Charging speed is merely moderate, enough to charge an older iPhone in a couple of hours. ESR also offers a faster-charging Qi2.2 device for twice the money, though I have not tested it.
★ A Good, Stylish Vent Charging Mount: Most vent chargers plant themselves directly into the airflow of your vent. But not all of them do. WIRED editor Julian Chokkattu recommends the Peak Design Car Vent Mount ($100). The mount stays secure on the vent, but an arm allows the charger a little distance from the vent. It's also a little bit stylish, a rarity for vent mounts. If you're using a Pixel or Samsung phone, we also like Peak Design's MagSafe phone cases.
Best Minimalist Car Phone Mount
Most people don't overwhelmingly want their car vent mount to be a defining feature in their car's interior. This Belkin takes this notion to the extreme. This silver and black air vent mount is minimalist, svelte, and—dare I say—almost classy. It grips phones surprisingly securely for a phone mount without feet to support the phone's bottom, according to WIRED reviewer Simon Hill, and you can rotate easily from portrait to landscape. There's also a handy rubber clip to hold charging cables in place. Just note that this will not be the best option for larger or heavier phones.
★ For larger phones: The Kenu Airframe Pro ($30) has a similar design but is built to accommodate thicker cases and larger phones, noted WIRED tester Simon Hill. The ball-and-socket joint allows 360-degree rotation and also lets you angle your phone for better viewing. It's a bit less sleek, however.
How I Test and Select Car Phone Mounts
Car phone mounts are and are not a sensitive technology. Bulky mounts can block your field of view while driving. And it's a genuine safety hazard if your car mount, or your phone, falls on the floor while you're driving down the freeway.
Every phone mount I and other WIRED testers recommend has been road-tested against this possibility, driven for hours on the road, and on long road trips, over sometimes bumpy roads. Often, I kept as many as eight devices at a time glued to my dash, windshield, and vents so that my car looked like a dollar-store communications center. For the most recent round of testing, this included multiple days of relatively humid, 90-degree Fahrenheit heat.
I pulled suction cups off of dashboards and windshields, over and over, to see if suction cups wore out the first time you had to move a device—or if the cups left residue on the windshield. I tested using multiple models of iPhone, a long folding Motorola Razr, and a large-model Nokia, onto each mount to see how it held up—with or without bulky cases.
I clamped each phone in and out repeatedly, to see how easy it is to remove a phone from the mount. I also turned each mount upside down and shook vigorously to see how violent I had to be to shake the phone loose from its mooring.
Where chargers were involved, I tested the charging capacity with ammeters and phone apps, as well as simply by marking how long it took to charge my phone compared to other chargers. I also tested the MagSafe charging speed vs. the speed if I'd just plugged the phone directly into my preferred USB car charger. (The USB always wins, for multiple reasons.)
For the most recent round of testing, I tested a dozen phone mounts during a sticky summer, selecting both best-selling and best-recommended mounts from both well-known brands and a new breed of hyper-specialized brands like Andobil and Andery that have made their name only on car phone mounts. My colleague Simon Hill likewise tested a dozen mounts in a previous round of testing.
Can Android Phones Use MagSafe and Qi2-Compatible Mounts?
MagSafe is a great technology for the more than half of cell phone owners in the US who use Apple products. The best phone mounts, with the fewest compromises, are pretty much all magnetic mounts.
But alas, most makers of Android phones have been more resistant to adding magnetic mounting capability. The Google Pixel 10 is an exception and offers built-in magnets and native Qi2-compatible charging support. Other phone makers, like Samsung, offer MagSafe-compatible cases for newer models like the Galaxy S26 series.
Some makers of MagSafe mounts offer little stick-on devices meant to affix to your non-magnetic phone. Don't bother with these; they don't work that well and don't stay affixed for long. If you'd like the convenience of a magnetic mount, you're going to have to get a MagSafe-compatible case for your phone. And for this, I refer you to WIRED's guide to the Best MagSafe Accessories.
Honorable Mentions
Belkin 15W MagSafe Mount for $80: This Belkin MagSafe charger and vent mount is an older device we've recommended previously as a top pick—with a secure magnet pad that offers 15-watt Qi2 charging. The mount positions itself in the air vent and blocks airflow a bit, but on summer days with the air-conditioner running, this positioning can help cool your phone while it charges. It's also a little bit sleek but also a bit on the spendy side for what it offers.
Andobil MagSafe Air Vent Mount for $37: This vent-mounted MagSafe device looks like a charger but isn't. The mount's broad, flat surface does stabilize the phone a bit. But in trade, it blocks airflow both to the phone and from the air vent. For these reasons, it's not really my favorite design. But the magnet is strong enough to hold the phone in place, and the vent mount is also stable.
iOttie iTap 3 Air Vent Holder for $16: This compact vent mount from iOttie is low-cost, and the MagSafe mount is strong enough. I can hold this thing upside down and shake it without dislodging my phone. But there's very little range of motion, and the phone can only be mounted where it'll block airflow from the vent. I also tend not to favor mounting mechanisms that use hooks, because it can make the mounts more difficult to remove when needed—though for unusual air vent geometries, the hook might be the only style of vent mount that works.
iOttie One Touch Dash and Windshield Mount for $28: This dash and windshield mount from iOttie was a favorite of WIRED tester Simon Hill when he tested it two years ago. But there's been a design update and some reports of durability issues, so until we test the newest model, I'm leaving this in the honorable mentions.
Vanmass Car Phone Holder for $40: Similar to the Andobil I recommend as a top pick, this Vanmass is a ball-socket mount with options for air vent or dashboard/windshield mounting. But it's a bit bulkier than the Andobil, and the air vent mount is a hook-based mount—which I tend to find more difficult to remove. The suction cup on the dash/windshield mount is ridiculously strong and is unllikely to dislodge even on hot days—and didn't leave residue when I removed it. But while Vanmass advertises “military-grade” tech, whatever this means for a phone mount, the plastic felt a bit flimsy, especially on a vacuum locking mechanism for the suction cup.
Bokilino Car Cup Mount for $16: This is a different sort of phone mount than most I tested: It affixes to a standard cup holder and holds up your phone like a liberty torch from atop a bendable gooseneck stem. This is all well and good when you're driving solo, notes WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, but during longer trips with family, it takes up a much-needed cup holder, and the stem can get in the way. In most cars, you'll have to look a bit too far away from the road to see the screen.
Not Recommended
Acer Gadget Car Phone Mount for $28: This little car mount from Acer mirrored the design of my top-pick Andery but fell far short on performance. The suction cup pretty much walked off the job after I removed and replaced it once, the magnet isn't as strong, and the mounting arm is shorter and doesn't rotate. There's no particular reason to buy it in a world where the Andery exists.
iOttie iTap 3 Dash and Windshield Mount for $25: MagSafe car phone mounts from iOttie have one chief merit: The magnet is strong and secure, unlikely to dislodge on even the bumpiest roads. But alas, the same cannot be said for the suction cup on this bulky dash and windshield mount, which gave up the ghost on a hot day.
Scosche Magic Mount for $13: This is maybe the most compact, low-cost MagSafe device I tested. Its S-branded design is both unobtrusive and winningly inscrutable: It looks like a talisman Jor-El might have brought back from Krypton. It's also the one with the weakest magnet. My iPhone lurched off at minor provocations.
iOttie Wireless 2 Qi Charging Phone Mount for $50: Don't mistake “Wireless 2 Qi Charger” for a Qi2 charger. A couple of years back, this MagSafe charging mount was a top pick for WIRED, but the charging is now a bit sluggish by modern standards.

In the "Forrest Gump" case, bail for Mudra and Mykytas has still not been paid — HACC
Kyiv • UNN
The HACC has not received bail for Iryna Mudra and Maksym Mykytas. Bail was set at UAH 20 million and UAH 30 million, respectively.
As of August 25, the judicial authorities had not received bail money for the defendants in the "Forrest Gump" case — former Deputy Head of the Office of the President (OP) Iryna Mudra and former parliamentarian Maksym Mykytas. This was reported by Kateryna Khomenko, press secretary of the High Anti-Corruption Court of Ukraine (HACC), in an exclusive comment to UNN.
A preventive measure was only imposed on Mudra today, so there had been nothing regarding her. No money has come in for Mykytas either (— ed.)
Context
The NABU and SAPO announced a special operation codenamed "Forrest Gump" on August 19. According to the investigation, members of a criminal organization arranged the legalization of UAH 150 million obtained through criminal means, which was subsequently used to post bail for one of the defendants in another anti-corruption investigation — the "Midas" case. Law enforcement officers are also investigating episodes related to the raider seizure of enterprises and real estate in Kyiv.
Among the defendants in the investigation are former Deputy Head of the Office of the President Iryna Mudra and former MP and property developer Maksym Mykytas. On August 19, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed Mudra from the position of Deputy Head of the OP. She herself denies involvement in criminal activity and says she is ready to cooperate with the investigation.
On August 21, the HACC imposed a preventive measure on Mykytas in the form of detention with the alternative of posting UAH 30 million in bail. The SAPO requested that bail be set at UAH 200 million.
On August 25, the HACC ordered Mudra to be held in custody with the possibility of posting UAH 20 million in bail. The SAPO insisted on bail of UAH 150 million. After the court's decision, Mudra said that she had part of the required amount herself and planned to ask friends and acquaintances for the rest.
We remind you
The SAPO currently sees no grounds to suspect other OP officials in the "Forrest Gump" case. SAPO prosecutor Vitaliy Hrechishkin said that the investigation is ongoing and that the situation may change.

- On 21 August, Russian forces attacked a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih twice with drones, killing 16 people and injuring 140 more.

China launches 7 new satellites
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:49:25 CST
19:49:25 KST

TAIYUAN, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- China on Tuesday launched a Long March-6C carrier rocket, placing seven satellites into space.
The rocket blasted off at 11:21 a.m. (Beijing Time) from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in north China's Shanxi Province and successfully sent the satellites into the planned orbit.
This launch marked the 665th flight mission of the Long March carrier rocket series, according to the launch center.
Two high-resolution Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites -- Zhongke Sat-14 and 15 -- carry dedicated space-based cloud payloads, breaking the traditional boundary between remote sensing and cloud computing to create an integrated platform that combines satellite sensing with onboard processing, according to developer GalaxySpace, a key supplier for China's internet satellite constellation project.
The company said this marks a breakthrough in space-based computing power and serves as an important step in the country's broader push for a space-based computing network.
The two satellites integrate onboard data reception, computing and analysis, delivering stable in-orbit computing power for tasks ranging from data acquisition to real-time delivery. They cut response times to minutes in flood or earthquake scenarios and significantly reduce bandwidth demand compared with traditional models, according to GalaxySpace.
GISTDA Cube Sat 1, also built by GalaxySpace, marks the company's first full-satellite and ground-system export to a Belt and Road partner country. Delivered to Thailand's Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (GISTDA), it will supply land-use, agricultural, and ecological surface data while supporting Thai universities in satellite design, telemetry, and remote-sensing education.
Other satellites aboard include the JAMX01, a microsatellite developed over eight years by Shanghai teachers and students in partnership with a Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology affiliate, aimed at promoting youth science education through hands-on aerospace projects. ■

Cheam Yeap, first vice-president of Cambodia's National Assembly, said the world is currently facing multiple crises, including the climate crisis and food insecurity.
"Our Southeast Asian region is not immune from these risks. Indeed, it is no longer a mere climate change but an acute climate crisis our global community needs to address together," he said at the opening ceremony of a parliamentary multi-stakeholder dialogue on responsible investment for food and climate security in the ASEAN region.

"Climate resilience is fundamental to food security, and it demands a holistic and coherent legal, policy, and societal response," Yeap said.

"It is necessary to invest more in developing climate-resilient agriculture, climate adaptation, water resource management, and smart early warning systems," he said.
Yeap highlighted that the ASEAN Guidelines on Promoting Responsible Investment in Food, Agriculture, and Forestry (ASEAN RAI), adopted in 2018, serve as a visionary framework.
"Crucially, the ASEAN RAI identifies food security, as well as climate change mitigation and adaptation, as central pillars of responsible investment," he said.
Yeap urged members of parliament across the region to actively monitor executive branches and relevant agencies to ensure that national agricultural strategies and investment promotion policies actually deliver on food and climate security.
Rebekah Bell, representative of the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization to Cambodia, warned that extreme heat, droughts, floods, and shifting rainfall patterns are pressuring Southeast Asia's agriculture, livelihoods, and food security.
"With El Nino conditions now present, the risks of extreme heat, water shortages, and reduced agricultural production could increase further in parts of the region," she said at the dialogue.
She added that building climate resilience is particularly critical for Cambodia, where farming remains heavily dependent on rainfall.
Echoing her concerns, ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly (AIPA) Secretary-General Chem Widhya noted that with a combined population of over 693 million, ASEAN is highly vulnerable to climate change.
In a pre-recorded video address, Widhya highlighted how rising temperatures and erratic weather disrupt regional food systems.
"Building a climate-resilient agriculture sector is therefore urgent, whereby adequate investment is profoundly needed," he said.
He noted that directing funds responsibly would foster sustainable agrifood systems that protect both livelihoods and the environment. ■

New Yellow River tunnel opens in east China, easing cross-river traffic
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:48:59 CST
19:48:59 KST

JINAN, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Drivers can now cross the Yellow River, China's second-longest river, in just about five minutes, as a new tunnel opened to traffic on Tuesday in Jinan, capital of east China's Shandong Province.
Stretching about 5.75 kilometers in total, the tunnel under Huanggang Road features a shield-driven section of roughly 3.3 kilometers, bored by the "Shanhe" shield tunneling machine with a cutting diameter of 17.5 meters, the largest of its kind among underwater shield tunnels in the country.
The single-tube, double-deck structure accommodates six lanes -- three on each level -- with a design speed of 60 kilometers per hour. "This layout makes full use of underground space resources, allowing two-way traffic with just one single bore by the shield tunneling machine, which significantly improves overall cost-effectiveness," said Zhang Tiyong, project director of Jinan City Construction Group, the project's investor.
The tunnel offers an internal clearance height of 4.2 meters, Zhang added, tall enough for buses, fire engines, and maintenance and rescue vehicles, greatly boosting cross-river traffic capacity between the southern and northern banks of the Yellow River.
According to Zhou Xiang, on-site project manager from China Railway 14th Bureau Group Corporation Limited, the project's constructor, the Yellow River section in Jinan is a typical "suspended river," with its bed rising about five meters above the urban area on the southern bank and complex geological conditions lying beneath the river.
"As the diameter of the shield tunneling machine increases, the engineering challenges and construction risks grow exponentially," Zhou said. Despite the extreme difficulties, the project team used intelligent, mechanized, and green technologies throughout construction to ensure safe, efficient boring.
Qian Qihu, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, said the successful application of these technologies will drive continuous progress in China's shield tunneling capabilities and mark a milestone for the country's underwater traffic tunnel construction.
The project also incorporates an intelligent rail-borne inspection robot equipped with a full suite of smart devices, including a 360-degree panoramic gimbal, infrared thermal imaging, and laser obstacle-avoidance radar, enabling fully autonomous inspection across the entire tunnel. In addition, the tunnel's fire suppression system has been upgraded with AI-powered image-based fire detection to markedly improve detection sensitivity and accuracy.
As the second major Yellow River crossing in Jinan after the tunnel under Jiluo Road, this new route is expected to further boost cross-river economic ties and accelerate the national strategy for the river's development and the construction of the city's pilot industrial transformation zone, local authorities said. ■

Peru to welcome Pope Leo with hymn honoring slain nun

Peru to welcome Pope Leo with hymn honoring slain nun
LIMA, Aug 25 - Peru will welcome Pope Leo XIV in November with a hymn in honor of a Catholic nun killed by Maoist insurgents, celebrating the pontiff's return to the country where he worked for decades as a missionary.
The song, featuring Andean rhythms and titled "Leon, Hermano del Camino" or "Leo, Brother on the Journey", will be performed by members of the Aguchita youth choir, named after Peruvian missionary Maria Agustina Rivas.
Rivas was killed by Shining Path rebels in 1990 while carrying out humanitarian work in Peru's remote Amazon jungle region.
Known as "Aguchita," she was beatified by the Vatican in 2022 under Pope Francis after the Church ruled she had been killed out of hatred for the Catholic faith.
Keverly Escobar, 27, one of the lead singers, told Reuters she was proud to be part of the choir honoring a Peruvian saint who gave "her life for the most humble."
The song's composer and musician, Jaime Montoya, said he was inspired to write the hymn because he saw a common thread —sacrifice — that unites the missionary and Pope Leo.
"The song came about partly while looking back on the life of our then-bishop, Robert Prevost," when the now-pontiff was a missionary in Peru, Montoya added.
Peru endured a brutal conflict between security forces and Shining Path, a guerrilla movement that sought to establish a communist state.
The violence left roughly 69,000 people dead or missing between 1980 and 2000, mostly in Peru's poorer indigenous and Amazon communities, according to official estimates.
"Aguchita knew she was confronting Shining Path, which at that time had the government under pressure and wanted to force all communities to join its cause," said Monsignor Pedro Castro of the Apostolic Vicariate of San Ramon, where the missionary served.
Pope Leo's visit comes soon after President Keiko Fujimori took office in July, pledging to unite the country following years of political turmoil.
Fujimori, the daughter of former President Alberto Fujimori, has praised her father's role in defeating the Shining Path insurgency in the 1990s, though his legacy remains divisive because of corruption and human rights abuses committed during his rule.
The hymn won a national competition to find a song symbolizing unity ahead of the Pope's November 11 to 16 visit to Peru, part of a South American tour that will include Argentina and Uruguay.
Pope Leo, the first U.S.-born pontiff, first arrived in Peru in 1985 and became a Peruvian citizen in 2015 after being appointed bishop of Chiclayo, where he stayed until 2023. REUTERS
